## Source unit 55 · printed entry 55

### English candidate

Aḥīḥa—written with two unpointed letters and in the diminutive form—ibn al-Julāḥ, with ḍamma on the jīm, an ungeminated lām, and an unpointed final letter. Mālik related in al-Muwaṭṭaʾ, from Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd, from ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr, that a man of the Anṣār called Aḥīḥa ibn al-Julāḥ had a young paternal uncle who was younger than Aḥīḥa and was staying with his maternal uncles. Aḥīḥa killed him. The slain uncle’s maternal uncles said to Aḥīḥa: ‘We were the ones who gathered and repaired his affairs until he came fully into possession of his flocks. Then you prevailed over us with respect to him, and his affair devolved upon his paternal uncle.’ ʿUrwa said: ‘It is for this reason that a killer does not inherit from the person he killed.’

I say: I have not found the lineage of this Aḥīḥa in the genealogies of the Anṣār. One of those who wrote works on the Companions mentioned him and claimed that he was Aḥīḥa ibn al-Julāḥ ibn Ḥuraysh—also said to be Khirāsh—ibn Jaḥjabā ibn Kulfa ibn ʿAwf ibn ʿAmr ibn Mālik ibn al-Aws. He was married to Salmā bint ʿAmr al-Khazrajiyya, who bore him ʿAmr ibn Aḥīḥa. After Aḥīḥa, Hāshim ibn ʿAbd Manāf married Salmā, and she bore him ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, the grandfather of the Prophet ﷺ. That author also claimed that this was the same ʿAmr ibn Aḥīḥa who narrated from Khuzayma ibn Thābit the prohibition against approaching women through the anus and from whom ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Sāʾib narrated. This would entail that his father Aḥīḥa had Companionship.

Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr rejected this emphatically. He said in al-Istīʿāb: ‘Ibn Abī Ḥātim mentioned him among those who narrated from the Prophet ﷺ and said that he also heard from Khuzayma ibn Thābit.’ Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said: ‘I do not know what this means, because Aḥīḥa belongs to a very early period, while [ʿAmr] was ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib’s maternal half-brother. It is impossible for one belonging to so early a generation to narrate from Khuzayma and for ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAlī ibn al-Sāʾib to narrate from him. Perhaps he was a grandson of ʿAmr ibn Aḥīḥa’—meaning that he was given his grandfather’s name.

I say: What he proposed is not compelled. Perhaps Aḥīḥa ibn al-Julāḥ, the father of ʿAmr, was another man, distinct from the well-known Aḥīḥa ibn al-Julāḥ. Al-Marzubānī mentioned ʿAmr ibn Aḥīḥa in Muʿjam al-Shuʿarāʾ and said that he was a mukhaḍram—that is, he lived through both the pre-Islamic period and Islam. He cited poetry that ʿAmr composed when al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī spoke before Muʿāwiya.

The well-known Aḥīḥa ibn al-Julāḥ was a distinguished man among his people in the pre-Islamic period. He died long before the Prophet ﷺ was born. Among his descendants was Muḥammad ibn ʿUqba ibn al-Julāḥ, one of those given the name Muḥammad in the pre-Islamic period in the hope that he would be the prophet who was to be sent. Muḥammad ibn ʿUqba died in the pre-Islamic period. His son al-Mundhir ibn Muḥammad embraced Islam, attended Badr and other campaigns, and was martyred at Biʾr Maʿūna during the lifetime of the Prophet ﷺ.

Among Aḥīḥa ibn al-Julāḥ’s descendants who had Companionship was ʿIyāḍ ibn ʿAmr ibn Bilāl ibn Bulayl ibn Aḥīḥa, who attended Uḥud and the campaigns thereafter. ʿAmr and Bulayl, the two sons of Bilāl ibn Aḥīḥa, also attended Uḥud, although no one included their father among the Companions. Another descendant of Aḥīḥa ibn al-Julāḥ was Fuḍāla ibn ʿUbayd ibn Nāqid ibn Qays ibn al-Aṣram ibn Jaḥjā; his mother was a daughter of the aforementioned Muḥammad ibn ʿUqba. This is among the proofs that whoever included the elder Aḥīḥa ibn al-Julāḥ among the Companions was mistaken.

ʿIyāḍ said in al-Mashāriq: ‘Some scholars misconstrued what occurs in al-Muwaṭṭaʾ. Aḥīḥa was a man of the pre-Islamic period who did not live to see Islam. “The Anṣār” is an Islamic designation for the Aws and the Khazraj, so how can he be called one of the Anṣār?’ ʿIyāḍ said that the wording may be explained as a loose usage: because Aḥīḥa belonged to the tribe later known by that designation, he was included among them as one of their kinsmen. End of quotation. This concedes that he died in the pre-Islamic period.

Al-Qāḍī Abū ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ḥadhdhāʾ made an extraordinary claim in Rijāl al-Muwaṭṭaʾ. He asserted that Aḥīḥa ibn al-Julāḥ died at an early date, yet in his notice of him he claimed that Aḥīḥa lived long enough to reach Islam, that he was the man about whom Mālik related the foregoing report, and that ʿUrwa did not meet him. He then said that the event itself occurred in the pre-Islamic period and that the report concerns a ruling made then and subsequently affirmed by Islam. End of quotation. He thus made Aḥīḥa reach Islam at one point and not reach it at another.

The correct view is that the famous Aḥīḥa died long ago, as I have explained. As for the man in the story, it appears to me that he was someone else, seemingly the father of the ʿAmr ibn Aḥīḥa who narrated from Khuzayma ibn Thābit. The Companion Aḥīḥa, father of ʿAmr, would therefore be distinct from Aḥīḥa ibn al-Julāḥ, the ancient pre-Islamic grandfather of Muḥammad ibn ʿUqba. It is possible that the younger man was a grandson of the elder and shared his own name, his father’s name, his grandfather’s name, and his son’s name. والله أعلم.

## Source unit 57 · printed entry 57

### English candidate

Al-Akhram al-Hujaymī. ʿAbd al-Ghanī and Ibn Mākūlā said that he is counted among the Companions. Khalīfa ibn Khayyāṭ, al-Bukhārī in his Tārīkh, and al-Baghawī transmitted, by way of Yaḥyā ibn al-Yamān al-ʿIjlī, from a man of Banū Taym al-Lāt named ʿAbd Allāh, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Akhram, from his father—who had Companionship—that he said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said on the day of Dhū Qār, ‘This is the first day on which the Arabs took their due from the Persians.’

## Source unit 60 · printed entry 60

### English candidate

Al-Akhnas al-Sulamī, the grandfather of Maʿn ibn Yazīd. His father’s name was Ḥabīb, though it is also said to have been Khabbāb. Al-Ṭabarī, Ibn al-Sakan, and others mentioned him. Ibn Saʿd included among the delegation of Banū Sulaym: ‘al-Akhnas ibn Yazīd.’

In his notice of Maʿn, al-Baghawī transmitted, by way of Yazīd ibn Abī Ḥabīb, that Maʿn ibn Yazīd ibn al-Akhnas al-Sulamī attended Badr together with his father and his grandfather. He said: ‘We know of no one other than al-Akhnas who attended it as a Muslim together with his son and his son’s son.’

Ibn Ḥibbān transmitted in his Ṣaḥīḥ, by way of Ṣafwān ibn ʿAmr, from Sulaym ibn ʿĀmir, from Abū Umāma al-Bāhilī, that Yazīd ibn al-Akhnas al-Sulamī asked the Messenger of God ﷺ a question; he then related the story. Al-Bukhārī transmitted by way of Abū al-Juwayriyya, from Maʿn ibn Yazīd, who said: ‘My father, my grandfather, and I pledged allegiance to the Prophet ﷺ.’ Ibn Manda claimed that the name of Maʿn’s grandfather was Thawr, so he included him under the letter thāʾ with three dots. والله أعلم.

## Source unit 61 · printed entry 61

### English candidate

Al-Akhnas ibn Sharīq ibn ʿAmr ibn Wahb ibn ʿIlāj ibn Abī Salama ibn ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā ibn Ghayra ibn ʿAwf ibn Thaqīf, al-Thaqafī, Abū Thaʿlaba, a confederate of Banū Zuhra. His personal name was Ubayy. He was given the sobriquet al-Akhnas because he turned Banū Zuhra back from Badr when news reached them that Abū Sufyān had escaped with the caravan. It was said, ‘Al-Akhnas withdrew with Banū Zuhra,’ and he was named for that.

Al-Akhnas later embraced Islam, became one of those whose hearts were to be reconciled, attended Ḥunayn, and died at the beginning of ʿUmar’s caliphate. Abū Mūsā mentioned this on the authority of Ibn Shāhīn, who said: Muḥammad ibn Ibrāhīm related to us; Muḥammad ibn Yazīd related to us, from his authorities. Ibn Fatḥūn likewise mentioned it on the authority of al-Ṭabarī.

Al-Dhuhlī mentioned in al-Zuhriyyāt, through a sound chain from al-Zuhrī, from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab, that Abū Sufyān, Abū Jahl, and al-Akhnas gathered secretly at night to listen to the Qurʾān. He then related the story, which says that al-Akhnas went to Abū Sufyān and asked, ‘What do you say?’ He replied, ‘I recognize some and reject some.’ Abū Sufyān asked, ‘And what do you say?’ Al-Akhnas replied, ‘I consider it the truth.’

Ibn ʿAṭiyya related from al-Suddī that al-Akhnas came to the Prophet ﷺ, professed Islam, and said, ‘God knows that I am truthful.’ He then fled. Passing by a group of Muslims, he burned their crops and killed their donkeys. Thereupon the verse was revealed: ‘Among the people is one whose speech in the life of this world impresses you, and who calls God to witness what is in his heart, though he is the fiercest of opponents’—through to His words—‘and wretched indeed is the resting place.’

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: ‘It has never been established that al-Akhnas embraced Islam.’ I say: Those previously mentioned did establish him among the Companions. There is nothing to prevent him from embracing Islam, then apostatizing, and then returning to Islam. والله أعلم.

## Source unit 67 · printed entry 67

### English candidate

Udhayna ibn Salama ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Khālid ibn ʿĀʾidh ibn Saʿd ibn Thaʿlaba ibn Ghanm ibn Mālik ibn Bahtha ibn ʿAbd al-Qays al-ʿAbdī, father of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān. It is also said that he was Udhayna ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Yaʿmar ibn ʿAmr ibn ʿAwf ibn Kaʿb ibn ʿĀmir ibn Layth ibn Bakr ibn ʿAbd Manāf ibn Kināna al-Laythī. These are two different lineages; Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr authenticated the first. He said some called him al-Shannī, but that was said to be unsound. Al-Rushāṭī objected that Shann ibn Amḍā belonged to ʿAbd al-Qays, so al-Shannī and al-ʿAbdī do not conflict. Ibn al-Athīr said that whoever called him Kinānī may have mistaken him for the father of the famous poet Ibn Udhayna. This Udhayna’s Companionship is disputed. He was the father of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, judge of Basra. Ibn Ḥibbān first said he had Companionship, then listed him among the Successors. Al-ʿAskarī said he headed ʿAbd al-Qays in Basra during ʿUthmān’s time and witnessed the Battle of the Camel. Al-Madāʾinī said he was their first leader, before al-Mundhir ibn al-Jārūd. Udhayna held offices for Ziyād. His son ʿAbd Allāh is mentioned with Muʿāwiya ibn Abī Sufyān and al-Muhallab ibn Abī Ṣufra. Abū Dāwūd al-Ṭayālisī transmitted from Abū al-Aḥwaṣ, from Abū Isḥāq, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Udhayna, from his father, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever swears an oath and then sees something better should do what is better and expiate his oath.” Al-Ṭabarānī, al-Baghawī, Ibn Shāhīn, Ibn al-Sakan, Abū ʿArūba, and others transmitted it through Abū al-Aḥwaṣ in Companion works. Al-Baghawī knew no other report from Udhayna and no other transmitter of it from Abū Isḥāq. Ibn al-Sakan said Companionship was ascribed to him and only Abū al-Aḥwaṣ—trustworthy though he was—transmitted the raised report, without stating that Udhayna heard it from the Prophet ﷺ. Al-Tirmidhī transmitted it in al-ʿIlal from Qutayba, from Abū al-Aḥwaṣ. Al-Bukhārī said in his History: “Udhayna al-ʿAbdī heard ʿUmar and transmitted from the Prophet ﷺ in mursal form.” Abū Nuʿaym al-Kūfī and Muslim listed him among the earliest Kufan Successors. ʿAbd al-Razzāq transmitted, by way of al-Ḥasan al-ʿUranī, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Udhayna, from his father: “I came to ʿUmar”—and he related his story. Al-Tirmidhī reported asking al-Bukhārī, who replied that it was mursal and Udhayna did not live into the time of the Prophet ﷺ; he was the man from whom ʿAmr ibn Dīnār transmitted, from Ibn ʿAbbās. If that last identification was al-Bukhārī’s, his statements differ, because his History distinguishes the two; Abū Ḥātim al-Rāzī followed that distinction. Ibn Abī Ḥātim separately listed Udhayna al-ʿAbdī of Basra, who transmitted from the Prophet ﷺ and ʿUmar through his son ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, and another Udhayna who transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās through ʿAmr ibn Dīnār and Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥārith. Ibn ʿUyayna said the latter was from Oman. Ibn Ḥibbān likewise distinguished them. If the identification was al-Tirmidhī’s wording, it is an error. والله أعلم.

أذينة بن سلمة بن الحارث بن خالد بن عائد بن سعد بن ثعلبة بن غنم بن مالك بن بهثة بن عبد القيس العبدي والد عبد الرحمن وقيل هو أذينة بن الحارث بن يعمر بن عمرو بن عوف بن كعب بن عامر بن ليث بن بكر بن عبد مناف بن كنانة الليثي وهاذان نسيان متغايران وصحح بن عبد البر الأول قال وقال بعضهم فيه الشني ولا يصح وتعقبه الرشاطي بأن شن بن أمضى بن عبد القيس فلا مغايرة بين الشني والعبدي وقال بن الأثير لعل من نسبه ## Source unit 72 · printed entry 72

### English candidate

Arṭāh ibn Kaʿb ibn Sharāḥīl ibn Kaʿb ibn Salāmān ibn ʿĀmir ibn Ḥāritha ibn Saʿd ibn Mālik ibn al-Nakhaʿ. Ibn Shāhīn transmitted through a weak isnād, by way of ʿAbd ibn ʿĀbis al-Nakhaʿī, from Qays ibn Kaʿb al-Nakhaʿī, that he came in a delegation to the Prophet ﷺ with his brothers Arṭāh ibn Kaʿb and al-Arqam. The two were among the handsomest and most eloquent men of their time. He invited them to Islam; they accepted, and he prayed for their welfare, wrote a document for Arṭāh, and tied a banner for him. Arṭāh witnessed al-Qādisiyya under that banner. His brother Zayd ibn Kaʿb then took the banner and was killed. Al-Rushāṭī related a similar account from Ibn al-Kalbī but named the brother Durayd ibn Kaʿb; Ibn Saʿd did likewise. Ibn Saʿd called him Arṭāh ibn Sharāḥīl ibn Kaʿb of Banū Ḥāritha ibn Saʿd ibn Mālik ibn al-Nakhaʿ, and related from Hishām ibn al-Kalbī, from his father, from Nakhaʿ elders, that he and al-Juhayish—whose name was al-Arqam—came to the Prophet ﷺ; he will appear under al-Arqam. Arṭāh is also mentioned through another route. Ibn Abī Shayba transmitted from Ibn Idrīs, from Ḥanash ibn al-Ḥārith, from his father: al-Nakhaʿ passed by ʿUmar, who inspected them—2,500 men under a man called Arṭāh—and said, “I see nobility firmly established among you. Go to your brethren in Iraq and fight.” They preferred Syria, but he directed them to Iraq, and they went. Abū Nuʿaym transmitted from Ḥanash, from Abū al-Ḥārith, that they came from Yemen and camped in Medina; ʿUmar inspected them and directed them to Iraq. At al-Qādisiyya many of al-Nakhaʿ were killed while few others were. Asked why, ʿUmar said, “Al-Nakhaʿ took charge of the greatest part of the affair by themselves.”

## Source unit 73 · printed entry 73

### English candidate

Al-Arqam ibn Abī al-Arqam, whose personal name was ʿAbd Manāf ibn Asad ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr ibn Makhzūm, with the kunya Abū ʿAbd Allāh. Ibn al-Sakan said his mother was Tumāḍir bint Ḥudhaym al-Sahmiyya; she is also called the daughter of ʿAbd al-Ḥārith al-Khuzāʿiyya. He was among the earliest converts. It is said that he accepted Islam after ten others. Al-Bukhārī said he had Companionship. Ibn Isḥāq and Mūsā ibn ʿUqba listed him among those at Badr. Al-Ḥākim related that he was the seventh to accept Islam. His house on al-Ṣafā was where the Prophet ﷺ sat during the early Islamic period. Al-Ḥākim related a long account: al-Arqam made the house an inalienable endowment, and his descendants later sold it to Abū Jaʿfar al-Manṣūr. Ibn Manda transmitted through a stronger route, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUthmān ibn al-Arqam, from his grandfather, a veteran of Badr: the Messenger of God ﷺ remained in his house near al-Ṣafā until the Muslims numbered forty; ʿUmar was the last of them to accept Islam, and when they reached forty they went out. Aḥmad transmitted from ʿUthmān ibn al-Arqam ibn Abī al-Arqam, from his father, a Companion of the Prophet ﷺ: “Whoever steps over people’s necks on Friday and separates two people after the imam has emerged is like one dragging his entrails in the Fire.” Al-Ḥākim also transmitted it, but al-Dāraquṭnī said Hishām ibn Ziyād—Abū al-Miqdām—alone transmitted it and had been weakened. Al-Ḥākim also related that al-Arqam directed that Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ pray over him. Ibn Manda transmitted from Ibrāhīm ibn al-Mundhir that al-Arqam died in 55 AH during Muʿāwiya’s caliphate; then through a weak chain from ʿUthmān ibn al-Arqam that his father died in 53 aged eighty-five and Saʿd prayed over him. Abū Nuʿaym and Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr transmitted through a disconnected chain that he died the day Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq died. Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr interpreted this as referring to his father Abū al-Arqam. Al-Arqam witnessed Badr, Uḥud, and every campaign; the Prophet ﷺ granted him a house in Medina. Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said Ibn Abī Ḥātim erred by making this al-Arqam the father of ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Arqam, ʿUthmān’s treasury official: that man was Zuhrī, while this one was Makhzūmī; the Zuhrī’s father was ʿAbd Yaghūth ibn Wahb ibn ʿAbd Manāf. I say: Al-Ṭabarānī transmitted, by way of al-Thawrī, from Ibn Abī Laylā, from al-Ḥakam, from Miqsam, from Ibn ʿAbbās, that the Prophet ﷺ appointed al-Arqam ibn Abī al-Arqam al-Zuhrī over alms collection. He sought the help of Abū Rāfiʿ, the client of the Prophet ﷺ. Abū Rāfiʿ came to the Prophet ﷺ, who said, “Abū Rāfiʿ, alms are forbidden to Muḥammad and the family of Muḥammad.” This indicates that the Zuhrī al-Arqam also had Companionship. Shuʿba, however, transmitted from al-Ḥakam, from Miqsam, “He appointed a man from Banū Makhzūm.” Abū Dāwūd and others likewise transmitted it, and their isnād is sounder than the first.

<div dir="rtl" lang="ar">

الأرقم بن أبي الأرقم وكان اسمه عبد مناف بن أسد بن عبد الله بن عمرو بن مخزوم يكنى أبا عبد الله قال بن السكن أمة تماضر بنت حذيم السهمية ويقال بنت عبد الحارث الخزاعية كان من السابقين الأولين قيل أسلم بعد عشرة وقال البخاري له صحبة وذكره بن إسحاق وموسى بن عقبة فيمن شهد بدرا وروى الحاكم في ترجمته في المستدرك أنه أسلم سابع سبعة وكانت داره على الصفا وهي الدار التي كان النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم يجلس فيها في الإسلام وذكر قصة طويلة لهذه الدار وأن الأرقم حبسها وأن احفاده بعد ذلك باعوها لأبي جعفر المنصور ورواه بن منده من طريق أقوى من طريق الحاكم وهي عن عبد الله بن عثمان بن الأرقم عن جده وكان بدريا وكان رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم في داره التي عند الصفا حتى تكاملوا أربعين رجلا مسلمين وكان آخرهم اسلاما عمر فلما تكاملوا أربعين رجلا خرجوا وروى أحمد من طريق عثمان بن الأرقم بن أبي الأرقم عن أبيه وكان من أصحاب النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال إن الذي يتخطى رقاب الناس يوم الجمعة ويفرق بين الإثنين بعد خروج الإمام كالجار قصبه في النار وأخرجه الحاكم أيضا لكن قال الدار قطني في الأفراد تفرد به هشام بن زياد وهو أبوالمقدام وقد ضعفوه وروى الحاكم أيضا أن الأرقم أوصى أن يصلي عليه سعد بن أبي وقاص وروى بن منده من طريق إبراهيم بن المنذر قال توفي الأرقم في خلافة معاوية سنة خمس وخمسين ثم روى بسند لين عن عثمان بن الأرقم قال توفي أبي سنة ثلاث وخمسين وهو بن خمس وثمانين سنة وصلى عليه سعد بن أبي وقاص وروى أبو نعيم وابن عبد البر بسند منقطع أنه توفي يوم مات أبو بكر الصديق وحمله بن عبد البر على أن المراد بذلك والده النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم الأرقم بن أبي الأرقم الزهري على السعاية فاستتبع أبا رافع مولى النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم فأتي النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم فقال يا أبا رافع إن الصدقة حرام على محمد وعلى آل محمد فهذا ## Source unit 80 · printed entry 80

### English candidate

Al-Azraq ibn ʿUqba, Abū ʿUqba al-Thaqafī, their client. He was one of Kalada al-Thaqafī’s slaves; it is also said, one of al-Ḥārith ibn Kalada’s. During the siege of al-Ṭāʾif he came down to the Prophet ﷺ and accepted Islam. The Prophet ﷺ freed him and entrusted him to Khālid ibn Saʿīd ibn al-ʿĀṣ to support and teach him. He became an ally of Banū Umayya, who married women to him and married women from his family. Al-Wāqidī mentioned this in al-Maghāzī, as did Ibn Isḥāq more briefly. Ibn Fatḥūn added him in a supplement. I say: He will be mentioned in the biography of al-Ḥārith ibn Kalada. Al-Balādhurī said that al-Azraq was a Roman blacksmith who married Sumayya, mother of ʿAmmār, after Yāsir separated from her. She bore him Salama ibn al-Azraq, who was therefore ʿAmmār’s maternal half-brother. Later, ʿAmmār’s sons ʿUmar and ʿUqba—who were not Sumayya’s sons—claimed descent from al-Ḥārith ibn Abī Shamir al-Ghassānī, saying they were allies of Banū Umayya; they attained standing in Mecca. Al-Ṭabarī related the same.

## Source unit 82 · printed entry 82

### English candidate

Azhar ibn ʿAbd ʿAwf ibn ʿAbd ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Zuhra ibn Kilāb, the Qurashī and Zuhrī, was the paternal uncle of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf and the father of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Azhar, who will be mentioned below. Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr claimed that he was Azhar ibn ʿAwf and that he was the brother of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Azhar ibn ʿAwf, but he erred in that. Al-Baghawī transmitted, by way of Yaʿqūb ibn Zayd ibn Ṭalḥa, from al-Zuhrī, from Abū al-Ṭufayl, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: “Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥanafiyya and I disputed over the office of providing drink to the pilgrims. Ṭalḥa, ʿĀmir ibn Rabīʿa, Azhar ibn ʿAbd ʿAwf, and Makhrama ibn Nawfal testified that the Prophet ﷺ handed it over to al-ʿAbbās on the day of the Conquest.” Al-Wāqidī is in its chain of transmission. It is also related from al-Zuhrī, from ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿAbd Allāh, that when ʿUmar assumed office he sent four men, who set up the boundary markers of the sanctuary: Makhrama, Azhar ibn ʿAbd ʿAwf, Saʿīd ibn Yarbūʿ, and Ḥuwayṭib ibn ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā. Al-Fākihī and others transmitted it. Al-Ṭabarānī included under this Azhar’s biography a report from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn Nāfiʿ al-Ṭaḥḥān, from Aḥmad ibn ʿAmr ibn al-Sarḥ, who said: “I found in my maternal uncle’s book, from ʿUqayl, from Ibn Shihāb, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Azhar, from his father, that a wine drinker was brought to the Messenger of God ﷺ while he was at Ḥunayn”—the report. This is an error by al-Ṭabarānī or his teacher. Abū Dāwūd and al-Nasāʾī transmitted it from Ibn al-Sarḥ through this chain, from al-Zuhrī, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Azhar, from his father. The report therefore belongs to the musnad of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Azhar, not to the musnad of Azhar. Ṣāliḥ ibn Kaysān likewise related it from al-Zuhrī, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Azhar himself, without saying “from his father.” Abū Salama ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān and Muḥammad ibn Ibrāhīm al-Taymī likewise related it from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Azhar himself. والله أعلم.

## Source unit 87 · printed entry 87

### English candidate

Usāma ibn Akhdarī, the Tamīmī and then the Shaqrī, settled in Basra. Ibn Ḥibbān said: He came to the Messenger of God ﷺ as a Muslim. End quote. He said, “Messenger of God, name him and supplicate for him.” He asked, “What is your name?” He replied, “Aṣram.” He said, “Rather, you are Zurʿa.” He asked, “What do you want him for?” He replied, “As a shepherd.” He then closed his fingers and said, “He is ʿĀṣim.” Abū Dāwūd and al-Ḥākim transmitted his report in al-Mustadrak. Ibn al-Sakan said: He has no report other than this one. ## Source unit 89 · printed entry 89

### English candidate

Usāma ibn Zayd ibn Ḥāritha ibn Sharāḥīl ibn ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā ibn Zayd ibn Imriʾ al-Qays ibn ʿĀmir ibn al-Nuʿmān ibn ʿĀmir ibn ʿAbd Wudd ibn ʿAwf ibn Kināna ibn Bakr ibn ʿAwf ibn ʿUdhra ibn Zayd al-Lāt ibn Rufayda ibn Thawr ibn Kalb ibn Wabara, the Kalbī, the beloved son of the beloved. His kunya was Abū Muḥammad, though Abū Zayd is also given. His mother was Umm Ayman, the woman who cared for the Prophet ﷺ. Ibn Saʿd said: Usāma was born in Islam, and when the Prophet ﷺ died he was twenty years old. Ibn Abī Khaythama said that he was eighteen. The Prophet ﷺ had appointed him commander over a great army, but died before he set out. Abū Bakr dispatched it. ʿUmar held Usāma in esteem and honored him, and allotted him more than he allotted his own son ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar. Usāma withdrew from the civil conflicts after ʿUthmān was killed and remained apart from them until he died late in Muʿāwiya’s caliphate. He had resided at al-Mizza in the district of Damascus; then he returned and lived in Wādī al-Qurā, after which he went down to Medina and died there at al-Jurf. Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr judged it sound that he died in the year fifty-four. Among the Companions, Abū Hurayra and Ibn ʿAbbās transmitted from Usāma; among the senior Followers, Abū ʿUthmān al-Nahdī, Abū Wāʾil, and others did so. His virtues are many and his reports well known.

## Source unit 90 · printed entry 90

### English candidate

Usāma ibn Sharīk al-Thaʿlabī, of Banū Thaʿlaba ibn Yarbūʿ, according to al-Ṭabarānī and Abū Nuʿaym. It is also said that he was of Banū Thaʿlaba ibn Saʿd, according to Ibn Ḥibbān; and it is said that he was of Banū Thaʿlaba ibn Bakr ibn Wāʾil, according to Ibn al-Sakan, Ibn Manda, and Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr. The latter also called him al-Dhubyānī al-Ghaṭafānī. Al-Rushāṭī objected that Bakr had no son named Thaʿlaba and that their describing his lineage as al-Dhubyānī al-Ghaṭafānī shows that he belonged to Banū Thaʿlaba ibn Saʿd ibn Dhubyān. والله أعلم. Al-Bukhārī said: Usāma ibn Sharīk, one of Banū Thaʿlaba, had Companionship. The compilers of the Sunan, Aḥmad, Ibn Khuzayma, Ibn Ḥibbān, and al-Ḥākim transmitted his report. Among his reports is: “I came to the Messenger of God ﷺ while his Companions were as still as though birds were perched on their heads.” In some routes it reads: “I went out with the Prophet ﷺ during the Farewell Pilgrimage. Some people came and said, ‘Messenger of God, Banū Yarbūʿ have killed us.’ He said, ‘No soul incurs guilt for another.’” Usāma ibn Sharīk also transmitted from Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī. Al-Azdī, Ibn al-Sakan, and more than one other scholar stated that Ziyād ibn ʿAlāqa alone transmitted from him.

## Source unit 94 · printed entry 94

### English candidate

Isḥāq al-Ghanawī. Al-Bukhārī transmitted in his Tārīkh, as did Samawayh, Abū Yaʿlā, and others, by way of Bashshār ibn ʿAbd al-Malik al-Muzanī, who said: My grandmother, Umm Ḥakīm bint Dīnār al-Muzaniyya, related to me from her patroness, Umm Isḥāq al-Ghanawiyya, that she and her brother Isḥāq emigrated from Mecca intending Medina. When they had reached a place along the road, her brother told her, “Sit here until I return to Mecca and fetch travel funds that I forgot.” She said, “I fear that the wicked man”—meaning her husband—“will kill you.” Her brother went to Mecca and left her. After three days a rider passed her and asked, “Umm Isḥāq, what is keeping you here?” She replied, “I am waiting for my brother.” He said, “There is no Isḥāq left for you. ## Source unit 97 · printed entry 97

### English candidate

Asad ibn Khuwaylid, in Khadīja’s lineage. Muḥammad ibn Jābir transmitted his report from Simāk and from someone who heard Asad ibn Khuwaylid; this is how Ibn Manda mentioned it. Abū ʿUmar said: Asad, son of Khadīja’s brother, transmitted from the Prophet ﷺ that he said, “Do not sell what you do not possess.” Al-ʿUqaylī mentioned him and said that there is criticism of its chain. End quote. Genealogists did not mention any brother of Khadīja other than al-ʿAwwām, father of al-Zubayr, who died in the pre-Islamic period, and Nawfal, who was killed as an unbeliever on the day of Badr. It is said that his brother’s son al-Zubayr killed him, and it is said that ʿAlī did. It is therefore possible that this Asad was a son of Nawfal, but they did not mention that.

## Source unit 100 · printed entry 100

### English candidate

Asad ibn Saʿya al-Quraẓī, one of the Jews who accepted Islam. Ibn al-Sakan transmitted, by way of Saʿīd ibn Buzaygh, from Ibn Isḥāq, who said: ʿĀṣim ibn ʿUmar ibn Qatāda related to me that an elder of Banū Qurayẓa told him that the conversion of Thaʿlaba ibn Saʿya, Asad ibn Saʿya, and Asad ibn ʿUbayd occurred because of the account of Ibn al-Hayyabān. He then related his story at length: Ibn al-Hayyabān had informed them before Islam that the Prophet ﷺ would come. On the night whose morning saw the conquest of Qurayẓa, these three said to them, “Assembly of Jews, by God, this is indeed the man whom Ibn al-Hayyabān described to us. Fear God and follow him.” They refused them. The three descended to the Prophet ﷺ and accepted Islam. He also transmitted it by way of Yaḥyā ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿAbbād al-Shajarī, from Ibn Isḥāq, from ʿĀṣim ibn ʿUmar, from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab, from Jābir; the first chain is stronger. Al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Manda transmitted by another route from Ibn Isḥāq, from Muḥammad ibn Abī Muḥammad, from Saʿīd or ʿIkrima, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: When ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām, Thaʿlaba ibn Saʿya, Asad ibn ʿUbayd, and Asad—or Usayd—ibn Saʿya accepted Islam, the Jews said, “Only our worst men have gone to Muḥammad.” God Most High then revealed, “They are not all alike; among the People of the Book...” through His words, “the righteous.”

Asad ibn Kurz ibn ʿĀmir ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbd Shams ibn ʿUqba ibn Jarīr ibn Shaqq ibn Ṣaʿb, al-Jabalī and then al-Qasrī, grandfather of Khālid, the governor of Iraq. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Aḥmad, in the additions to al-Musnad, and Abū Yaʿlā and al-Baghawī transmitted by way of Ismāʿīl ibn Wāsiṭ al-Bajalī, from Khālid al-Qasrī, from his grandfather Asad ibn Kurz, that he heard the Prophet ﷺ say, ‘A sick person’s sins fall away’—the report. ## Source unit 111 · printed entry 111

### English candidate

Asʿad ibn Zurāra ibn ʿAdas ibn ʿUbayd ibn Thaʿlaba ibn Ghanm ibn Mālik ibn al-Najjār, Abū Umāma, al-Anṣārī al-Khazrajī al-Najjārī. He embraced Islam early, witnessed both pledges at al-ʿAqaba, and was the naqīb of his tribe. None of the naqībs was younger than he. It is also said that he was the first to pledge allegiance on the night of al-ʿAqaba. Al-Wāqidī reported, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, from Khubayb, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, who said: Asʿad ibn Zurāra and Dhakwān ibn ʿAbd Qays went out to Mecca, intending to submit their dispute over precedence to ʿUtba ibn Rabīʿa. They heard about the Messenger of God ﷺ, went to him, and he presented Islam to them and recited the Qurʾān to them. They accepted Islam, did not go near ʿUtba, and returned to Medina. They were the first two to bring Islam to Medina. Ibn Isḥāq, however, said that Asʿad accepted Islam only at the First ʿAqaba, with the group of six; الله أعلم. Ibn Manda erred when he said that Asʿad was naqīb over Banū Sāʿida. It is also said that he was the first to pledge on the night of al-ʿAqaba. Ibn Isḥāq said that he witnessed the first, second, and third ʿAqabas. Abū Dāwūd and al-Ḥākim transmitted, through ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Kaʿb ibn Mālik, who said: I used to guide my father after his sight failed. Whenever I took him out for Friday prayer and he heard the call to prayer, he would ask forgiveness for Asʿad ibn Zurāra—the report. It states that Asʿad was the first to conduct the Friday congregation for us in Medina, before the Prophet ﷺ arrived, in the lava field of Banū Bayāḍa, at Naqīʿ al-Khaḍamāt. Al-Wāqidī stated that he died nine months after the Hijra. Al-Ḥākim related this in al-Mustadrak through al-Wāqidī, from Ibn Abī al-Rijāl. It includes: Banū al-Najjār came and said, ‘O Messenger of God, our naqīb has died, so appoint a naqīb over us.’ He replied, ‘I am your naqīb.’ Ibn Isḥāq stated that Asʿad died while the Prophet ﷺ was building the mosque. Al-Wāqidī said that this occurred in Shawwāl. Al-Baghawī said: I have been informed that he was the first of the Companions to die after the Hijra, and the first deceased person over whom the Prophet ﷺ performed the funeral prayer. Al-Wāqidī transmitted, through ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Bakr ibn Ḥazm: The first person buried in al-Baqīʿ was Asʿad ibn Zurāra; that is the position of the Anṣār. The Emigrants, however, said that the first person buried there was ʿUthmān ibn Maẓʿūn. Al-Ḥākim transmitted, by way of al-Sarrāj in his History, then through Muḥammad ibn ʿUmāra, from Zaynab bint Nubayṭ, that the Prophet ﷺ adorned her mother and her maternal aunt with dangling earrings of unminted gold and gold, set with pearls. Their father, Asʿad ibn Zurāra, had entrusted them to the Messenger of God ﷺ. ʿAbd al-Razzāq reported, from Maʿmar, from al-Zuhrī, from Abū Umāma ibn Sahl, who said: The Prophet ﷺ entered upon Asʿad ibn Zurāra, one of the naqībs on the night of al-ʿAqaba, when he had been afflicted by al-shawka—a spreading redness or eruption—and cauterized him—the report. Al-Ḥākim likewise transmitted it through Yūnus, from al-Zuhrī. I say: this is the preserved version. ʿAbd al-Aʿlā related it from Maʿmar, from al-Zuhrī, from Anas; al-Ḥākim also transmitted that version, but it is anomalous. Ibn Abī Dhiʾb related it from al-Zuhrī, from ʿUrwa, from ʿĀʾisha; that version is anomalous as well. Zamʿa ibn Ṣāliḥ related it from al-Zuhrī, from Abū Umāma ibn Sahl, from ‘Abū Umāma Asʿad ibn Zurāra.’ This agrees with ʿAbd al-Razzāq’s version, because by saying ‘from Abū Umāma Asʿad ibn Zurāra’ he did not mean that Abū Umāma narrated from Asʿad; he meant ‘concerning the account of Asʿad ibn Zurāra.’ والله أعلم. The authorities on campaigns and histories agree that he died during the Prophet’s ﷺ lifetime, before Badr. A report in al-Ṭabarānī, through al-Shaʿbī, from Zufar ibn Wathīma, from al-Mughīra ibn Shuʿba, states that Asʿad ibn Zurāra said to ʿUmar: The Prophet ﷺ wrote to al-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Sufyān that he should give the wife of Ashyam al-Ḍibābī an inheritance from her husband’s blood-money. This is problematic. Perhaps the text originally read ‘Saʿd ibn Zurāra’ and was corrupted in transmission; والله أعلم. Otherwise, it must be understood as referring to another Asʿad ibn Zurāra. End.

## Source unit 121 · printed entry 121

### English candidate

Al-Asqaʿ—with qāf—the father of Wāthila ibn al-Asqaʿ al-Bakrī al-Laythī, the well-known Companion. Abū Saʿd cited in Sharaf al-Muṣṭafā something indicating that the father had Companionship. He transmitted, through Hishām ibn ʿAmmār, from Muḥammad ibn Shuʿayb, from Yaḥyā ibn Abī ʿAmr, from ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd Allāh, from Wāthila ibn al-Asqaʿ, who said: I went out to the Messenger of God ﷺ, and he led the people in prayer—the report. It includes: Then I returned and found my father seated, facing the sun in the forenoon. I greeted him with the greeting of Islam. He said, ‘Have you become a Ṣābiʾ?’ I said, ‘Yes, I have accepted Islam.’ He said, ‘May God perhaps place good for you and for us in that.’ He said: I then remained with him—meaning until the time of the Conquest—the report. I later found an even more explicit report. Abū Nuʿaym transmitted in Dalāʾil al-Nubuwwa, through Abū ʿĀṣim, who said: Hishām ibn ʿAmmār related to us; ʿUmar ibn al-Darfas related to us; ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Qasīma related to me, from Wāthila ibn al-Asqaʿ, who said: We were in the Ṣuffa, twenty men in all. Hunger afflicted us, and I was among the youngest of my companions, so they sent me to the Prophet ﷺ to complain to him of their hunger.

## Source unit 122 · printed entry 122

### English candidate

Al-Aslaʿ al-Aʿrajī—with rāʾ—of Banū al-Aʿraj ibn Kaʿb ibn Saʿd ibn Zayd Manāt ibn Tamīm. Ibn al-Sakan said, “His hadith is counted among those of the Basrans, but it is open to question.” Ibn Ḥibbān said, “Al-Aslaʿ al-Saʿdī was a man of Banū al-Aʿraj ibn Kaʿb. It is said that he had Companionship, but al-Rabīʿ ibn Badr occurs in the chain of his report.”

In the heading, al-Ṭabarānī called him “al-Aslaʿ ibn Sharīk al-Ashjaʿī.” He then related his hadith by two routes from al-Rabīʿ ibn Badr: “My father related to me, from his father, from a man called al-Aslaʿ, who said: I used to serve the Prophet ﷺ and saddle his mount. One day he said to me, ‘Al-Aslaʿ, get up and saddle it.’ I said, ‘Messenger of God, I am in a state of major ritual impurity.’ The Messenger of God ﷺ remained silent, and Gabriel came to him with the verse concerning clean earth. The Messenger of God ﷺ then said, ‘Get up, al-Aslaʿ, and perform tayammum.’ I got up, performed tayammum, and then saddled his mount. He traveled until he passed some water and said to me, ‘Al-Aslaʿ, touch—or cause this to touch—your skin.’ He demonstrated tayammum to me: one strike for the face and one strike for the hands up to the elbows.” End of report.

Al-Ṭabarānī then related it through Yaḥyā al-Ḥimmānī from al-Rabīʿ, who said, “Al-Aslaʿ was a man of Banū al-Aʿraj ibn Kaʿb.” Ismāʿīl al-Qāḍī likewise transmitted it in al-Aḥkām from Yaḥyā.

Al-Ṭabarānī also related, through al-Haytham ibn Ruzayq, from his father, from al-Aslaʿ ibn Sharīk, who said: “I used to saddle the she-camel of the Prophet ﷺ. One cold night I entered a state of major ritual impurity, and the Messenger of God ﷺ intended to depart. I disliked saddling his she-camel while in that state, and I feared that if I washed with the cold water I would die or fall ill. I therefore instructed a man of the Helpers to saddle it. I placed stones in a fire, heated water with them, and washed. Then I caught up with the Messenger of God ﷺ and his Companions. He said, ‘Al-Aslaʿ, why do I see that your saddling has changed?’ I said, ‘Messenger of God, I did not saddle it; a man of the Helpers did.’ He asked, ‘Why?’ I replied, ‘I entered a state of major ritual impurity and feared the cold for myself, so I told him to saddle it. I placed stones in a fire, heated water, and washed with it.’ God then sent down: ‘O you who believe, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated ...’ through His words, ‘Ever Pardoning, Ever Forgiving.’”

I say: this account bears a slight resemblance to the first, but the two differ plainly. Al-Ṭabarānī and a group of scholars understood all of it to have happened to al-Aslaʿ. This is supported by Ibn Manda, who headed his entry “Al-Aslaʿ ibn Sharīk ibn ʿAwf al-Aʿrajī,” and then transmitted through Qays ibn Ḥafṣ al-Dārimī, who said: “I asked some of al-Aslaʿ’s paternal cousins about him, and they said, ‘He is al-Aslaʿ ibn Sharīk ibn ʿAwf.’” End of quotation.

Khalīfa said in his Tārīkh: “Of Banū al-Aʿraj ibn Kaʿb was al-Aslaʿ ibn Sharīk, who transmitted from the Prophet ﷺ concerning tayammum.” I have seen nothing in any route of this report calling him Ashjaʿī, nor is that compatible with his belonging to Banū al-Aʿraj ibn Kaʿb. It may be an aural scribal corruption: the speaker intended to say al-Aʿrajī but said al-Ashjaʿī.

Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr, however, separated the two accounts and assigned them to two men, each called al-Aslaʿ. He said that the first was al-Aslaʿ ibn al-Asqaʿ, whose hadith al-Rabīʿ ibn Badr transmitted, and that the second was al-Aslaʿ ibn Sharīk al-Aʿrajī al-Tamīmī. Yet his attribution of the second to al-Aʿraj indicates that he is the first, for it is established that the first was Aʿrajī. I do not know where he obtained the name of the first man’s father, al-Asqaʿ. If it is established, perhaps the man was named Sharīk and nicknamed al-Asqaʿ.

In Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr’s original, in his own handwriting, it appeared as al-Aʿwajī, with wāw. Al-Rushāṭī criticized this and said that it is with rāʾ. It likewise appeared as al-Taymī, and al-Rushāṭī criticized that as well. Ibn al-Sakan also said of the Aʿrajī that he was called Ibn Sharīk. This indicates that the reports concern one man. والله أعلم.

Ibn Manda related from ʿAlī ibn Saʿīd al-ʿAskarī that al-Aslaʿ’s name was al-Ḥārith ibn Kaʿb. I think this is an error. والله أعلم.

Notice: in his commentary on al-Bukhārī, at the beginning of the Book of Tayammum, Shaykh Mughlaṭāy attributed this account of al-Aslaʿ to al-Jāḥiẓ in the Book of al-Burhān. His wording was: “Al-Aslaʿ al-Aʿrajī used to saddle for the Prophet ﷺ. He said to the Prophet ﷺ, ‘I am in a state of major ritual impurity and have no water,’ so God sent down the verse of tayammum.” This is a grave shortcoming on his part, despite the breadth of his reading.

## Source unit 125 · printed entry 125

### English candidate

Aslam ibn Bajra—with fatḥa on the bāʾ and sukūn on the jīm—al-Anṣārī. Ibn al-Kalbī gave his lineage as Aslam ibn Bajra ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Ghayyān—with dotted ghayn and a geminated subscript yāʾ—ibn Thaʿlaba ibn Ṭarīf ibn al-Khazraj ibn Sāʿida, al-Khazrajī al-Sāʿidī. This is how Ibn al-Kalbī gave his lineage.

Al-ʿAdawī, however, gave Aws in place of Ghiyāth. Ibn Mākūlā, and al-Dāraquṭnī before him, gave “Aslam ibn Aws ibn Bajra,” with the rest of the lineage the same. Ibn Shāhīn likewise mentioned it from Muḥammad ibn Ibrāhīm, from Muḥammad ibn Yazīd, from his authorities. All of them followed al-ʿAdawī, for this is how he listed him in the genealogy of the Helpers, and he said that Aslam witnessed Uḥud.

Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said, “His lineage is not soundly established in my view, and his Companionship is open to question.” I say: Ibn al-Kalbī did give his lineage, and he is the principal authority among genealogists, as we have mentioned. Ibn Shāhīn, Ibn Qāniʿ, and others followed him.

Al-Ṭabarānī transmitted in al-Ṣaghīr, through al-Zubayr ibn Bakkār, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr al-Fihrī, from Muḥammad ibn Ibrāhīm ibn Muḥammad ibn Aslam, from his father, from his grandfather Aslam al-Anṣārī, who said: “The Prophet ﷺ placed me in charge of the captives of Qurayẓa”—the rest of the hadith. Al-Ṭabarānī said, “No one transmits from Aslam except by this chain; al-Zubayr alone transmitted it.” End of quotation.

Al-Ṭabarānī himself also transmitted it in al-Kabīr by another route, through Isḥāq ibn Abī Farwa, from Ibrāhīm ibn Muḥammad ibn Aslam ibn Bajra, from his father, from Aslam ibn Bajra, with the same report. Ibn al-Sakan transmitted it by this second route and said, “It is not established.” Ibn Manda called it singular. Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said, “His hadith revolves around Isḥāq.” That is what he said.

Ibn al-Athīr distinguished Aslam ibn Bajra from Aslam ibn Aws ibn Bajra, but they are one man, as you can see. It remains remotely possible that one was the other’s nephew and that they shared a name. والله أعلم.

Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said that Aslam was one of those who prevented ʿUthmān from being buried in al-Baqīʿ.

Al-Baghawī transmitted from Abū ʿUbayd: “Aslam ibn al-Ḥuṣayn ibn al-Nuʿmān al-Awsī had the kunya Abū Jabīra. He is not Abū Jabīra Qays ibn al-Ḍaḥḥāk.” I say: Ibn Shabba transmitted this in the report about Medina, through Makhlad ibn Khufāf, from ʿUrwa: “Those who prevented them from burying ʿUthmān in al-Baqīʿ included Aslam ibn Aws ibn Bajra al-Sāʿidī.”

## Source unit 132 · printed entry 132

### English candidate

Aslam, the Black shepherd. Ibn Isḥāq said in al-Maghāzī: “My father, Isḥāq ibn Yasār, related to me that a Black shepherd came to the Prophet ﷺ while he was besieging one of the fortresses of Khaybar. The shepherd had with him sheep for whose Jewish owner he was a hired hand. He said, ‘Messenger of God, explain Islam to me,’ and he embraced Islam.”

This is how Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr mentioned him. Ibn al-Athīr objected that none of the versions states that his name was Aslam. This is a well-directed objection. Abū Nuʿaym named him Yasār, as will appear under the subscript letter yāʾ, إن شاء الله تعالى.

Al-Rushāṭī said in al-Ansāb: “Aslam the Abyssinian embraced Islam on the day of Khaybar, fought, and was killed without having performed a single prayer.” The Prophet ﷺ said, “With him now is his wife from among the maidens of Paradise.”

## Source unit 137 · printed entry 137

### English candidate

Asmāʾ ibn Ḥāritha ibn Saʿīd ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ghiyāth ibn Saʿd ibn ʿAmr ibn ʿĀmir ibn Thaʿlaba ibn Mālik ibn Afṣā al-Aslamī. His kunya was Abū Hind. Ibn al-Kalbī gave this lineage. Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said, “Asmāʾ ibn Ḥāritha ibn Hind ibn ʿAbd Allāh,” with the remainder the same. Including Hind in his lineage is an error; Hind was his brother. Aḥmad and Ibn Manda transmitted by way of Yaḥyā ibn Hind ibn Ḥāritha. Hind had been among the Companions at al-Ḥudaybiya, while his brother was the one whom the Messenger of God ﷺ sent to his people to order them to fast on ʿĀshūrāʾ; that brother was Asmāʾ ibn Ḥāritha. Yaḥyā ibn Hind related from Asmāʾ ibn Ḥāritha that the Messenger of God ﷺ sent him and said, “Go command your people to fast on this day”—the report. A similar report is related from al-Awzāʿī, from Ibn Ḥarmala, from Abū Salama ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, from Asmāʾ ibn Ḥāritha; and from Mūsā ibn ʿUqba, from Isḥāq ibn Yaḥyā, from ʿUbāda ibn al-Ṣāmit, who said: The Prophet ﷺ sent Asmāʾ ibn Ḥāritha. Al-Ḥākim transmitted in al-Mustadrak, by way of al-Wāqidī, from Saʿīd ibn ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Marwān, from his father, from his grandfather, from Asmāʾ ibn Ḥāritha. He also transmitted by way of Yazīd ibn Ibrāhīm, from Ibn Sīrīn, from Abū Hurayra, who said: “Because Hind and Asmāʾ, the two sons of Ḥāritha, remained so constantly at the Messenger of God’s ﷺ door and served him, I used to think that they were nothing but servants of his.” Ibn Saʿd related from al-Wāqidī that Asmāʾ died in Basra in the year sixty-six at the age of eighty, and that he was one of the People of the Bench. He also said: Al-Wāqidī stated that he died during Muʿāwiya’s caliphate, in the days of Ziyād; but Ziyād died in the year fifty-three.

## Source unit 140 · printed entry 140

### English candidate

Ismāʿīl, a man from among the Companions who settled in Basra. Muslim transmitted, by way of Wakīʿ, from Ismāʿīl ibn Abī Khālid, Misʿar ibn Kidām, and al-Bukhtarī ibn al-Mukhtār; al-Nasāʾī transmitted by way of Abū Isḥāq al-Sabīʿī; and Muslim also transmitted by way of ʿAbd al-Malik ibn ʿUmayr. All of them related from Abū Bakr ibn ʿUmāra ibn Ruwayba, from his father, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said, “No man who prayed before sunrise and before sunset will enter the Fire.” We also related it in the account of ʿAbd Allāh al-Jābirī, who said: Ibn Abī al-Muthannā related to us; Jaʿfar ibn ʿAwn related to us, from Ismāʿīl ibn Abī Khālid, from Abū Bakr ibn ʿUmāra ibn Ruwayba, who said: An old man from Basra came to my father and said, “Relate to us what you heard from the Messenger of God ﷺ.” He then related it. The old man asked, “Did you hear it yourself?” He replied, “My two ears heard it and my heart retained it.” The old man said, “I too heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say it, and I did not know that anyone corroborated me concerning it.” Ibn Khuzayma transmitted it in his Ṣaḥīḥ from Bundār, from Yazīd ibn Hārūn, from Ismāʿīl, and his version says: “An old man from Basra named Ismāʿīl.” Ibn Manda transmitted it from Ibrāhīm ibn Muḥammad, from Ibn Khuzayma. We know this old man’s name from this sound transmission alone. والله أعلم.

## Source unit 141 · printed entry 141

### English candidate

Ismāʿīl ibn Saʿīd ibn ʿUbayd ibn Usayd ibn ʿAmr ibn ʿIlāj al-Thaqafī. It will be stated in his father’s biography that his father had Companionship. This Ismāʿīl was with him and witnessed the death of Umayya ibn Abī al-Ṣalt. Al-Bukhārī related this in his Tārīkh from al-Jarrāḥ ibn Makhlad, from al-ʿAlāʾ ibn al-Faḍl, who heard Muḥammad ibn Ismāʿīl ibn Ṭurayḥ ibn Ismāʿīl ibn Saʿīd ibn ʿUbayd relate from his father, from his grandfather, from his father’s grandfather, who said: “I witnessed Umayya ibn Abī al-Ṣalt at the time of death.” He then related the report at length. Ibn Manda transmitted it in the biography of Ṭurayḥ, by way of ʿAmr ibn ʿAlī, from al-ʿAlāʾ ibn al-Faḍl, from Muḥammad ibn Ismāʿīl ibn Ṭurayḥ, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: “I was present with Umayya.” Ibn al-Sakan likewise transmitted it from al-Maḥāmilī, from Muḥammad ibn Ṣāliḥ, from al-ʿAlāʾ. Al-Bukhārī’s wording is the authoritative one. The second transmission can be reconciled with the first if the pronoun in “his grandfather” refers to Ismāʿīl rather than to Muḥammad. Ibn Qāniʿ and Ibn Manda omitted Ismāʿīl between Ṭurayḥ and Saʿīd, which is an error. Al-Zubayr ibn Bakkār gave his lineage correctly. والله أعلم. Umayya ibn Abī al-Ṣalt died some time after the battle of Badr. Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr mentioned that after the Farewell Pilgrimage no one from Quraysh or Thaqīf remained without accepting Islam. Ibn Fatḥūn added him as an omission.

Ismāʿīl ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Ghifārī; al-Ashjaʿī is also given. Al-Thaʿlabī mentioned in his Qurʾānic commentary, and Hibat Allāh ibn Salāma in his work on abrogation, from al-Kalbī and Muqātil, that during the lifetime of the Messenger of God ﷺ he divorced his wife Qutayla without knowing that she was pregnant. He later learned of the pregnancy and took her back. She gave birth, then both she and her child died. The verse was then revealed: “Divorced women shall wait by themselves for three qurūʾ”—the verse. Ibn Fatḥūn added him as an omission.

## Source unit 147 · printed entry 147

### English candidate

Al-Aswad ibn Abī al-Aswad al-Nahdī. Ibn Manda transmitted, by way of Yūnus ibn Bukayr, from ʿAnbasa ibn al-Azhar, from Ibn al-Aswad al-Nahdī, from his father, who said: “The Messenger of God ﷺ rode to the cave, and his finger bled, so he said: ‘You are nothing but a finger that has bled;
what you have met was in the path of God.’” In the biographical heading Ibn Manda called him al-Aswad ibn Abī al-Aswad. This was his customary practice when he did not know a father’s name: he made a kunya for the father from the subject’s own name. Al-Baghawī had entered him earlier as “al-Aswad,” without a lineage, and then gave his report with the wording “from Abū al-Aswad—or Ibn al-Aswad—from his father.” He said: I know no other report with this chain. Abū Nuʿaym said: The correct version is what al-Thawrī, Shuʿba, Ibn ʿUyayna, and others related from al-Aswad ibn Qays, from Jundub al-Bajalī, who said: “I was with the Prophet ﷺ in a cave, and his finger bled”—the report. Ibn al-Athīr objected that Jundub was not with the Prophet ﷺ in the Cave, meaning the cave he entered when he emigrated to Medina. I say: The correct wording is, “I was with the Prophet ﷺ in a cave.” This is how it is established in the sound routes. He meant one cave among many, not the well-known Cave. والله أعلم.

### Arabic authority

<div dir="rtl" lang="ar">

الأسود بن أبي الأسود النهدي روى بن منده من طريق يونس بن بكير عن عنبسة بن الأزهر عن بن الأسود النهدي عن أبيه قال ركب رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم إلى الغار فدميت أصبعه فقال <br />
 هل أنت الا أصبع دميت <br />
 وفي سبيل الله ما لقيت قال بن منده في الترجمة الأسود بن أبي الأسود وهذه عادته فيمن لا يعرف اسم أبيه يجعل له من اسم صاحب الترجمة كنية وقد ترجم له قبله البغوي فقال الأسود ولم ينسبه ثم ساق حديثه ووقع عنده عن أبي الأسود أو بن الأسود عن أبيه وقال لا أعلم بهذا الإسناد غيره قال أبو نعيم الصحيح ما رواه الثوري وشعبة وابن عيينة وغيرهم عن الأسود بن قيس عن جندب البجلي قال كنت مع النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم في الغار فدميت أصبعه الحديث وتعقبه بن الأثير بأن جندبا لم يكن مع النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم في الغار يعني دخله لما هاجر إلى المدينة قلت وصواب العبارة كنت مع النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم في غار كذا ثبت في الطرق الصحيحة وأراد غارا من الغيران لا الغار المعهود والله أعلم

## Source unit 148 · printed entry 148

### English candidate

Al-Aswad ibn Aṣram al-Muḥāribī. Ibn Ḥibbān said: He was counted among the people of Syria, and his transmission is among theirs. Abū Zurʿa al-Dimashqī, Ibn Sumayʿ, and Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr mentioned him among the Companions who settled in Syria. Ibn al-Sakan said that his report is transmitted among the Syrians. Al-Ṭabarānī related, by way of ʿAbd al-Wahhāb ibn Bukht, from Sulaymān ibn Ḥabīb al-Muḥāribī, from al-Aswad ibn Aṣram al-Muḥāribī, that during a drought he brought some fat camels of his to Medina and took them to the Prophet ﷺ. The Prophet asked, “What do you want for them?” He replied, “A servant.” He asked, “Who has a servant?” ʿUthmān said, “I do.” He went to him with the camels. When ʿUthmān saw them, he said, “I want their like.” Al-Aswad said, “Take them,” and the Messenger of God ﷺ took possession of his camels. Al-Aswad then said, “Messenger of God, counsel me.” He replied, “Say with your tongue only what is right, and extend your hand only toward what is good.” Al-Baghawī transmitted it in abridged form and said: I know no other report of his, and no one other than Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥīm related it from ʿAbd al-Wahhāb. End quote. Ibn al-Sakan, al-Bukhārī in his Tārīkh, and Ibn Abī al-Dunyā in al-Ṣamt transmitted it through another route from Sulaymān, who said, “Al-Aswad ibn Aṣram related to me,” with similar wording. Al-Bukhārī, however, said: There is question concerning its chain.

<div dir="rtl" lang="ar">

الأسود بن أصرم المحاربي قال بن حبان عداده في أهل الشام وروايته فيهم وذكره أبو زرعة الدمشقي وابن سميع وابن عبد البر فيمن نزل الشام من الصحابة وقال بن السكن مخرج حديثه في أهل الشام ورواه الطبراني من طريق عبد الوهاب بن بخت عن سليمان بن حبيب المحاربي عن أسود بن أصرم المحاربي أنه قدم بإبل له سمان إلى المدينة في زمن محل فأتى بها النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم فقال له ما أردت بها قال خادما فقال من عنده خادم فقال عثمان عندي فأتاه بها فلما رآها قال مثلها أريد قال فخذها وقبض رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم إبله فقال أسود يا رسول الله أوصني قال لا تقل بلسانك إلا معروفا ولا تبسط يدك الا إلى خير أخرجه البغوي مختصرا وقال لا أعلم له غيره ولم يحدث به غير أبي عبد الرحيم عن عبد الوهاب انتهى وقد أخرجه بن السكن والبخاري في تاريخه وابن أبي الدنيا في الصمت من وجه آخر عن سليمان قال حدثني أسود بن أصرم نحوه لكن قال البخاري في إسناده نظر

## Source unit 149 · printed entry 149

### English candidate

Al-Aswad ibn Abī al-Bakhtarī, whose name was al-ʿĀṣ ibn Hāshim ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Asad ibn ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā ibn Quṣayy, the Qurashī and Asadī. His mother was ʿĀtika bint Umayya ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Asad. His father was killed as an unbeliever on the day of Badr, while he accepted Islam on the day of the Conquest. Al-Zubayr ibn Bakkār said: Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna related to us, from ʿAmr ibn Dīnār, who said: Muʿāwiya sent Busr ibn Abī Arṭāh to Medina and ordered him to consult a man of Banū Asad called al-Aswad ibn so-and-so. When Busr entered the mosque, he barred the doors and intended to kill them, until al-Aswad stopped him. Al-Zubayr said: He was al-Aswad ibn Abī al-Bakhtarī. The people of Medina had agreed upon him during the war between ʿAlī and Muʿāwiya. Al-Zubayr also mentioned that when al-Aswad’s sister Umm ʿAbd Allāh bint Abī al-Bakhtarī received a message from her husband ʿAdī ibn Nawfal asking her to join him after ʿUmar had appointed him over Ḥaḍramawt, al-Aswad told her, “The summons from your cousin has reached you, so set out to him.” She did so. A woman said concerning his son Saʿīd ibn al-Aswad: “If only I could buy, with my sash and my bracelet,
a single glance at Saʿīd ibn Aswad.” This Saʿīd ibn al-Aswad was a man living in the days of ʿUthmān. Ibn Abī Shayba said: ʿAffān related to us; Muʿtamir related to us; I heard my father relate from Abū Naḍra, from Abū Saʿīd, the client of Banū Usayd. He then related at length the report of ʿUthmān’s killing. It includes: “I saw Saʿīd ibn al-Aswad ibn Abī al-Bakhtarī striking a man with the flat of his sword. Had he wished to kill him, he could have done so; but ʿUthmān had bound them by a solemn command, so they held back.”

### Arabic authority

<div dir="rtl" lang="ar">

الأسود بن أبي البختري واسمه العاص بن هاشم بن الحارث بن أسد بن عبد العزى بن قصي القرشي الأسدي أمة عاتكة بنت أمية بن الحارث بن أسد قتل أبوه يوم بدر كافرا وأسلم هو يوم الفتح وقال الزبير بن بكار حدثنا سفيان بن عيينة عن عمرو بن دينار قال بعث معاوية بسر بن أبي أرطاة إلى المدينة وأمره أن يستثير رجلا من بني أسد يقال له الأسود بن فلان فلما دخل المسجد سد الأبواب وأراد قتلهم حتى نهاه الأسود قال الزبير هو الأسود بن أبي البختري وكان الناس اصطلحوا عليه بالمدينة أيام حرب علي ومعاوية وذكر الزبير أيضا أنه قال لأخته أم عبد الله بنت أبي البختري لما أرسل زوجها عدي بن نوفل يطلبها إذا استعمله عمر على حضر موت قد بلغ الأمر من بن عمك فاشخصي إليه ففعلت وفي ابنه سعيد بن الأسود تقول امرأة <br />

## Source unit 154 · printed entry 154

### English candidate

Al-Aswad ibn Khuzāʿī al-Aslamī, a confederate of Banū Salama of the Anṣār. Mūsā ibn ʿUqba, from Ibn Shihāb, mentioned him among the killers of Ibn Abī al-Ḥuqayq. He said: The Messenger of God ﷺ sent ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAtīk, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Unays, Abū Qatāda, Masʿūd ibn Sinān, al-Aswad ibn Khuzāʿī, and al-Aswad ibn Ḥarām—and he related the account. Ibn Isḥāq called him Khuzāʿī ibn al-Aswad, as did Maʿmar, from al-Zuhrī. Ibn Manda transmitted, by way of al-Wāqidī, from Usāma ibn Zayd ibn Aslam, from his father, from ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasār, from Abū Rāfiʿ: When [the expedition to] Khaybar arrived, the Prophet ﷺ ordered ʿAlī to fight them. A fully armored man came forward, and al-Aswad ibn Khuzāʿī went down to meet him. Al-Aswad killed him and took his spoils. Al-Ṭabarī said that al-Aswad ibn Khuzāʿī witnessed Uḥud. Al-Wāqidī mentioned that he traveled with ʿAlī to Yemen when the Prophet ﷺ sent him there. He also mentioned that al-Aswad testified in favor of Abū Qatāda’s right to the spoils of the man he killed on the Day of Ḥunayn.

Al-Aswad ibn Khaṭāma al-Kinānī. ## Source unit 156 · printed entry 156

Al-Aswad ibn Khalaf ibn Asʿad ibn ʿĀmir ibn Bayāḍa al-Khuzāʿī. Khalīfa mentioned him among the Companions. Ibn Ḥibbān said: he is said to have had Companionship, although there is some question concerning its chain. Ibn Saʿd erred in his entry: he included there the report of al-Aswad ibn Khalaf ibn ʿAbd Yaghūth, who appears next. Al-Dhahabī noticed the problem, but did not state his intended correction plainly. Instead, after placing this man’s entry immediately after that of Ibn ʿAbd Yaghūth, he said, ‘He is the preceding man, as I see it.’ End. ## Source unit 157 · printed entry 157

### English candidate

Al-Aswad ibn Khalaf ibn ʿAbd Yaghūth al-Qurashī. This is how al-Bukhārī gave his lineage in al-Aswad’s entry and in the entry of his son Muḥammad. Ibn al-Sakan said that he is said to have belonged to Banū Jumaḥ, and Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr preferred that view. Ibn al-Athīr objected that no one among Banū Jumaḥ was named ʿAbd Yaghūth. Ibn Manda said that al-Aswad was Zuhrī. Al-ʿAskarī said: Muṭayyan said that he was Qurashī, accepted Islam on the Day of the Conquest, and that ʿAbd Yaghūth was ibn Wahb ibn Zuhra. ʿAbd Yaghūth had a son called al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd Yaghūth, who was one of the mockers and died an unbeliever. Al-Aswad ibn Khalaf was named after his paternal uncle. والله أعلم. Imām Aḥmad said in his Musnad: ʿAbd al-Razzāq related to us; Ibn Jurayj informed us; Ibn Khuthaym informed me that Muḥammad ibn al-Aswad ibn Khalaf informed him that his father, al-Aswad, saw the Prophet ﷺ taking pledges from the people at Qarn Maṣqala. Al-Ḥākim transmitted it by way of Ibn Jurayj, wording it: ‘that his father related to him that he saw.’ Al-Baghawī and Ibn al-Sakan said: no one other than Ibn Jurayj transmitted it. Al-Baghawī transmitted, by way of ʿAbd al-Razzāq, from Maʿmar, from Ibn Khuthaym, with this chain, that the Prophet ﷺ took Ḥasan, kissed him, and said, ‘A child makes one miserly and cowardly.’ Al-Baghawī, Ibn al-Sakan, and al-Dāraquṭnī said that Maʿmar alone transmitted it. Al-Baghawī and Ibn al-Sakan said: al-Aswad has no reports other than these two. End. I have found a third for him. Al-Bazzār transmitted it from Bishr ibn Muʿādh, from Fuḍayl ibn Sulaymān, from Ibn Khuthaym, from Muḥammad ibn al-Aswad ibn Khalaf, from his father: the Prophet ﷺ ordered him to renew the boundary markers of the Sanctuary. Al-Ṭabarānī transmitted it from al-Bazzār. He has a fourth. Al-Bukhārī said in his History: Muʿallā related to us; Wuhayb related to us, from Ibn Khuthaym: Muḥammad ibn al-Aswad ibn Khalaf ibn ʿAbd Yaghūth related to me, from his father: They found a writing beneath the Station, so Quraysh summoned a man from Ḥimyar. He said, ‘It contains a line which, if I were to tell it to you, you would kill me.’ He said: We thought it contained mention of Muḥammad ﷺ, so we concealed it.

## Source unit 158 · printed entry 158

### English candidate

Al-Aswad ibn Rabīʿa ibn al-Aswad al-Yashkurī. Ibn Manda transmitted, by way of al-Ḥārith ibn ʿUbayd al-Iyādī, who said: ʿAbāya—or Ibn ʿAbāya—a man of Banū Thaʿlaba, related to me, from al-Aswad ibn Rabīʿa ibn al-Aswad al-Yashkurī: When the Prophet ﷺ conquered Mecca, he stood to deliver an address and said, ‘Behold: the blood claims of the pre-Islamic period and all other [pre-Islamic claims] are beneath my feet, except the provision of water and custody of the House.’ Its chain is unknown. Abū ʿUbayda, however, mentioned him in Kitāb al-Arḥāʾ wa-l-Maḥājim wa-Maʾāthir al-ʿArab. He said: Among the glories of Yashkur in the pre-Islamic period was that the Prophet ﷺ addressed the people on the Day of the Conquest and said, ‘Behold: every noble distinction that existed in the pre-Islamic period I have placed beneath my feet, except the provision of water and custody of the House.’ Al-Aswad ibn Rabīʿa ibn Abī al-Aswad ibn Mālik ibn Rabīʿa ibn Jamīl ibn Thaʿlaba ibn ʿAmr ibn ʿUthmān ibn Ḥabīb ibn Yashkur stood before him and said, ‘O Messenger of God, my father assigned some of his wealth as charity for the wayfarer during the pre-Islamic period. If that counts as a noble distinction for me, leave it in force; if it does not, then I have the greater right to it.’ He replied, ‘Rather, it is a noble distinction for you, so accept it.’ He said: It was this that al-Farazdaq meant when he said to Jarīr: ‘Come to the arbiters—Bakr ibn Wāʾil—
and do not be like the bewildered, wavering man.
[Come] to the noble Yashkurīs, noble are their deeds,
the descendants of the feeder of guests, among the house of Aswad.’

## Source unit 160 · printed entry 160

Al-Aswad ibn Zayd ibn Thaʿlaba ibn ʿUbayd ibn ʿAdī ibn Ghanm ibn Kaʿb ibn Salama ibn Saʿd ibn ʿAlī ibn Asad ibn Sārida, al-Anṣārī al-Khazrajī. ## Source unit 161 · printed entry 161

### English candidate

Al-Aswad ibn Sarīʿ ibn Ḥumayr ibn ʿUbāda ibn al-Nazzāl ibn Murra ibn ʿUbayd ibn Muqāʿis ibn ʿAmr ibn Kaʿb ibn Saʿd ibn Zayd Manāt ibn Tamīm, al-Tamīmī al-Saʿdī, the well-known poet. Al-Bukhārī transmitted in his History, from Muslim ibn Ibrāhīm, from al-Sarī ibn Yaḥyā, from al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, who said: al-Aswad ibn Sarīʿ related to us, saying, ‘I went on four expeditions with the Prophet ﷺ.’ Ibn Ḥibbān and Ibn al-Sakan transmitted it by way of al-Sarī. Al-Bukhārī transmitted another report of his in al-Adab al-Mufrad. Aḥmad said: ʿAlī ibn ʿAbd Allāh related to us; Muʿādh ibn Hishām related to us; my father related to me, from Qatāda, from al-Aḥnaf ibn Qays, from al-Aswad ibn Sarīʿ; and from Qatāda, from al-Ḥasan, from Abū Rāfiʿ, from Abū Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said, ‘Four will present a plea on the Day of Resurrection’—the report. Ibn Ḥibbān transmitted it in his Ṣaḥīḥ by way of Isḥāq ibn Ibrāhīm, from Muʿādh ibn Hishām. Al-Ḥākim transmitted, by way of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Bakr, from al-Aswad ibn Sarīʿ, that he said, ‘O Messenger of God, shall I not recite praises to you?’—the report. Al-Baghawī said: He was a poet. At the beginning of Islam he was also a storyteller. Al-Baghawī then transmitted, through al-Sarī ibn Yaḥyā, from al-Ḥasan, that he was the first person to deliver religious stories in the mosque of Basra. Khalīfa said: He had a house near the congregational mosque in Basra. He died during the reign of Muʿāwiya. Ibn Abī Khaythama reported, from Aḥmad and Ibn Maʿīn, that he died in the year forty-two. Al-Bukhārī said: ʿAlī said, ‘He disappeared during the Days of the Camel.’ Abū Ḥātim, Abū Dāwūd, Ibn al-Sakan, Ibn Ḥibbān, Ibn Zabr, and others decided categorically in favor of that view. Al-Bāwardī transmitted from al-Ḥasan: When ʿUthmān was killed, al-Aswad boarded a ship, took his household and dependents with him, and set out; he was never seen afterward.

## Source unit 162 · printed entry 162

Al-Aswad ibn Sufyān ibn ʿAbd al-Asad ibn Hilāl ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar ibn Makhzūm, al-Qurashī al-Makhzūmī. He was the son of the brother of Abū Salama ibn ʿAbd al-Asad, the husband of Umm Salama. ## Source unit 165 · printed entry 165

### English candidate

Al-Aswad ibn ʿAbs ibn Asmāʾ ibn Wahb ibn Riyāḥ ibn ʿAwidh ibn Munqidh ibn Kaʿb ibn Rabīʿat al-Jūʿ ibn Mālik ibn Ḥanẓala ibn Zayd Manāt ibn Tamīm. Hishām al-Kalbī mentioned that he came as a delegate to the Prophet ﷺ and said, “I have come so that, through your companionship, I may draw near to God.” He therefore named him al-Muqarrab, “the one brought near.”

Sayf ibn ʿUmar related from Warqāʾ ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Ḥanẓalī that al-Aswad ibn Rabīʿa, a descendant of Rabīʿa ibn Mālik ibn Ḥanẓala, came to the Messenger of God ﷺ. He asked, “What has brought you?” He replied, “That through your companionship I may draw near.” The name al-Aswad was set aside and he was called al-Muqarrab. He accompanied the Prophet ﷺ and was present with ʿAlī at Ṣiffīn.

Al-Ṭabarī related that ʿUmar appointed al-Aswad ibn Rabīʿa, one of Banū Rabīʿa ibn Mālik, over the Basran army. He was a Companion and an Emigrant, and it was he who said, “I have come so that I may draw near,” and was therefore named al-Muqarrab. One of the hadith masters said, “Perhaps someone traced him to his higher ancestor Rabīʿa.” والله أعلم.

## Source unit 172 · printed entry 172

### English candidate

Al-Aswad ibn Wahb ibn ʿAbd Manāf ibn Zuhra, al-Qurashī al-Zuhrī, maternal uncle of the Prophet ﷺ.

Ibn al-Aʿrābī transmitted in his Muʿjam, by way of ʿAnbasa ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Qurashī, from Muḥammad ibn Rustum al-Thaqafī, who said: “I heard ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr say that the Messenger of God ﷺ said to his maternal uncle al-Aswad ibn Wahb, ‘Shall I teach you words which, when God desires good for someone, He teaches him and then never lets him forget them?’ He said, ‘Yes, Messenger of God.’ He said, ‘O God, I am weak, so strengthen my weakness in pursuit of Your good pleasure; take me by the forelock toward goodness; and make Islam the utmost limit of my satisfaction’”—to the end of the hadith.

Ibn Manda also transmitted, by way of Muḥammad ibn al-ʿAbbās ibn Khalaf, from ʿAmr ibn Abī Salama, from Ṣadaqa al-Samīn, from Abū Muʿīd Ḥafṣ ibn Ghaylān, from Zayd ibn Aslam, who said: “Wahb ibn al-Aswad ibn Wahb, the maternal uncle of the Messenger of God ﷺ, related to me that the Messenger of God ﷺ said to him, ‘Shall I tell you something by which God may benefit you?’ He said, ‘Yes, Messenger of God.’ He said, ‘Ribā has many doors. One of its doors is equivalent to seventy sins; the least of them in wickedness is like a man lying with his mother. The gravest ribā is a man’s wrongful violation of his brother’s honor.’”

Ibn Qāniʿ transmitted it in his Muʿjam by way of Abū Bakr ibn al-Aʿyun, from ʿAmr ibn Abī Salama, but he said, “from Wahb ibn al-Aswad, the maternal uncle of the Messenger of God ﷺ,” and did not say, “from his father.” He inserted al-Ḥakam al-Aylī between Ṣadaqa and Zayd. Both al-Ḥakam and Ṣadaqa are weak.

It was also transmitted from al-Qāsim, from ʿĀʾisha, that al-Aswad ibn Wahb, maternal uncle of the Prophet ﷺ, asked permission to enter upon him. He said, “Maternal uncle, come in.” He entered, and the Prophet spread out his cloak for him—to the end of the hadith. Ibn Shāhīn transmitted it. In its chain is ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muḥammad ibn Rabīʿa al-Qudāmī, who is weak.

## Source unit 175 · printed entry 175

### English candidate

Asīd ibn Abī Anās ibn Zanīm ibn ʿAmr ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jābir ibn Maḥmiya ibn ʿAbd ibn ʿAdī ibn al-Duʾil ibn Bakr ibn ʿAbd Manāt ibn Kināna, al-Kinānī al-Duʾalī, the son of Sāriya’s brother. Al-ʿAskarī and al-Dāraquṭnī vocalized his name with fatḥa on its first letter; al-Marzubānī gave it with ḍamma, and Ibn Mākūlā rejected that.

Ibn Shāhīn transmitted, by way of al-Madāʾinī from his authorities through many routes reaching Ibn ʿAbbās and others, that they said: A delegation of Banū ʿAbd ibn ʿAdī came to the Messenger of God ﷺ. Among them were al-Ḥārith ibn Wahb, ʿUwaymir ibn al-Akhram, Ḥabīb and Rabīʿa, the two sons of Milla, and a group of their people. They related their story at length. In it they said, “We do not wish to fight you, but if you were to fight anyone other than Quraysh, we would fight alongside you.” They then embraced Islam and sought protection for their people, except for one of their men whose blood the Prophet ﷺ had declared licit, a man called Asīd ibn Abī Anās; they disavowed him.

When word of that reached Asīd, he went to al-Ṭāʾif and stayed there. In the Year of the Conquest, Sāriya ibn Zanīm went out to al-Ṭāʾif and said to him, “Nephew, go out to him, for he does not kill anyone who comes to him.” Asīd went out to him, embraced Islam, and placed his hand in his. The Prophet ﷺ granted him safe-conduct, and Asīd praised the Prophet ﷺ in verses. In this account, when Asīd set out to meet the Prophet ﷺ, his pregnant wife accompanied him and gave birth to a child for him at Qarn al-Thaʿālib.

Al-ʿAskarī mentioned that Asīd had composed an elegy for the people of Badr and that the Prophet ﷺ declared his blood licit for that reason. He said, “Ibn Durayd informed us of that, from Abū Ḥātim, from Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar ibn al-Muthannā.” A story analogous to his has been transmitted concerning Anas ibn Zanīm, as will appear in his biography. It is possible that it happened to both of them. والله أعلم.

The judge Abū Bakr ibn al-ʿArabī transmitted from Abū ʿĀmir al-ʿAbdarī that he said, “This Asīd embraced Islam and accompanied the Prophet ﷺ, and I think he lived to see Uḥud.” Ibn al-ʿArabī rejected this statement of his teacher on the basis of what preceded.

I then found, in a compilation on the merits of ʿAlī ﵁ by al-Mufīd ibn al-Nuʿmān al-Rāfiḍī, something like what al-ʿAbdarī mentioned. He related the story of Badr and then said at its end, concerning what ʿAlī ﵁ did on the day of Badr, that Asīd ibn Abī Anās addressed Quraysh with these words:

At every gathering, a champion has disgraced you—
a young colt surpassing mature, battle-seasoned steeds.
This is the son of Fāṭima, the one who annihilated you
by slaughter and killing; hatred of him brought no profit.
How astonishing of you! Will you not yet remember?
The noble free man may remember and feel shame.

Al-Zubayr, however, stated that Asīd recited these verses to Quraysh when they marched to Uḥud.

أسيد بن أبي أناس بن زنيم بن عمرو بن عبد الله بن بن جابر بن محمية بن عبد بن عدي بن الدئل بن بكر بن عبد مناة بن كنانة الكناني الدئلي بن أخي سارية ضبطه العسكري والدارقطني بفتح أوله المرزباني بضم أوله ورد ذلك بن ماكولا وروى بن شاهين من طريق المدائني عن رجاله من طرق كثيرة إلى بن عباس وغيره قالوا قدم على رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم وفد بني عبد بن عدي فيهم الحارث بن وهب وعويمر بن الأخرم وحبيب وربيعة ابنا ملة ومعهم رهط من قومهم فذكر قصتهم مطولة وفيها قالوا إنا لانريد قتالك ولو قاتلت غير قريش لقاتلنا معك ثم أسلموا واستأمنوا لقومهم سوى رجل منهم اهدر النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم دمه يقال له أسيد بن أبي أناس فتبرءوا منه فبلغ أسيدا ذلك فأتى الطائف فأقام به فلما كان عام الفتح خرج سارية بن زنيم إلى الطائف فقال له بابن أخي أخرج إليه فإنه لا يقتل من أتاه فخرج إليه فأسلم ووضع يده في يده فأمنه النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم ومدح النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم بأبيات وفي هذه القصة أن اسيدا لما أراد الاجتماع بالنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم خرج معه بامرأته وهي حامل فوضعت له ولدا في قرن الثعالب وذكر العسكري أنه كان رثى أهل بدر فأهدر النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم دمه بذلك قال أخبرنا بذلك بن دريد عن أبي حاتم عن أبي عبيدة معمر بن المثنى وقد رويت نظير قصته لأنس بن زنيم كما سيأتي في ترجمته ويحتمل وقوع ذلك لهما والله أعلم ونقل أبو بكر بن العربي القاضي عن أبي عامر العبدري أنه قال أسلم أسيد هذا وصحب النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم وأظنه أدرك أحدا ورد ذلك بن العربي على شيخه بما تقدم ثم وجدت في فضائل علي رضي الله عنه جمع المميد بن النعمان الرافضي نحو ما ذكر العبدي فإنه ذكر قصة بدر ثم قال في آخرها فيما صنعه رضي الله عنه يوم بدر يقول أسيد بن أبي أناس يخاطب قريشا بقوله <br />
 في كل مجمع غاية اخزاكم <br />
 جذع يفوق على المذاكي القرح <br />
 هذا بن فاطمة الذي أفناكم <br />
 ذبحا وقتلا بغضه لم يربح <br />
 لله دركم ألما تذكروا <br />
 قد يذكر الحر الكريم ويستحي والذي ذكره الزبير أن أسيدا أنشد قريشا هذه الأبيات لما ساروا إلى أحد

## Source unit 176 · printed entry 176

Asīd ibn Jāriya ibn Asīd ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salama ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ghīra ibn ʿAwf ibn Thaqīf, al-Thaqafī, an ally of Banū Zuhra. Al-ʿAskarī and others counted him among the Companions. ## Source unit 181 · printed entry 181

### English candidate

Usayd ibn Uḥayḥa ibn Umayya ibn Khalaf ibn Wahb ibn Ḥudhāfa ibn Jumaḥ, al-Qurashī al-Jumaḥī, son of the brother of Ṣafwān ibn Umayya. He was among those who accepted Islam at the Conquest. Al-Zubayr ibn Bakkār said: Uḥayḥa ibn Umayya ibn Khalaf fathered Usayd ibn Uḥayḥa; Usayd fathered ʿAlī. ʿAlī’s kunyā was Abū Rayḥāna. He was one of Muʿāwiya’s companions and was opposed to ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr. He and his cousin ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ṣafwān ibn Umayya exchanged words concerning Ibn al-Zubayr. He then traveled to Syria and returned with the armies of Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiya, after which he besieged Ibn al-Zubayr. He was the cousin of Abū Dahbal, Wahb ibn Zamʿa ibn Usayd ibn Uḥayḥa. Al-Fākihī related from al-Zubayr that he was also called ʿUlayl, in the diminutive; that he joined ʿAbd al-Malik and asked him to reinforce al-Ḥajjāj; and that ʿAbd al-Malik reinforced him with Ṭāriq at the head of four thousand men. Abū Rayḥāna looked down from Abū Qubays and cried, ‘Has God not disgraced you?’ Ibn Abī ʿAtīq, who was with Ibn al-Zubayr, replied, ‘Indeed, by God.’

## Source unit 185 · printed entry 185

### English candidate

Usayd ibn al-Ḥuḍayr ibn Simāk ibn ʿAtīk ibn Imriʾ al-Qays ibn Zayd ibn ʿAbd al-Ashhal, al-Anṣārī al-Ashhalī. His kunyās were Abū Yaḥyā and Abū ʿAtīk. His father, Ḥuḍayr, was the horseman of al-Aws and their leader on the Day of Buʿāth. Usayd was among the earliest converts to Islam and one of the naqībs on the night of al-ʿAqaba. He accepted Islam at the hands of Muṣʿab ibn ʿUmayr, before Saʿd ibn Muʿādh. Authorities disagreed over whether he witnessed Badr. Ibn Saʿd said: He was a complete and eminent noble. The Messenger of God ﷺ established brotherhood between him and Zayd ibn Ḥāritha. He was among those who stood firm on the Day of Uḥud, when he received seven wounds. Ibn al-Sakan said that he witnessed Badr and al-ʿAqaba and was one of the naqībs. Others rejected counting him among the people of Badr. He has reports in the two Ṣaḥīḥs and elsewhere. Al-Baghawī said: Ibn Zanbūr related to us; Ibn Abī Ḥāzim related to us, from Suhayl, from his father, from Abū Hurayra, that the Prophet ﷺ said, ‘What an excellent man Usayd ibn Ḥuḍayr is.’ Ibn Isḥāq said: Yaḥyā ibn ʿAbbād ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr related to us, from his father, from ʿĀʾisha, who said: There were three men of the Anṣār whom no one could match in merit, all of them from Banū ʿAbd al-Ashhal: Saʿd ibn Muʿādh, Usayd ibn Ḥuḍayr, and ʿAbbād ibn Bishr. Aḥmad transmitted in his Musnad, by way of Fāṭima bint al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī, from ʿĀʾisha, who said: Usayd ibn Ḥuḍayr was among the most excellent of people. He used to say, ‘If only I could always be as I am in three states: when I hear the Qurʾān or recite it; when I hear the sermon of the Messenger of God ﷺ; and when I attend a funeral.’ Al-Wāqidī transmitted, by way of ʿAbd Allāh al-Taymī, who said: Abū Bakr did not prefer anyone among the Anṣār over Usayd ibn Ḥuḍayr. Al-Bukhārī transmitted in his History, from Ibn ʿUmar: When Usayd ibn Ḥuḍayr died, ʿUmar said to his creditors—and he related an account showing that Usayd died during ʿUmar’s caliphate. Ibn al-Sakan transmitted, through Ibn ʿUyayna, from Hishām ibn ʿUrwa, from his father: When Usayd ibn Ḥuḍayr died, ʿUmar sold the yield of his property for three years and thereby paid his debt. He said, ‘I will not leave the sons of my brother destitute.’ He therefore returned the land and sold its produce. Al-Baghawī and others dated his death to the year twenty; al-Madāʾinī said the year twenty-one.

## Source unit 194 · printed entry 194

### English candidate

Usayr, without further lineage, ending in the letter rāʾ. Al-Bukhārī in his History, Ibn Saʿd, al-Baghawī, Ibn al-Sakan, and Ibn Shāhīn transmitted, by way of Abū ʿAwāna, from Dāwūd ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Awdī, from Ḥumayd ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, who said: We entered upon Usayr, a man among the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ. He said: The Prophet ﷺ said, ‘Only good comes to you from modesty.’ Al-Baghawī said: no other report of Usayr is known. Someone other than Abū ʿAwāna transmitted it from Dāwūd as ‘from a man among the Companions,’ without naming him. Al-Bukhārī also mentioned him as Yusayr, with yāʾ below the line, and added: When Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiya was appointed caliph, Yusayr said, ‘They say that Yazīd is not the best of Muḥammad’s community, and I say the same. Yet for God to unite Muḥammad’s community is dearer to me than for it to be divided.’ Muḥammad ibn Saʿd likewise mentioned him through Yaḥyā ibn Ḥammād, from Abū ʿAwāna; his version is fuller.

I said, ‘O Messenger of God, teach me some of what God has taught you.’ He replied, ‘Never disdain any act of kindness.’ This is not Usayr ibn Jābir the Successor, who will be mentioned later among the mukhaḍrams. ## Source unit 205 · printed entry 205

### English candidate

Al-Ashʿath ibn Qays ibn Maʿdīkarib ibn Muʿāwiya ibn Jabala ibn ʿAdī ibn Rabīʿa ibn Muʿāwiya al-Akramīn ibn Thawr al-Kindī. His kunya was Abū Muḥammad. Ibn Saʿd said that in the year ten he came in a delegation to the Prophet ﷺ with seventy riders from Kinda. He was one of the kings of Kinda and held the right to the mirbāʿ in Ḥaḍramawt, according to Ibn al-Kalbī. Al-Bukhārī and Muslim transmitted his report in their Ṣaḥīḥs. His name was Maʿdīkarib, and al-Ashʿath was only a sobriquet. Muḥammad ibn Yazīd related from his authorities that his name was Maʿdīkarib and that his hair was always disheveled, so he was called al-Ashʿath. Ismāʿīl ibn Abī Khālid related from Qays ibn Abī Ḥāzim, who said: “I attended a funeral at which al-Ashʿath and Jarīr were present. Al-Ashʿath put Jarīr forward and said, ‘He did not apostatize, whereas I did apostatize.’” Ibn al-Sakan and others transmitted it. Al-Ashʿath had apostatized with those Kindīs who apostatized. He was captured and brought before Abū Bakr; he then accepted Islam, so Abū Bakr released him and married him to his sister Umm Farwa, in a long account. Al-Wāqidī said: Hishām ibn Saʿd related to us, from Zayd ibn Aslam, from his father, who said: I heard al-Ashʿath ibn Qays say to Abū Bakr when he was brought to him during the apostasy, “Spare me for your wars and marry me to your sister.” He did so. Al-Ṭabarānī said: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Salm related to us; ʿAbd al-Muʾmin ibn ʿAlī related to us; ʿAbd al-Salām ibn Ḥarb related to us, from Ismāʿīl ibn Abī Khālid, from Qays ibn Abī Ḥāzim, who said: When al-Ashʿath was brought as a prisoner before Abū Bakr, he released him from his bonds and married him to his sister. Al-Ashʿath drew his sword, entered the camel market, and hamstrung every male or female camel he saw. The people shouted, “Al-Ashʿath has disbelieved!” When he had finished, he threw down his sword and said, “By God, I have not disbelieved. This man married me to his sister, and had we been in our own country the wedding feast would not have been like this. People of Medina, eat! Owners of the camels, come and take their equivalents.” Al-Ashʿath then took part in al-Yarmūk in Syria, al-Qādisiyya and other battles in Iraq. He settled in Kufa and was present with ʿAlī at Ṣiffīn; accounts concerning him and ʿAlī are known. Khalīfa, Abū Nuʿaym, and more than one other authority said that he died forty nights after ʿAlī was killed and that al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī performed the funeral prayer over him. It is also said that he died in the year forty-two. Al-Ṭabarānī has a report, by way of Abū Isrāʾīl al-Malāʾī, from Abū Isḥāq, which might indicate that he lived beyond that time, since Abū Isḥāq was young during ʿAlī’s lifetime. In this account al-Ashʿath was owed a debt by a man of Kinda; Abū Isḥāq entered their mosque and performed the dawn prayer, and a purse, a robe, and a sandal were placed before him. When he asked about them, they said, “Al-Ashʿath arrived from Mecca last night.” Another route in the same work states that al-Ashʿath sought permission to enter upon Muʿāwiya in Kufa while al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī and Ibn ʿAbbās were with him, and then relates his story; but this does not overturn what preceded. Abū Ḥassān al-Ziyādī said that he died at the age of sixty-three.
