<div dir="rtl" lang="ar">

الأشعث بن قيس بن معديكرب بن معاوية بن جبلة بن عدي بن ربيعة بن معاوية الاكرمين بن ثور الكندي يكنى أبا محمد قال بن سعد وفد على النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم سنة عشر في سبعين راكبا من كندة وكان من ملوك كندة وهو صاحب مرباع حضر موت قاله بن الكلبي وأخرج البخاري ومسلم حديثه في الصحيح وكان اسمه معد يكرب وإنما لقب بالأشعث قال محمد بن يزيد عن رجاله كان اسمه معد يكرب وكان أبدا أشعث الرأس فسمي الأشعث وقال إسماعيل بن أبي خالد عن قيس بن أبي حازم شهدت جنازة فيها الأشعث وجرير فقدم الأشعث جريرا وقال أنه لم يرتد وقد كنت ارتددت ورواه بن السكن وغيره وكان الأشعث قد ارتد فيمن ارتد من الكنديين وأسر فأحضر إلى أبي بكر فأسلم فاطلقه وزوجه أخته أم فروة في قصة طويلة قال الواقدي حدثنا هشام بن سعد عن زيد بن أسلم عن أبيه قال سمعت الأشعث بن قيس يقول لأبي بكر حين أتى به في الردة استبقني لحربك وزوجني أختك ففعل وقال الطبراني حدثنا عبد الرحمن بن سلم حدثنا عبد المؤمن بن علي قال حدثنا عبد السلام بن حرب عن إسماعيل بن أبي خالد عن قيس بن أبي حازم قال لما قدم بالأشعث أسيرا على أبي بكر أطلق وثاقه وزوجه أخته فاخترط سيفه ودخل سوق الإبل فجعل لا يرى جملا أو ناقة الا عرقبه فصاح الناس كفر الأشعث فلما فرغ طرح سيفه وقال إني والله ما كفرت ولكن زوجني هذا الرجل أخته ولو كنا في بلادنا كانت وليمة غير هذه يأهل المدينة كلوا ويا أصحاب الإبل تعالوا خذوا شرواها ثم شهد الأشعث اليرموك بالشام والقادسية وغيرها بالعراق وسكن الكوفة وشهد مع علي صفين وله معه أخبار قال خليفة وأبو نعيم وغير واحد مات بعد قتل علي بأربعين ليلة وصلى عليه الحسن بن علي وقيل مات سنة اثنتين وأربعين وفي الطبراني من طريق أبي إسرائيل الملائي عن أبي إسحاق ما يدل على أنه تأخر عن ذلك فإن أبا إسحاق كان صغيرا على عهد علي وقد ذكر في هذه القصة أنه كان له على رجل من كندة دين وأنه دخل مسجدهم فصلى الفجر فوضع بين يديه كيس وحلة ونعل فسأل عن ذلك فقالوا قدم الأشعث الليلة من مكة وفيه أيضا من وجه آخر استأذن الأشعث على معاوية بالكوفة وعنده الحسن بن علي وابن عباس فذكر قصته لكن هذا لا يدفع ما تقدم وقال أبو حسان الزيادي مات وله ثلاث وستون سنة

## Source unit 206 · printed entry 206

### English candidate

Al-Ashʿath al-Anṣārī, without a lineage. He is mentioned in a disconnected report. Ibn Abī Shayba said in his Muṣannaf: Wakīʿ related to us, from ʿĀṣim, from al-Shaʿbī, who said: There were two Anṣārī brothers, one of whom was called Ashʿath. He went out on campaign in one of the Muslim armies. His wife said to his brother, “Would you care to see a man with your brother’s wife, talking to her?” The brother climbed up and looked down upon him. The man was on her bed while she was plucking a chicken, and he was saying: “Ashʿath, whom Islam has sent campaigning away from me—
I have been alone with his wife through the full-moon night”—and the remaining verses. The brother leapt at the man, struck him with his sword until he killed him, and then cast him down. When this reached ʿUmar, he said, “I adjure by God any man who has knowledge of this to stand and disclose it,” and the account continues. I have included al-Ashʿath even though the account does not explicitly state that he had Companionship, because at the Prophet’s ﷺ death there was no non-Muslim among the Anṣār, and it is inconceivable that a man could go on campaign in ʿUmar’s time without having reached the age of discernment during the Prophet’s ﷺ lifetime, even if he had not yet reached manhood. This account has another route, transmitted by Ibn Manda by way of Abū Bakr al-Hudhalī, from ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Yaʿlā al-Laythī: Bakr ibn Shaddākh al-Laythī killed a Jewish man during ʿUmar’s reign. ʿUmar went out, mounted the pulpit, and said, “I adjure by God any man who has knowledge of this to inform me.” Bakr ibn Shaddākh stood before him and said, “I know about it.” ʿUmar said, “God is greatest.” Bakr said: “So-and-so went out on campaign and entrusted me with his household. I came to his door and found this Jewish man saying, ‘Ashʿath, whom Islam has sent campaigning away from me’”—and the verses. ʿUmar accepted his account as true and declared the dead man’s blood without claim.

<div dir="rtl" lang="ar">

## Source unit 212 · printed entry 212

### English candidate

Al-Aṣamm al-ʿĀmirī, then al-Bakkāʾī. Ibn Shāhīn mentioned, by way of ʿAlī ibn Muḥammad al-Madāʾinī, from Abū Maʿshar, from Yazīd ibn Rūmān; and from Khallād ibn ʿUbayda, from ʿAlī ibn Zayd, from al-Ḥasan; and from Asad ibn al-Qāsim, from al-Suddī, from Abū Mālik; and from authorities of al-Madāʾinī, that they said: A delegation from Banū al-Bakkāʾ came consisting of Muʿāwiya ibn Thawr ibn ʿUbāda, his son Bishr ibn Muʿāwiya, al-Fujayʿ ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jandaʿ ibn al-Bakkāʾ, al-Aṣamm, and some other men of Banū al-Bakkāʾ. Their chief, Muʿāwiya ibn Thawr, was one hundred years old. They accepted Islam and remained for some days as guests of the Messenger of God ﷺ. When the time for their departure came, they bade farewell to the Messenger of God ﷺ. Muʿāwiya said to him, “I seek blessing through your touch. I have grown old, and this son of mine, Bishr, is dutiful to me, so stroke his face.” He stroked his face, gave him some dust-colored she-goats, and prayed for blessing for him. Thereafter a year of drought would strike Banū al-Bakkāʾ but would not strike the family of Muʿāwiya. He wrote a document for al-Fujayʿ, and they departed. Aṣyad—on the pattern of Aḥmad—ibn Salama al-Sulamī. Abū Mūsā transmitted by way of Saʿīd ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Walīd al-Waṣṣāfī, from his father, who was one of the weak transmitters, from Abū Jaʿfar Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn, from his father, from his grandfather ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ dispatched a raiding party. They took captive a man of Banū Sulaym called Aṣyad ibn Salama. When the Messenger of God ﷺ saw him, he felt compassion for him and presented Islam to him, and he accepted Islam. Aṣyad had a very elderly father. When the news reached him, he wrote to his son: “Who will ride safely toward Medina
to convey what I say to Aṣyad?
Have you abandoned the religion of your father and of the lofty nobles who have passed away,
and followed Muḥammad this very morning?”—in a number of verses. Aṣyad sought the Prophet’s ﷺ permission to answer him, and he gave permission. He wrote: “He who raised the sky by His power,
exalted and alone in His dominion,
sent the one whose like has never passed before,
the Prophet Muḥammad, calling to His mercy”—in a number of verses. When his father read his son’s letter, he came to the Prophet ﷺ and accepted Islam.

## Source unit 214 · printed entry 214

### English candidate

Aṣyad ibn Salama ibn Qurayẓ ibn ʿUbayd ibn Abī Bakr ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Kilāb al-Kilābī. Al-Wāqidī and al-Ṭabarī said that he accepted Islam and that the Prophet ﷺ sent him in an army with al-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Sufyān al-Kilābī against his own people. When the two sides drew up in battle lines, Aṣyad called his father to Islam, but he refused. Aṣyad charged him and hamstrung his horse. Salama fell and leaned upon his spear, and Aṣyad refrained from attacking him out of filial respect. The Muslims caught up with Salama and killed him. Ibn Shāhīn transmitted it from Muḥammad ibn Ibrāhīm, from Muḥammad ibn Yazīd, from his authorities; but Ibn Shāhīn conflated him with the preceding man, whereas the correct course is to distinguish them.

## Source unit 215 · printed entry 215

### English candidate

Uṣayl—in the diminutive, with a final lām—ibn Sufyān; it is also said ibn ʿAbd Allāh, al-Hudhalī; it is also said al-Ghifārī or al-Khuzāʿī. It includes that the Messenger of God ﷺ said, “Enough, Uṣayl; do not make us grieve.” Abū Mūsā transmitted it in al-Dhayl by another route, through Aḥmad ibn Bakkār ibn Abī Maymūna, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Saʿīd, from Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Qurashī, from Badīḥ—also said Ibn Sidra—al-Sulamī, who said: Uṣayl al-Hudhalī arrived, and he related a similar account in abridged form. It includes that the Prophet ﷺ said to him, “Easy, Uṣayl; let hearts come to rest.” Al-Jāḥiẓ mentioned him in his Kitāb al-Bayān, saying that the Prophet ﷺ asked Uṣayl al-Khuzāʿī, “Uṣayl, how did you leave Mecca?” and he related something similar. In the work of al-Yashkurī the genealogist, when he mentioned Khafāja ibn Ghifār, he said: They are the clan of Uṣayl ibn Sufyān, whom the Prophet ﷺ asked about Mecca.

## Source unit 221 · printed entry 221

### English candidate

Al-Aʿwar ibn Bashāma ibn Naḍla ibn Sinān ibn Jundab ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Jahma ibn ʿAdī ibn Jundab ibn al-ʿAnbar ibn ʿAmr ibn Tamīm. Ibn al-Kalbī said that his name was Nāshib and al-Aʿwar was a sobriquet.

Ibn ʿAbdān said in al-Ṣaḥāba: “Muḥammad ibn Muḥammad ibn Marzūq related to us; Sālim ibn ʿAdī ibn Saʿīd al-ʿAnbarī related to us, from Bakr ibn Mirdās, from al-Aʿwar ibn Bashāma, Wardān ibn Makhram, and a son of Rabīʿa ibn Rafīʿ, all of al-ʿAnbar. They came to the Prophet ﷺ while he was asleep in his chamber, just as ʿUyayna ibn Ḥiṣn arrived with captives from Banū al-ʿAnbar. We said, ‘What has happened to us, Messenger of God? We have been taken captive although we came as Muslims.’ He said, ‘Swear that you came as Muslims.’ Thus I, Wardān, and Khalaf ibn Rabīʿa ...”—to the end of the hadith. Its chain contains persons who are not known.

Ibn Shāhīn said: “Aḥmad ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Naṣr al-Qāḍī related to us; al-ʿAbbās ibn Ṣāliḥ ibn Musāwir related to us; Muḥammad ibn Sulaymān related to us; ʿAlī ibn Ghurāb al-Fazārī related to us; Abū Bakr al-Makkī related to me, from ʿUmayr ibn Muḥammad, from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: Banū al-ʿAnbar incurred blood liabilities among their people, so they departed and settled among their maternal uncles of Khuzāʿa. The Messenger of God ﷺ sent an alms collector to Khuzāʿa, and he collected their alms and then those of Banū al-ʿAnbar. When Banū al-ʿAnbar saw that he had secured the alms, they sprang upon them and wrested them away.

“The collector came to the Messenger of God ﷺ and said, ‘Messenger of God, Banū al-ʿAnbar have withheld the alms.’ He sent ʿUyayna ibn Ḥiṣn against them with one hundred and seventy men. He found the main body of the people absent and drove away nine men, eleven women, and some children. When news of this reached Banū al-ʿAnbar, seventy of their men rode to the Messenger of God ﷺ, among them al-Aqraʿ ibn Ḥābis and al-Aʿwar ibn Bashāma al-ʿAnbarī, who was the youngest of them.

“When they reached Medina, the women and children eagerly greeted them. The men rushed upon the chambers of the Prophet ﷺ while he was taking his midday rest and cried out to him, ‘Muḥammad, why are our women being taken captive when we have not withdrawn a hand from obedience to you?’ He came out to them and said, ‘Appoint an arbiter between me and you.’ They said, ‘Messenger of God, al-Aʿwar ibn Bashāma.’ He said, ‘Rather, your chief, Ibn ʿAmr.’ They said, ‘Messenger of God, al-Aʿwar ibn Bashāma.’ The Messenger of God ﷺ appointed him arbiter, and he ruled that half should be ransomed and half set free.”

## Source unit 222 · printed entry 222

Aʿyan ibn Ḍubayʿa ibn Nājiya ibn ʿIqāl ibn Muḥammad ibn Sufyān ibn Mujāshiʿ ibn Dārim, al-Tamīmī al-Ḥanẓalī al-Dārimī. He was the son of the brother of Ṣaʿṣaʿa ibn Nājiya, the grandfather of al-Farazdaq. The author of al-Istīʿāb mentioned him but cited nothing indicating that he had Companionship.

## Source unit 223 · printed entry 223

### English candidate

Al-Agharr ibn Yasār al-Muzanī, also said to be al-Juhanī, one of the Emigrants. Muslim, Aḥmad, Abū Dāwūd, and al-Nasāʾī transmitted for him, by way of Abū Burda ibn Abī Mūsā, from al-Agharr al-Muzanī, that he heard the Prophet ﷺ say, “People, repent to God, for I repent one hundred times by day and night.” In Muslim’s and Aḥmad’s versions: “from al-Agharr al-Muzanī, who had Companionship.” In a version of al-Baghawī, from Ḥumayd ibn Hilāl, from Abū Burda, he said: “I entered upon a man of the Emigrants whose humility impressed me.”

Abū Nuʿaym said: “It was transmitted from Nāfiʿ, from Ibn ʿUmar, from al-Agharr—a man of Muzayna who had Companionship with the Messenger of God ﷺ—that he was owed several wasqs of dates by a man of Banū ʿAmr ibn ʿAwf.” He then related the hadith concerning salam. Al-Baghawī transmitted it under the biography of al-Agharr al-Muzanī, and we heard it in al-Bukhārī’s al-Adab al-Mufrad. It says that al-Agharr was owed several wasqs by a man of Banū ʿAmr ibn ʿAwf. He said, “I came to the Prophet ﷺ, and he sent Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq with me.” He then related the account of salam.

Abū Nuʿaym then mentioned the hadith of Muʿāwiya ibn Qurra from al-Agharr al-Muzanī concerning witr, by way of Khālid ibn Abī Karīma from Muʿāwiya. Its wording is: “A man came to the Prophet ﷺ and said, ‘Messenger of God, I reached morning without having performed witr.’ He said, ‘Witr is only at night.’” Abū Nuʿaym said, “Some people”—meaning Ibn Manda—“treated the transmitter of the witr hadith as different from the preceding man, but he is one and the same.” Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr likewise stated decisively that al-Agharr al-Muzanī and al-Agharr al-Juhanī were one man.

Abū ʿAlī ibn al-Sakan said: “Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan related to us, from al-Bukhārī, who said: Misʿar used to call him al-Agharr al-Juhanī in his transmission, but al-Muzanī is more sound.” Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said, “It is said that Sulaymān ibn Yasār transmitted from al-Agharr al-Muzanī, but that is not sound.” Ibn al-Athīr inclined toward separating the Muzanī from the Juhanī, but that is baseless, because the route of the hadith is one. Al-Bukhārī clarified the defect in it: Misʿar alone called him al-Juhanī, thereby removing the difficulty.

الأغر بن يسار المزني ويقال الجهني من المهاجرين روى له مسلم وأحمد وأبو داود والنسائي من طريق أبي بردة بن أبي موسى عن الأغر المزني أنه سمع النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم يقول يا أيها الناس توبوا إلى الله فإني أتوب في اليوم والليلة مائة مرة وفي رواية مسلم وأحمد عن الأغر المزني وكانت له صحبة وفي رواية للبغوي عن حميد بن هلال عن أبي بردة قال دخلت على رجل من المهاجرين يعجبني تواضعه قال أبو نعيم وروى عن نافع عن بن عمر عن الأغر وهو رجل من مزينة كانت له صحبة مع رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم وأنه كانت له أوسق من تمر على رجل من بني عمرو بن عوف فذكر الحديث في السلم وقد أخرجه البغوي في ترجمة الأغر المزني وسمعناه في الأدب المفرد للبخاري وفيه أن الأغر كانت له أوسق على رجل من بني عمرو بن عوف قال فجئت النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم فأرسل معي أبا بكر الصديق فذكر قصة السلم ثم ذكر أبو نعيم حديث معاوية بن قرة عن الأغر المزني في الوتر من طريق خالد بن أبي كريمة عن معاوية ولفظه إن رجلا أتى النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم فقال يا رسول الله إني أصبحت ولم أوتر قال إنما الوتر بالليل وقال أبو نعيم غاير بعض الناس يعني بن منده بين صاحب حديث الوتر وبين الذي قبله وهو واحد وكذا جزم بن عبد البر بان الأغر المزني والجهني واحد وقال أبو علي بن السكن حدثنا محمد بن الحسن عن البخاري قال كان مسعر يقول في روايته عن الأغر الجهني والمزني أصح وقال بن عبد البر يقال إن سليمان بن يسار روى عن الأغر المزني ولا يصح ومال بن الأثير إلى التفرقة بين المزني والجهني وليس بشيء لأن مخرج الحديث واحد وقد أوضح البخاري العلة فيه وأن معشرا تفرد بقوله الجهني فأزال الاشكال

## Source unit 225 · printed entry 225

### English candidate

Al-Aghlab ibn Juthm ibn ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayda ibn Ḥāritha ibn Dulaf ibn Jusham ibn Qays ibn Saʿd ibn ʿIjl, al-ʿIjlī, the famous rajaz poet. Ibn Qutayba said that he lived to see Islam, embraced it, and migrated. He was then among those who went to Iraq with Saʿd. He settled in Kufa and was martyred at the Battle of Nahāwand. Ibn al-Athīr added him as an omission.

I say: the statement that he migrated does not prove that he migrated to the Prophet ﷺ. It may mean that he migrated to Medina after the Prophet’s death ﷺ. For that reason, no one included him among the Companions. Al-Marzubānī said in his Muʿjam that he was a mukhaḍram.

Abū al-Faraj al-Iṣbahānī transmitted, with his chain to al-Shaʿbī, who said: ʿUmar wrote to al-Mughīra ibn Shuʿba, who was governor of Kufa, instructing him to ask the poets in his jurisdiction to recite what they had composed in Islam. Labīd went and wrote Sūrat al-Baqara on a sheet. He said, “God has given me this in Islam in place of poetry.” Al-Aghlab came to al-Mughīra and said to him:

Do you want rajaz or a qaṣīda?
You have sought something easy and readily found.

Al-Mughīra wrote of that to ʿUmar, who wrote back: “Deduct five hundred from al-Aghlab’s stipend and add it to Labīd’s stipend.”

Ibn Durayd transmitted a similar account in al-Akhbār al-Manthūra from al-Riyāshī, from Abū Maʿmar, from ʿAbd al-Wārith, from Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ. Al-Marzubānī also cited these verses by al-Aghlab:

The ordeals—and then they clear away;
then they depart and never come to us.

And his saying:

Man ever yearns for what he has not attained;
death follows him, while hope distracts him.

Abū al-Faraj cited a rajaz poem in which al-Aghlab satirized Sajāḥ, who claimed prophethood and married Musaylima the Liar.

## Source unit 227 · printed entry 227

### English candidate

Aflah, brother of Abū al-Quʿays and ʿĀʾisha’s uncle through suckling. Ibn Manda said that he is counted among Banū Sulaym, while Abū ʿUmar said that he is said to have been one of the Ashʿarīs. We transmitted, in the report of Zayd ibn Abī Unaysa as extracted by al-Ismāʿīlī, through ʿIrāk, from ʿUrwa, from ʿĀʾisha, that she said: ‘Aflah ibn Qays al-Makhzūmī entered upon me, so I veiled myself from him’; and she related the report. Its basis is in Muslim. His mention is established in the two Ṣaḥīḥs and elsewhere by way of Mālik, from al-Zuhrī, from ʿUrwa, from ʿĀʾisha: Aflah, brother of Abū al-Quʿays, came to seek permission to enter upon her. He was her uncle through suckling, and this was after the command of veiling had been revealed. This is how it appears in most narrations. In one of Muslim’s narrations it occurs as ‘Aflah ibn Abī al-Quʿays’; the same appears through another route in al-Baghawī. In another narration of Muslim it is ‘Aflah ibn Qays,’ which is more plausible. Muslim also has, by way of ʿAṭāʾ, from ʿUrwa, from ʿĀʾisha: ‘My uncle Abū al-Jaʿd sought permission to enter upon me’; it is as though this was Aflah’s kunyā. One of Muslim’s narrations says: ‘Abū al-Quʿays sought permission to enter upon her.’ This is an error by one of its transmitters—Abū Muʿāwiya, who transmitted it from Hishām—for Ḥammād ibn Zayd contradicted him in transmitting it from Hishām. Ḥammād had a better memory than Abū Muʿāwiya for Hishām’s reports, and he said: ‘the brother of Abū al-Quʿays.’ Al-Ṭabarānī transmitted it in al-Awsaṭ through another route agreeing with Abū Muʿāwiya’s narration. He said: Ibrāhīm—that is, Ibn Hāshim—related to us; Hudba related to us; Muḥammad ibn Bakr related to us; ʿAbbād ibn Manṣūr related to us, from al-Qāsim ibn Muḥammad, who said: Abū al-Quʿays related to us that he came to ʿĀʾisha to seek permission to enter upon her. Although this narration contains an error in the naming, it establishes that the man concerned in the incident lived until al-Qāsim heard from him. والله أعلم. Al-Baghawī transmitted, by way of Khalaf al-Azdī, from al-Ḥakam, from ʿIrāk ibn Mālik, from Aflah ibn Abī al-Quʿays, that he came to ʿĀʾisha and she veiled herself from him. He said, ‘I am your uncle,’ and related the report. Al-Baghawī said: ‘He thus gave it a chain from Aflah.’ Shuʿba transmitted it from al-Ḥakam, however, saying: from ʿIrāk, from ʿUrwa, from ʿĀʾisha.

## Source unit 229 · printed entry 229

### English candidate

Aflah, a client of the Messenger of God ﷺ. He is mentioned among the Prophet’s clients; Abū ʿUmar said this. Ibn Manda said: His report was transmitted by Yūsuf ibn Khālid, from Salm ibn Bashīr, who heard Ḥabīb al-Makkī say that he heard Aflah, client of the Messenger of God ﷺ, say that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: ‘After me, I fear for my community the deviation of capricious doctrines and the pursuit of desires.’ Aflah said: ‘I have forgotten the third.’ End quote. Al-Ḥakīm al-Tirmidhī transmitted it by this route and named the third as self-admiration. Ibn Shāhīn transmitted it and named the third as heedlessness after knowledge. ## Source unit 231 · printed entry 231

### English candidate

Al-Aqraʿ ibn Ḥābis ibn ʿIqāl ibn Muḥammad ibn Sufyān, al-Tamīmī al-Mujāshiʿī al-Dārimī. The relevant discussion of his lineage appeared in the entry on Aʿyan. Ibn Isḥāq said: He came to the Prophet ﷺ as a member of a delegation and witnessed the Conquest of Mecca, Ḥunayn, and al-Ṭāʾif. He was one of those whose hearts were won over, and his Islam thereafter became sound. Al-Zubayr said in his Genealogy: Al-Aqraʿ was an arbiter in the pre-Islamic period. Jarīr—or, it is said, someone else—said concerning him, when he and al-Farāfiṣa, or Khālid ibn Arṭāh, submitted their competing claims to him: ‘O Aqraʿ ibn Ḥābis, O Aqraʿ!
If today you throw down your brother, you yourself will be thrown down.’ Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī ʿĀṣim, and al-Baghawī transmitted by way of Wuhayb, from Mūsā ibn ʿUqba, from Abū Salama ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, from al-Aqraʿ ibn Ḥābis, that he called to the Prophet ﷺ from behind the apartments, ‘O Muḥammad!’ He did not answer him. He called, ‘O Muḥammad! By God, my praise is an adornment and my censure a disgrace.’ The Messenger of God ﷺ replied, ‘That is God.’ Ibn Manda said: It was also transmitted from Abū Salama, in mursal form, that al-Aqraʿ ibn Ḥābis called out; and he related it. This is the sounder form. Al-Ruyānī likewise transmitted it by way of ʿUmar ibn Abī Salama, from his father, who said in mursal form: ‘Al-Aqraʿ called out’; and he related it. Aḥmad transmitted it in both forms. Ibn Jarīr’s version expressly states that Abū Salama heard from al-Aqraʿ, and this indicates that al-Aqraʿ lived to a later date. In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, by way of al-Zuhrī, from Abū Salama, from Abū Hurayra, it is related that al-Aqraʿ ibn Ḥābis saw the Messenger of God ﷺ kissing al-Ḥasan; and the report follows. The two works also contain, in the report of Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, that ʿAlī sent the Prophet ﷺ a small piece of gold from Yemen, and he divided it among four men, one of whom was al-Aqraʿ ibn Ḥābis. In al-Bukhārī, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr, it is related that a mounted delegation from Banū Tamīm came to the Messenger of God ﷺ, and Abū Bakr said, ‘Messenger of God, appoint al-Aqraʿ’; and the report follows. Ibn Shāhīn transmitted by way of al-Madāʾinī, from his authorities, that when ʿUyayna ibn Ḥiṣn took captives from Banū al-ʿAnbar, their delegation arrived; and he related the account. It says that al-Aqraʿ ibn Ḥābis spoke to the Messenger of God ﷺ about the captives. He had been in Medina before the captives arrived, and ʿUyayna ibn Ḥiṣn disputed the matter with him. Concerning this, al-Farazdaq said, boasting of his uncle al-Aqraʿ: ‘Before the Messenger of God stood Ibn Ḥābis,
with the resolve of an aswār—a cavalier—firmly bent on glory.
On his account the captives were released—the ones whose necks,
fettered in their bonds, were chained in iron bits.’ Al-Bukhārī in his Short History and Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān transmitted with a sound chain, by way of Muḥammad ibn Sīrīn, from ʿAbīda ibn ʿAmr al-Salmānī, that ʿUyayna and al-Aqraʿ asked Abū Bakr for grants of land. ʿUmar said to them, ‘The Prophet ﷺ used to win you over to Islam. Now, however, exert yourselves to the utmost,’ and he tore up the document. ʿAlī ibn al-Madīnī said in al-ʿIlal: ‘This is disconnected, because ʿAbīda did not live early enough to encounter the incident, nor is it transmitted from ʿUmar that ʿAbīda heard it from him.’ He said: ‘Nothing is transmitted from ʿUmar with an isnād better than this one.’ Sayf ibn ʿUmar transmitted it at length in al-Futūḥ and added that they witnessed al-Yamāma and other campaigns with Khālid ibn al-Walīd. Al-Aqraʿ then went on and witnessed Dūmat al-Jandal with Shuraḥbīl ibn Ḥasana, and he witnessed Khālid’s war against the people of Iraq, including al-Anbār. Ibn Durayd said: Al-Aqraʿ ibn Ḥābis’s personal name was Firās. He was called al-Aqraʿ because of baldness on his head. He was a nobleman in both the pre-Islamic period and Islam. ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĀmir appointed him over an army that he dispatched to Khurasan; al-Aqraʿ and the army were killed at al-Jūzjān. This was during the time of ʿUthmān. Ibn al-Kalbī mentioned that he had been a Magian before accepting Islam. I read in the handwriting of al-Raḍī al-Shāṭibī: ‘Al-Aqraʿ ibn Ḥābis was killed at al-Yarmūk together with ten of his sons.’ والله أعلم.

## Source unit 232 · printed entry 232

### English candidate

Al-Aqraʿ ibn Shafī al-ʿAkkī. The Prophet ﷺ visited him during his illness. No one other than Lifāf ibn Kurz transmitted from him. This is how Abū ʿUmar included him. Al-Rushāṭī said: ‘It appears in his work as Lifāf ibn Kurz, with rāʾ and zāy, but the correct form is Ibn Kadan, with an open dāl followed by nūn.’ The report to which he alluded was transmitted by Ibn al-Sakan and Ibn Manda by way of Muḥammad ibn Fihr ibn Jamīl ibn Abī Karīm ibn Lifāf, from Umayya and Lifāf ibn al-Faḍl ibn Abī Karīm, from al-Mufaḍḍal ibn Abī Karīm, from his father, from his grandfather Lifāf ibn Kadan, from al-Aqraʿ ibn Shafī al-ʿAkkī. He said: The Prophet ﷺ entered upon me during my illness. I said, ‘I think that I will surely die during this illness.’ He replied, ‘No. You will certainly remain alive, migrate to the land of Syria, and die and be buried at al-Rabwa in the land of Palestine.’ Ibn al-Sakan said: ‘We know none of the men in this isnād.’ Ibn Manda said: Ismāʿīl ibn Rashīd also transmitted it from Ḍamra ibn Rabīʿa, from Qādim ibn Maysūr, from a man of ʿAkk, from al-Aqraʿ al-ʿAkkī, with similar wording. Ḍamra said: ‘This al-Aqraʿ died during ʿUmar’s caliphate.’ I say: This is a second route and refutes Abū ʿUmar’s categorical statement. Hishām ibn ʿAmmār transmitted in his Fawāʾid, from al-Mughīra ibn al-Mughīra, from Yaḥyā ibn Abī ʿAmr al-Shaybānī, who said: ‘A man of ʿAkk called al-Aqraʿ fell ill’; and he related something similar. At its end he said that al-Aqraʿ was buried at al-Ramla. Ibn ʿAsākir transmitted it in the introduction to his History by this route. This is therefore a third route.

## Source unit 234 · printed entry 234

### English candidate

Al-Aqraʿ al-Ghifārī. Ibn Manda said: Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Abī Saʿd informed us; ʿAlī ibn Saʿīd related to us; ʿAlī ibn Muslim related to us; Abū Dāwūd related to us; Shuʿba related to us, from ʿĀṣim, from Abū Ḥājib, from al-Aqraʿ al-Ghifārī, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he forbade a man to perform ablution with water left over from a woman’s ablution. Ibn Manda said: ‘I know of no one other than this man who named him.’ We transmitted it by a route from Abū Dāwūd in which he said, ‘from a man among the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ,’ without naming him. I say: This report is well known by way of Shuʿba, from ʿĀṣim, from Abū Ḥājib, from al-Ḥakam ibn ʿAmr al-Ghifārī. That is how the leading transmitters among Shuʿba’s associates related it from him. Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān transmitted it from Ibn Bashshār, from Abū Dāwūd, with his chain, saying: ‘from al-Ḥakam ibn ʿAmr, who is al-Aqraʿ.’ It is therefore clear that al-Aqraʿ is al-Ḥakam ibn ʿAmr. This also refutes Ibn Manda’s claim that ʿAlī ibn Muslim alone named him, for another transmitter from Shuʿba named him as well. Ibn Shāhīn said: Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿIṣma related to us; Aḥmad ibn ʿUmar ibn Bisṭām in Merv related to us; Khalaf ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz related to us; my father informed me, from my grandfather, from Shuʿba, from ʿĀṣim, from Abū Ḥājib, who said: ‘Al-Aqraʿ al-Ghifārī related to us’; and he related the report. Ibn Shāhīn said: ‘I reckon it to be an error by one of the transmitters.’ Thus he said.

## Source unit 236 · printed entry 236

### English candidate

Al-Aqʿas ibn Salama. He is counted among the people of al-Yamāma and possessed companionship, Ibn Ḥibbān said. It is also said that his name was al-Uqayṣir ibn Salama al-Ḥanafī. Al-Baghawī said: Aḥmad ibn Isḥāq related to us; Sulaymān ibn Muḥammad related to us; ʿUmāra ibn ʿUqba related to us; Muḥammad ibn Jābir related to us, from al-Minhāl ibn ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Ḍamra ibn Hawdha, who said: I heard my father say, ‘I bear witness that al-Uqayṣir ibn Salama came with the water flask that the Messenger of God ﷺ had sent, and he sprinkled its contents in the mosque of Qurān.’ Al-ʿAskarī relied upon that and therefore gave al-Uqayṣir a heading. Ibn Manda said, ‘The correct form of his name is al-Aqʿas.’ He then transmitted the report by another route from Muḥammad ibn Jābir, in which he said: from al-Minhāl ibn ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Ḍamra ibn Hawdha, from his father, who said, ‘I bear witness that al-Aqʿas came.’ Al-Rushāṭī related from Abū ʿUbayd that al-Aqʿas ibn Salama ibn ʿUbayd ibn ʿAmr ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā ibn Suḥaym came to the Messenger of God ﷺ in the delegation of Banū Suḥaym. He embraced Islam and practiced it well. The Messenger sent them back to their people and ordered them to call them to Islam. He gave them a water flask containing water into which he had expectorated lightly or spat, and said, ‘Carry my message to Banū Suḥaym: let them sprinkle their mosque with this flask, and let them hold their heads high, since God has raised them.’ He said: Not one man among them followed Musaylima, nor did any Kharijite ever emerge from among them. The expression aliknī has an open hamza, a kasra on the lām, and a quiescent kāf; it means ‘convey my message.’ A message is called an alūka.

## Source unit 240 · printed entry 240

### English candidate

Aktham ibn al-Jawn, or ibn Abī al-Jawn. His name was ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā ibn Munqidh ibn Rabīʿa ibn Aṣram ibn Ḍubays ibn Ḥarām ibn Ḥabashiyya ibn Kaʿb ibn ʿAmr ibn Rabīʿa al-Khuzāʿī. He was the paternal uncle of Sulaymān ibn Ṣurad al-Khuzāʿī. Aḥmad said: Muḥammad ibn Bashīr related to us; Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr related to us, from Abū Salama, from Abū Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said, ‘The Fire was shown to me, and in it I saw ʿAmr ibn Luḥayy ibn Qamaʿa ibn Khindif dragging his entrails in the Fire. He was the first to alter Abraham’s covenant: he set the sāʾibas loose, slit the ears of the baḥīras, protected the ḥāmī, and set up idols. The person I have seen who most resembles him is Aktham ibn Abī al-Jawn.’ Aktham asked, ‘Messenger of God, will my resemblance to him harm me?’ He replied, ‘No. You are a Muslim, whereas he was an unbeliever.’ Al-Ḥākim transmitted it by way of Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Anṣārī, from Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr, in the same form. The two of them also transmitted it by way of ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿAmr al-Raqqī, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿAqīl, from al-Ṭufayl ibn Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, from his father, in a long account. Ibn Abī ʿArūba and Ibn Manda transmitted by way of Ibn Isḥāq: Muḥammad ibn Ibrāhīm ibn al-Ḥārith related to me, from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Abū Hurayra, who said: I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say to Aktham ibn Abī al-Jawn, ‘Aktham, I saw ʿAmr ibn Luḥayy ibn Qamaʿa ibn Khindif dragging his entrails in the Fire’—the report. It includes Aktham ibn al-Jawn’s question and the reply to him. Abū Salama’s version is more complete. The report is included in Muslim by way of Suhayl ibn Abī Ṣāliḥ, from his father, in a shorter form that omits the story of Aktham. In the Book of Genealogy, al-Zubayr transmitted the story of Aktham through two other disconnected routes. Aḥmad transmitted it by another route from Jābir, where it reads, ‘The person I have seen who most resembles him is Maʿbad ibn Aktham.’ He then related it, and it is possible that there were multiple persons. In Ibn al-Kalbī’s Jamharat al-Nasab, when he mentioned this Aktham and stated decisively that he was the son of Abū al-Jawn, I saw that he said: He is the one about whom the Prophet ﷺ said, ‘The Dajjāl was shown to me. Behold, he was a dark-complexioned, curly-haired man, and the member of Banū ʿAmr ibn Kaʿb who most resembled him was Aktham ibn ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā.’ Aktham stood and asked, ‘Messenger of God, will my resembling him harm me at all?’ He replied, ‘No. You are a Muslim, whereas he is an unbeliever.’ I say: On its face this conflicts with what preceded. It is possible, however, that the pronoun in ‘resembled him’ refers to ʿAmr ibn Kaʿb, who is ʿAmr ibn Luḥayy, in which case the two reports do not conflict. They would then be two independent reports, one describing the Dajjāl and the other concerning the resemblance of ʿAmr ibn Kaʿb. The person reported to resemble the Dajjāl is ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā ibn Qaṭan. Al-Ṭabarānī and Ibn Manda transmitted by way of Ḍamra, from Ibn Shawdhab, from Abū Nahīk, from Shibl ibn Khalīd al-Muzanī, from Aktham ibn al-Jawn al-Khuzāʿī, who said: We said, ‘Messenger of God, so-and-so is indeed bold in battle.’ He replied, ‘He is in the Fire’—the full report. Its chain is fair. This episode occurred at Khaybar, as established in the Ṣaḥīḥ from the report of Sahl ibn Saʿd; one therefore learns that Aktham ibn Abī al-Jawn was present there. Ibn Abī Ḥātim in al-ʿIlal, al-ʿAskarī in al-Amthāl, al-Baghawī, and Ibn Manda transmitted by way of Abū Salama al-ʿĀmilī, from al-Zuhrī, from Anas, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said, ‘Aktham, go on campaign with people other than your own; your character will improve.’ Ibn Abī Ḥātim said: I heard my father say, ‘Abū Salama al-ʿĀmilī is abandoned, and the report is false.’ End. Ibn Manda transmitted it by another route from Aktham himself, and Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr alluded to it. والله أعلم.

## Source unit 244 · printed entry 244

### English candidate

Akīna, ancestor of Rizq Allāh ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhāb al-Tamīmī. Ibn Mākūlā said: Rizq Allāh told me that his ancestor Akīna possessed companionship. Ibn Mākūlā also related from Rizq Allāh that his ancestor ʿAbd Allāh came to the Prophet ﷺ. His name had been ʿAbd al-Lāt, so the Prophet named him ʿAbd Allāh. He is Rizq Allāh ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhāb ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Asad ibn al-Layth ibn al-Aswad ibn Sufyān ibn Yazīd ibn Akīna ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Tamīmī. Al-Khaṭīb transmitted from ʿAbd al-Wahhāb, Rizq Allāh’s father, from his forefathers, a report ending with the aforementioned Akīna, who said, ‘I heard ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib...’; he then related a report. Yazīd does not occur in the genealogy given by al-Khaṭīb. Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ likewise gave it that way in ʿUlūm al-Ḥadīth. Al-Khaṭīb expressly stated that there were nine forefathers, which is correct only if Yazīd is included. Ibn Mākūlā gave Akīna’s lineage as ibn Yazīd ibn al-Haytham ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Kalada ibn Ḥanẓala ibn Zayd Manāt ibn Tamīm. We transmitted it in the session that Rizq Allāh al-Tamīmī dictated in Isfahan. He said: I heard my father, ʿAbd al-Wahhāb, say: I heard my father, Abū al-Ḥasan ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, say: I heard my father, Abū Bakr al-Ḥārith, say: I heard my father, Asad, say: I heard my father, Sulaymān, say: I heard my father, al-Aswad, say: I heard my father, Sufyān, say: I heard my father, Yazīd, say: I heard my father, Akīna, say: I heard my father, al-Haytham, say: I heard my father, ʿAbd Allāh, say: I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say, ‘No people gather for remembrance without the angels surrounding them and mercy covering them.’ Al-Dhahabī said, ‘Most of his forefathers have no mention in any history or among the names of transmitters.’ Al-Layth, the father of Asad, has fallen out of this chain, although al-Khaṭīb included him in his History when he gave the biography of ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz. I say: Al-Haytham, however, does not occur in al-Khaṭīb’s version. The ḥāfiẓ al-ʿAlāʾī, the teacher of our teachers, said the same in al-Washy al-Muʿlam.

## Source unit 246 · printed entry 246

### English candidate

Elijah, God’s prophet ﵇. Some accounts about him will appear in the biography of al-Khiḍr. Including al-Khiḍr among the Companions requires us to include Elijah as well. Among the strangest reports transmitted concerning him is that he is al-Khiḍr. Ibn Mardawayh transmitted in his commentary on Sūrat al-Anʿām, by way of Hishām ibn ʿUbayd Allāh al-Rāzī, from Ibrāhīm ibn Abī Jazī, from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ḥārith, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said, ‘Al-Khiḍr is Elijah.’ He transmitted it from Ṭāhir ibn Aḥmad ibn Ḥamdān, from Muḥammad ibn Jaʿfar al-Ushnānī, from Muḥammad ibn Yūsuf ibn Farrāʾ, from Hishām.

## Source unit 247 · printed entry 247

### English candidate

Amānah—with an nūn—ibn Qays ibn Shaybān ibn al-ʿĀtik ibn Muʿāwiya al-Akramīn al-Kindī. Ibn Saʿd related from Ibn al-Kalbī that he came in a delegation to the Prophet ﷺ. He had lived for a very long time. ʿAwaḍa, the Nakhaʿī poet from Banū Barāʾ, said of him:

Would that I had been granted life, O Umm Mālik,
as long as Amānah ibn Qays ibn Shaybān’s life!
He lived until it was said, ‘He will never die,’
and he outlasted multitudes of mature men and youths.

It is said that he lived for three hundred and twenty years. Al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Shāhīn also included him among the Companions, as did Ibn Fatḥūn in the Supplement. His son Yazīd embraced Islam with him, then apostatized and was killed during the caliphate of Abū Bakr.

## Source unit 248 · printed entry 248

### English candidate

Amad ibn Abad al-Ḥaḍramī. Al-Ṭabarānī said: ʿAlī ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz related to us; Abū ʿUbayd al-Qāsim related to us; Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar related to us; my brother Yazīd ibn al-Muthannā related to me, from Salama ibn Saʿīd, who said: We were with Muʿāwiya when he said, ‘I wish that we had someone who could tell us about bygone times and whether they resembled our own day.’ He was told that in Ḥaḍramawt there was a man who had lived for three hundred years. Muʿāwiya sent for him, and the man was brought. When he entered, Muʿāwiya seated him and then asked, ‘What is your name?’ He replied, ‘Amad ibn Abad,’ and related a long story. In it Muʿāwiya asked, ‘Did you see Muḥammad?’ He replied, ‘Why did you not say, “the Messenger of God”?’ ‘Yes, I saw him.’ Muʿāwiya said, ‘Describe him to me.’ He replied, ‘I saw him—may my father and mother be his ransom—and I never saw anyone like him before or after him.’

Abū Mūsā transmitted it in al-Dhayl. There is an obvious break in its chain, and the story contains an objectionable element: it states that he saw a woman traveler set out from Syria for Mecca needing neither food nor drink, eating from the fruits and drinking from the springs. This is false.

Abū Ḥātim al-Sijistānī mentioned in Kitāb al-Muʿammarīn, from Abū ʿĀmir, from a man of Basra, who said—and Abū al-Junayd al-Ḍarīr also related it from his teachers—that they said: Muʿāwiya said, ‘I would like to meet a man of great age who can tell us what he has seen.’ He then related the story. This version does not contain that objectionable addition. Rather, it states that the man had seen Hāshim ibn ʿAbd Manāf and Umayya ibn ʿAbd Shams. Muʿāwiya asked him, ‘What was your occupation?’ He replied, ‘I was a merchant.’ He asked, ‘How far did your trade reach?’ He replied, ‘I did not buy at a loss, and I did not turn down a profit.’ Muʿāwiya said to him, ‘Ask something of me.’ He replied, ‘I ask you to restore my youth to me.’ Muʿāwiya said, ‘That is not in my power.’ He said, ‘Then I ask you to admit me into Paradise.’ Muʿāwiya said, ‘That is not in my power.’ He replied, ‘I see that nothing of this world or the Hereafter is in your power, so return me to the place from which you brought me.’ Muʿāwiya said, ‘That, at least, I can do.’

<div dir="rtl" lang="ar">

أمد بن أبد الحضرمي قال الطبراني حدثنا علي بن عبد العزيز حدثنا أبو عبيد القاسم حدثنا أبو عبيدة معمر حدثني أخي يزيد بن المثنى عن سلمة بن سعيد قال كنا عند معاوية فقال وددت أن عندنا من يحدثنا عما مضى من الزمن هل يشبه ما نحن فيه اليوم فقيل له بحضر موت رجل قد أتت عليه ثلاثمائة سنة فأرسل إليه معاوية فأتى به فلما دخل عليه اجلسه ثم قال ما اسمك قال أمد بن أبد فذكر قصة طويلة وفيها فهل رأيت محمدا قال الا قلت رسول الله نعم رأيته قال فصفه لي قال رأيته بأبي وأمي فما رأيت قبله ولا بعده مثله أخرجه أبو موسى في الذيل وفي الإسناد إرسال ظاهر وفي القصة نكارة من جهة أنه وقع فيها أنه رأى الظعينة تخرج من الشام إلى مكة لا تحتاج إلى طعام ولا إلى شراب تأكل من الثمار وتشرب من العيون وهذا باطل وذكر أبو حاتم السجستاني في كتاب المعمرين عن أبي عامر عن رجل من أهل البصرة قال وحدث به أبو الجنيد الضرير عن أشياخه قالوا قال معاوية إني لاحب أن ألقى رجلا قد أتى عليه سن يخبرنا عما رأى فذكر القصة وليس فيها تلك الزيادة المنكرة بل فيها أنه رأى هاشم بن عبد مناف وأمية بن عبد شمس وأنه قال له ما كان صنعتك قال كنت تاجرا قال فما بلغت تجارتك قال كنت لا اشتري غبنا ولا أرد ربحا وإن معاوية قال له سلني قال أسألك أن ترد علي شبابي قال ليس ذاك بيدي قال فأسألك أن تدخلني الجنة قال ليس ذاك بيدي قال لا أرى بيدك شيئا من الدنيا والآخرة فردني من حيث جئت بي قال أما هذه فنعم

## Source unit 249 · printed entry 249

## Source unit 250 · printed entry 250

### English candidate

Imruʾ al-Qays ibn ʿĀbis ibn al-Mundhir ibn Imruʾ al-Qays ibn al-Simṭ ibn ʿAmr ibn Muʿāwiya al-Akramīn, al-Kindī. Al-Baghawī said, in these exact words: ‘In al-Bukhārī’s book naming those who related from the Prophet ﷺ: Imruʾ al-Qays ibn ʿĀbis settled in Kufa.’

Al-Nasāʾī, Aḥmad, and al-Baghawī transmitted, by way of Rajāʾ ibn Ḥaywa, from ʿAdī ibn ʿUmayra, who said: There was a dispute between Imruʾ al-Qays and a man of Ḥaḍramawt, and they brought their case before the Prophet ﷺ. He said to the Ḥaḍramī, ‘Your proof; otherwise, his oath.’ The man said, ‘Messenger of God, if he swears, my land is gone.’ He said, ‘Whoever swears a false oath by which he appropriates his brother’s right will meet God while He is angry with him.’ Imruʾ al-Qays said, ‘Messenger of God, what awaits the person who relinquishes it while knowing that he is in the right?’ He replied, ‘Paradise.’ Imruʾ al-Qays said, ‘Then I call you to witness that I have relinquished it.’ Its chain is sound. The hadith will appear later, through another route, in the entry on Rabīʿa ibn ʿAydān, with the statement that he was the opposing litigant. ʿAydān is vocalized with a fatḥa on the ʿayn followed by a lower-dotted yāʾ.

Sayf ibn ʿUmar said in al-Futūḥ that on the day of al-Yarmūk, Imruʾ al-Qays commanded a contingent. Al-Marzubānī mentioned that he was among those present at the siege of the fortress of al-Nujayr. When the apostates were brought out to be executed, he sprang upon his paternal uncle to kill him. His uncle said, ‘Woe to you! Will you kill me when I am your uncle?’ He replied, ‘You are my uncle, but God is my Lord,’ and killed him.

Ibn al-Sakan said that he was among those who remained steadfast in Islam and that he denounced al-Ashʿath’s apostasy. Ibn Isḥāq recited poetry of his in which he urged his people to remain steadfast in Islam. Among his verses are:

‘Stand at the dwellings, as one held back would stand,
and tarry, for you are not despairing.
The storm winds have played over them—
winds passing among those that efface the traces.’

In it he says:

‘How many a woman will weep for me,
and many a reciter for me in gatherings.
Do not be amazed if you should hear:
“Imruʾ al-Qays ibn ʿĀbis has perished.”’

During the apostasy he wrote to Abū Bakr:

‘Let a messenger carry word to Abū Bakr,
and carry it to all the Muslims:
No houses shall stand beside my house
whose people deny what the Prophet said.’

The grandfather of his father was Imruʾ al-Qays ibn al-Simṭ. He was called Ibn Tamlik—with a tāʾ bearing two dots above—and she was his mother. The poet Imruʾ al-Qays mentioned him in his ode rhyming in rāʾ, saying ‘Imruʾ al-Qays ibn Tamlik,’ thus tracing him through his mother. Ibn al-Kalbī said: Rajāʾ ibn Ḥaywa, the famous Successor and companion of ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, was from his clan. He was Rajāʾ ibn Ḥaywa ibn Jandal ibn al-Aḥnaf ibn al-Simṭ. His father lived into the Islamic period, but the authorities did not expressly state that he had Companionship; it therefore appears that he did not come as a delegate during the lifetime of the Prophet ﷺ.

امرىء القيس بن عابس بن المنذر بن امرئ القيس بن عمرو بن معاوية الاكرمين الكندي قال البغوي ما نصه في كتاب البخاري في تسمية من روى عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم امرؤ القيس بن عابس سكن الكوفة وروى النسائي وأحمد والبغوي من طريق رجاء بن حيوة عن عدي بن عميرة قال كان بين امرئ القيس ورجل من حضر موت خصومة فارتفعا إلى النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم فقال للحضرمي بينتك وإلا فيمينه فقال يا رسول الله إن حلف ذهب بأرضي فقال من حلف على يمين كاذبة يقتطع بها حق أخيه لقي الله وهو عليه غضبان فقال امرؤ القيس يا رسول الله فما لمن تركها وهو يعلم أنه محق قال الجنة قال فإني أشهدك أني قد تركتها إسناده صحيح وسيأتي الحديث في ترجمة ربيعة بن عيدان من وجه آخر وأنه هو المخاصم وعيدان بفتح العين بعدها ياء تحتانية وقال سيف بن عمر في الفتوح كان امرؤ القيس يوم اليرموك على كردوس وذكر المرزباني أنه كان ممن حضر حصار حصن النجير فلما أخرج المرتدون ليقتلوا وثب على عمه ليقتله فقال له عمه ويحك اتقتلني وأنا عمك قال أنت عمي والله ربي فقتله وقال بن السكن كان ممن ثبت على الإسلام وأنكر على الأشعث ارتداده وأنشد له بن إسحاق شعرا يحرض فيه قومه على الثبات على الإسلام ومن شعره <br />

## Source unit 252 · printed entry 252

### English candidate

Umayya ibn Asʿad ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Khuzāʿī. His father was mentioned above. As for Umayya, Aḥmad ibn Sayyār al-Marwazī mentioned him in Tārīkh Marw, among the names of the naqībs of Banū al-ʿAbbās. He said: ‘As for the seven who were Arabs, among them was Abū Muḥammad Sulaymān ibn Kathīr ibn Umayya ibn Asʿad ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Khuzāʿī, one of the people of Medina, from the quarter of Ḥarthān. His grandfather Umayya was one of the seventy who pledged allegiance to the Messenger of God ﷺ beneath the tree.’

Ibn ʿAsākir transmitted it in his Tārīkh by way of Ibn Manda, from al-Qāsim ibn al-Qāsim al-Sayyārī, from his grandfather Aḥmad ibn Sayyār, with exactly the same wording. Muḥammad ibn Ḥamduwayh also mentioned it in Tārīkh Marw, but he said ‘Umayya ibn Saʿd,’ without an alif; this is an error. Abū Zakariyyā ibn Manda made another muddle in his entry, which we have discussed in the final section.

## Source unit 253 · printed entry 253

### English candidate

Umayya ibn al-Askar—with an unpointed sīn, according to the form that al-Jayyānī deemed correct, although Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr wrote it with the pointed letter—ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Zuhra ibn Zubayna ibn Jundaʿ ibn Layth ibn Bakr ibn ʿAbd Manāt ibn Kināna, al-Kinānī al-Laythī al-Jundaʿī. He lived in al-Ṭāʾif. His son Ubayy was mentioned previously. Abū al-Faraj al-Iṣfahānī said that Abū ʿAmr al-Shaybānī said: Kilāb ibn Umayya ibn al-Askar emigrated, and his father composed poetry about him; the Prophet ﷺ therefore ordered Kilāb to maintain ties with his father and remain obedient to him. Abū al-Faraj said: ‘This is an error by Abū ʿAmr. It was ʿUmar who ordered him to do that, when Kilāb campaigned against the Persians during ʿUmar’s caliphate.’ He then transmitted, from Ibn al-Madāʾinī, from Abū Bakr al-Hudhalī, from al-Zuhrī, from ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr: When Kilāb ibn Umayya ibn al-Askar emigrated to Medina during ʿUmar’s caliphate, he remained there for some time. He then met Ṭalḥa and al-Zubayr and asked them which deeds were best. They answered, ‘Struggle in God’s path.’ He asked ʿUmar, who sent him on campaign. His father had grown old and weak. When Kilāb’s absence became prolonged, his father said: ‘For whose sake have two aged parents called out for Kilāb?
By God’s Book—if only he would accept the Book!
I call to him, but he turns away in proud refusal;
no, by Kilāb’s father, he has not acted rightly.
In seeking reward while leaving me behind, you are
like one seeking water who follows a mirage.’ He then recited verses to ʿUmar complaining of his intense longing for Kilāb. ʿUmar wept and ordered that Kilāb be returned to him. Ibrāhīm al-Ḥarbī said in his Gharīb al-Ḥadīth: Ibn al-Junayd related to us; Ibn Abī al-Zinād related to us, from his father, from a trustworthy man, that ʿUmar returned to his father a man who had been on campaign. His father had been weeping for him and saying: ‘Righteousness after neglecting both his parents?
No, by Kilāb’s father, he has not acted rightly.’ ʿUmar said, ‘Indeed—by Kilāb’s father, he has not acted rightly.’ Al-Fākihī said in Akhbār Makka: Ibn Abī ʿUmar related to us; Sufyān related to us, from Abū Saʿīd al-Aʿwar: Whenever someone arriving from elsewhere came before ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, he would ask him about the people. One traveler arrived, and ʿUmar asked where he came from. He replied, ‘Al-Ṭāʾif.’ ʿUmar asked, ‘What is happening there?’ He replied, ‘I saw an old man there saying: “You left your father with trembling hands,
and your mother unable to swallow a drink.
When the doves coo in the valley of Wajj
over their eggs, they remind her of Kilāb.”’ ʿUmar asked, ‘Who is Kilāb?’ The traveler replied, ‘The old man’s son; he was away on campaign.’ ʿUmar wrote concerning him and had him sent home. ʿAlī ibn Mushir transmitted from Hishām ibn ʿUrwa, from his father, who said: Umayya ibn al-Askar lived into Islam as a very old man and was a nobleman among his people. He had two sons who fled from him, one named Kilāb. Umayya lamented them in poems. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb returned them to him and made them swear not to leave him until he died. Al-Dūlābī transmitted in al-Kunā by way of Abū Saʿd ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Jumaḥī, from al-Zuhrī, who said: I passed by ʿUrwa while he was sitting in a covered portico. He said, ‘Would you like an unusual report? Umayya ibn al-Askar al-Jundaʿī had become senile, and two sons of his had emigrated with Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ. Umayya said in his verse: “Two emigrants came to him and left him prostrate;
servants of God, they disobeyed and failed.
You left your father…”’ The verses include: ‘I call to him, but he turns his back to me;
no, by Kilāb’s father, he has not acted rightly.’ Al-Zubayr transmitted this story at length in al-Muwaffaqiyyāt. Umayya ibn al-Askar also has an account in the Sacrilegious War, which Ibn Isḥāq mentioned in the Greater Sīra. He said that Ibn Abī Asmāʾ ibn al-Ḍarība said: ‘We were the kings among the people of Najd,
defenders of the lands when honor was at stake.
There we struck Kināna such a blow
that afterward they kept company with grazing pregnant she-camels.’ Umayya ibn al-Askar answered him: ‘Tell Ḥamma ibn al-Ḍarība that we
killed your chiefs in the Sacrilegious War.
We gave you undiluted death to drink
and carried off the plunder and the young she-camels.’ Muḥammad ibn Ḥabīb transmitted from Abū ʿUbayda another poem by him about the Sacrilegious War, which he spoke concerning Wahb ibn Muʿattib al-Thaqafī: ‘Manhood is Wahb—Wahb of the house of Muʿattib;
the misguided have wearied, but you have not yet wearied.
He strives; the heat of its fuel kindles it;
and when your people’s peace is ready, you swear against it.’ He gave the poet’s name, however, as Umayya ibn Ḥarthān ibn al-Askar. Aslam ibn Sahl also transmitted his story in the History of Wāsiṭ, by way of Shabīb ibn Shayba ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ahtam al-Tamīmī, from his father. He said: There was a man who had two aged parents; and he related the story, including the poetry. Al-Madāʾinī said, from Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ, that Umayya lived so long that he became senile. Abū Ḥātim al-Sijistānī said in the Book of Long-Lived Persons that Umayya ibn al-Askar lived for a very long time. He said, yearning for his son Kilāb: ‘O reproaching woman, you reproached without knowledge;
what do you know—woe to you—of what I suffer?
If you would reproach me, then return
Kilāb, now that he has set out for Iraq.
I shall appeal against al-Fārūq to a Lord
to whom the pilgrims lift their voices at Bisāq,
if al-Fārūq does not return Kilāb
to two old parents whose heads cry aloud.’ His poetry reached ʿUmar, who wrote to Saʿd ordering him to send Kilāb home. When Kilāb arrived, ʿUmar sent for Umayya and asked him what he desired most. He replied, ‘To look upon my son Kilāb.’ ʿUmar summoned Kilāb. When Umayya saw him, he embraced him and wept intensely. ʿUmar wept and said, ‘Kilāb, remain with your father and mother as long as they live.’ I say: I did not defer him to the section on the mukhaḍramūn because of Abū ʿAmr al-Shaybānī’s statement with which we began. Nothing in the remaining reports negates it, so the possibility remains—especially for a Kinānī man from the neighbors of Quraysh. The account of Kilāb will appear under kāf. Ibn al-Kalbī mentioned that the other son’s name was Ubayy ibn Umayya.

## Source unit 257 · printed entry 257

### English candidate

Umayya ibn Abī ʿUbayda ibn Hammām ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Bakr ibn Zayd ibn Mālik ibn Ḥanẓala ibn Mālik ibn Zayd Manāt ibn Tamīm, al-Tamīmī al-Ḥanẓalī, a confederate of Banū Nawfal. He was the father of Yaʿlā ibn Umayya, who is also called Yaʿlā ibn Munya. Yaʿlā is a well-known Companion. Al-Nasāʾī transmitted by way of ʿAmr ibn al-Ḥārith, from al-Zuhrī, that ʿAmr ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, the son of Yaʿlā ibn Umayya’s brother, related to him that his father informed him that Yaʿlā ibn Umayya said: ‘I brought my father to the Messenger of God ﷺ on the Day of the Conquest and said, “Messenger of God, accept my father’s pledge to emigrate.” He replied, “There is no emigration after the Conquest.”’ Ibn Abī ʿĀṣim transmitted it from Abū al-Rabīʿ, from Fulayḥ, from al-Zuhrī, from ʿAmr ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Yaʿlā, from his father, from Yaʿlā, with similar wording. Ibn Manda said: ‘ʿUqayl transmitted it from al-Zuhrī similarly, except that he said ʿAmr ibn ʿAbd Allāh.’ I say: Al-Nasāʾī transmitted it by way of ʿUqayl and said ʿAmr ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān. Ibn Manda also transmitted it by way of ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Abī Ziyād al-Qaddāḥ, from Dāwūd ibn Sābūr, from Mujāhid, from Yaʿlā. These chains strengthen one another.

## Source unit 261 · printed entry 261

### English candidate

Anjasha, the Black camel-driver. He had a beautiful voice when chanting to the camels. Al-Balādhurī said that he was Abyssinian and had the kunyā Abū Māriya. Abū Dāwūd al-Ṭayālisī transmitted in his Musnad, from Ḥammād ibn Salama, from Thābit, from Anas, who said: Anjasha used to chant for the women, while al-Barāʾ ibn Mālik used to chant for the men. When the camels quickened their pace, the Prophet ﷺ said, ‘Anjasha, gently! Drive the glass vessels slowly.’ The two Shaykhs transmitted it in abridged form by way of Ḥammād ibn Zayd, from Thābit, from Anas, and by way of Ḥammād ibn Zayd, from Ayyūb, from Abū Qilāba, from Anas. Muslim transmitted by way of Sulaymān ibn Ṭarkhān al-Taymī, from Anas, who said: The Prophet ﷺ had a camel-driver called Anjasha. The Prophet ﷺ said to him, ‘Gently! Drive the glass vessels slowly.’ Ibn Manda said: ‘It is well known from Sulaymān.’ By way of Abū Qilāba, from Anas, it is related that the Messenger of God ﷺ was on one of his journeys and a Black youth called Anjasha was chanting to the camels. By way of Qatāda, from Anas, it is related that the Messenger of God ﷺ had a camel-driver with a beautiful voice. Al-Nasāʾī transmitted by way of Zuhayr, from Sulaymān al-Taymī, from Anas, from his mother, that she was with the wives of the Prophet ﷺ while a driver was driving them; and he related the report. A report of Wāthila ibn al-Asqaʿ says that Anjasha was among the mukhannathūn—effeminate men—in the time of the Messenger of God ﷺ. Al-Ṭabarānī transmitted with a weak chain, by way of ʿAnbasa ibn Saʿīd—also printed as ʿUtba—from Ḥammād, a client of Banū Umayya, from Janāḥ, from Wāthila ibn al-Asqaʿ, who said: ‘The Messenger of God ﷺ cursed the mukhannathūn and said, “Expel them from your houses.” The Prophet ﷺ expelled Anjasha, and ʿUmar expelled a certain unnamed man.’

## Source unit 266 · printed entry 266

### English candidate

Anas ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Nabīh. Ibn al-Sakan said, ‘There is cause for scrutiny in his report.’ Ibn Manda said that he was counted among the people of Kufa. Al-Bukhārī said: ‘Anas ibn al-Ḥārith was killed with al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī; he heard the Prophet ﷺ.’ Muḥammad related this from Saʿīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik al-Ḥarrānī, from ʿAṭāʾ ibn Muslim: Ashʿath ibn Suḥaym related to us, from his father, who said: I heard Anas ibn al-Ḥārith. Al-Baghawī, Ibn al-Sakan, and others transmitted it by this route. Its text is: I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say, ‘This son of mine’—meaning al-Ḥusayn—‘will be killed in a land called Karbalāʾ. Whoever among you is present for that must support him.’ He said: Anas ibn al-Ḥārith therefore went to Karbalāʾ and was killed there with al-Ḥusayn. Al-Bukhārī said, ‘They criticize Saʿīd’—meaning the transmitter. Al-Baghawī said, ‘I do not know anyone other than him to have transmitted it.’ Ibn al-Sakan said, ‘It is transmitted only by this route, and no other report is known from Anas.’ I say: His father, al-Ḥārith ibn Nabīh, will be mentioned in his proper place. In al-Dhahabī’s al-Tajrīd it reads, ‘He had no companionship, and his report is mursal.’ Al-Mizzī said, ‘He had companionship, so [al-Dhahabī] erred.’ End. The basis for rejecting that view is plain from what we stated earlier. How can his report be mursal when he said, ‘I heard’? Al-Baghawī, Ibn al-Sakan, Ibn Shāhīn, al-Daghūlī, Ibn Zabr, al-Bāwardī, Ibn Manda, Abū Nuʿaym, and others included him among the Companions.

## Source unit 267 · printed entry 267

### English candidate

Anas ibn Zunaym al-Kinānī. His full lineage appeared earlier in the biography of his nephew, Usayd ibn Abī Unās ibn Zunaym. Ibn Isḥāq mentioned in al-Maghāzī that ʿAmr ibn Sālim al-Khuzāʿī went out with forty riders to seek the aid of the Messenger of God ﷺ against Quraysh, and recited to him:

O God, I appeal to Muḥammad
by the ancient covenant of our father and his father...

Then he said, ‘Messenger of God, Anas ibn Zunaym has lampooned you.’ The Messenger of God ﷺ therefore declared his blood forfeit. When news of that reached Anas, he came to him apologetically and recited verses praising him. Nawfal ibn Muʿāwiya al-Dīlī interceded for him, so he pardoned him. Al-Wāqidī and al-Ṭabarī likewise gave the story as concerning Anas ibn Zunaym. Ibn Shāhīn cited, through a disconnected chain to Ḥizām ibn Hishām ibn Khālid al-Kaʿbī, from his father, who said: When the delegation of Khuzāʿa came seeking the Prophet’s ﷺ aid—then he related approximately this story. It includes that on the Day of the Conquest Anas ibn Zunaym embraced Islam. He is the one who said, among other verses:

Know, Messenger of God, that you will overtake me,
and that a threat from you is like being seized by the hand.

Ibn Saʿd transmitted it from Muḥammad ibn ʿUmar: Ḥizām ibn Hishām ibn Khālid related to me, from his father, approximately the same. It includes that Nawfal said, ‘You are most entitled to pardon. Which of us did not offend and oppose you? In the Age of Ignorance we did not know what to adopt and what to leave until God guided us through you and rescued us from destruction.’ He replied, ‘I have pardoned him.’ Nawfal said, ‘May my father and mother be your ransom.’ The beginning of the poem includes:

No she-camel ever bore above her saddle
one more righteous or more faithful to a covenant than Muḥammad.

It also includes:

The Messenger of God was told that I had lampooned him;
if so, may my hand never again lift my whip to me.
I violated no honor and shed no blood;
so remember, knower of truth, and be just.
Except that I said, ‘Alas for young men
struck by misfortune on the day of Ṭalq and Asʿad!
They were struck by one who was no equal for their blood,
and my protective zeal and restless grief grew fierce:
Dhuʾayb, Kulthūm, Salmā, and Sāʿid,
all together; if the eye does not weep, it wastes away in grief.
Yet among them there was none like Salmā,
and his brothers—are there kings like slaves?’

This poem also contains the line:

No she-camel ever bore above her saddle
one more chaste or more faithful to a covenant than Muḥammad.

Diʿbil ibn ʿAlī said in Ṭabaqāt al-Shuʿarāʾ, ‘This is the truest verse the Arabs ever spoke.’ I say: Anas ibn Zunaym also has reports involving ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Ziyād, governor of Iraq, which Abū al-Faraj al-Iṣbahānī included in the biography of Ḥāritha ibn Badr al-Ghudānī. Among them is that ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Ziyād used to provoke poets against one another, so he ordered Ḥāritha to lampoon Anas ibn Zunaym. He composed verses against him, including:

I was told of Anas that he
is scant in trustworthiness, a betrayer of it.

Anas answered him with verses beginning:

An offensive message reached me,
and my answer was to forgive it.

Al-Marzubānī related by way of al-Walīd ibn Hishām al-Jaʿdī, who said: ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĀmir promised Anas ibn Abī Unās something, as he had accustomed him to such favors, but was slow in fulfilling it. Anas stood before him and recited:

Would that I knew concerning my friend what it was
that destroyed his affection until he bade it farewell.
Let not your raincloud’s lightning be a deceptive flash;
the best lightning is that which brings rain.
Do not demean me after having honored me,
for a firmly rooted habit is hard to uproot.

I say: This one is the brother of Usayd ibn Abī Unās, not his paternal uncle; perhaps he was named after him. Anas ibn Zunaym was the brother of Sāriya ibn Zunaym, who will appear in his proper place.

## Source unit 270 · printed entry 270

### English candidate

Anas ibn Ẓahīr, brother of Usayd ibn Ẓahīr. Abū Ḥātim and al-ʿAskarī mentioned that he took part in Uḥud. Al-Bukhārī said in his History: Ibrāhīm ibn al-Mundhir said to me: Muḥammad ibn Ṭalḥa related to us, from Ḥusayn ibn Thābit ibn Anas ibn Ẓahīr, from his sister Saʿdā bint Thābit, from her father, from her grandfather, who said: On the Day of Uḥud, Rāfiʿ ibn Khadīj presented himself. The Prophet ﷺ considered him too young and intended to turn him back. His paternal uncle Ẓahīr said, ‘Messenger of God, my brother’s son is an archer,’ so the Prophet ﷺ permitted him to take part. Ibn al-Sakan transmitted it by way of al-Bukhārī, who said: Ibrāhīm ibn al-Mundhir related to us. Ibn Manda transmitted it from ʿAlī ibn al-ʿAbbās al-Miṣrī, from Jaʿfar ibn Sulaymān, from Ibrāhīm ibn al-Mundhir, in the same form, except that it reads, ‘My paternal uncle Rāfiʿ ibn Ẓahīr ibn Rāfiʿ said to him.’ In the biography of Usayd ibn Ẓahīr, al-Ṭabarānī said: Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-ʿAdanī related to us; ʿUthmān ibn Yaʿqūb al-ʿUthmānī related to us; Muḥammad ibn Ṭalḥa related to us; Bashīr ibn Thābit and his sister Saʿdā bint Thābit related to us, from their father Thābit, from their grandfather Usayd ibn Ẓahīr. That is how it occurs in his work, and it is erroneous in several places. Abū Nuʿaym was misled by it and claimed that Ibn Manda had miscopied Usayd ibn Ẓahīr as Anas ibn Ẓahīr. The correct position is Ibn Manda’s, as you can see, except for his wording ‘Rāfiʿ ibn Ẓahīr’; the correct form is ‘Ẓahīr ibn Rāfiʿ.’ والله أعلم.

## Source unit 271 · printed entry 271

### English candidate

Anas ibn ʿAbbās ibn Anas ibn ʿĀmir ibn Ḥayy ibn Riʿl ibn Mālik ibn ʿAwf ibn Imriʾ al-Qays ibn Bahtha ibn Sulaym, al-Sulamī and then al-Riʿlī. Ibn Saʿd related from Abū Maʿshar, from his teachers, who said: In the Year of the Conquest, seven hundred men of Banū Sulaym came to the Messenger of God ﷺ. Among them were ʿAbbās ibn Mirdās, Anas ibn ʿAbbās ibn Riʿl, and Rāshid ibn ʿAbd Rabbih, and they embraced Islam. I say: His father will also be mentioned later. The expression ‘ʿAbbās ibn Riʿl’ attributes him to the grandfather of his grandfather. Ibn al-Kalbī mentioned that this Anas was a chief, and that Khathʿam later killed him. His son Razīn ibn Anas ibn ʿAbbās is also mentioned and will appear under the letter rāʾ. If that is sound, they are three Companions in succession: Razīn ibn Anas ibn ʿAbbās. Sayf mentioned in al-Futūḥ that Razīn was commander of the rear guard of the Iraqi cavalry when Abū ʿUbayda sent them back there after the conquest of Damascus, at ʿUmar’s command. He was present at al-Qādisiyya. Ibn ʿAsākir included him among those present at al-Yarmūk, and Ibn Fatḥūn added him as an omitted Companion. He will also be mentioned in the biography of his father ʿAbbās.

Anas ibn Fuḍāla ibn ʿAdī ibn Ḥarām ibn al-Hutaym ibn Ẓafar al-Anṣārī al-Ẓafarī. ## Source unit 277 · printed entry 277

### English candidate

Anas ibn Mālik ibn al-Naḍr ibn Ḍamḍam ibn Zayd ibn Ḥarām ibn Jundab ibn ʿĀmir ibn Ghanm ibn ʿAdī ibn al-Najjār, Abū Ḥamza al-Anṣārī al-Khazrajī, servant of the Messenger of God ﷺ and one of those who related abundantly from him. It is soundly reported from him that he said, ‘The Prophet ﷺ arrived in Medina when I was ten years old.’ His mother, Umm Sulaym, brought him to the Prophet ﷺ when he arrived and said, ‘This is Anas, a boy who will serve you,’ and he accepted him. The Prophet ﷺ gave him the kunyah Abū Ḥamza after a herb that he used to gather. The Prophet ﷺ also joked with him and said, ‘O you with the two ears!’

Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Anṣārī said: ‘Anas went out with the Messenger of God ﷺ to Badr as a boy serving him. My father informed me, from a client of Anas, that he asked Anas, “Did you witness Badr?” Anas replied, “Where would I have been absent from Badr? May you be bereft of your mother!”’ I say: He was not listed among the men of Badr only because he was not old enough to fight.

Al-Tirmidhī said: Maḥmūd ibn Ghaylān related to us; Abū Dāwūd related to us, from Abū Khalda, who said: ‘I asked Abū al-ʿĀliya, “Did Anas hear from the Prophet ﷺ?” He replied, “He served him for ten years, and the Prophet ﷺ prayed for him.”’ Anas had an orchard that bore fruit twice each year. It contained sweet basil from which came the fragrance of musk. After the Prophet ﷺ, Anas remained in Medina, then participated in the conquests, then settled in Basra and died there. ʿAlī ibn al-Madīnī said: ‘He was the last of the Companions to die in Basra.’

Al-Bukhārī said: Mūsā related to us; Isḥāq ibn ʿUthmān related to us: ‘I asked Mūsā ibn Anas, “How many campaigns did Anas undertake with the Prophet ﷺ?” He replied, “Eight campaigns.”’ Ibn al-Sakan transmitted by way of Ṣafwān ibn Hubayra, from his father, who said: Thābit al-Bunānī said to me: ‘Anas ibn Mālik said to me, “This is a hair from the hair of the Messenger of God ﷺ. Place it beneath my tongue.” I placed it beneath his tongue, and he was buried with it beneath his tongue.’ Muʿtamir related from his father that he heard Anas ibn Mālik say, ‘No one remains who prayed toward both qiblahs except me.’

Jarīr ibn Ḥāzim said: ‘I asked Shuʿayb ibn al-Ḥabḥāb, “When did Anas die?” He replied, “In the year 90.”’ Ibn Shāhīn transmitted it. Saʿīd ibn ʿUfayr, al-Haytham ibn ʿAdī, and Muʿtamir ibn Sulaymān said that he died in 91. Ibn Shāhīn said: ʿUthmān ibn Aḥmad related to us; Ḥanbal related to us; Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal related to us; Muʿtamir ibn Sulaymān related to us, from Ḥumayd, with the same report, adding that he was one hundred years old less one year. Ibn Saʿd related from al-Wāqidī, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Zayd al-Hudhalī, that he was present with Anas ibn Mālik in the year 92. Abū Nuʿaym al-Kūfī said that Anas died in 93. Al-Madāʾinī and Khalīfa also dated his death to that year, and Khalīfa added that he was 103 years old. Ibn Shāhīn related from Yaḥyā ibn Bukayr that he died at the age of 101. He said that it was also said that he was 107. Al-Baghawī transmitted the same from ʿUmar ibn Shabba, from Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Anṣārī.

Al-Ṭabarānī said: Jaʿfar al-Firyābī related to us; Ibrāhīm ibn ʿUthmān al-Maṣṣīṣī related to us; Makhlad ibn al-Ḥusayn related to us, from Hishām ibn Ḥassān, from Ḥafṣa, from Anas, who said: ‘Umm Sulaym said, “Messenger of God, pray to God for Anas.” He said, “O God, increase his wealth and his children, and bless him in them.”’ Anas said, ‘I have buried 125 of my direct offspring, not counting my grandchildren, and my land bears fruit twice each year.’

Jaʿfar ibn Sulaymān related from Thābit, from Anas: ‘Umm Sulaym brought me to the Prophet ﷺ when I was a boy and said, “Messenger of God, this is Anas; pray to God for him.” The Prophet ﷺ said, “O God, increase his wealth and his children, and admit him into Paradise.”’ Anas said, ‘I have seen two of these, and I hope for the third.’

Jaʿfar also related from Thābit: ‘I was with Anas when his estate manager came and said, “Abū Ḥamza, our land is parched.” Anas rose, performed ablution, went out into the open country, prayed two rakʿahs, and then supplicated. I saw the clouds join together; then it rained until it filled everything. When the rain subsided, Anas sent one of his family and said, “See how far the rain reached.” He looked and found that it had extended only a little beyond Anas’s land. This occurred in summer.’

ʿAlī ibn al-Jaʿd related from Shuʿba, from Thābit, that Abū Hurayra said: ‘I have not seen anyone whose prayer more closely resembled that of the Messenger of God ﷺ than the son of Umm Sulaym’—meaning Anas. Al-Ṭabarānī transmitted in al-Awsaṭ, by way of ʿUbayd ibn ʿAmr al-Aṣbaḥī, from Abū Hurayra: ‘Anas ibn Mālik informed me that the Prophet ﷺ used to gesture during prayer.’ Al-Ṭabarānī said: ‘We know of no hadith that Abū Hurayra related from Anas other than this one.’

Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Anṣārī said: Ibn ʿAwn related to us, from Mūsā ibn Anas, that when Abū Bakr became caliph he sent for Anas in order to dispatch him to Bahrain to collect the alms levy. ʿUmar came in, and Abū Bakr consulted him. ʿUmar said, ‘Send him, for he is intelligent and a scribe.’ So he sent him. The merits and virtues of Anas are exceedingly numerous.

## Source unit 278 · printed entry 278

### English candidate

Anas ibn Mālik al-Kaʿbī al-Qushayrī, Abū Umayya; he is also said to have been Abū Umayma or Abū Mayya. He settled in Basra and related from the Prophet ﷺ a hadith concerning the lifting of the fast from a traveler; the report includes an incident involving him and the Prophet. The compilers of the Sunan and Aḥmad transmitted it, and al-Tirmidhī and others graded it sound.

In Ibn Mājah’s version he is described as ‘Anas ibn Mālik, a man of Banū ʿAbd al-Ashhal,’ which is an error. Abū Dāwūd’s version says, ‘Anas ibn Mālik, a man of Banū ʿAbd Allāh ibn Kaʿb, the brothers of Qushayr.’ This is correct, and al-Bukhārī stated it decisively in his entry. On this basis he was Kaʿbī, not Qushayrī: Qushayr was a son of Kaʿb, and Kaʿb had another son named ʿAbd Allāh, so Anas belonged to Qushayr’s brothers, not to Qushayr himself.

Al-Rushāṭī criticized Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr’s statement, ‘He was Qushayrī, and it is also said Kaʿbī,’ by saying, ‘Kaʿb was Qushayr’s brother, not a descendant of Qushayr.’ Yet Kaʿb was Qushayr’s father, not his brother. والله أعلم.

A version transmitted by al-Baghawī and Ibn Shāhīn, by way of ʿIṣām ibn Yaḥyā, from Abū Qilāba, from ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Ziyād, from Abū Umayma, a man of Banū Juʿda, likewise relates the hadith.

## Source unit 280 · printed entry 280

### English candidate

Anas ibn Mudrik ibn Kaʿb ibn ʿAmr ibn Saʿd ibn ʿAwf ibn al-ʿAtīk ibn Jābir ibn ʿĀmir ibn Taym Allāh ibn Mubashshir ibn Aklub—with a ḍamma on the lām—al-Khathʿamī, then al-Aklabī. His kunyah was Abū Sufyān. Ibn Shāhīn mentioned him among the Companions and transmitted from Muḥammad ibn Ibrāhīm, from Muḥammad ibn Yazīd, from his authorities, who gave this genealogy and then said, ‘I know of no hadith of his.’ Ibn al-Kalbī also mentioned him and gave his genealogy. He said that Anas was a poet who attained leadership, but, as was his practice with such men, did not say that he had Companionship. Abū ʿUbayd, Ibn Jundab, and Ibn Ḥazm followed Ibn al-Kalbī.

Ibn Fatḥūn mentioned him in the supplement to al-Istīʿāb, from al-Ṭabarī, and said that he was a poet and was killed while fighting alongside ʿAlī. Abū Ḥātim al-Sijistānī mentioned him in al-Muʿammarīn and said: ‘He was the chief and horseman of Khathʿam in the pre-Islamic period. He lived into Islam, embraced it, and lived 154 years.’ When he reached that age he said:

‘When a man has lived al-Hunayda—a hundred years—in safety,
and fifty years after that, and four,
the bitterness of life replaces its sweetness,
and he soon wears away and begins to totter;
a hostage to the innermost house, never leaving it,
a cast-off thing, lying there, never quitting his bed;
he tells of those who died until it is as though
he had seen al-Ṣaʿb Dhū al-Qarnayn or seen Tubbaʿ.’

Another authority said that Khālid ibn al-Walīd married Anas’s daughter, and she bore him ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, ʿAbd Allāh, and al-Muhājir. Al-Marzubānī said that Anas was one of the horsemen of Khathʿam in the pre-Islamic period; he later embraced Islam and settled in Kufa. He is the one who said:

‘I enter wars while my coat is double mail
covering my fingertips, and my sword a keen, stalwart blade.’

His accounts from the pre-Islamic period are numerous. Among them is what Abū ʿUbayda related in al-Dībāj, from al-Muntajiʿ ibn Nabhān, who said: Al-Sulayk ibn al-Sulaka, the famous poet, used to give ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Muwaylik al-Khathʿamī tribute from his spoils as payment for his protection. Returning from one of his raids, he passed a house belonging to Khathʿam whose men were away. In it was a plump young woman. He asked her, ‘Where are the people?’ She said, ‘Away.’ He forced himself upon her. When he had finished and risen from her, she hurried to the water and told the people what had happened. Anas ibn Mudrik al-Khathʿamī mounted, caught al-Sulayk, and killed him. ʿAbd al-Malik said, ‘I will kill his killer, or he must pay his blood price.’ Anas replied, ‘By God, I will never pay it, because of his depravity.’

Abū al-Faraj al-Iṣfahānī also related a long story involving Anas and Durayd ibn al-Ṣimma in the pre-Islamic period. Al-Zubayr ibn Bakkār mentioned in al-Nasab that ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ḥārith al-Wādiʿī used to come to Mecca every year. Anas ibn Mudrik al-Khathʿamī encountered him, raided him, and stripped him of his possessions. He then said verses about it, among them:

‘My she-camel did not set out because my face was evil,
that a gatekeeper should bar her from your bounty.
Anas transgressed after the midday halt and turned us
from the House when means of gain had failed him.’

## Source unit 281 · printed entry 281

### English candidate

Anas ibn Abī Marthad al-Ghanawī. Abū Marthad’s name was Kannāz ibn al-Ḥuṣayn; his complete genealogy will appear in his father’s entry. Anas’s kunyah was Abū Yazīd. Ibn Manda said that the difference in age between him and his father was twenty years.

Abū Dāwūd, al-Nasāʾī, al-Baghawī, al-Ṭabarānī, and Ibn Manda transmitted by way of Abū Tawba, from Muʿāwiya ibn Sallām, from Zayd ibn Sallām, who heard Abū Sallām say: ‘Al-Salūlī—that is, Abū Kabsha—related to us that Sahl ibn al-Ḥanẓaliyya related to him that they traveled with the Prophet ﷺ on the day of Ḥunayn. They prolonged their march until evening, when the noon prayer came due.’ He then related the hadith, which includes the Messenger of God ﷺ asking, ‘Who will guard us tonight?’ Anas ibn Abī Marthad al-Ghanawī replied, ‘I will, Messenger of God.’ At the end of the hadith, the Messenger of God ﷺ asked him, ‘Did you dismount during the night?’ He replied, ‘No, except to pray or relieve myself.’ He said, ‘You have made [Paradise] incumbent for yourself; it will not harm you if you do no deed after this.’ Its chain meets the criteria of the Ṣaḥīḥ.

Ibn Ḥibbān and Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr mentioned that he was named Unays. Al-Baghawī distinguished Anas ibn Abī Marthad from Unays ibn Abī Marthad. Ibn Shāhīn likewise distinguished Anas ibn Abī Marthad al-Ghanawī from Unays ibn Marthad ibn Abī Marthad. In the entry on Unays he said: ‘Ibn Saʿd said: He was the Prophet’s ﷺ scout at Awṭās, his kunyah was Abū Yazīd, he died in the year 20, and the difference in age between him and his father was twenty-one years.’ All of these are descriptions of Anas ibn Abī Marthad, as set out above. والله أعلم. Al-Bukhārī made this clear, saying: ‘Anas ibn Abī Marthad; he is also called Unays ibn Abī Marthad.’

## Source unit 283 · printed entry 283

### English candidate

Anas ibn al-Naḍr ibn Ḍamḍam, the Anṣārī of the Khazraj, paternal uncle of Anas ibn Mālik, the servant of the Prophet ﷺ. His full lineage was given above in the biography of Anas ibn Mālik.

Al-Bukhārī transmitted, by way of Ḥumayd, from Anas, that his uncle Anas ibn al-Naḍr had been absent from the fighting at Badr. He said, “O Messenger of God, I was absent from the first battle in which you fought the polytheists. By God, if God lets me witness battle against the polytheists, God will certainly see what I do.” When the Day of Uḥud came and the Muslims broke ranks, he said, “O God, I apologize to You for what these people have done”—meaning the Muslims—“and I declare myself innocent before You of what these people have brought”—meaning the polytheists. He then advanced and met Saʿd ibn Muʿādh. He said, “O Saʿd! It is Paradise, by the Lord of Anas! I can smell its fragrance on this side of Uḥud.” Saʿd said, “I could not do what he did.” Anas was killed that day; the report continues.

The report is also in al-Bukhārī by way of Thumāma, from Anas. Ibn Manda transmitted it by way of Ḥammād ibn Salama, from Thābit, from Anas. He will also be mentioned in the biography of al-Rubayyiʿ bint al-Naḍr, إن شاء الله تعالى.
