## Source unit 517 · printed entry 517

### English candidate

Usāma ibn Mālik, Abū al-ʿAshrāʾ al-Dārimī. Abū Mūsā said: 'ʿAbdān included him and erred, for Abū al-ʿAshrāʾ had no companionship; rather, the companionship belonged to his father. There is extensive disagreement over his name and his father's name.' I say: He also stated decisively among the Companions that the name of Abū al-ʿAshrāʾ's father was Usāma ibn Mālik ibn Qahṭam ibn Ḥayyān, saying under the letter alif: 'Usāma ibn Mālik ibn Qahṭam, the father of Abū al-ʿAshrāʾ al-Dārimī. It is also said that his name was ʿUṭārid ibn Barz, and it is said Yasār ibn Balz.' He then cited his report by way of Ḥammād ibn Salama, from Abū al-ʿAshrāʾ, from his father. I say: What is recognized among hadith scholars is that Usāma was the name of Abū al-ʿAshrāʾ, not the name of his father. والله أعلم.

## Source unit 521 · printed entry 521

### English candidate

Asad al-Turkī. He is mentioned in a fabricated report. Al-Dhahabī mentioned him in al-Tajrīd in this abbreviated form. What is astonishing is not Bahrām's narration from al-Ḥāmidī; what is astonishing is ʿUmar al-Nasafī's transmitting this in his book without denouncing him—indeed, transmitting it as one who thought it a hadith.' ## Source unit 524 · printed entry 524

### English candidate

The Bishop of Najrān. Abū Mūsā mentioned him in the Supplement and said: 'I do not know whether he accepted Islam.' He then cited the report of Ibn Isḥāq, from Jabala, from Ibn Masʿūd, that the Bishop of Najrān came to the Prophet ﷺ and said, 'Send with me a trustworthy man.' The Prophet ﷺ said, 'I shall certainly send with you a man who is trustworthy—truly trustworthy,' to the end of the report. It contains no mention of his accepting Islam. Ibn Isḥāq stated that the Bishop of Najrān did not accept Islam. It has been said that this Bishop of Najrān was named al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAlqama, of the Banū Bakr ibn Wāʾil. 'Bishop' is a title borne by the leading Christians.

## Source unit 525 · printed entry 525

### English candidate

Aslam the shepherd, Abū Salmā. Ibn Mandah said that he was martyred at Khaybar. He then cited the report of Abū Salām, who said: 'Abū Salmā the shepherd related to us, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: “Excellent, excellent are five! How heavy they are in the Scale.”' Abū Nuʿaym said: 'He erred in naming Abū Salmā, whose name was actually Ḥurayth, and in saying that he was martyred at Khaybar, because someone martyred at Khaybar could not be described by Abū Salām as having related to us.' This is a well-directed objection, because Abū Salām had no companionship. The truth is that two biographies became conflated for Ibn Mandah: the shepherd who was killed at Khaybar is not the shepherd whose kunya was Abū Salmā. والله أعلم.

## Source unit 528 · printed entry 528

### English candidate

Ismāʿīl ibn Abī Ḥakīm al-Muzanī, then one of the Banū Fuḍayl. Ibn Mandah included him and said: 'Al-Bukhārī listed him in al-Afrād, but I know of neither companionship nor transmission for him.' In my view, this isnad is disconnected.' I say: It is an error. The correct wording is 'Ismāʿīl ibn Abī Ḥakīm al-Madanī, from one of the Banū Fuḍayl.' Al-Madanī was corrupted into al-Muzanī, and ʿan, 'from,' into thumma, 'then.' ## Source unit 529 · printed entry 529

### English candidate

Ismāʿīl ibn Zayd ibn Thābit al-Anṣārī. Abū Mūsā mentioned him in the Dhayl and transmitted, by way of Ibn Mardawayh with his chain, from Zakariyyā ibn Ismāʿīl al-Zaydī, a descendant of Zayd ibn Thābit, from his father, who said: ‘A group of us Companions went out with the Messenger of God ﷺ on one of the military expeditions. We reached a junction of roads, and a Bedouin appeared holding his camel’s halter’—the rest of the hadith.

Abū Mūsā said, ‘Ismāʿīl is ibn Zayd ibn Thābit. He is a Successor who transmitted from his father, and I do not know that he lived during the Prophet’s time ﷺ.’ Ibn al-Athīr argued for the correctness of that judgment on the ground that Zayd was young during the time of the Prophet ﷺ. He said, ‘Ismāʿīl is a Successor, and no weight should be given to his transmitting this hadith without naming the intermediary, for the Successors continually transmitted disconnected reports.’ Thus he spoke.

That argument is open to objection. If the wording were sound, it would establish Companionship for Ismāʿīl. A Successor may indeed transmit a disconnected report, but he does not report of something he did not witness that he witnessed it. As you can see, the wording says, ‘We went out with the Messenger of God ﷺ until we stopped …’ It is possible to take that figuratively, but that is contrary to the apparent sense. My view is that either ‘from his grandfather’ fell out of the chain, or Zakariyyā intended by ‘from his father’ his grandfather Zayd, since a grandfather is a father.

Ibn Ḥibbān listed Ismāʿīl ibn Zayd ibn Thābit among the Successors and said that his kunya was Abū Muṣʿab and that he was Zayd ibn Thābit’s youngest child. Al-Bukhārī likewise listed him among the Successors and recorded from him, on his father’s authority, a report that stops at the Companion.

### Arabic authority

<div dir="rtl" lang="ar">

إسماعيل بن زيد بن ثابت الأنصاري ذكره أبو موسى في الذيل وأخرج من طريق بن مردويه بسنده عن زكريا بن إسماعيل الزيدي من ولد زيد بن ثابت عن أبيه قال خرجنا جماعة من الصحابة غزاة من الغزوات مع رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم حتى وقفنا في مجمع طرق وطلع أعرابي عند خطام بعيره الحديث قال أبو موسى إسماعيل هو بن زيد بن ثابت وهو تابعي يروي عن أبيه لا أعلم له إدراكا للنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم واستدل بن الأثير على صحة ذلك بان زيدا كان صغيرا على عهد النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم وقال إسماعيل تابعي ولا عبرة بإرسال هذا الحديث فإن التابعين لم يزالوا يرون المراسيل كذا قال وفيه نظر لأن السياق لو صح لأثبت لإسماعيل الصحبة فإن التابعي وإن كان يرسل لكن لايخبر بشيء لم يشاهده أنه شاهده وأنت ترى في السياق قوله خرجنا مع رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم حتى وقفنا لكن يجوز أن يحمل على المجاز وهو خلاف الظاهر والذي عندي أنه إما أن يكون سقط من الإسناد عن جده أو أراد زكريا بقوله عن أبيه عن جده زيد لأن الجد أب وقد ذكر إسماعيل بن زيد بن ثابت في التابعين بن حبان وقال يكنى أبا مصعب وهو أصغر ولد زيد بن ثابت وكذا ذكره البخاري في التابعين وذكر له عن أبيه حديثا موقوفا

## Source unit 532 · printed entry 532

### English candidate

Al-Aswad ibn Ḥāritha. ## Source unit 533 · printed entry 533

### English candidate

Al-Aswad, without a patronymic. Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said: Hushaym and Abū ʿAwāna transmitted from Yaʿlā ibn ʿAṭāʾ, from ʿĀmir ibn al-Aswad, from his father, that he witnessed the Farewell Pilgrimage with the Messenger of God ﷺ. He said, ‘I attended the dawn prayer with him in the mosque of al-Khayf. When he had completed his prayer, there were two men at the rear of the people who had not prayed. They were brought to him with their shoulder muscles trembling. He asked, “What kept you from praying with us?”’—the rest of the hadith.

Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said that Shuʿba differed from them, transmitting it from Yaʿlā ibn ʿAṭāʾ, from Jābir ibn Yazīd ibn al-Aswad, from his father, with exactly the same report. I say: this is an error produced by a copyist’s corruption and omission. Hushaym and Abū ʿAwāna did not differ from Shuʿba, nor did Shuʿba differ from them. All of them agreed on Yaʿlā ibn ʿAṭāʾ, from Jābir ibn Yazīd ibn al-Aswad, from his father. Abū Dāwūd transmitted it from Ḥafṣ ibn ʿUmar, from Shuʿba. Al-Tirmidhī, al-Nasāʾī, and al-Baghawī transmitted it from Hushaym, while al-Baghawī also transmitted it from Abū ʿAwāna; his version is the fullest.

I think that in the version which reached Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr, Yazīd—the father of Jābir—fell out, and Jābir was miscopied as ʿĀmir. He therefore read it as ‘ʿĀmir ibn al-Aswad, from his father’ and created a biography for al-Aswad. I then saw the same erroneous omission in al-Fākihī’s Kitāb Makka: al-Fākihī said, ‘Ḥusayn ibn Ḥasan related to us: Hushaym related to us, from Yaʿlā ibn ʿAṭāʾ, from Jābir ibn al-Aswad, from his father.’ It agrees with the group in reading Jābir rather than corrupting it, but attributes Jābir to his grandfather.

It is astonishing that Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr included this very hadith in al-Tamhīd, in the biography of Zayd ibn Aslam, by way of ʿAlī ibn al-Madīnī, from Hushaym, from Yaʿlā ibn ʿAṭāʾ, from Jābir ibn Yazīd ibn al-Aswad, from his father—the correct form. Immediately afterward he said, ‘Shuʿba transmitted it from Yaʿlā ibn ʿAṭāʾ in exactly the same way,’ explicitly affirming the agreement of Shuʿba and Hushaym, contrary to what he wrote in al-Istīʿāb. God is the granter of success.

## Source unit 534 · printed entry 534

### English candidate

Al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd al-Asad ibn Hilāl al-Makhzūmī, brother of Abū Salama. Abū Mūsā mentioned him on the authority of ʿAbdān, who said, ‘No transmission is known from him, except that Ibn ʿAbbās mentioned him.’ Ibn al-Athīr objected that Ibn al-Kalbī and al-Zubayr ibn Bakkār stated that he was killed at Badr as an unbeliever. It is as they said. Kaʿb ibn Mālik mentioned him in a poem about the battle of Badr, including:

‘At the trampled watering place, seventy of them remained—
ʿUtba among them, and al-Aswad.’

Ibn ʿAbbās mentioned him only among the mockers, so there is no basis for including him among the Companions. As for his nephew al-Aswad ibn Sufyān ibn ʿAbd al-Asad, he was discussed earlier in the first section. ʿAbdān cannot have intended him, because Ibn ʿAbbās did not mention him.

This al-Aswad had a daughter named Fāṭima. Ibn Saʿd mentioned her and said that she embraced Islam and pledged allegiance. She is the woman whose hand was cut off for theft, according to the sound view. The explanation of that will come in her biography, إن شاء الله تعالى.

## Source unit 535 · printed entry 535

### English candidate

Asīd—with an open first letter and a kasra on the sīn—ibn Abī Usayd—the latter with a ḍamma and in the diminutive—al-Sāʿidī. Abū Mūsā mentioned him on the authority of ʿAbdān, who said: Muḥammad ibn Sinān related to us: Abū ʿĀṣim related to us, from Mūsā ibn ʿUbayda: ʿUmar ibn al-Ḥakam related to me, from Asīd ibn Abī Usayd, that the Messenger of God ﷺ married a woman of the Banū al-Jawn. Asīd said, ‘He sent me, and I brought her and lodged her in the ravine’—then he related the story of the woman who sought refuge.

Abū Mūsā objected that ʿUmar ibn al-Ḥakam in fact transmitted it from Abū Usayd himself. Al-Ḥasan ibn Sufyān likewise included it in his Musnad from Muḥammad ibn al-Faraj, from Muḥammad ibn al-Zibriqān, from Mūsā ibn ʿUbayda; this is the well-known version. I say: Mūsā ibn ʿUbayda is weak, as is Muḥammad ibn Sinān. It is possible that ‘from his father’ fell out of the first chain, for Asīd ibn Usayd is a well-known Successor whose death was delayed until the caliphate of Abū Jaʿfar al-Manṣūr, as Ibn Ḥibbān mentioned in al-Thiqāt among the Successors. Al-Bukhārī also transmitted the hadith of the woman who sought refuge by way of Ḥamza ibn Abī Usayd, from his father.

## Source unit 539 · printed entry 539

### English candidate

Usayd—with a ḍamma—described as a nephew of Rāfiʿ ibn Khadīj. Ibn Manda mentioned him and said: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Yaḥyā related to us: Abū Masʿūd related to us: Ḥammād ibn Masʿada related to us, from Ibn Jurayj, from ʿIkrima ibn Khālid, that Usayd related to him that the Messenger of God ﷺ said, ‘When a man finds his stolen property and its holder is not suspected, he may, if he wishes, take it for its price’—the rest of the hadith.

Abū Nuʿaym objected that Abū Masʿūd, by whose route Ibn Manda transmitted it, included the report in the Musnad of Usayd ibn Ẓuhayr. I say: Abū Masʿūd did not supply his lineage, for a reason I shall mention. Abū Dāwūd and al-Nasāʾī transmitted it from Hārūn al-Ḥammāl, from Ḥammād ibn Masʿada, and in their versions the name occurs as Usayd ibn Ḥuḍayr. Abū Dāwūd added: Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal said, ‘In Ibn Jurayj’s book it is Usayd ibn Ẓuhayr, but this is how he related it to them in Basra.’ ʿAbd al-Razzāq also transmitted it from Ibn Jurayj as Usayd ibn Ẓuhayr; Isḥāq ibn Rāhawayh included it in his Musnad from ʿAbd al-Razzāq, and al-Nasāʾī included it by another route from him. Rawḥ ibn ʿUbāda corroborated ʿAbd al-Razzāq in transmitting it from Ibn Jurayj. From this it is known that the narrator is Usayd ibn Ẓuhayr. Ibn Manda had already mentioned him, so there is no basis for separating the two entries.

There is a further objection to the phrase ‘nephew of Rāfiʿ’: Usayd ibn Ẓuhayr was Rāfiʿ’s cousin, not his nephew. Rāfiʿ did, however, have a brother’s son named Usayd, counted among the Successors; Ibn Ḥibbān and others mentioned him. That Usayd transmitted from his paternal uncle Rāfiʿ ibn Khadīj. والله أعلم.

## Source unit 540 · printed entry 540

### English candidate

Usayr—with a ḍamma and a final rāʾ—a man of Aslam. ## Source unit 541 · printed entry 541

### English candidate

Al-Ashajj. He is mentioned in a fabricated report forged by Maḥmūd ibn ʿAlī al-Ṭarāzī, one of the liars who lived after the year 500. He said: ‘Al-Ashajj, a Companion of the Prophet ﷺ, related to us: “Four hundred and fifty men of us set out for trade. I embraced Islam at the hand of ʿAlī, who took me to the Prophet ﷺ while he was dividing the spoils of Badr”’—the rest of the hadith.

Abū Hurayra informed me, from al-Dhahabī by authorization, from Ibrāhīm ibn Ḥamawayh: al-Ẓahīr al-Bukhārī informed us: Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Sattār al-Kurdī informed us, from Maḥmūd ibn ʿAlī, from this al-Ashajj, with another, different report. I then came upon a copy containing more than forty hadiths by another route, from Qays ibn Tamīm, from al-Ashajj. It related this story and other hadiths, most of which are fabricated; their fabrication is glaringly obvious. I shall discuss that under the letter qāf, إن شاء الله تعالى.

I read in a book by Abū Saʿd al-Samʿānī that he said, ‘I saw Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn al-Shāshī. He was a shaykh much given to weeping, who recited poems and narrated tales. He would say, “I saw al-Ashajj, and I heard my teacher al-Ashajj say: I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say, ‘From stick to stick, the backs of the woodcutters grow heavy; and from slip to slip, the sins of the sinners multiply.’”’ End of quotation. I do not know whether he was Qays or someone else.

## Source unit 544 · printed entry 544

### English candidate

Ashʿab ibn Umm Ḥumayda, known for greed. Mughlaṭāy mentioned him in his marginalia on Usd al-Ghāba and said: “He was born in the ninth year after the Hijra, and his mother used to visit the wives of the Prophet ﷺ.” Abū al-Faraj al-Iṣbahānī mentioned this. End.

By this he intended to establish that Ashʿab was born during the lifetime of the Messenger of God ﷺ, so that he would be counted in the second division. I cannot see that this is sound, because Abū al-Faraj mentioned it only through a feeble route from ʿUbayda ibn Ashʿab, from his father.

Ibn ʿAsākir, however, transmitted in Ashʿab’s biography, through Naṣr ibn ʿAlī al-Jahḍamī, from al-Aṣmaʿī, who said: Ashʿab told me, “I was born on the day ʿUthmān was killed.”

As for what Wakīʿ al-Qāḍī transmitted in Ghurar al-Akhbār, from Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Ḥamza, from al-Māzinī, from al-Aṣmaʿī, who said: Ashʿab related to me, “I heard Ṭuways sing these two verses at the wedding of Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam to Umm ʿAbd al-Malik,” followed by a story—this is also open to question, because ʿAbd al-Malik was born during ʿUthmān’s caliphate.

It is therefore evident that Ashʿab cannot be trusted in what he says. Had that claim been sound, he would have transmitted from the senior Companions. Yet we have found no transmission of his from a Companion except Ibn ʿUmar and ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar. His transmissions from the Successors are numerous, such as Sālim, al-Qāsim, and Fāṭima bint al-Ḥusayn.

It is enough to disprove the first view that they agreed he died in 154 AH. We have already established that, after 110 AH, no one remained who had lived into the time of the Prophet ﷺ. Ashʿab’s biography is given at length in my book Lisān al-Mīzān.

## Source unit 549 · printed entry 549

### English candidate

Ukaydir of Dūma. He was Ukaydir ibn ʿAbd al-Malik ibn ʿAbd al-Jinn ibn Aʿyā ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Muʿāwiya ibn Ḥalāwa ibn Usāma ibn Salama ibn Shukāma ibn Shabīb ibn al-Sakūn, the lord of Dūmat al-Jandal. Ibn Manda and Abū Nuʿaym listed him among the Companions. They said that the Prophet ﷺ wrote to him and sent a detachment against him with Khālid ibn al-Walīd; then he accepted Islam and presented the Prophet ﷺ with a striped silk robe, which he gave to ʿUmar.

Ibn al-Athīr objected to this, saying: He merely presented a gift to the Prophet ﷺ and made a treaty with him; he did not accept Islam. There is no disagreement about this among the biographers. Whoever says that he accepted Islam has made an obvious error. Rather, he was a Christian. After the Prophet ﷺ made a treaty with him, he returned to his fortress and remained there. Khālid ibn al-Walīd later captured him during the days of Abū Bakr and killed him as an unbeliever.

Al-Balādhurī, however, states that when Ukaydir of Dūma came to the Prophet ﷺ with Khālid, he accepted Islam and returned to Dūma. When the Prophet ﷺ died, he apostatized and withheld what he had previously undertaken; when Khālid ibn al-Walīd traveled from Iraq to Syria, he killed him. Ibn al-Athīr said: In any event, he ought not to be listed among the Companions. I say: Ibn al-Kalbī states that when he withheld what he had agreed by treaty to pay, Abū Bakr expelled him to al-Ḥīra; another report says that ʿUmar expelled him.

Ibn Manda’s principal evidence that he accepted Islam is a report he transmitted by way of Bilāl ibn Yaḥyā, from Ḥudhayfa: the Prophet ﷺ sent a force to Dūmat al-Jandal and said, “You will find Ukaydir of Dūma outside.” He then related a report of Ukaydir’s acceptance of Islam; that is how it appears in his version. We have related it in the Additions to the Maghāzī by way of Yūnus ibn Bukayr, from Saʿd ibn Aws, from Bilāl ibn Yaḥyā, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ appointed Abū Bakr over the Emigrants going to Dūmat al-Jandal and appointed Khālid ibn al-Walīd over the Bedouins accompanying him. He said, “Go, for you will find Ukaydir of Dūma hunting wild animals. Seize him firmly, send him to me, and do not kill him.” They proceeded, besieged its people, seized him, and sent him to the Prophet. This account does not mention that he accepted Islam.

Abū Yaʿlā and Ibn Shāhīn related, by way of ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Iyāḍ ibn Laqīṭ, who said, “I heard my father Iyāḍ relate,” from Qays ibn al-Nuʿmān al-Sakūnī: The cavalry of the Messenger of God ﷺ rode out. When Ukaydir of Dūmat al-Jandal heard of it, he went to the Messenger of God ﷺ and said, “Messenger of God, I have heard that your cavalry has ridden out, and I fear for my land and my property. Write me a document so that they will not molest anything belonging to me, for I acknowledge the obligation that is rightly due from me.” The Messenger of God ﷺ wrote for him. Ukaydir then brought out a gold-woven brocade qabāʾ of the sort Khusraw used to clothe them in and said, “Messenger of God, accept this from me; I have given it to you as a gift.” He said, “Take your qabāʾ back. No one who wears this in the present world but will be forbidden it in the Hereafter.” Ukaydir carried it back to his baggage until he reached his lodging. Then it troubled him that his gift had been returned, so he came back and said, “Messenger of God, we are a household for whom it is hard to have our gift returned. Accept my gift from me.” He said, “Give it to ʿUmar,” and the narrator related the rest of the story. Perhaps the basis of those who said that Ukaydir accepted Islam was his address, “Messenger of God,” in this report.

In Aḥmad’s Musnad, by way of Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr ibn ʿAlqama, from Wāqid ibn ʿAmr ibn Saʿd ibn Muʿādh, from Anas: “The Messenger of God ﷺ sent a detachment against Ukaydir of Dūma, and Ukaydir sent the Messenger of God ﷺ a brocade robe interwoven with gold. The Messenger of God ﷺ put it on, then stood—or sat—upon the pulpit, and the people began to touch it.” Al-Tirmidhī and al-Nasāʾī transmitted the report by this route. Aḥmad also transmitted, by way of ʿAlī ibn Zayd, from Anas: “Ukaydir of Dūma gave the Prophet ﷺ a jar of manna, and he gave each person a piece,” to the end of the report.

Ibn Manda also transmitted by way of ʿAlī ibn Isḥāq, who said: Rizq ibn Abī Rizq ibn Ṣadaqa ibn Mahdī ibn Ḥurayth ibn Ukaydir ibn ʿAbd al-Malik related to us; our elders—that is, their fathers—related to us that the Prophet ﷺ went out with the people on campaign to Tabūk. He then related a long report. Ibn Manda said that another narrator related it “from his fathers, from his forefathers, down to Ukaydir.” Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal said, “This Ukaydir is Ukaydir of Dūma.” Ibn Manda therefore relied on Ukaydir’s transmission as evidence that he accepted Islam, but this inference is open to question.

Ibn Isḥāq recorded his story in the Maghāzī. He said: Yazīd ibn Rūmān and ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Bakr related to us that the Messenger of God ﷺ sent Khālid ibn al-Walīd to Ukaydir ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, a man of Kinda who ruled Dūma and was a Christian, saying, “You will find him hunting wild cattle.” He then related the story at length. It includes that Khālid killed Ḥassān, Ukaydir’s brother, and brought Ukaydir before the Messenger of God ﷺ, who spared his blood, made a treaty with him for payment of the jizya, released him, and allowed him to return to his town. ʿUrwa likewise related substantially the same story in the Maghāzī, in Ibn Lahīʿa’s transmission from Abū al-Aswad, from ʿUrwa. On this account, his arrival in Medina in Qays ibn al-Nuʿmān’s report occurred afterward.

This story will appear at length in the biography of Bujayr ibn Bajara al-Ṭāʾī under the letter bāʾ, if God Most High wills. Al-Bāwardī’s discussion will also appear in the biography of Ḥurayth ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, Ukaydir’s brother, under the letter ḥāʾ. Ibn Ḥabīb said, concerning Ḥassān’s famous poem rhyming in lām:

“If you see that the color of my head has changed—
gray, until it has become like whitened thaghām—
my two companions indeed once saw me as though
I were in Dūma’s palace, or at the very center of the sanctuary.”

Dūma lies between Syria and the Hijaz; it is Dūmat al-Jandal, belongs to Kalb, and was ruled by Ukaydir ibn ʿAbd al-Malik al-Sakūnī. The Prophet ﷺ sent Khālid ibn al-Walīd against him, and Khālid killed him there. Dūmān ibn Ismāʿīl had inhabited it.

Abū al-Saʿādāt Ibn al-Athīr, the brother of the author of Usd al-Ghāba, said: Some people say that Ukaydir accepted Islam, but this is not sound. Among those whose wording indicates that he accepted Islam is al-Wāqidī. He said in the Maghāzī: A shaykh from Dūma related to me that the Messenger of God ﷺ wrote this document for Ukaydir: “In the name of God, the All-Merciful, the Ever-Merciful. From the Messenger of God to Ukaydir, when Islam came and rival gods and idols were cast off, with Khālid ibn al-Walīd, the Sword of God, at Dūmat al-Jandal. They shall establish the prayer and give the alms. In that regard God’s covenant and compact rest upon you, and you are owed truthfulness and faithful fulfillment.”

What appears most likely is that Ukaydir initially made a treaty for payment of the jizya, as Ibn Isḥāq said. It remains possible that he accepted Islam afterward, as al-Wāqidī said, and then apostatized after the Prophet ﷺ together with those who apostatized, as al-Balādhurī said, and died in that state. والله أعلم.

أكيدر دومة هو أكيدر بن عبد الملك بن عبد الجن بن اعيا بن الحارث بن معاوية بن خلاوة بن أبامة بن سلمة بن شكامة بن شبيب بن السكون صاحب دومة الجندل ذكره بن منده وأبو نعيم في الصحابة وقال كتب إليه النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم وأرسل إليه سرية مع خالد بن الوليد ثم إنه أسلم وأهدى النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم حلة سيراء فوهبها لعمر وتعقب ذلك بن الأثير فقال إنما أهدى إلى النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم وصالحه ولم يسلم وهذا البلاذري أن أكيدر دومة لما قدم على النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم مع خالد أسلم وعاد إلى دومة فلما مات النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم ارتد ومنع ما قبله فلما سار خالد بن الوليد من العراق إلى الشام قتله قال بن الأثير فعلى كل حال لا ينبغي أن يذكر في الصحابة قلت وذكر بن الكلبي أنه لما منع ما صالح عليه اجلاه أبو بكر إلى الحيرة ويقال بل اجلاه عمر وعمدة بن منده في أنه أسلم ما أخرجه من طريق بلال بن يحيى عن حذيفة أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم بعث بعثا إلى دومة الجندل فقال إنكم ستجدون أكيدر دومة خارجا ثم ذكر حديث إسلامه كذا وقع فيه وقد رويناه في زيادات المغازي من طريق يونس بن بكير عن سعد بن أوس عن بلال بن يحيى قال بعث رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم أبا بكر على المهاجرين إلى دومة الجندل وبعث خالد بن الوليد على الأعراب معه وقال انطلقوا فإنكم ستجدون أكيدر دومة يقتنص الوحش فخذوه أخذا فابعثوا به إلى ولا تقتلوه فمضوا وحاصروا أهلها فأخذوه فبعثوا به إليه ولم يذكر في هذه القصة أنه أسلم وروى أبو يعلى وابن شاهين من طريق عبيد الله بن إياد لقيط سمعت أبي إيادا يحدث عن قيس بن النعمان السكوني قال خرجت خيل رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم فسمع بها أكيدر دومة الجندل فانطلق إلى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم فقال يا رسول الله بلغني أن خيلك انطلقت وإني خفت على ارضي ومالي فاكتبوا لي كتابا لا يعرضون في شيء هولي فإني أقر بالذي هو علي من الحق فكتب له رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم ثم إن أكيدر أخرج قباء من ديباج منسوج بالذهب مما كان كسرى يكسوهم فقال يا رسول الله أقبل مني هذا فإني اهديته لك فقال ارجع بقبائك فإنه ليس أحد يلبس هذا في الدنيا الا حرمه في الآخرة فرجع به إلى رحله حتى أتى منزله ثم إنه وجد في نفسه أن يرد عليه هديته فرجع فقال يا رسول الله إنا أهل بيت يشق علينا أن ترد هديتنا فاقبل مني هديتي فقال ادفعه إلى عمر فذكر القصة فلعل مستند أحمد من قال إنه أسلم قوله في هذا الحديث يا رسول الله وفي مسند أحمد من طريق محمد بن عمرو بن علقمة عن واقد بن عمرو بن سعد بن معاذ عن أنس قال بعث رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم بعثا إلى أكيدر دومة فأرسل إلى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم بجبة من ديباج منسوج فيها الذهب فلبسها رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم ثم قام على المنبر أو جلس فجعل الناس يلمسونها الحديث أخرجه الترمذي والنسائي من هذا الوجه وأخرجه أحمد أيضا من طريق علي بن زيد عن أنس أهدى أكيدر دومة للنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم جرة من من فأعطى لكل واحد قطعة الحديث وروى بن منده أيضا من طريق علي بن إسحاق قال حدثنا رزق بن أبي رزق بن صدقة بن مهدي بن حريث بن أكيدر بن عبد الملك قال حدثنا أشياخنا يعني آباءهم أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم خرج بالناس غازيا إلى تبوك فذكر حديثا طويلا قال ورواه غيره فقال عن آبائه عن أجداده إلى أكيدر قال أحمد بن حنبل أكيدر هذا هو أكيدر دومة فتمسك بن مندة لكونه أسلم بروايته وفيها نظر وقد ذكر بن إسحاق قصته في المغازي قال حدثنا يزيد بن رومان وعبد الله بن أبي بكر أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم بعث خالد ## Source unit 550 · printed entry 550

### English candidate

Umayya ibn Khālid. Ibn Ḥibbān said: 'He transmits mursal reports. Whoever claims that he had companionship has erred.' I say: A group mentioned him among the Companions, but it is an error, as we shall explain. The first to mention him, to my knowledge, was al-Baghawī, who said: 'Al-Qawārīrī related to us; Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd related to us, from Sufyān: Abū Isḥāq related to me, from Umayya ibn Khālid, who said: “The Messenger of God ﷺ used to seek victory through the indigent Emigrants.”' Al-Baghawī said: 'Umayya ibn Khālid—I do not think he had companionship, except that al-Qawārīrī and Ibn Abī Shayba included this report in their Musnads.' Ibn Qāniʿ said: 'Umayya ibn Khālid—I think that he had sight of the Prophet.' Al-ʿAskarī said: 'Umayya ibn Khālid ibn Usayd. Some mentioned that he had sight of the Prophet.' Al-Ṭabarānī also mentioned him. Ibn Mandah said: 'Umayya ibn Khālid ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Usayd al-Umawī. His companionship is open to question. He is counted among the Successors and died in the year eighty-six.' He then cited the report by way of Qays ibn al-Rabīʿ, from Abū Isḥāq, from al-Muhallab, from Umayya ibn Khālid ibn Usayd, and mentioned it. The lineage under which he gave the heading is inverted. Abū Nuʿaym mentioned him correctly, saying: 'Umayya ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Khālid ibn Usayd ibn Abī al-ʿĪṣ ibn Umayya.' He then cited his report, and its route correctly read 'from Umayya ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Khālid.' He said that his companionship was disputed. Al-Bāwardī before him said the same, and Ibn al-Jawzī followed him. Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr, however, said: 'Umayya ibn Khālid—his companionship is not sound in my view.' He said: 'It is also said that he was Umayya ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Khālid ibn Usayd.' I say: Al-Bukhārī clarified his case, saying: 'Umayya ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Khālid ibn Usayd heard Ibn ʿUmar.' He said: 'Ibn Mahdī reported from Sufyān, from Abū Isḥāq, from Umayya ibn Khālid ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Usayd.' Abū ʿUbayd said: 'In my view, he is Umayya ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Khālid'—meaning that the other form had inverted the lineage. Al-Ṭabarānī transmitted his report in al-Muʿjam al-Kabīr and gave his lineage correctly, saying: 'Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq ibn Rāhawayh related to us; my father related to us; ʿĪsā ibn Yūnus related to us, from his father, from his grandfather Abū Isḥāq, from Umayya ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Usayd, who said: “The Messenger of God ﷺ used to seek victory through the indigent Emigrants.”' By this same isnad up to Ibn Isḥāq, he said: 'Umayya ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Khālid ibn Usayd led us in prayer in Khurasan and, between the two sūras, recited, “Indeed, we seek Your help.”' I say: This Umayya had neither companionship nor sight of the Prophet, for the companionship belonged to his grandfather Khālid, who was the brother of ʿAttāb, the governor of Mecca. His father, ʿAbd Allāh, was a young child when the Prophet ﷺ died, and Muʿāwiya appointed him over Fārs. ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān appointed Umayya, the subject of this biography, over Khurasan. The account of his governorship is well known in the historical works. Al-Muhallab was with him in his army, as was Abū Isḥāq, as noted above. This Umayya's mother was Umm Ḥajar bint Shayba ibn ʿUthmān, herself a Successor. Umayya was sometimes ascribed to his grandfather Khālid, until some thought that Umayya ibn Khālid was a paternal uncle of Umayya ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Khālid. Were it not for the identity of the report and the fact that genealogists such as al-Zubayr and other Qurashī scholars mention no son of Khālid ibn Usayd other than ʿAbd Allāh, we could have allowed that possibility. In al-Bayhaqī's al-Sunan al-Kabīr, by way of al-Walīd ibn Muslim, from Saʿīd ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, from ʿAṭiyya ibn Qays, it says: 'Ibn ʿUmar and Abū Salama ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān wrote to Umayya ibn Khālid ibn Usayd, and he read their letter to us,' and he mentioned a story. In this route Umayya was ascribed to his grandfather. After mentioning Umayya ibn Khālid and what we cited earlier, Ibn Ḥibbān also said among the Successors: 'Umayya ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Khālid ibn Usayd narrates from Ibn ʿUmar; Abū Isḥāq al-Sabīʿī narrated from him. He died in the year eighty-six.' The critics faulted Ibn Ḥibbān for making them two persons, for he is one person, as we have explained. Al-Madāʾinī said that he died in the year eighty-seven.

## Source unit 551 · printed entry 551

### English candidate

Umayya ibn Khuwaylid ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Iyās ibn ʿAbd Nāshira ibn Kaʿb ibn Judayy ibn Ḍamra ibn Bakr ibn ʿAbd Manāt ibn Kināna, Abū ʿAmr al-Ḍamrī. Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said: 'He had companionship, and his son ʿAmr had companionship; ʿAmr's companionship is better known.' His report was narrated by Ibrāhīm ibn Ismāʿīl ibn Mujammiʿ, from Jaʿfar ibn ʿAmr ibn Umayya, from his father, from his grandfather, that the Prophet ﷺ sent him out alone as a spy, and he mentioned the report. I read in his handwriting, in the margin of Ibn al-Sakan's book: 'Umayya al-Ḍamrī—his report is with his descendants.' He then cited by way of Hishām ibn ʿUrwa, from al-Zuhrī, from ʿAmr ibn Umayya al-Ḍamrī, from his father, who said: 'I saw the Prophet ﷺ eat, then rise and pray without performing ablution.' As for the first report, Ibn Mandah gave it in the biography of Umayya ibn ʿAmr—also said to be Ibn Abī Umayya al-Ḍamrī—and said: 'He is counted among the people of the Hijaz. His son ʿAmr ibn Umayya narrated from him.' He then cited by way of Jaʿfar ibn ʿAwn, from Ibrāhīm ibn Ismāʿīl ibn Mujammiʿ: Jaʿfar ibn ʿAmr ibn Umayya informed me, from his father, from his grandfather, that the Messenger of God ﷺ sent him alone as a spy to Quraysh. He said: 'I came to Khubayb's wooden scaffold while I feared the watchers. I climbed it and cut Khubayb down,' to the end of the report. This story is recorded in the works on military biography as belonging to ʿAmr ibn Umayya, not to his father, and it is famous through him, not his father. ʿAlī ibn al-Madīnī explained its case conclusively in Kitāb al-ʿIlal. After citing the report by the aforementioned route of Ibn Mujammiʿ, he said: 'This Jaʿfar ibn ʿAmr is not the immediate son of ʿAmr ibn Umayya al-Ḍamrī. Rather, he is Jaʿfar ibn ʿAmr ibn so-and-so ibn ʿAmr ibn Umayya. The report is actually from his father ʿAmr, from that father's grandfather ʿAmr ibn Umayya.' I say: The pronoun in the words 'from his grandfather' refers to Jaʿfar's father, ʿAmr ibn so-and-so, not to Jaʿfar. It is thus clear that the report belongs to the Musnad of ʿAmr ibn Umayya al-Ḍamrī, not that of Umayya. Note: In al-Ṭabarānī's al-Muʿjam, the cited report appears as 'from Jaʿfar ibn ʿAwf, from Ibrāhīm ibn Ismāʿīl ibn Mujammiʿ, from al-Zuhrī: Jaʿfar informed me,' to the end. The words 'from al-Zuhrī' are among the additions inserted into an otherwise connected isnad. As for the second report, a single word—ibn—has fallen out. The correct route is 'from al-Zuhrī, from a son of ʿAmr ibn Umayya, from his father.' Al-Zuhrī did not meet ʿAmr ibn Umayya; rather, he narrated from his son Jaʿfar, as we shall explain. Ibn Mandah also said: 'ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Yaḥyā informed us; Abū Masʿūd informed us; ʿAbd al-Razzāq informed us, from Maʿmar, from al-Zuhrī, from ʿAmr ibn Umayya al-Ḍamrī, from his father, who said: “I saw the Prophet ﷺ eat a sheep's shoulder, then pray without performing ablution.”' Ibn Mandah said: 'This is how ʿAbd al-Razzāq transmitted it. Ibrāhīm ibn Saʿd transmitted it from al-Zuhrī, from Jaʿfar ibn ʿAmr ibn Umayya, from his father, which is correct.' I say: The error should not be attributed to ʿAbd al-Razzāq alone, since it may have arisen from him while he was relating it to Abū Masʿūd, or from Ibn Abī Masʿūd. Al-Tirmidhī transmitted it from Maḥmūd ibn Ghaylān, from ʿAbd al-Razzāq, in the correct form. It likewise appears correctly in ʿAbd al-Razzāq's Muṣannaf through Isḥāq al-Dabarī's transmission from him. Al-Bukhārī also transmitted it by way of Ibn al-Mubārak, from Maʿmar. ʿUqayl, Ṣāliḥ, Shuʿayb, Yūnus, and ʿAmr ibn al-Ḥārith all transmitted it from al-Zuhrī, and all of those routes are sound. It is therefore clear that the second report likewise belongs to the Musnad of ʿAmr ibn Umayya. والله أعلم.

## Source unit 552 · printed entry 552

### English candidate

Umayya ibn Abī al-Ṣalt al-Thaqafī, the famous poet. Ibn al-Sakan mentioned him among the Companions and said: 'He did not attain Islam. The Prophet ﷺ affirmed him as truthful in some of his poetry and said, “Umayya nearly accepted Islam.”' He then related the story of Muʾta by way of Muḥammad ibn Ismāʿīl ibn Ṭurayḥ ibn Ismāʿīl al-Thaqafī, from his father, from his grandfather. He next transmitted the report of ʿIkrima, from Ibn ʿAbbās, that the Prophet ﷺ was recited these words of Umayya:

'Saturn and a bull beneath His right foot;
the eagle for the other, and a lion lying in wait.'

He said: 'He spoke truthfully. This is the description of the bearers of the Throne.' I say: It is soundly transmitted from al-Sharīd ibn ʿAmr that the Prophet ﷺ asked him to recite some of Umayya's poetry, then said: 'He nearly accepted Islam.' In al-Bukhārī, from Abū Hurayra, traced to the Prophet, within a report, are the words: 'Umayya ibn Abī al-Ṣalt nearly accepted Islam.' Umayya's mother was Ruqayya bint ʿAbd Shams ibn ʿAbbād ibn ʿAbd Manāf. For that reason Umayya ibn Abī al-Ṣalt lamented those killed at Badr in his famous ode: among the principal men killed there were ʿUtba and Shayba, the two sons of Rabīʿa ibn ʿAbd Shams, who were his maternal cousins. Abū al-Ṣalt, Umayya's father, was a poet, as was Umayya's son al-Qāsim ibn Umayya, who will be mentioned as having companionship. Abū ʿUbayda said: 'The Arabs agreed that Umayya was the finest poet of Thaqīf.' Al-Zubayr ibn Bakkār said: 'My uncle related to me that, during the pre-Islamic period, Umayya studied and read the scriptures, wore sackcloth, and at first devoted himself to the remembrance of Abraham and Ishmael and to the Ḥanīfiyya. He prohibited wine and avoided idols. He aspired to prophethood because he had read in the scriptures that a prophet would be sent in the Hijaz, and he hoped that he would be that prophet. When the Prophet ﷺ was sent, he envied him and did not accept Islam.' It was Umayya who lamented those killed at Badr in the ode beginning:

'What is at Badr and al-ʿAqanqal?
Mighty marzbāns—great chiefs!'

The author of al-Mirʾāt mentioned in Umayya's biography, from Ibn Hishām, that Umayya had believed in the Prophet ﷺ and came to the Hijaz to collect his property from al-Ṭāʾif and emigrate. When he stopped at Badr, he was asked, 'Where are you going, Abū ʿUthmān?' He replied, 'I want to follow Muḥammad.' He was asked, 'Do you know who is in this well?' He said no. They told him, 'It contains Shayba and ʿUtba, your two maternal cousins, and so-and-so and so-and-so.' He cut the nose of his she-camel, tore his garment, wept, and went to al-Ṭāʾif, where he died. That author mentioned this among the events of the second year. The well-known position, however, is that he died in the ninth year. The chroniclers did not disagree that he died an unbeliever, and it is soundly established that he lived long enough to lament the people of Badr. It is said that he was the one concerning whom God Most High's words were revealed: 'the one to whom We gave Our signs, but he cast them off.' It is also said that he died an unbeliever in al-Ṭāʾif in the ninth year after the Hijra, before Thaqīf accepted Islam. Al-Marzubānī said: 'Abū al-Ṣalt's name was ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rabīʿa ibn ʿAwf ibn ʿUqda ibn Ghayra ibn ʿAwf ibn Thaqīf. It is also said: he was Abū al-Ṣalt ibn Wahb ibn ʿIlāj ibn Abī Salama.' Umayya had the kunya Abū ʿUthmān, and it is also said Abū al-Qāsim. He died during the siege of al-Ṭāʾif after Ḥunayn. In al-Ṭabarānī's al-Muʿjam al-Kabīr, from Abū Sufyān ibn Ḥarb, it is related that he set out to trade in a group that included Umayya ibn Abī al-Ṣalt. He mentioned a story in which Umayya said that a prophet from Quraysh would be sent in the Hijaz. Umayya had thought that he himself would be that prophet until it became clear to him that the prophet would be from Quraysh and would be sent at the beginning of his fortieth year. ʿUtba ibn Rabīʿa asked Umayya about him and said, 'But he has passed that age.' Abū Sufyān said: 'When I returned to Mecca, I found that the Prophet ﷺ had been sent. I met Umayya and he said to me, “Follow him, for he is upon the truth.” I asked, “And you?” He said, “Were it not for shame before the young women of Thaqīf! I used to tell them that I was he, and now they would see me following a youth of Banū ʿAbd Manāf.”' Among Umayya's poetry, from one ode, are the words:

'Every religion on Resurrection Day, before God,
save the Ḥanīfiyya, is false.'

And from another ode:

'Lord, never make me an unbeliever;
make the inward state of my heart faith forever.'

There is much of this kind in his poetry. Hence the Prophet ﷺ said: 'His poetry believed, but his heart disbelieved.' Ibn al-Aʿrābī mentioned in al-Nawādir that Umayya went on one of his journeys and, in the course of a story, saw an old man of the jinn. The old man said: 'You are followed by a spirit. From which direction does your companion come to you?' Umayya said: 'From my left ear.' He asked, 'What does he command you to wear?' Umayya said: 'Black.' The old man said: 'That is an orator of the jinn. You nearly became a prophet, but did not. A prophet's companion comes to him from the right ear and commands him to wear white.' ʿUmar ibn Shabba mentioned, with an isnad of his, from al-Zuhrī, that Umayya entered upon his sister and slept on a bed belonging to her. Two birds appeared. One landed on his chest, split it open, and removed his heart. The other asked, 'Did it comprehend?' It replied, 'Yes.' It asked, 'Did it accept?' It replied, 'It refused,' and returned his heart to its place. Then it rose, and Umayya followed it with his gaze, saying:

'At your service, both of you, at your service;
here I am before you both.'

They returned and did the same thing three times, then departed. On the third occasion he added:

'If You forgive, O God, You forgive a multitude;
and which servant of Yours has not sinned?'

The ceiling then closed, and Umayya stood rubbing his chest. His sister asked, 'My brother, what do you feel?' He replied, 'Nothing, except that I feel heat in my chest.' From al-Zubayr, from his uncle Muṣʿab ibn ʿUthmān, from Thābit ibn al-Zubayr, it is related that, when Umayya fell ill with his final sickness, he began saying: 'My end has drawn near. I know that the Ḥanīfiyya is true, but doubt about Muḥammad enters me.' When his death drew near, he fainted briefly, then recovered while saying, 'At your service, both of you, at your service.' He related something like the preceding account. Then Umayya died without believing in the Prophet ﷺ.

## Source unit 558 · printed entry 558

### English candidate

Umayya, grandfather of ʿAmr ibn ʿUthmān al-Thaqafī, a Medinan. His report states that the Messenger of God ﷺ prayed in water and mud while mounted, gesturing, with his prostration lower than his bowing. This is how Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr transmitted it, but it is an error. Al-Tirmidhī narrated the cited report by way of Kathīr ibn Ziyād, from ʿAmr ibn ʿUthmān ibn Yaʿlā ibn Murra, from his father, from his grandfather: they were with the Prophet ﷺ on a journey and reached a narrow pass; the time for prayer arrived and rain fell on them, to the end of the report. Al-Tirmidhī said: 'Strange.' I say: Its isnad is unobjectionable, and its Companion is Yaʿlā ibn Murra, not Umayya. Al-Ṭabarānī, however, transmitted it in his Muʿjam as 'from ʿAmr ibn ʿUthmān ibn Yaʿlā ibn Umayya, from his father, from his grandfather.' Mentioning Umayya is an error; the correct name is Murra. On either reading, the Companion is Yaʿlā, not Umayya. If a transmission from Umayya, the father of Yaʿlā, is established, then he is Umayya al-Tamīmī, who was mentioned in the first section.

## Source unit 562 · printed entry 562

### English candidate

Anas ibn Rāfiʿ, Abū al-Ḥaysar al-Awsī. Ibn Manda mentioned him and said, ‘He came to the Prophet ﷺ in Mecca. The Prophet ﷺ went to them, and they embraced Islam.’ He then gave the report by way of Salama ibn al-Faḍl, from Ibn Isḥāq, from Ḥuṣayn ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, from Maḥmūd ibn Labīd, to this effect. Thus he said. Yet what Ibn Isḥāq related in al-Maghāzī through this chain indicates that he did not embrace Islam. The story has already been given in full in the biography of Iyās ibn Muʿādh. His statement that ‘he came to the Prophet ﷺ’ is questionable. Rather, Abū al-Ḥaysar came with a band of young men of Banū ʿAbd al-Ashhal to Quraysh, seeking an alliance with them against al-Khazraj. The Prophet ﷺ went to them and invited them to Islam, but they did not embrace Islam at that time. They returned, and the celebrated Battle of Buʿāth then took place between them. This Abū al-Ḥaysar had a son who witnessed Badr and a daughter whom ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf married. It was on her account that he was told, ‘Give a wedding feast, even if only with a sheep.’

## Source unit 567 · printed entry 567

### English candidate

Aws ibn Bashīr, a man of Yemen said to be from Jayshān, came to the Prophet ﷺ and embraced Islam. His hadith is transmitted by al-Layth ibn Saʿd from ʿĀmir al-Jayshānī. Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr entered him thus, following Ibn Abī Ḥātim. It contains errors, which we shall explain. One is his saying ‘ibn Bashīr’; it is actually ibn Bishr. Another is his saying that he was from Jayshān; he was actually al-Maʿāfirī. Another is his saying that he came to the Prophet ﷺ; he did not come to him, but merely related the story of a man from Jayshān who did come and question him. Another is his saying ‘ʿĀmir al-Jayshānī’; it is actually al-Maʿāfirī. Abū Mūsā transmitted the hadith in al-Dhayl by way of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ṣāliḥ, from al-Layth, from ʿĀmir ibn Yaḥyā, from Aws ibn Bashīr: a man from Yemen, from Jayshān, came to the Prophet ﷺ and said, ‘We have a drink called mizr, made from millet.’ He asked, ‘Does it intoxicate?’ The man said, ‘Yes.’ He said, ‘Then do not drink it.’ Abū Mūsā said, ‘This hadith has been transmitted from Daylam al-Jayshānī, and I think he was the questioner.’ I say: al-Bukhārī mentioned him in al-Tārīkh and said, ‘Aws ibn Bishr al-Maʿāfirī is counted among the Egyptians. He accompanied Companions of the Prophet ﷺ. ʿĀmir ibn Yaḥyā al-Maʿāfirī and Wāhib ibn ʿAbd Allāh transmitted from him, and he heard ʿUqba ibn ʿĀmir.’ Ibn Ḥibbān likewise mentioned him among the trustworthy Successors.

## Source unit 568 · printed entry 568

### English candidate

Aws ibn Thābit al-Anṣārī. Al-Ṭabarānī distinguished him from Aws ibn Thābit, the brother of Ḥassān, but they are the same man. In this man’s biography he transmitted from ʿUrwa, among those of Banū ʿAmr ibn Mālik ibn al-Najjār who witnessed al-ʿAqaba and Badr: Aws ibn Thābit ibn al-Mundhir. He then mentioned him from Mūsā ibn ʿUqba among those who witnessed Badr: Aws ibn Thābit ibn al-Mundhir, who left no descendants. Al-Ṭabarānī was confused for two reasons: first, he did not give the lineage of Aws ibn Thābit, Ḥassān’s brother; second, he said that he was the father of Shaddād, then saw Mūsā’s statement that he left no descendants and judged him to be someone else.

## Source unit 569 · printed entry 569

### English candidate

Aws ibn Ḥāritha ibn Laʾm ibn ʿAmr ibn Thumāma ibn ʿAmr ibn Ṭarīf al-Ṭāʾī. Ibn Qāniʿ mentioned him. It has already been explained, in the biography of Aws ibn Ḥāritha in the first section, that this was an error. Al-Marzubānī mentioned him in Muʿjam al-Shuʿarāʾ and said that he was a pre-Islamic poet. Ibn al-Kalbī related that Hāniʾ ibn Qabīṣa ibn Aws ibn Ḥāritha ibn Laʾm was a Christian and had as his wife a Christian daughter of his paternal uncle. She embraced Islam, so ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb separated them. Had Aws ibn Ḥāritha embraced Islam, his grandson Hāniʾ ibn Qabīṣa would not have been allowed to remain a Christian. Abū Ḥātim al-Sijistānī mentioned in al-Muʿammarīn that Aws ibn Ḥāritha ibn Laʾm lived for two hundred and twenty years, until he became decrepit and lost his hearing and reason. He had been the chief and leader of his people. Ibn al-Kalbī related this from his father, who said, ‘We were informed that his sons moved away and left him in their courtyard until he died there, neglected. They are reproached for that to this day.’ This supports what we have said: he did not live to see Islam.

### Arabic authority

<div dir="rtl" lang="ar">

أوس بن حارثة بن لأم بن عمرو بن ثمامة بن عمرو بن طريف الطائي ذكره بن قانع وقد تقدم أنه وهم في ترجمة أوس بن حارثة في القسم الأول وذكره المرزباني في معجم الشعراء وقال إنه شاعر جاهلي وذكر بن الكلبي أن هانئ بن قبيصة بن أوس بن حارثة بن لأم كان نصرانيا وكان تحته بنت عم له نصرانية فأسلمت ففرق عمر بن الخطاب بينهما فلو كان أوس بن حارثة أسلم لم يقر حفيده هانئ بن قبيصة على النصرانية وذكر أبو حاتم السجستاني في المعمرين قال عاش أوس بن حارثة بن لأم مائتين وعشرين سنة حتى هرم وذهب سمعه وعقله وكان سيد قومه ورئيسهم ذكر ذلك بن الكلبي عن أبيه قال فبلغنا أن بنية ارتحلوا وتركوه في عرصتهم حتى هلك فيها ضيعة فهم يسبون بذلك إلى اليوم فهذا يؤيد ماقلناه إنه لم يدرك الإسلام

## Source unit 573 · printed entry 573

### English candidate

Aws, without a lineage. Ibn Qāniʿ also mentioned him and transmitted from Ibn Lahīʿa, from ʿAbd Rabbih ibn Saʿīd, from Yaʿlā ibn Aws, from his father, who said, ‘During the time of the Messenger of God ﷺ, we used to count ostentation as minor polytheism.’ This is an error caused by an omission. This hadith is actually transmitted by Yaʿlā ibn Shaddād ibn Aws from his father, so Companionship belongs to Shaddād ibn Aws. When Yaʿlā appeared in this version attributed to his grandfather Aws, Ibn Qāniʿ took the wording at face value. The hadith is well known from Shaddād ibn Aws through several routes. ## Source unit 574 · printed entry 574

### English candidate

Iyās ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Bahzī. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Yasār transmitted from him. He witnessed Ḥunayn, and his hadith is in the Musnad of al-Ṭayālisī. Al-Dhahabī entered him thus in al-Tajrīd and marked him with the symbol of Baqī ibn Makhlad, indicating that Baqī transmitted a hadith for him. He then separately mentioned Iyās ibn ʿAbd al-Fihrī, without ‘Allāh’ in the patronymic. I say: they are one man. What appears in Usd al-Ghāba is ‘Iyās ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Fihrī,’ with fāʾ and rāʾ, from whom ʿAbd Allāh ibn Yasār transmitted. It then gives, by way of the Musnad of al-Ṭayālisī, a hadith of Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Fihrī without naming him. It next says, ‘Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr, Ibn Manda, and Abū Nuʿaym included him,’ although Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said ‘Iyās ibn ʿAbd,’ without ‘Allāh.’ It is therefore clear that making them two men was an error, and that the nisba is al-Fihrī, with fāʾ and rāʾ. That is also how it appears in the Musnad of al-Ṭayālisī, although he is not named in the text of his hadith. There is disagreement over his name, as will be discussed under the kunyās, إن شاء الله تعالى.

## Source unit 575 · printed entry 575

### English candidate

Iyās ibn Mālik ibn Aws ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ḥajar al-Aslamī. Ibn Manda mentioned him and said, ‘Al-Sarrāj included him among the Companions, although he is a Successor.’ He then transmitted for him a hadith that Iyās related without naming the Companion intermediary. ## Source unit 576 · printed entry 576

### English candidate

Iyās ibn Muʿāwiya al-Muzanī. Al-Ṭabarānī mentioned him among the Companions, and Abū Mūsā supplied him as an addition. He transmitted by way of al-Ṭabarānī, with his chain, from Ibn Isḥāq, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Ḥārith, from Iyās ibn Muʿāwiya al-Muzanī, who said: the Messenger of God ﷺ said, ‘There must be prayer during the night, even if only for the time it takes to milk a she-camel or a sheep. Whatever comes after the final evening prayer counts as night prayer.’ Whoever made him a Companion erred. He was only a younger Successor, well known as Iyās the judge and celebrated for his intelligence. His ancestor Iyās ibn Hilāl ibn Riʾāb has already been mentioned, and Qurra ibn Iyās will be mentioned under the letter qāf. Abū Nuʿaym thought that the hadith just cited belonged to this Iyās ibn Hilāl and gave it in his earlier biography, but that is an error, for Qurra’s father has no transmission, as previously stated. Abū Mūsā said, ‘This hadith is transmitted by Iyās ibn Muʿāwiya ibn Qurra. He transmitted from Anas and from Successors. Companionship belongs only to his grandfather Qurra, not even to his father Muʿāwiya.’ I say: Iyās ibn Muʿāwiya died in the year 121; it is also said, in 122. It is said that he had not reached forty years of age.

## Source unit 578 · printed entry 578

### English candidate

Ayfaʿ ibn ʿAbd al-Kalāʿī. He was a junior Successor. Abū Mūsā supplied this omitted entry and said that al-Ismāʿīlī had included him among the Companions. Al-Ismāʿīlī said: Aḥmad ibn al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAbd al-Jabbār related to us; al-Ḥakam ibn Mūsā related to us, from al-Walīd ibn Muslim, from Ṣafwān ibn ʿAmr, who said: I heard Ayfaʿ ibn ʿAbd al-Kalāʿī say from the pulpit of Ḥimṣ, “The Messenger of God ﷺ said: ‘When God has admitted the people of Paradise into Paradise and the people of the Fire into the Fire, He will say: O people of Paradise, how many years did you remain on earth?’” and he continued the report. Abū Yaʿlā corroborated al-Ismāʿīlī’s route, transmitting from al-Haytham ibn Khārija, from al-Walīd. The men of its chain are trustworthy, but it is mursal or muʿḍal. It cannot be established that Ayfaʿ heard from any Companion. Ibn Abī Ḥātim mentions only his transmission from Rāshid ibn Saʿd. ʿAbdān said: I heard Muḥammad ibn al-Muthannā say, “Ayfaʿ died in the year 106.” Al-Dārimī said in his Musnad: Yazīd ibn Hārūn informed us, from Ḥarīz ibn ʿUthmān, from Ayfaʿ ibn ʿAbd, from the Prophet ﷺ, concerning the merit of the Throne Verse. ## Source unit 579 · printed entry 579

### English candidate

Ayman ibn Yaʿlā, Abū Thābit al-Thaqafī, was a well-known Successor. He was not a son of Yaʿlā, although he did transmit from him. Ibn Manda said: Muḥammad ibn Ayyūb ibn Ḥabīb and Khaythama ibn Sulaymān informed us, saying: Hilāl ibn al-ʿAlāʾ related to us; my father and ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar related to us, saying: ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿAmr related to us, from Yazīd ibn Abī Unaysa, from Ismāʿīl ibn Abī Khālid, from al-Shaʿbī, from Abū Thābit, Ayman ibn Yaʿlā al-Thaqafī, who said: I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say, “Whoever steals a span of land, or its produce, will come on the Day of Resurrection carrying it upon his neck down to the lowest of the earths.”

Ibn Manda said: ʿAmr ibn Zurāra likewise related it from ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿAmr. A group related it from ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿAmr but omitted al-Shaʿbī. ʿAlī ibn Maʿbad related it from ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿAmr as “from Abū Thābit, from Yaʿlā ibn Murra al-Thaqafī.” More than one narrator likewise related it from Abū Yaʿfūr, from Abū Thābit, from Yaʿlā; this is the correct version.

I say: Al-Baghawī related it from ʿAmr ibn Zurāra exactly as in ʿAlī ibn Maʿbad’s version. Ayman Abū Thābit transmitted from the aforementioned Yaʿlā and from Ibn ʿAbbās. Al-Bukhārī and Ibn Abī Ḥātim mention him on that basis. Ibn Ḥibbān also cites this report through Abū Yaʿfūr, from Ayman Abū Thābit, who said, “I heard Yaʿlā,” and included it in his Ṣaḥīḥ by way of al-Rabīʿ ibn ʿAbd Allāh, from Ayman, from Yaʿlā ibn Murra.

## Source unit 581 · printed entry 581

### English candidate

Ayman, without a patronymic. He has a mursal report. He also transmitted from Tubayʿ, the son of Kaʿb’s wife, from Kaʿb. ʿAṭāʾ and Mujāhid transmitted from him. It is said that he was a client of al-Zubayr or of Ibn al-Zubayr. Al-Nasāʾī said, “I do not think that he had Companionship.”

In his Tārīkh, al-Bukhārī related by way of Manṣūr, from al-Ḥakam, from Mujāhid and ʿAṭāʾ, from Ayman al-Ḥabashī, that he said, “The thief’s hand is cut off.” This is mursal. Al-Shāfiʿī said: Whoever claims that he was Ayman ibn Umm Ayman, the maternal brother of Usāma ibn Zayd, is mistaken, because that man was killed on the day of Ḥunayn. Al-Dāraquṭnī said: Ayman, the transmitter of the theft report, was a Successor; he met neither the Prophet ﷺ nor the caliphs after him. It has also been said that he was Ayman al-Ḥabashī, the father of ʿAbd al-Wāḥid ibn Ayman, a client of the Banū Makhzūm, for whom al-Bukhārī transmitted. والله أعلم.

## Source unit 583 · printed entry 583

### English candidate

Bāqūm—also said to be Bāqūl, with lām and a ḍamma on the qāf—the carpenter, a client of the Banū Umayya. ʿAbd al-Razzāq said in his Muṣannaf: Ibrāhīm ibn Abī Yaḥyā informed us, from Ṣāliḥ, the client of al-Tawʾama, that Bāqūl, the client of al-ʿĀṣ ibn Umayya, made for the Messenger of God ﷺ his pulpit, of tamarisk, with three steps. This chain is weak and the report is mursal. Ibn Manda transmitted it by this route.

Ibn al-Sakan transmitted by way of Isḥāq ibn Idrīs: Abū Isḥāq related to us, from Bāqūl, that he made it, and he related the report. Ibn al-Sakan said: I think Abū Isḥāq was Ibrāhīm ibn Abī Yaḥyā, while Ṣāliḥ was the client of al-Tawʾama. We have received it only by this route, and it is weak. End.

Abū Nuʿaym transmitted by way of Muḥammad ibn Ismāʿīl al-Masmūlī, one of the weak transmitters, from Abū Bakr ibn Abī Sayra, from Ṣāliḥ, the client of al-Tawʾama: Bāqūm, the client of Saʿīd ibn al-ʿĀṣ, related to me, saying, “I made for the Messenger of God ﷺ a pulpit from the tamarisk of al-Ghāba, three levels: the seat and two steps.” He presented it with a connected chain, but it too is weak.

There is extensive disagreement over the name of the pulpit’s maker, which I have explained in my commentary on al-Bukhārī. In the Ṣaḥīḥ, the report of Sahl ibn Saʿd says that he was the slave-boy of a woman of the Anṣār. Yet there is no contradiction between the statements that he was a client of the Banū Umayya and the slave-boy of an Anṣārī woman: he may have served the woman after migrating to Medina and thus become known through her.

Ibn ʿUyayna related in his Jāmiʿ, from ʿAmr ibn Dīnār, from ʿUbayda ibn ʿUmayr, who said: “The man who built the Kaaba for Quraysh was named Bāqūm. He was a Roman aboard a ship which the wind detained. Quraysh went out to it, took its timber, and told him, ‘Build it in the manner in which churches are built.’” The men of this chain are trustworthy, though it is mursal. The story of the Roman’s building of the Kaaba is well known; al-Fākihī and others mention it.

In the transmission of ʿUthmān ibn Sāj, from Ibn Jurayj, a Roman named Bāqūm used to trade with al-Mandab. His ship was wrecked at al-Shuʿayba, so he sent to Quraysh, asking: “Will you carry my caravan goods with your caravan goods—that is, in trade? I will supply you with as much timber as you wish and a carpenter, so that you may build with it the House of Abraham.” The purpose of this route is to establish his name. It is possible that this was the same man who later made the pulpit. God knows best.

Another Bāqūm. ## Source unit 587 · printed entry 587

### English candidate

Bujayd, in the diminutive, ibn ʿImrān al-Khuzāʿī. He is mentioned in the Maghāzī. Ibn Hishām said in the story of the Conquest: Bujayd ibn ʿImrān al-Khuzāʿī said:

“God raised the clouds to bring us victory—
masses of heavily laden, piled-up clouds.
Our emigration was within our own land; there we held
a document from the best one to dictate and write.
For our sake a sanctity at Mecca was made lawful,
that we might exact vengeance with cutting swords.”

Ibn Fatḥūn and others supplied him as an omitted entry under the letter bāʾ. Some have Bujayr, ending in rāʾ, but the correct form, as in the Sīra, ends in dāl. A late writer claimed that he was Bujayd ibn ʿImrān ibn Ḥuṣayn, but that is baseless: the man whose grandfather is Ḥuṣayn has a name beginning with nūn and is a well-known Successor. The poet is evidently someone else.

## Source unit 589 · printed entry 589

### English candidate

Bujayr ibn Bajara—with a fatḥa on the first letter and a sukūn on the jīm—al-Ṭāʾī. Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said: He left exploits and verses concerning the fighting against the apostates, which Ibn Isḥāq mentioned in the Maghāzī.

Yazīd ibn Rūmān and ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Bakr related to me that the Messenger of God ﷺ sent Khālid ibn al-Walīd to Ukaydir ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, a man of Kinda who ruled Dūma and was a Christian. The Messenger of God ﷺ said, “You will find him hunting wild cattle.” The source then related the story, including that Khālid killed Ḥassān, Ukaydir’s brother, and brought Ukaydir before the Messenger of God ﷺ. He spared Ukaydir’s blood, made a treaty with him for payment of the jizya, released him, and allowed him to return to his town. A man of Ṭayyiʾ called Bujayr ibn Bajara then recited verses about this.

Ibn Manda said: “This is mursal, but it has reached us with a connected chain.” He then transmitted by way of Abū al-Maʿārik al-Shammākh ibn Maʿārik ibn Murra ibn Ṣakhr ibn Bujayr ibn Bajara al-Ṭāʾī: “My father related to me, from my grandfather, from his father Bujayr ibn Bajara, who said: I was in Khālid ibn al-Walīd’s army when the Prophet of God ﷺ sent him to Ukaydir, king of Dūmat al-Jandal. The Prophet ﷺ said, ‘You will find him hunting wild cattle.’ We encountered him on a moonlit night after he had gone out just as the Messenger of God ﷺ had described him. We seized him and killed his brother, who had fought us. Ukaydir was wearing a brocade qabāʾ, and Khālid ibn al-Walīd sent it to the Prophet ﷺ. When we came to the Prophet ﷺ, I recited verses to him, including:

‘Blessed is the Driver of the wild cattle; truly,
I have seen God guide every guide.’

The Prophet ﷺ said, ‘May God never cause your mouth to lose its teeth.’ He lived to the age of ninety, and not one tooth moved.”

Ibn al-Sakan and Abū Nuʿaym transmitted it by this route. Abū al-Maʿārik and his forefathers have no entries in the biographical books on transmitters. Sayf ibn ʿUmar stated in the Futūḥ that Bujayr ibn Bajara was martyred at al-Qādisiyya.

## Source unit 591 · printed entry 591

### English candidate

Bujayr ibn Zuhayr ibn Abī Sulmā—with a ḍamma on the sīn—al-Muzanī, the poet. He was the brother of Kaʿb ibn Zuhayr, likewise a famous poet. He accepted Islam before his brother. This will be recounted in detail in the biography of Kaʿb, إن شاء الله تعالى. Ibn Isḥāq recited the following by him concerning the day of the Conquest of Mecca:

“We struck them in Mecca on the day the good Prophet
conquered, with swift white swords.
We gave the Messenger of God from among ourselves
solemn pledges of sincere concord.
We came upon them at dawn with a thousand men of Sulaym,
and a thousand of the Banū ʿUthmān, fully present.
We returned as victors, having gained what we desired;
they returned regretting their opposition.”

These are among a longer set of verses.

## Source unit 608 · printed entry 608

### English candidate

Budayl ibn Umm Aṣram was Budayl ibn Salama ibn Khalaf ibn ʿAmr ibn al-Aḥabb ibn Miqbās ibn Ḥabtar ibn ʿAdī ibn Salūl ibn Kaʿb ibn ʿAmr al-Khuzāʿī al-Salūlī. Ibn al-Kalbī said that his mother was Umm Aṣram bint al-Aḥjam ibn Dandana ibn ʿAmr ibn al-Qayn, who was likewise of Khuzāʿa. Abū Mūsā said: 'ʿAbdān included him and said, “We know of no report from him beyond his mention and his story.”' He was the man who answered al-Aḥraz ibn Laqīṭ al-Dīlī when the latter related what they had inflicted upon Khuzāʿa; that was at the time of the truce of al-Ḥudaybiyya. Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said that he was the man whom the Prophet ﷺ sent to Banū Kaʿb, together with Busr ibn Sufyān al-Khuzāʿī, to summon them for the campaign to Mecca. Al-Marzubānī mentioned him in Muʿjam al-Shuʿarāʾ and cited these lines that he addressed to Anas ibn Zunaym at the conquest of Mecca:

'Anas wept over a calamity, and weeping made him wail;
he became fearful when a kindler kindled war.
You wept for slain men drenched in their own blood,
and by it the straightened Samharī spear was dyed.'

Ḥanthar: al-Dāraquṭnī vocalized it with fatḥa on the unpointed initial letter, a quiescent nūn, and then a three-dotted letter; Ibn Mākūlā, however, vocalized it with a single-dotted letter followed by a two-dotted letter.

### Arabic authority

<div dir="rtl" lang="ar">

بديل بن أم أصرم هو بن سلمة بن خلف بن عمرو بن الأحب بن مقباس بن حبتر بن عدي بن سلول بن كعب بن عمرو الخزاعي السلولي وقال بن الكلبي أمة أم أصرم بنت الاحجم بن دندنة بن عمرو بن القين خزاعية أيضا قال أبو موسى أورده عبدان وقال لا نحفظ له حديثا الا ذكره وقصته وهو الذي أجاب الاحرز بن لقيط الديلي ذكر ما أصابوا من خزاعة وذلك حين صلح الحديبية وقال بن عبد البر هو الذي بعثه النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم إلى بني كعب ليستنفرهم لغزو مكة هو وبشر بن سفيان الخزاعي وذكره المرزباني في معجم الشعراء وأنشد له يخاطب أنس بن زنيم في فتح مكة <br />

## Source unit 612 · printed entry 612

### English candidate

Budayl—also said to be Barīl, with rāʾ in place of dāl, and also Barīr, with two rāʾs, while still other forms are reported—ibn Abī Maryam; it is also said ibn Abī Māriya al-Sahmī, a client of ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ. Al-Tirmidhī transmitted, by way of Ibn Isḥāq, from Abū al-Naḍr, from Bādham, from Ibn ʿAbbās, from Tamīm al-Dārī, concerning the verse, 'O you who believe, testimony between you when death approaches one of you at the time of a bequest ...' Tamīm said: 'All people were clear of its implication except me and ʿAdī ibn Baddāʾ.' The two were Christians who regularly traveled to Syria before Islam. They went to Syria for their trade, and a client of Banū Sahm called Budayl ibn Abī Maryam came to them with merchandise, including a silver cup; and he related the report. I say: Abū al-Naḍr is Muḥammad ibn al-Sāʾib al-Kalbī, who is weak. Ibn Mandah transmitted it by way of Muḥammad ibn Marwān al-Suddī, from al-Kalbī, giving the name as Budayl ibn Abī Māriya and stating that Budayl was a Muslim. The basis of the report is in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī by another route from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: 'ʿAdī and Tamīm set out ...' and related it, but did not name the Sahmī. Ibn Barīra mentioned in his Tafsīr that there is no disagreement among the exegetes that Budayl was a Muslim from among the Emigrants.

## Source unit 614 · printed entry 614

### English candidate

Budayl ibn Warqāʾ ibn ʿAmr ibn Rabīʿa ibn ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā ibn Rabīʿa ibn Jurayy ibn ʿĀmir ibn Māzin ibn ʿAdī ibn ʿAmr ibn Rabīʿa al-Khuzāʿī. Ibn al-Sakan said that he had companionship and lived in Mecca. It is said that he was killed at Ṣiffīn. I say: The man killed at Ṣiffīn was his son ʿAbd Allāh. Ibn Mandah transmitted from Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Ibrāhīm, from Muḥammad ibn Saʿīd, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Ḥakam, from Bishr, that Bishr was asked about Budayl ibn Warqāʾ and replied: 'He died before the Prophet ﷺ.' In the maghāzī accounts from Ibn Isḥāq and others, Quraysh took refuge on the day of the conquest of Mecca in the house of Budayl ibn Warqāʾ and in the house of his client Rāfiʿ. Budayl accepted Islam before the conquest; it is also said that he did so on the day of the conquest. Al-Bukhārī in his Tārīkh and al-Baghawī transmitted by way of Ibn Isḥāq, who said: Ibrāhīm ibn Abī ʿAbla related to me, from a son of Budayl ibn Warqāʾ, from his father, that the Prophet ﷺ ordered him to detain the captives and property at al-Jiʿrāna until the Prophet came to him, and he did so. Its isnad is fair. Abū Nuʿaym transmitted by way of Ibn Jurayj, from Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā ibn Ḥibbān, from Umm al-Ḥārith bint ʿAyyāsh ibn Abī Rabīʿa, that she saw Budayl ibn Warqāʾ circling at Minā on a gray camel and saying: 'The Messenger of God ﷺ forbids you to fast on these days, for they are days of eating and drinking.' Al-Baghawī also transmitted it by way of Ibn Jurayj, but said: 'It reached me from Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā.' Ibn al-Sakan transmitted by way of Mufaḍḍal ibn Ṣāliḥ, from ʿAmr ibn Dīnār, from Ibn ʿAbbās, that the Prophet ﷺ gave Budayl the order, and he related something similar. Ismāʿīl ibn ʿAlī ibn Razīn ibn ʿUthmān ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Budayl ibn Warqāʾ transmitted from his father, from his father, from his father, from his father, from his father, from his father: 'I heard Budayl ibn Warqāʾ say: “On the day of the conquest, the Messenger of God ﷺ said to me, when he saw blackness on the sides of my beard, ‘How old are you?’ I said, ‘Ninety-seven.’ He said, ‘May God increase you in beauty and blackness,’”' and he related the report. Ibn Abī ʿĀṣim said: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Muḥammad ibn Bishr ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salama ibn Budayl ibn Warqāʾ related to us: 'My father related to me, from his father ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, from his father Muḥammad ibn Bishr, from his father Bishr ibn ʿAbd Allāh, from his father ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salama, from his father Salama, who said: “My father Budayl ibn Warqāʾ handed me a document and said, ‘My son, this is a document of the Messenger of God ﷺ. Take good care of it. You will continue to fare well so long as it remains among you.’”' He related the report, in which it is stated that the document was in the handwriting of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib. In the biography of Ismāʿīl ibn ʿAlī ibn Razīn ibn ʿUthmān ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Budayl ibn Warqāʾ, from his father, from his father, from his father, from his father, it is related: 'I heard Budayl ibn Warqāʾ say: “Ibn ʿAbbās stationed me before the Prophet ﷺ and said, ‘This is Budayl ibn Warqāʾ.’ The Prophet asked him, ‘How old are you?’ and saw blackness on the sides of his beard. He replied, ‘Ninety-seven.’ The Prophet said, ‘May God increase you in beauty and blackness.’”'

## Source unit 617 · printed entry 617

### English candidate

Al-Barāʾ ibn Ḥazm. Ibn Ḥibbān mentioned him among the Companions and said that the Prophet ﷺ collected the alms-tax from them. Al-Bāwardī transmitted through Yaʿlā ibn al-Ashdaq—one of the weak, abandoned narrators—who said: “I met ten of the Companions, among them al-Barāʾ ibn Ḥazm and ʿAbd Allāh Jurād. They said: ‘The Prophet ﷺ took from us two jadhaʿa she-camels out of every hundred camels.’”

## Source unit 618 · printed entry 618

### English candidate

Al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib ibn al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAdī ibn Jusham ibn Majdaʿa ibn Ḥāritha ibn al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAmr ibn Mālik ibn al-Aws, al-Anṣārī al-Awsī. His kunya was Abū ʿUmāra, and it is also said Abū ʿAmr. Both he and his father were Companions. Ibn al-Kalbī did not include Majdaʿa in his genealogy, and that is more correct.

Aḥmad said: Yazīd related to us, from Sharīk, from Abū Isḥāq, from al-Barāʾ, who said: “The Messenger of God ﷺ considered Ibn ʿUmar and me too young on the day of Badr and sent us back, so we did not witness it.” Abū Dāwūd al-Ṭayālisī said in his Musnad: Shuʿba related to us, from Abū Isḥāq, who heard al-Barāʾ say: “Ibn ʿUmar and I were considered too young on the day of Badr.” ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwsaja related something similar from al-Barāʾ and added, “I did witness Uḥud”; al-Sarrāj transmitted it.

It is related from him that he went on fourteen campaigns with the Messenger of God ﷺ, and in another version fifteen; its chain is sound. It is also related from him that he said: “I traveled with the Messenger of God ﷺ on eighteen journeys”; Abū Dharr al-Harawī transmitted it. Aḥmad related through al-Thawrī, from Ibn Isḥāq, from al-Barāʾ, that he said: “Not everything we relate to you from the Messenger of God ﷺ did we hear from him. Our companions related it to us, for tending the camels kept us occupied.”

He was the one who conquered al-Rayy in the year 24, according to Abū ʿAmr al-Shaybānī; others disagreed with him. He witnessed the campaign of Tustar with Abū Mūsā, and he fought alongside ʿAlī at the Battle of the Camel, Ṣiffīn, and against the Khārijites. He settled in Kufa and built a house there. He died during the governorship of Muṣʿab ibn al-Zubayr; Ibn Ḥibbān dated his death to the year 72.

He transmitted a body of hadith from the Prophet ﷺ, and also from his father, Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, and other senior Companions. Abū Juḥayfa, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Yazīd al-Khaṭmī, and a group of others transmitted from him; the last of them was Abū Isḥāq al-Sabīʿī.

## Source unit 620 · printed entry 620

### English candidate

Al-Barāʾ ibn Mālik ibn al-Naḍr al-Anṣārī, the brother of Anas. His genealogy has preceded in the biography of Anas. Abū Ḥātim said that he was Anas’s brother through their father. Ibn Saʿd said that he was his full brother and that their mother was Umm Sulaym. End quote. This is open to question, because the biography of Sharīk ibn Saḥmāʾ will state that he was al-Barāʾ ibn Mālik’s maternal brother and that their mother was Saḥmāʾ, whereas Anas’s mother was unquestionably Umm Sulaym.

It was stated in the biography of Anjasha that al-Barāʾ was a camel-driver for the Prophet ﷺ. In al-Mustadrak, through Ibn Isḥāq, from ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Anas, Anas ibn Mālik said: “Al-Barāʾ ibn Mālik had a fine voice and used to chant rajaz for the Messenger of God ﷺ on some of his journeys. He told him, ‘Beware the glass vessels,’ so he stopped.” Al-Sarrāj transmitted through Ḥammād, from Thābit, from Anas: “Al-Barāʾ was the men’s camel-driver.” A fuller version has preceded under Anjasha.

Al-Barāʾ witnessed the campaigns with the Messenger of God ﷺ except Badr. He had celebrated exploits on the day of al-Yamāma. He was martyred at the fortress of Tustar during ʿUmar’s caliphate, in the year 20; it is said earlier than that, and it is also said in the year 23. Sayf mentioned that al-Hurmuzān was the one who killed him. His brother Anas transmitted from him.

Al-Baghawī transmitted with a sound chain from Muḥammad ibn Sīrīn, from Anas, who said: “I entered upon al-Barāʾ ibn Mālik while he was singing. I said to him, ‘God has given you something better than this.’ He replied, ‘Do you fear that I shall die in my bed? No, by God, God would not deprive me of that, for I have killed one hundred men single-handedly, apart from those in whose killing I shared.’”

Baqī ibn Makhlad said in his Musnad: Khalīfa related to us; Abū Bakr related to us, from Abū Isḥāq, who said: “On the day of al-Yamāma the Muslims advanced against the polytheists until they forced them into a garden in which was the enemy of God, Musaylima. Al-Barāʾ ibn Mālik said, ‘Muslims, throw me over to them!’ They carried him until, when he looked over the wall, he plunged in and fought them for control of the garden until the Muslims opened it and entered upon them; then God killed Musaylima.” Khalīfa related to us; al-Anṣārī related to us, from his father, from Thumāma, from Anas, who said: “Al-Barāʾ threw himself upon them and fought until he opened the gate. He had more than eighty wounds, including wounds from arrows and blows. He was carried to his quarters for treatment, and Khālid personally tended him for a month.”

In al-Sarrāj’s History, through Yūnus, from al-Ḥasan and Ibn Sīrīn, from Anas, Khālid ibn al-Walīd said to al-Barāʾ on the day of al-Yamāma, “Rise, al-Barāʾ.” He mounted his horse, praised and extolled God, and then said: “People of Medina, there is no Medina for you today. It is only God, alone, and Paradise.” He charged, and the people charged with him, and the people of al-Yamāma were routed. Al-Barāʾ met Muḥakkam al-Yamāma, struck him, and felled him. He took Muḥakkam al-Yamāma’s sword and struck with it until it broke.

Al-Baghawī transmitted through Ayyūb, from Ibn Sīrīn, from Anas, from al-Barāʾ, who said: “On the day of Musaylima I met a man called Ḥimār al-Yamāma, a huge man with a white sword in his hand. I struck his legs, and it was as though the blow had missed him; then he was uprooted and fell on his back. I took his sword and sheathed mine. I did not strike a blow with it before it broke.”

Al-Ṭabarānī transmitted through Isḥāq ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Ṭalḥa: “While Anas ibn Mālik and his brother were at one of the enemy’s fortresses”—meaning at the burning—they cast grappling hooks on heated chains; when one caught a man, they raised him up to themselves. They did that to Anas. Al-Barāʾ came forward until he was visible upon the wall, then seized the chain with his hand and did not let go until the rope snapped. He looked at his hand and its bones were visible, all the flesh upon them having gone. God thereby saved Anas ibn Mālik.

Al-Tirmidhī transmitted through Thābit and ʿAlī ibn Zayd, from Anas, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Many a disheveled, dusty man to whom no attention is paid—if he swore an oath by God, God would fulfill it for him. Al-Barāʾ ibn Mālik is among them.” When the day of Tustar in the land of Persia came and the people broke, the Muslims said, “Al-Barāʾ, adjure your Lord.” He said: “My Lord, I adjure You to grant us their shoulders and to join me to Your Prophet.” He charged, and the people charged with him. Marzubān al-Zāra, one of the Persian grandees, killed him and took his spoils. The Persians were routed and al-Barāʾ was killed. Al-Mustadrak contains a similar report through Salāma, from ʿUqayl, from al-Zuhrī, from Anas.

## Source unit 621 · printed entry 621

### English candidate

Another al-Barāʾ ibn Mālik. Ibn Shāhīn mentioned him among the Companions and transmitted through Saʿīd ibn ʿUthmān al-Balawī, from Ḥuṣayn ibn Waḥwaḥ, that al-Barāʾ ibn Mālik came to the Prophet ﷺ and said, “Command me to do whatever you wish.” He said, “Go and kill your father.” When he turned away, he said, “Call him back. I was not sent to sever ties of kinship.” Then al-Barāʾ ibn Mālik fell ill and the Prophet ﷺ visited him. He related the hadith concerning his death and the Prophet’s ﷺ words: “O God, meet al-Barāʾ ibn Mālik while smiling upon him.” End quote.

This story is known only concerning Ṭalḥa ibn al-Barāʾ, as will come in the letter ṭāʾ. The mistake in the name may have come from ʿAbd al-Wahhāb ibn al-Ḍaḥḥāk, one of Ibn Shāhīn’s transmitters. I have not asserted decisively that he erred, because it remains possible that the story happened to two men. This al-Barāʾ ibn Mālik is not the previously mentioned brother of Anas, for he lived after the Prophet ﷺ, as stated above.

## Source unit 622 · printed entry 622

### English candidate

Al-Barāʾ ibn Maʿrūr ibn Ṣakhr ibn Khansāʾ ibn Sinān ibn ʿUbayd ibn ʿAdī ibn Ghanm ibn Kaʿb ibn Salama ibn Saʿd ibn ʿAlī ibn Asad ibn Sārida ibn Tazīd ibn Jusham ibn al-Khazraj, al-Anṣārī al-Khazrajī al-Sulamī, Abū Bishr.

Mūsā ibn ʿUqba related from al-Zuhrī that he was among the group who gave the first pledge at al-ʿAqaba. According to Ibn Isḥāq, he was the first to pledge allegiance, the first to face the qibla, and the first to bequeath one-third of his property. He was one of the twelve chiefs. Ibn Isḥāq said: Maʿbad ibn Kaʿb related to me that his brother ʿAbd Allāh—one of the most learned of the Anṣār—related to him that his father, who witnessed al-ʿAqaba, said: “We set out on pilgrimage with our people after we had begun to pray and had gained understanding, and with us was al-Barāʾ ibn Maʿrūr, our elder and leader.” He then related at length the account of the night of al-ʿAqaba, saying: “The first person to clasp the hand of the Messenger of God ﷺ was al-Barāʾ ibn Maʿrūr.”

Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān transmitted in his History through Ibn Shihāb, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Kaʿb, that Kaʿb said: “Al-Barāʾ ibn Maʿrūr was the first to face the Kaaba, both while alive and when death approached, before the Messenger of God ﷺ faced it. News of that reached the Messenger of God ﷺ, and he ordered him to face Jerusalem, which he obeyed. When he was dying, he instructed his family to turn him toward the Kaaba.”

Ibn Shāhīn transmitted, with a weak chain, through ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Qatāda: “My mother related to me from my father that al-Barāʾ ibn Maʿrūr died before the Hijra. His grave was oriented toward the Kaaba. He had made a bequest to the Messenger of God ﷺ, who accepted his bequest and then returned it to his children. He prayed over him”—meaning at his grave—“and pronounced four takbīrs.”

Al-Ṭabarānī transmitted by another route from Abū Qatāda that al-Barāʾ ibn Maʿrūr bequeathed one-third of his property to the Prophet ﷺ, for him to dispose of as he wished, but the Prophet ﷺ returned it. Ibn Isḥāq and others said that al-Barāʾ ibn Maʿrūr died one month before the Prophet ﷺ arrived.

## Source unit 632 · printed entry 632

### English candidate

Burayda ibn al-Ḥuṣayb ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ḥārith ibn al-Aʿraj ibn Saʿd ibn Razāḥ ibn ʿAdī ibn Sahm ibn Māzin ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Salāmān ibn Amḍā al-Aslamī. Ibn al-Sakan said that he embraced Islam at al-Ghamīm when the Prophet ﷺ passed him during the Emigration. He remained where he was until Badr and Uḥud had passed, and then came afterward. It is also said that he embraced Islam after the Prophet ﷺ returned from Badr. He settled in Basra when it was conquered. In the two Ṣaḥīḥs it is related from him that he took part in sixteen campaigns with the Prophet ﷺ. Abū ʿAlī al-Ṭūsī Aḥmad ibn ʿUthmān, a companion of Ibn al-Mubārak, said that Burayda’s name was ʿĀmir and that Burayda was a byname. Burayda’s reports are numerous and his merits well known. He campaigned in Khurasan during the time of ʿUthmān, then moved to Marw and lived there until he died during the caliphate of Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiya. Ibn Saʿd said that he died in the year 63.
