## Source unit 639 · printed entry 640

### English candidate

Basbasa ibn ʿAmr ibn Thaʿlaba ibn Kharasha ibn Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Saʿd ibn Dhibyān ibn Rashdān ibn Ghaṭafān ibn Qays ibn Juhayna al-Juhanī, an ally of Banū Ṭarīf ibn al-Khazraj ibn Sāʿida ibn Kaʿb ibn al-Khazraj. The name has two open bāʾs with a vowelless undotted sīn between them, followed by an open undotted sīn. He is also called Basbas, without the final letter; this is the view of Ibn Isḥāq and others. By agreement, he witnessed Badr. He is mentioned in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim in the hadith of Anas, who said, ‘The Messenger of God ﷺ sent Basbasa as a scout to see what Abū Sufyān’s caravan was doing.’ He then related the hadith concerning the Battle of Badr. The name appears with two bāʾs on the pattern faʿlala. ʿIyāḍ related that Muslim has it with one bāʾ, in the diminutive. Abū Dāwūd also transmitted it, and there the name appears in a diminutive form. Ibn al-Athīr likewise said that he saw it in an original copy of Ibn Manda’s work, but without hāʾ. The first form is correct. Ibn al-Kalbī stated that he is the man whom the poet intended in these lines:

Turn their chests forward, Basbas;
the people’s mounts are not to be held back.

## Source unit 641 · printed entry 642

### English candidate

Busr ibn Arṭāʾa—or ibn Arṭāʾa. Ibn Ḥibbān said, ‘Whoever says ibn Abī Arṭāʾa has erred.’ Abū Arṭāʾa’s name was ʿUmayr ibn ʿUwaymir ibn ʿImrān ibn al-Ḥulays ibn Sayyār ibn Nizār ibn Maʿīṣ ibn ʿĀmir ibn Luʾayy, al-Qurashī al-ʿĀmirī. Busr’s kunya was Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān. There is disagreement over his Companionship. The Syrians said that he heard from the Prophet ﷺ when he was young. In Sunan Abī Dāwūd, through a strong Egyptian chain, Junāda ibn Abī Umayya said, ‘We were with Busr ibn Abī Arṭāʾa at sea when a thief was brought to him. He said, “I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say: ‘Hands are not to be cut off while traveling.’”’ Ibn Ḥibbān transmitted in his Ṣaḥīḥ by way of Ayyūb ibn Maysara ibn Ḥulays: ‘I heard Busr ibn Abī Arṭāʾa say: I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say, “O God, make our outcome good in all our affairs”’—the rest of the hadith. Al-Wāqidī, however, said that he was born two years before the Prophet’s death ﷺ. Yaḥyā ibn Maʿīn said that the Prophet ﷺ died while Busr was young. Al-Dāraquṭnī said that he had Companionship. Ibn Yūnus said, ‘He was one of the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ. He witnessed the conquest of Egypt, marked out a house there, and was a partisan of Muʿāwiya. Muʿāwiya sent him to Yemen and the Ḥijāz at the beginning of the year 40 and ordered him to find those who obeyed ʿAlī and strike them; he did so. He also commanded the naval forces for Muʿāwiya and became mentally disordered near the end of his life.’ Ibn al-Sakan said that he died senile. Ibn Ḥibbān said, ‘He held offices for Muʿāwiya, and when he prayed, his supplication was sometimes answered. He has famous reports concerning the civil wars with which one ought not occupy oneself.’ Ibn al-Sakan said that he died during the days of Muʿāwiya. It is also said that he survived into the caliphate of ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān; this is Khalīfa’s view, which Ibn Ḥibbān stated with certainty. It is also said that he died during al-Walīd’s caliphate, in the year 86; al-Masʿūdī related that view.

<div dir="rtl" lang="ar">

بسر بن أرطاة أو بن أرطاة قال بن حبان من قال بن أبي أرطاة فقد وهم واسم أبي أرطاة عمير بن عويمر بن عمران بن الحليس بن سيار بن نزار بن معيص بن عامر بن لؤي القرشي العامري يكنى أبا عبد الرحمن مختلف في صحبته فقال أهل الشام سمع من النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم وهو صغير وفي سنن أبي داود بإسناد مصري قوي عن جنادة بن أبي أمية قال كنا مع بسر بن أبي أرطاة في البحر فأتى بسارق فقال سمعت رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يقول لا تقطع الأيدي في السفر وروى بن حبان في صحيحه من طريق أيوب بن ميسرة بن حليس سمعت بسر بن أبي أرطاة يقول سمعت رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يقول اللهم أحسن عاقبتنا في الأمور كلها الحديث وأما الواقدي فقال ولد قبل النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم بسنتين وقال يحيى بن معين مات النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم وهو صغير وقال الدارقطني له صحبة وقال بن يونس كان من أصحاب رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم شهد فتح مصر واختط بها وكان من شيعة معاوية وكان معاوية وجهه إلى اليمن والحجاز في أول سنة أربعين وأمره أن ينظر من كان في طاعة على فيوقع بهم ففعل ذلك وقد ولي البحر لمعاوية ووسوس في آخر أيامه قال بن السكن مات وهو خرف وقال بن حبان كان يلي لمعاوية الأعمال وكان إذا دعا ربما استجيب له وله أخبار شهيرة في الفتن لا ينبغي التشاغل بها وقيل مات أيام معاوية قاله بن السكن وقيل بقي إلى خلافة عبد الملك بن مروان وهو قول خليفة وبه جزم بن حبان وقيل مات في خلافة الوليد سنة ست وثمانين حكاه المسعودي

## Source unit 642 · printed entry 643

### English candidate

Busr ibn Abī Busr al-Māzinī, the father of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Busr, of Banū Māzin ibn Manṣūr ibn ʿIkrima. His mention is established in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim in the hadith of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Busr, who said, ‘The Prophet ﷺ stayed with my father, and we served him food’—the rest of the hadith. Al-Nasāʾī’s version has ʿAbd Allāh ibn Busr transmitting from his father. In the Book of Fasting he transmitted the hadith concerning fasting on Saturday from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Busr, from his father; it is also said, from his sister, from her father; and it is also said, from ʿAbd Allāh without an intermediary. Abū Zurʿa al-Dimashqī said, ‘Busr accompanied the Prophet ﷺ, as did his two sons and his daughter.’ Ibn al-Sakan transmitted by way of Muʿāwiya ibn Ṣāliḥ, from a son of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Busr, from his father ʿAbd Allāh, from his father Busr, that the Prophet ﷺ came to them riding a she-mule that they used to call ‘the Syrian she-ass.’

## Source unit 643 · printed entry 644

### English candidate

Busr ibn Jiḥāsh—with kasra on the jīm, followed by a lightly pronounced unpointed ḥāʾ; it is also said with fatḥa on the jīm, followed by a doubled ḥāʾ and then a dotted shīn after the alif—was a Qurashī who settled in Homs. Maḥmūd ibn Sumayʿ stated this and mentioned that he belonged to Banū ʿĀmir ibn Luʾayy. Ibn Mandah said: 'The people of Iraq pronounce it Busr with an unpointed sīn, while the people of Syria pronounce it Bishr with a dotted shīn.' Al-Dāraquṭnī and Ibn Zabr said that the dotted form is not sound. Abū ʿAlī al-Hajarī likewise recorded it with an unpointed sīn in his Nawādir, but called his father Jaḥsh. Muslim, Ibn al-Sakan, and others said that no one except Jubayr ibn Nufayr narrated from him. His report is in Aḥmad and Ibn Mājah by way of Jubayr, with a sound isnad. Ibn Mandah said that he was counted among the Syrians and died in Homs.

## Source unit 644 · printed entry 645

### English candidate

Bishr ibn Rāʿī al-ʿAyr al-Ashjaʿī. Al-Dārimī, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Ḥibbān, and al-Ṭabarānī transmitted by way of ʿIkrima ibn ʿAmmār, from Iyās ibn Salama ibn al-Akwaʿ, from his father, that the Prophet ﷺ saw Busr ibn Rāʿī al-ʿAyr eating with his left hand and said, 'Eat with your right hand.' He replied, 'I cannot.' The Prophet said, 'May you never be able!' Thereafter his right hand never reached his mouth. Muslim transmitted it by this route without naming Busr and added: 'Nothing prevented him except arrogance.' ʿIyāḍ inferred in his commentary on Muslim that the man was a hypocrite. Al-Nawawī rejected that in his own commentary, relying on the fact that Ibn Mandah, Abū Nuʿaym, Ibn Mākūlā, and others listed him among the Companions. This inference is open to objection, because everyone who listed him cited no basis other than this report; the possibility therefore remains. The accounts can perhaps be reconciled by supposing that at the time he had not yet accepted Islam and did so later. His name is also said to be Bishr, with dotted shīn. Ibn Mandah listed him in that form, but Abū Nuʿaym objected and ascribed it to a copyist's error. Al-Dāraquṭnī and Ibn Mākūlā related no disagreement that it was with unpointed sīn. Al-Bayhaqī, however, stated in al-Sunan that the dotted form was sounder. Ibn Fatḥūn made the unusual move of adding him under the name Bashīr, as will follow.

## Source unit 645 · printed entry 646

### English candidate

Busr ibn Sufyān ibn ʿAmr ibn ʿUwaymir ibn Ṣirma ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmayr ibn Ḥubshiyya ibn Salūl al-Khuzāʿī. Ibn al-Kalbī said that the Prophet ﷺ wrote to him and that he was a notable man. Abū ʿUmar said that he accepted Islam in the sixth year, and he is mentioned in the report of al-Ḥudaybiyya and elsewhere. Ibn Abī Shayba said: ʿAbd al-Raḥīm ibn Salmān related to us, from Zakariyyā ibn Abī Zāʾida, who said: 'I was with Abū Isḥāq—that is, al-Sabīʿī—between Mecca and Medina. A man of Khuzāʿa traveled alongside him and brought out for us a letter of the Messenger of God ﷺ to Khuzāʿa, written that day. It contained: “In the name of God, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful. From Muḥammad, the Messenger of God, to Budayl ibn Warqāʾ, Busr, and the chiefs of Banū ʿAmr ...”' and he related the report. Al-Ṭabarānī transmitted it at length from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Muḥammad ibn Busr ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salama ibn Budayl ibn Warqāʾ, from his forefathers, father after father, as far as Budayl, and related it. Al-Fākihī included it by ʿAbd al-Raḥmān's route and stated that he dictated it to them from his document. Ibn Mākūlā and others vocalized Busr with ḍamma on the bāʾ and sukūn on the unpointed sīn. I likewise saw the sign marking the letter as unpointed in the relied-upon copy of al-Fākihī's book. Aḥmad said in his Musnad: Yazīd ibn Hārūn related to us; Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq informed us, from al-Zuhrī, from ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr, from al-Miswar ibn Makhrama and Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam, who said: 'The Messenger of God ﷺ set out in the year of al-Ḥudaybiyya intending to visit the House, not intending to fight, and drove seventy sacrificial camels. When he reached ʿUsfān, Busr ibn Sufyān al-Kaʿbī met him and said, “Messenger of God, Quraysh has heard of your advance and has come out with nursing she-camels and their young ...”' and they related the report at length. It is in al-Bukhārī by way of Maʿmar, from al-Zuhrī, with the wording: 'Then Budayl ibn Warqāʾ came with a group of his people ...' and it relates the report without naming Busr. ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zibaʿrā addressed him in connection with the Banū Makhzūm demand that Khuzāʿa pay for the blood of al-Walīd ibn al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra:

'Indeed, convey to Busr ibn Sufyān that
the lone well-informed man conveys it from me ...'

and he continued the ode. Busr took his son by the hand and said: 'People of Quraysh, this son of mine is a pledge to you for the blood-money.' Khālid ibn al-Walīd took him, fed him, clothed him in a robe, perfumed him, and said, 'Go to your father.' Busr ibn Sufyān then carried the blood-money of al-Walīd to them.

## Source unit 653 · printed entry 654

### English candidate

Bishr ibn al-Barāʾ ibn Maʿrūr. His lineage was given recently in the biography of his father, who was one of the twelve chiefs and died before the Hijra. Bishr attended al-ʿAqaba with his father, witnessed Badr and the subsequent campaigns, and died after Khaybar from a morsel he had eaten with the Prophet ﷺ from the sheep into which poison had been placed. Ibn Isḥāq stated this. Yaʿqūb ibn Sufyān in his Tārīkh, Abū al-Shaykh in al-Amthāl, and al-Walīd ibn Abān in Kitāb al-Jūd transmitted by way of Ṣāliḥ ibn Kaysān, from Ibn Shihāb, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Kaʿb ibn Mālik, from Kaʿb ibn Mālik, that the Prophet ﷺ said: 'Who is your leader, Banū Naḍla?' They said, 'Jadd ibn Qays.' He asked, 'Why do you regard him as your leader?' They replied, 'He has the most wealth among us, although we nevertheless suspect him of miserliness.' He said, 'What malady is more malignant than miserliness? This man is not your leader.' They asked, 'Then who is our leader, Messenger of God?' He said, 'Bishr ibn al-Barāʾ ibn Maʿrūr.' Ibn Isḥāq corroborated it from al-Zuhrī and in his version said: 'Rather, your leader is the fair-complexioned, curly-haired Bishr ibn al-Barāʾ.' Yūnus and Ibrāhīm ibn Saʿd likewise transmitted it from al-Zuhrī in al-Uwaysī's narration from him. Yaʿqūb ibn Ibrāhīm ibn Saʿd differed, transmitting it from his father without a Companion in the chain; Ibn Abī ʿĀṣim included it. Maʿmar likewise transmitted it without a Companion; it is in ʿAbd al-Razzāq's Muṣannaf, Masāwiʾ al-Akhlāq by al-Kharāʾiṭī, the route of Ibn Akhī al-Zuhrī from his uncle in al-Amthāl by Abū ʿArūba, and the route of Shuʿayb from al-Zuhrī in the recension of Ibn Abī al-Yamān. It has a corroborating report from ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Jābir ibn ʿAtīk, from Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh, in al-Maʿrifa. Another comes from Abū Hurayra in al-Mustadrak, al-Amthāl by Abū ʿArūba, and al-Kāmil by Ibn ʿAdī. Ibn ʿAdī included it in the biography of Saʿīd ibn Muḥammad al-Warrāq, in his narration from Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr, from Abū Salama, from Abū Hurayra. Saʿīd did not transmit it alone: al-Naḍr ibn Shumayl corroborated him in the works of al-Walīd ibn Abān and Abū al-Shaykh, as did Muḥammad ibn Yaʿlā in al-Ḥākim's work. Abū al-Shaykh also transmitted it from Ibn ʿUmar with a weak isnad.

## Source unit 662 · printed entry 663

### English candidate

Bishr ibn ʿĀṣim ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar ibn Makhzūm al-Makhzūmī, an official of ʿUmar. Ibn Rushdayn gave his lineage in this form among the Companions. Al-Bukhārī, Ibn Ḥibbān, Ibn al-Sakan, and more than one scholar who followed them, however, called him Bishr ibn ʿĀṣim. Some called him al-Thaqafī, and some called him Bishr ibn ʿĀṣim ibn Sufyān. This last form is an error, for Bishr ibn ʿĀṣim ibn Sufyān ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Thaqafī—who narrates from his father, from his grandfather Sufyān ibn ʿAbd Allāh, that he had been an official of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb—is someone other than the Companion Bishr ibn ʿĀṣim. Al-Bukhārī, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Ibn Ḥibbān, and others distinguished between the two.

Al-Bukhārī said, “Bishr ibn ʿĀṣim, a Companion of the Prophet ﷺ.” He then said, “Bishr ibn ʿĀṣim ibn Sufyān ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rabīʿa al-Thaqafī, a Ḥijāzī; Ibn ʿUyayna heard from him,” and gave his biography. Ibn Ḥibbān said, “Bishr ibn ʿĀṣim had companionship.” Ibn Abī Ḥātim said, “Bishr ibn ʿĀṣim had companionship. Abū Wāʾil narrated from him. I heard my father say that.” He also said, “No one except Suwayd ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz mentioned him from Abū Wāʾil.” End quote.

This refers to Suwayd’s report from Sayyār Abū al-Ḥakam, from Abū Wāʾil: ʿUmar appointed Bishr ibn ʿĀṣim over the alms of Hawāzin, but Bishr held back. ʿUmar met him and said, “What kept you back? Do we not have a claim upon you to hear and obey?” He answered, “Yes, but I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say: ‘Whoever assumes charge of any matter of the Muslims will be brought with it on the Day of Resurrection until he is made to stand upon a bridge over Hell…’” and he related the report. Al-Bukhārī transmitted it by way of Suwayd and said, “So far as I know, no one other than Suwayd narrated it from Sayyār, and there is some weakness in his hadith.” End quote.

It has also reached us by a route other than Suwayd. Ibn Abī Shayba transmitted it from Ibn Numayr, from Fuḍayl ibn Ghazwān, from Muḥammad al-Rāsibī, from Bishr ibn ʿĀṣim, who said: “ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb wrote out my commission, but I said, ‘I have no need of it. I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say…’” and he related the report. Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr stated that this Muḥammad was Sulaym al-Rāsibī. If he is as Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said, the isnad is disconnected, because he did not meet Bishr ibn ʿĀṣim.

It has another route, transmitted by Ibn Mandah through Salama ibn Tamīm, from ʿAṭāʾ ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Sufyān, from Bishr ibn ʿĀṣim, who said: “ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb sent Bishr ibn ʿĀṣim to collect the alms of Mecca and Medina, but Bishr remained and did not set out. ʿUmar met him…” and he related the report at length. Ibn Mandah said, “In this hadith it has been said, ‘from Bishr ibn ʿĀṣim, from his father,’ but the inclusion of ‘from his father’ is not sound.”

What we have set out makes clear that Bishr ibn ʿĀṣim ibn Sufyān had no companionship; rather, he was among the followers of the Followers. The Companion Bishr ibn ʿĀṣim is not given a lineage in the sound reports beyond what was cited above from Ibn Rushdayn. If that is preserved correctly, he was Qurashī; otherwise, he was in any event certainly not al-Thaqafī. Ibn al-Athīr’s discussion conflicts with this, and his error becomes apparent upon considering carefully what I have critically established. God is the guide.

## Source unit 666 · printed entry 667

### English candidate

Bishr ibn ʿArfaṭa ibn al-Khashkhāsh al-Juhanī; he is also called Bashīr, which is the more common form. Ibn Mandah said that the first form is sounder. His report is with al-Walīd ibn Muslim: ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd ibn ʿAdī al-Juhanī related to us, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ḥumayd al-Juhanī, who said that a man of Juhayna named Bishr ibn ʿArfaṭa ibn al-Khashkhāsh said in verses of his:

“We, on the morning of the Conquest, beside Muḥammad,
came forth before the people, a thousand in the vanguard.
On the day of Ḥunayn we witnessed its raging;
it was a day dark and steeped in death.”

These are verses in which he says:

“I fight in al-Baṭḥāʾ, shielding Muḥammad,
against battalions who were more undutiful and more unjust.”

Al-Ḥasan ibn Sufyān transmitted it in his Musnad from Hishām ibn Khālid, and al-Ghanawī in his History from Ṣafwān ibn Ṣāliḥ, both from al-Walīd; both called him Bashīr. Muḥammad ibn ʿĀʾidh likewise mentioned him in the Campaigns from al-Walīd. Al-Khaṭīb included it in al-Muʾtalif by way of Hishām, and I saw it in his handwriting as Bashīr, on the morphological pattern of ʿaẓīm.

Al-Baghawī said, “I know no report with this isnad other than this hadith, and it is an unknown isnad.” I say: Abū Ḥātim said that ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd was acceptable, but I do not know his shaykh.

Hishām ibn ʿAmmār transmitted the cited report from al-Walīd, but in his version it is from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ḥumayd, from Bashīr ibn ʿArfaṭa, who said: “When the Prophet ﷺ called the tribes to Islam, Juhayna came, one thousand strong from among them and those who followed them. They accepted Islam and were present with the Prophet ﷺ in campaigns and engagements.” Bashīr composed the verses about that, and he then cited the poetry. I have not seen any of the routes name him Bishr without the yāʾ, and Ibn Mandah did not give his isnad back to al-Walīd for that form.

 كتائب هم كانوا اعق واظلما أخرجه الحسن بن سفيان في مسنده عن هشام بن خالد والغنوى في تاريخه عن صفوان بن صالح كلاهما عن الوليد وسمياه بشيرا وكذلك ذكره محمد بن عائد في المغازي عن الوليد وأورده الخطيب في المؤتلف من طريق هشام ورأيته بخطة بشير بوزن عظيم وقال البغوي لا أعلم بهذا الإسناد غير هذا الحديث وهو إسناد مجهول قلت عبد الحميد قال أبو حاتم إنه صالح وأما شيخه فلا أعرفه وقد روى الحديث المذكور هشام بن عمار عن الوليد فقال فيه عن عبد الله بن الحميد عن بشير بن عرفطة قال لما دعا النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم جاءت جهينة في ألف منهم وممن تبعهم فأسلموا وحضروا مع النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم مغازي ووقائع وفي ذلك يقول بشير فذكر الشعر ولم أر في شيء من الطرق تسميته بشرا بالسكون ولم يسق بن منده إسناده إلى الوليد بذلك

## Source unit 668 · printed entry 669

### English candidate

Bishr ibn ʿIṣma al-Muzanī. Kathīr ibn Aflaḥ, the client of Abū Ayyūb, narrated from him that he said, “I heard the Prophet ﷺ say: ‘Khuzāʿa are of me, and I am of them.’” Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Abū Aḥmad al-ʿAskarī, and Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr mentioned him. It has already been stated that al-Āmidī gave his name as Busr—with ḍamma on the bāʾ and a quiescent, unpointed sīn. Sayf mentioned in the Conquests that he was one of the commanders whom Abū ʿUbayda dispatched to his tribal subdivision, each of whom had companionship. Ibn ʿAsākir included him among those named Bishr, as he is named here. والله أعلم.

## Source unit 669 · printed entry 670

### English candidate

Bishr ibn ʿAṭiyya. Ibn Ḥibbān mentioned him and said, “I do not rely upon the isnad of his report.” Al-Bāwardī transmitted through Burd ibn Sinān, from Makḥūl, from Bishr ibn ʿAṭiyya, who said: “Before his death, the Messenger of God ﷺ cursed twenty-four practices. He said, ‘Indeed, the curse of God, the angels, and all people is upon anyone who diminishes any part of my right…’” and he related the report at length. Ibn Mandah transmitted through Makḥūl, from Ghuḍayf ibn al-Ḥārith, from Abū Dharr, that Bishr ibn ʿAṭiyya asked the Prophet ﷺ about something and he answered him. ## Source unit 670 · printed entry 671

### English candidate

Bishr ibn ʿUqruba al-Juhanī, Abū al-Yamān. He and his father had companionship, as will follow. He is also called Bashīr, with an added yāʾ. Ibn al-Sakan transmitted from al-Bukhārī that Bishr is sounder. I say: that is likewise how al-Bukhārī headed his biography in his History. He said: “ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUthmān said to me: Ḥujr ibn al-Ḥārith related to us: I heard ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAwf say: I heard Bishr ibn ʿUqruba say, ‘My father was martyred with the Messenger of God ﷺ in one of his campaigns. The Prophet ﷺ passed by me while I was weeping and said, “Be still. Would you not be content that I be your father and ʿĀʾisha your mother?” I said, “Yes.”’” Al-Bukhārī said, “ʿUthmān said to me: Bishr is well known in Palestine.” Muḥammad ibn al-Mubārak likewise transmitted it from Ḥujr ibn al-Ḥārith and named him Bishr.

Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr called him Bashīr. I say: that occurs in another hadith. I recited to Abū al-Faraj ibn Ḥammād that ʿAlī ibn Ismāʿīl informed them: Ismāʿīl ibn ʿAbd al-Qawī informed us, from Fāṭima bint Saʿd al-Khayr—by audition—from Fāṭima al-Jūzdāniyya—by audition—that Ibn Rīdha informed them: al-Ṭabarānī informed us: Abū Yazīd al-Qarāṭīsī and ʿAlī ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz related to us; they said: Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr related to us: Ḥujr ibn al-Ḥārith al-Ghassānī related to us, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAwf al-Kinānī, who was ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz’s official over al-Ramla. He witnessed ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān say to Bishr ibn ʿUqruba al-Juhanī on the day ʿAmr ibn Saʿīd was killed, “Abū al-Yamān, I have need of your words, so speak.” Bishr replied, “I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say: ‘Whoever stands to deliver an address seeking by it nothing but ostentation and reputation, God will station him in a station of ostentation and reputation.’”

Aḥmad transmitted it from Saʿīd, so we concurred with him through a higher chain. Al-Baghawī transmitted it from ʿAlī ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, so we likewise concurred with him. Ibn al-Sakan said, “This is a well-known hadith.” I say: it has another route, through Ismāʿīl ibn ʿAyyāsh, from Ḍamḍam ibn Zurʿa, from Shurayḥ ibn ʿUbayd, from Bishr ibn ʿUqruba, with a similar report. Abū Ḥātim preferred Bashīr, but Ibn Ḥibbān took the opposite position and said, “Whoever claims that he is Bashīr has erred.”

Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said that Bishr ibn ʿUqruba died after the year 85. Ibn Ḥibbān said that he died in a village within one of the districts of Palestine. Ibn Sumayʿ included him among those who settled in Palestine and named him Bishr.

He is also mentioned in another report in which he is called Bashīr—with fatḥa on the first letter and kasra on the dotted shīn. Isḥāq ibn Ibrāhīm al-Ramlī said in his Fawāʾid, in material I read in al-Silafī’s handwriting: al-Ḥasan ibn Bishr related to us; my father related to us that he heard his father, al-Ḥasan ibn Mālik ibn Nāqid, from his father, from his grandfather: “I heard Bashīr ibn ʿUqruba al-Juhanī say: ‘My father, ʿUqruba al-Juhanī, came to the Prophet ﷺ. He asked, “Who is this with you, ʿUqruba?” He replied, “My son, Baḥīr.” He said, “Come near.” I drew near until I sat on his right. He passed his hand over my head and asked, “What is your name?” I replied, “Baḥīr, Messenger of God.” He said, “No; rather, your name is Bashīr.” There was a knot in my tongue, so the Prophet ﷺ blew into my mouth and the knot in my tongue was released. Everything on my head turned white except the place where he had laid his hand, which remained black.’”

Isḥāq then transmitted it from al-Ḥasan ibn Suwayd, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿUqba al-Juhanī, from his father, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Bashīr ibn ʿUqruba, who said, “I heard my father say…” and he related a similar report. In both places he vocalized Baḥīr with fatḥa on its first letter and kasra on the unpointed ḥāʾ.

## Source unit 677 · printed entry 678

### English candidate

Bishr ibn Muʿādh al-Asadī. Abū Mūsā transmitted in al-Dhayl, by way of Abū Naṣr Aḥmad ibn Aḥyad ibn Nūḥ al-Bazzāz, that Aḥmad heard Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-ʿUqaylī in the year 246. Jābir said: 'Bishr ibn Muʿādh al-Asadī related to me that he and his father prayed with the Prophet ﷺ when Bishr was a boy ten years old. Gabriel was in front of the Prophet ﷺ, and the Prophet was looking at Gabriel's outline, resembling the shadow of a cloud. Whenever the outline moved, the Prophet ﷺ bowed.' Bishr ibn Muʿādh possessed no report other than this one. Abū Naṣr said that Jābir had reached the age of one hundred and fifty. I say: On that reckoning, Bishr ibn Muʿādh would have remained alive until after the year 100 of the Hijra. Jābir, however, was a liar notorious for lying. Ghanjār said in his Tārīkh that the emir Khālid ibn Aḥmad banished him from Bukhara because he claimed that he heard al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī say: 'When I was born, I was carried to the Prophet ﷺ.' Abū Saʿd al-Mālīnī also transmitted Bishr's report in his al-Muʾtalif, by way of Abū Jaʿfar ʿAnbasa ibn Muḥammad al-Marwazī: 'Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ayman al-Yamānī related to us; Bishr ibn Muʿādh al-Tawzī, of the people of Tawz, related to us. It is said that he had companionship, and he was then one hundred and sixty years old. He said: “My father and I prayed behind the Prophet ﷺ when I was a boy ten years old,”' and he related the report.

## Source unit 678 · printed entry 679

### English candidate

Bishr ibn Muʿāwiya ibn Thawr ibn Muʿāwiya ibn ʿUbāda ibn al-Bakkāʾ—whose name was Rabīʿa—ibn ʿĀmir ibn Ṣaʿṣaʿa al-ʿĀmirī al-Bakkāʾī. Al-Bukhārī, al-Baghawī, and others transmitted by way of ʿImrān ibn Māʿiz—and in Ibn Mandah's book the name is Ṣāʿid ibn al-ʿAlāʾ ibn Bishr—who said: 'My father related to me from his father, from Bishr ibn Muʿāwiya, that Bishr came with his father Muʿāwiya ibn Thawr to the Messenger of God ﷺ. The Messenger stroked Bishr's head and prayed for him,' and he related the report. It states that the trace of the Prophet's touch ﷺ was upon his face like a blaze and that nothing he touched failed to be cured. Al-Baghawī said: 'ʿImrān is unknown.' Ibn Mandah said: 'We know it only by this route.' I say: It has another route, transmitted by Abū Nuʿaym by way of Abū al-Haytham Ṣāʿid ibn Ṭālib al-Bakkāʾī, who said: 'My father related to me, from his father Nawwās ibn Ribāṭ, from his father Wāṣil ibn Kāhil, from his father, from his father Mujālid ibn Thawr, from Bishr ibn Muʿāwiya ibn Thawr—who was Ṣāʿid's maternal grandfather—that Bishr and his father came in a delegation to the Prophet ﷺ. He taught them Yā Sīn, al-Fātiḥa, and the two sūras of seeking refuge, and taught them to begin the prayer with the basmala,' and he related a long report. Its isnad is unknown from Ṣāʿid upward. It has another route that Ibn Shāhīn included by way of Ziyād ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Bakkāʾī, from Muʿāwiya ibn Bishr ibn Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiya ibn Thawr, who said: 'Bishr ibn Muʿāwiya ibn Thawr came to the Messenger of God ﷺ, who stroked his face and prayed for him.' This route is disconnected. Ibn Shāhīn also transmitted, as did Thābit in al-Dalāʾil, by way of Hishām ibn al-Kalbī, who said: 'Abū Miskīn, a client of Abū Hurayra, related to me; al-Jaʿd ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Māʿiz ibn Mujālid ibn Thawr al-Bakkāʾī related to me from his father, who said: Muʿāwiya ibn Thawr ibn ʿUbāda al-Bakkāʾ came to the Prophet ﷺ as a very old man, accompanied by a son called Bishr, al-Hajnaʿ ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jundaʿ ibn al-Bakkāʾ, and Jahm al-Aṣamm. Muʿāwiya said, “Messenger of God, stroke the face of this son of mine.” He did so,' and he related the report. Muḥammad ibn Bishr ibn Muʿāwiya composed concerning this:

'By my father, whose head the Prophet stroked,
and for whom he prayed for good and blessings.'

Bishr will also be mentioned in the biography of ʿAbd ibn ʿAmr ibn Kaʿb and in the biography of his father, Muʿāwiya ibn Thawr.

Bashīr ibn al-Ḥārith al-Anṣārī. Ibn Qāniʿ and others mentioned him among the Companions. Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said Ibn Abī Ḥātim mentioned him. Ibn Qāniʿ transmitted by way of Dāwūd al-Awdī, from al-Shaʿbī, from Bashīr ibn al-Ḥārith, that the Prophet ﷺ said, ‘When you differ between yāʾ and tāʾ, write it with yāʾ.’ He mentioned the Qurʾān. ## Source unit 693 · printed entry 694

### English candidate

Bashīr ibn Saʿd ibn Thaʿlaba ibn Jilās—with ḍamma on the jīm and the word undoubled. ## Source unit 703 · printed entry 704

### English candidate

Bashīr ibn Maʿbad; it is also said ibn Nadhīr ibn Maʿbad ibn Sharāḥīl ibn Sabuʿ ibn Ḍubārā ibn Sadūs ibn Shaybān ibn Dhuhl al-Sadūsī, known as Ibn al-Khaṣāṣiyya. The khāʾ has fatḥa and the undotted ṣād is undoubled. Al-Khaṣāṣiyya is a matronym from Khaṣāṣa, whose name was al-Āʾa bint ʿAmr ibn Kaʿb ibn al-Ḥārith ibn al-Ghiṭrīf the Younger ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĀmir ibn al-Ghiṭrīf the Elder al-Azdī. She was the mother of Bashīr’s remote ancestor Ḍubārā ibn Sadūs. Al-Dimyāṭī established this from Ibn al-Kalbī. Al-Rāmahurmuzī stated it categorically and said her name was Kabsha. It is also said Māwiya bint ʿAmr ibn al-Ḥārith al-Ghiṭrīfiyya, or bint ʿAmr ibn Kaʿb ibn al-Ghiṭrīf. Abū ʿUmar said al-Khaṣāṣiyya was not his mother but his grandmother. In his lineage he wrote Ḍubāb instead of Ḍubārā, which is a scribal error, and called his father Yazīd instead of Nadhīr. In Ibn al-Sakan’s book, in Ibn Mufarrij’s hand, it is Budayr, and that is correct. His hadith is in al-Adab al-Mufrad of al-Bukhārī and in the Sunan. His name had been Zaḥm—with zāy and a vowelless undotted ḥāʾ—but the Prophet ﷺ changed it. He has other hadiths besides this one.

### Arabic authority

## Source unit 704 · printed entry 705

### English candidate

Bashīr ibn Maʿbad, Abū Maʿbad al-Aslamī. Ibn Ḥibbān said he had Companionship and was counted among the Kufans; his son transmitted his hadith. Al-Bukhārī said, ‘Bashīr al-Aslamī had Companionship; his hadith is among the Kufans. Ṭalq ibn Ghannām told me: Muḥammad ibn Bishr ibn Bashīr al-Aslamī related from his father, from his grandfather, that ashes used for washing were brought to him for ablution. He took them with his right hand. When this was questioned, he said, “We take good things only with our right hands.”’ Ibn Manda transmitted it by way of Abū Aḥmad al-Zubayrī, from Muḥammad, ‘from his grandfather, who had Companionship.’ We related it by way of ʿAbbās al-Dūrī, from Ṭalq ibn Ghannām, with the wording that he witnessed the Pledge of Riḍwān. Al-Baghawī transmitted by way of Qays ibn al-Rabīʿ, from Bishr ibn Bashīr al-Aslamī, from his father, who had Companionship, another hadith. Ibn al-Sakan transmitted it by another route from Qays, saying he was one of the Companions of the Tree. In none of these routes did I find his father named Maʿbad, except that Abū Ḥātim stated it categorically. Ibn Ḥibbān mistakenly separated Bashīr al-Aslamī, whose hadith his son Bishr transmitted, from Bashīr ibn Maʿbad al-Aslamī. They are one man. Ibn al-Sakan said, ‘Bashīr al-Aslamī had Companionship; it is said he was Bashīr ibn Maʿbad.’ Then, by way of Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿlā, from Muḥammad ibn Bishr, from his father, from his grandfather Bashīr ibn Maʿbad, he gave the preceding hadith. Thus we have found the basis for naming his father Maʿbad. والله أعلم. He has another hadith, transmitted by al-Baghawī by way of al-Bukhārī, from Abū Masʿūd, from Abū Salama Bishr ibn Bashīr al-Aslamī, from his father, concerning the well of Rūma.

## Source unit 705 · printed entry 706

### English candidate

Bashīr ibn Muʿāwiya, Abū ʿAlqama al-Najrānī. Al-Ḥākim mentioned him in al-Iklīl, Abū Saʿd in Sharaf al-Muṣṭafā, and al-Bayhaqī in al-Dalāʾil, by way of Yūnus ibn Bukayr, from Salama ibn ʿAbd Yasūʿ. In Abū Saʿd’s version it is from Saʿīd ibn ʿAmr, from his father, from his grandfather, who had been a Christian and embraced Islam: the Messenger of God ﷺ wrote to the people of Najrān, and a delegation from them came to him and returned. While the bishop was reading his letter, his mount stumbled. A brother of his named Bashīr ibn Muʿāwiya, Abū ʿAlqama, spoke ill of Muhammad ﷺ. The bishop rebuked him and said, ‘You have mentioned a messenger-prophet.’ Bashīr replied, ‘By God, then I shall not get down from this mount until I join him.’ He turned his mount toward Medina, saying:

To you she runs, her girth quivering,
opposing Christianity, her former faith.

He remained with the Messenger of God ﷺ until Abū ʿAlqama was later martyred. I have abridged this story, which extends for about three folios. He will be mentioned under the kunyās, إن شاء الله.

## Source unit 708 · printed entry 709

### English candidate

Bashīr ibn Yazīd al-Ḍubaʿī; in al-Baghawī it appears as Bashīr ibn Zayd. Ibn al-Sakan said his hadith was among the Basrans. Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted from his father that he had Companionship. Al-Baghawī said, ‘I have heard of him only in this hadith,’ then gave it by way of al-Ashhab al-Ḍubaʿī, from him: the Messenger of God ﷺ said on the Day of Dhū Qār, ‘This is the first day on which the Arabs obtained justice from the Persians.’ Baqī ibn Makhlad transmitted it in his Musnad by this route, as did al-Bukhārī in al-Tārīkh. Their wording and Ibn al-Sakan’s say that he had lived into the pre-Islamic age. Al-Bukhārī said Khalīfa once called him Yazīd ibn Bishr. Abū ʿUmar said the first form is sounder. Ibn Ḥibbān listed him among the Successors and said, ‘An early shaykh who lived into the pre-Islamic age and transmitted disconnected reports.’ I say: none of the report’s routes states that he heard directly. الله أعلم. The Day of Dhū Qār is a famous battle of the Arabs, fought between the army of Khusraw and Bakr ibn Wāʾil for reasons whose explanation would be lengthy; the chroniclers have recorded them. Ibn al-Kalbī said it occurred some months after Badr. He said: al-Kalbī informed me, from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said that the Battle of Dhū Qār was mentioned in the Prophet’s presence ﷺ. He said, ‘That was the first day on which the Arabs obtained justice from the Persians, and through me they were granted victory.’

<div dir="rtl" lang="ar">

بشير بن يزيد الضبعي ووقع عند البغوي بشير بن زيد قال بن السكن حديثه في البصريين وقال بن أبي حاتم عن أبيه له صحبة وقال البغوي لم أسمع به الا في الحديث ثم ساقه من طريق الأشهب الضبعي عنه قال قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يوم ذي قار هذا أول يوم انتصفت فيه العرب من العجم وأخرجه بقي بن مخلد في مسنده من هذا الوجه وكذلك البخاري في تاريخه ووقع في سياقه وفي سياق بن السكن وكان قد أدرك الجاهلية قال البخاري وقال خليفة مرة يزيد بن بشر قال أبو عمر الأول أصح وذكره بن حبان في التابعين فقال شيخ قديم أدرك الجاهلية يروي المراسيل قلت وليس في شيء من طرق حديثه له سماع فالله أعلم ويوم ذي قار من أيام العرب المشهورة كان بين جيش كسرى وبين بكر بن وائل لاسباب يطول شرحها قد ذكرها الاخباريون وذكر بن الكلبي أنها كانت بعد وقعة بدر بأشهر قال وأخبرني الكلبي عن أبي صالح عن بن عباس قال ذكرت وقعة ذي قار عند النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم فقال ذاك أول يوم انتصفت فيه العرب من العجم وبي نصروا

## Source unit 711 · printed entry 712

### English candidate

Bashīr al-Ḥārithī al-Kaʿbī, father of ʿIṣām. Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from his father that he had companionship and that his hadith was with Saʿīd ibn Marwān al-Rahāwī. ʿUmayra ibn ʿAbd al-Muʾmin corroborated him, from ʿIṣām ibn Bashīr al-Ḥārithī al-Kaʿbī, who said: “My father related to me: ‘My people, Banū al-Ḥārith ibn Kaʿb, sent me as their delegate to the Prophet ﷺ. He asked, “From where have you come?” I replied, “I am my people’s delegate to you, bringing their acceptance of Islam.” He said, “Welcome. What is your name?” I replied, “My name is Akbar.” He said, “You are Bashīr.”’” Al-Nasāʾī transmitted it in al-Yawm wa-l-Layla, as did al-Bukhārī in his History and Ibn al-Sakan. Ibn Mandah said, “It is uncommon; we know it only from the report of the people of al-Jazīra, from ʿIṣām.” In al-Bukhārī’s version, ʿIṣām reached one hundred and ten years of age.

## Source unit 716 · printed entry 717

### English candidate

Baṣra ibn Aktham al-Anṣārī; he is also said to have been al-Khuzāʿī. He has a hadith concerning marriage, narrated from him by Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab and transmitted by Abū Dāwūd and others. His name is also given as Busra—with ḍamma on the first letter and an unpointed sīn—and as Naḍla, with nūn and a dotted ḍād, and as Naḍra, the same except that rāʾ replaces lām. The first form is preferable and is the form preserved through Ṣafwān ibn Sulaym from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab.

Some transmitters differed from ʿAbd al-Razzāq concerning it. Some gave it with nūn and dotted ḍād; among those, some then used lām and others rāʾ. Yaḥyā ibn Abī Kathīr likewise transmitted from Yazīd ibn Nuʿaym, from Saʿīd, the form Naḍra with nūn and dotted ḍād; Ibn Mandah and others transmitted it. It was also transmitted from Muḥammad ibn Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab, from his father, with uncertainty between Baṣra or Naḍra: either with bāʾ and an unpointed ṣād, or with nūn and a dotted ḍād. Ibn Mandah transmitted it by that route as Busra, with bāʾ and an unpointed sīn, and gave his affiliation as al-Ghifārī or al-Kindī. The narrator from Muḥammad is very weak: Isḥāq ibn Abī Farwa.

Al-Ṭabarānī placed the cited marriage report in the biography of Baṣra ibn Abī Baṣra al-Ghifārī, who is mentioned next. Ibn al-Kalbī listed among the children of Aktham ibn Abī al-Jawn sons named Maʿbad and Baṣra, and a daughter named Jaldiyya. It is therefore possible that Baṣra is the subject of this hadith, if the form “ibn Aktham al-Khuzāʿī” is correctly preserved.

## Source unit 720 · printed entry 721

### English candidate

Buqayla the Elder al-Ashjaʿī, of Banū Bakr ibn Ashjaʿ, was known as Abū al-Minhāl. His name is Buqayla, with qāf, in the diminutive. Al-Āmidī mentioned him under the letter bāʾ and said that it is reported that he reinforced the Prophet ﷺ on the day of Uḥud; it is also said that he commanded the cavalry on the day of Uḥud—meaning the cavalry of Ashjaʿ—while another report says that the cavalry commander was Misʿar al-Ashjaʿī.

Buqayla was a great chief and a poet. During one of his campaigns he wrote these lines to ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb:

“Let a messenger carry word to Abū Ḥafṣ:
my waist-wrapper be your ransom—from a trustworthy brother.
Our young she-camels—may God guide you—indeed
we were kept from you throughout the time of siege.”

The story will follow in the biography of Jaʿda al-Sulamī, إن شاء الله تعالى.

Among the poetry of this Buqayla are the lines:

“Clothe your kinsman if his rags are worn;
there is no new garment for one who will not wear the old.
The most poetic verse that you can utter
is a verse that, when you recite it, is called true.
Poetry is only the core of a man, which he displays
before gatherings—whether wisdom or folly.”

ʿUmar ibn Shabba said in his History of Medina: “Buqayla ibn al-Minhāl al-Ashjaʿī said…” He was among those who witnessed al-Qādisiyya with Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ. Some people call him Nufayla—with nūn and fāʾ. ʿUmar ibn Shabba then cited poetry of his yearning for Medina. In al-Muwaffaqiyyāt, after citing poetry of his, al-Zubayr ibn Bakkār said, “I heard al-ʿUtbī corrupt his name and call him Nufayla, with nūn.”

## Source unit 721 · printed entry 722

### English candidate

Bakr ibn Umayya al-Ḍamrī, brother of ʿAmr; his lineage will appear in his brother’s biography. Ibn Ḥibbān, al-Bukhārī, and Ibn al-Sakan mentioned him among the Companions. Abū Ḥātim said that he had companionship. Ibn Ḥibbān said that his hadith was with his nephew al-Faḍl ibn ʿAmr ibn Umayya.

I say: his hadith reached me in Ibn Abī al-Dunyā’s Mujābī al-Daʿwa and in al-Muwaffaqiyyāt, through Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq: “Al-Ḥasan ibn al-Faḍl ibn al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAmr ibn Umayya related to me, from his father, from his paternal uncle Bakr ibn Umayya, who said: ‘In the territory of Banū Ḍamra there was, in the early days of Islam, a neighbor from Juhayna, while at that time we were still in our polytheism.’” He then related the story of the Juhanī with Rīsha al-Muḥāribī: Rīsha’s wrongdoing against him and the Juhanī’s supplication against Rīsha.

All the collectors transmitted it by way of Ibn Isḥāq, and it is known only through this isnad. I consider it disconnected, because Bakr ibn Umayya was the paternal uncle of al-Faḍl’s father, and the report comes by his route only with an ʿanʿana chain.

## Source unit 722 · printed entry 723

### English candidate

Bakr ibn Jabala ibn Wāʾil ibn Qays ibn Bakr ibn ʿĀmir ibn ʿAwf ibn Bakr ibn ʿAwf ibn ʿUdhra ibn Zayd al-Lāt al-Kalbī. His name had been ʿAbd ʿAmr, and the Prophet ﷺ renamed him Bakr. Ibn al-Kalbī mentioned him.

Ibn Mandah transmitted through Hishām ibn al-Kalbī, who said: al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAmr and others related to us that ʿAbd ʿAmr ibn Jabala said, “We had an idol called ʿAyr, which they used to venerate. We passed by it, and I heard a voice say, ‘Bakr ibn Jabala, do you know Muḥammad?’” He then related the hadith, which contains the story of his acceptance of Islam. This is how Ibn Mandah transmitted it in abridged form.

Al-Marzubānī also alluded to his story and cited poetry by him, including:

“I came to the Messenger of God when he brought guidance,
and after denial I became a believer in God.”

Among the descendants of his brother was Saʿīd ibn al-Abrash al-Kalbī, the well-known commander under the Marwānid dynasty: Saʿīd ibn al-Walīd ibn ʿAbd ʿAmr ibn Jabala.

## Source unit 723 · printed entry 724

### English candidate

Bakr ibn al-Ḥārith al-Anmārī, Abū al-Minqaʿa; he is also called Abū Munayqiʿa. Al-Tirmidhī and Ibn Shāhīn mentioned him among the Companions, as did Abū Bakr ibn ʿĪsā al-Baghdādī among the Companions who settled in Homs. Abū Bakr said: “I asked ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Makhramī for Abū al-Minqaʿa’s name. He replied, ‘Jābir ibn al-Nimr ibn Ḥabīb and Anas ibn Khālid informed me that Abū Munayqiʿa’s name was Bakr ibn al-Ḥārith, a Companion of the Messenger of God ﷺ.’”

One manuscript reads Bakr ibn al-Ḥubāb and gives his kunya as Abū ʿAbd al-Samīʿ. Ibn al-Dabbāgh, Ibn al-Amīn, and Ibn Fatḥūn added him as an omitted entry. Ibn Qāniʿ also mentioned him and called him Bakr ibn al-Ḥārith; he then transmitted his hadith through Kulayb ibn Minqaʿa, from his grandfather, who said, “Messenger of God, to whom should I show the greatest dutiful kindness?” He answered, “Your mother…” and the report continues.

## Source unit 724 · printed entry 725

### English candidate

Bakr ibn Ḥāritha al-Juhanī. Al-Dūlābī mentioned him and transmitted through al-Ḥasan ibn Bishr, from his father Bishr ibn Mālik, from his father Mālik ibn Nāqid, from his father Nāqid ibn Mālik al-Juhanī: Bakr ibn Ḥāritha al-Juhanī related to me, saying, “I was in a detachment sent by the Messenger of God ﷺ. We and the polytheists fought.” He then related a hadith concerning the revelation of God Most High’s words, “It is not for a believer to kill a believer except by mistake.” He said, “The Messenger of God ﷺ then brought me near.” Ibn Mandah also transmitted it.

Al-Maʿmarī transmitted from Isḥāq ibn Ibrāhīm al-Ramlī, from al-Ḥasan, from Bishr, with this isnad to Bakr ibn Ḥāritha al-Juhanī, that he fought the polytheists. The Messenger of God ﷺ asked him, “What did you do today, Bakr?” He replied, “I barbartu them with lances—a fine barbarah.” The Messenger of God ﷺ therefore named him al-Barbīr.

It will be stated in the biography of al-Ḥārith ibn Yazīd that the reason for the revelation of this verse was his story with ʿAyyāsh ibn Abī Rabīʿa.

## Source unit 727 · printed entry 728

### English candidate

Bakr ibn al-Shaddākh al-Laythī; he is also called Bukayr. He was mentioned above in the biography of Ashʿath. Ibn Mandah transmitted through Abū Bakr al-Hudhalī, from ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Yaʿlā al-Laythī, that Bakr ibn Shaddākh al-Laythī was among those who served the Prophet ﷺ while he was a boy. When he reached puberty, he informed the Prophet ﷺ, who prayed for him.

Hishām ibn al-Kalbī mentioned this story in the Book of Genealogy, but called him Bukayr ibn Shaddād ibn ʿĀmir ibn al-Mulawwaḥ ibn Yaʿmur, who is al-Shaddākh ibn ʿAwf ibn Kaʿb ibn ʿĀmir ibn Layth al-Laythī. He related the cited story and then said that Bukayr was the rider of Aṭlāl, whom al-Shammākh meant in his verse:

“I was kept from cavalry at Mūqān that surrendered
Bukayr of Banū al-Shaddākh, the rider of Aṭlāl.”

Aṭlāl was the name of his horse. He had a story with her that Sayf ibn ʿUmar mentioned in the Conquests. Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ had appointed him over his people when they entered Iraq. When they wished to ford the Tigris, the people were apprehensive about entering the water. Bukayr said, “Leap, Aṭlāl!” She said, “I leapt—by Sūrat al-Baqara!”

Bakr had many accounts with Saʿd which Sayf and others mentioned, but in some of them he was called Bakr ibn ʿAbd Allāh. It is possible that Bakr ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Laythī was another person. The apparent explanation is that al-Hudhalī attributed him to his higher ancestor al-Shaddākh, while Ibn al-Kalbī is the authority to whom genealogy is referred. He was the man who conquered Mūqān; Surāqa ibn ʿAmr had sent him there.

## Source unit 735 · printed entry 736

### English candidate

Bilāl ibn Rabāḥ al-Ḥabashī, the muezzin. He was also Bilāl ibn Ḥamāma; she was a bondwoman. Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq purchased him from the polytheists while they were torturing him for affirming divine oneness, and he freed him. Bilāl then remained constantly with the Prophet ﷺ, called the prayer for him, and witnessed every campaign with him. The Prophet ﷺ established brotherhood between Bilāl and Abū ʿUbayda ibn al-Jarrāḥ. After the Prophet ﷺ, Bilāl went out to fight in God's cause until he died in Syria. Abū Nuʿaym said that he was the same age as Abū Bakr and was treasurer to the Messenger of God ﷺ. Abū Isḥāq al-Jawzajānī transmitted in his Tārīkh by way of Manṣūr, from Mujāhid, who said that ʿAmmār stated: 'Everyone said what they wanted'—meaning the polytheists—'except Bilāl.' His merits are numerous and well known. Ibn Isḥāq said that he was born among the clients of Banū Jumaḥ and that his mother's name was Ḥamāma. When the midday heat grew intense, Umayya ibn Khalaf would bring him out, cast him on his back in the gravel plain of Mecca, order a huge rock placed upon his chest, and then say: 'You will remain like this until you die or disbelieve in Muḥammad.' While enduring this, Bilāl would say: 'One! One!' Abū Bakr passed by him and purchased him from Umayya in exchange for a strong black slave belonging to him. Al-Bukhārī said that Bilāl died in Syria during ʿUmar's time. Ibn Bukayr said that he died in the plague of ʿAmwās. ʿAmr ibn ʿAlī said that he died in the year twenty. Ibn Zabr said that he died at Dārayyā. Ibn Mandah's al-Maʿrifa says that he was buried in Aleppo.

## Source unit 746 · printed entry 747

### English candidate

Banna al-Juhanī—the name has, after the initial bāʾ, an open doubled nūn. Ibn Luhayʿa narrated his report from Abū al-Zubayr, from Jābir, from Banna, concerning the prohibition against handing an unsheathed sword to another. Al-Baghawī said: 'I know of no report that he narrated except this one, nor anyone who transmitted it except Ibn Luhayʿa.' I say: Rushdayn ibn Saʿd corroborated him, narrating it from both Abū ʿAmr al-Tujībī and Ibn Luhayʿa, from Abū al-Zubayr; Abū Nuʿaym transmitted it. Ḥammād ibn Salama differed from him and did not mention Banna in the isnad. There is disagreement over the vocalization of his name. The majority gave it with initial bāʾ. Ibn al-Sakan entered the name with initial yāʾ instead of bāʾ. ʿAbbās al-Dūrī related from Ibn Maʿīn that he said, 'It is Nubayh'—meaning with initial nūn bearing ḍamma, followed by bāʾ, in the diminutive form. ## Source unit 748 · printed entry 749

### English candidate

Bahz al-Qushayrī, also said to be al-Bahzī. Al-Baghawī and others mentioned him among the Companions and transmitted by way of Thubayt ibn Kathīr al-Ḍabbī—Thubayt begins with thāʾ, then bāʾ, and ends with tāʾ, in the diminutive form—from Yaḥyā, from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab, from Bahz, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ used the tooth-stick crosswise. Al-Baghawī said: 'I know of no report narrated by Bahz except this one, and it is objectionable.' Ibn Mandah said that ʿAbbād ibn Yūsuf narrated it from Thubayt but said 'from al-Qushayrī' in place of 'from Bahz.' Mukhayyis ibn Tamīm narrated it from Bahz ibn Ḥakīm, from his father, from his grandfather, saying that Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab had heard it only from Bahz ibn Ḥakīm; the transmitter from Saʿīd rendered it mursal, and some people therefore supposed Bahz to be a Companion. I say: Ibn Mandah, however, mentioned that Sulaymān ibn Salama al-Janāʾizī narrated it from al-Yamān ibn ʿAdī, from Thubayt, from Yaḥyā, from Saʿīd, from Muʿāwiya al-Qushayrī. On that basis, Saʿīd may have heard it from Muʿāwiya, the grandfather of Bahz ibn Ḥakīm, and on one occasion said 'from Bahz,' with the word 'grandfather' omitted by one of the transmitters. ## Source unit 749 · printed entry 750

Bahlūl ibn Dhuʾayb, the grave robber. He is mentioned in a report that is not established. ## Source unit 752 · printed entry 753

### English candidate

Būlā, without a lineage given. ʿAbdān listed him among the Companions and transmitted, by way of Khaṭṭāb ibn Muḥammad ibn Būlā, from his father, from his grandfather, that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: “Beware of hot food…” The chain is unknown. So I read in Mughalṭāy’s handwriting, though I did not find it in al-Mushtabih. That work contains only ʿAbd Allāh ibn Tūlā, who narrated from ʿUthmān and from whom Abū Ḥāzim narrated; the name there begins with tāʾ. Ibn Qāniʿ corrupted it and said, among the Companions, “Būlā, father of ʿAbd Allāh.” He then transmitted, by way of ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Abī Ḥāzim, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Būlā, from his father—one of the Prophet’s Companions ﷺ—that the Prophet ﷺ came to the Red Mountain and saw a dead ewe, whereupon we held our noses… The report includes: “This world is more insignificant to God than this is to its people.” Ibn Qāniʿ entered the name with bāʾ, thereby corrupting it, and he also erred in the chain. The correct form is ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Abī Ḥāzim, from his father, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Tūlā, without “from his father.” والله أعلم.

## Source unit 753 · printed entry 754

### English candidate

Bayḥara—with an unpointed ḥāʾ bearing a fatḥa, preceded by a quiescent yāʾ—ibn ʿĀmir. Ibn Ḥibbān included him among the Companions and said that he came as a delegate to the Prophet ﷺ. Ibn al-Sakan said that he had companionship and one hadith. He, al-Ṭabarānī, and others transmitted, by way of al-Mundhir al-ʿAṣarī, that he heard Bayḥara ibn ʿĀmir say: “We came to the Messenger of God ﷺ, accepted Islam, and asked him to excuse us from the late-evening prayer. We said, ‘We are occupied with milking our camels.’ He replied, ‘إن شاء الله, you will milk them and you will pray.’” Abū Nuʿaym said Yaḥyā ibn Rāshid alone transmitted it from al-Raḥḥāl ibn al-Mundhir, from his father. I say: Yaḥyā is weak. Abū ʿUmar corrupted the name as Baḥrāh, apparently writing it from memory, for I saw it carefully vocalized in a copy of Ibn al-Sakan’s book as first reported. Ibn Mandah related that it is also said as Baḥra and counted him among the Bedouins of Basra. I suspect this man belonged to ʿAbd al-Qays. As for identifying him as Bayḥara ibn Firās ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salama ibn Kaʿb ibn Qushayr al-Qushayrī, Ibn al-Kalbī reported that this man prodded the Messenger of God’s she-camel ﷺ, so the Messenger of God ﷺ cursed him. He is someone else. I have seen no one include him among the Companions; apparently he did not accept Islam. His report will come in the entry on Ḍubāʿa in the Book of Women, إن شاء الله تعالى. I later saw in Ibn al-Sakan’s book that the subject of this entry was an Azdī.

## Source unit 754 · printed entry 755

### English candidate

Bashīr ibn Abī Masʿūd al-Anṣārī al-Badrī. Ibn Mandah transmitted by way of Abū Dāwūd al-Ṭayālisī, from Ayyūb ibn ʿUtba, from Ibn Ḥazm al-Anṣārī, that ʿUrwa informed him: “Abū Masʿūd—or Bashīr ibn Abī Masʿūd—related to me,” and that both had lived to the time of the Prophet ﷺ; he then related the report on prayer times. ʿAlī ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz likewise transmitted it in his Musnad from Aḥmad ibn Yūnus, from Ayyūb ibn ʿUtba, but his wording says both had accompanied the Prophet ﷺ. This is part of Ayyūb ibn ʿUtba’s confusion. The report is in fact from ʿUrwa, from Bashīr, from his father, as in the two Ṣaḥīḥs and elsewhere. Ibn Mandah also transmitted from Saʿīd ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, from Ibn Ḥalbas, from Bashīr—‘and he was one of the Companions’—and from Misʿar, from Thābit ibn ʿUbayd: “I saw Bashīr, and he had companionship.” I say: in both routes the pronoun may refer to Abū Masʿūd. We related the third report in the Fawāʾid of Abū al-ʿAbbās al-Aṣamm: Abū ʿUtba related to us; Baqiyya related to us; Saʿīd related to us, from Ibn Ḥalbas, who said: Bashīr—‘and he was one of the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ’—said: “Fear God and hold fast to the community, for God would not unite the community of Muḥammad upon error.” The report is mawqūf. Were this securely preserved, Bashīr would unquestionably be a Companion. In my judgment, “from his father” fell out, because this saying is securely preserved from Abū Masʿūd; al-Ḥākim and others transmitted several routes from him. والله أعلم. Al-Bukhārī, al-ʿIjlī, Muslim, Abū Ḥātim, and others state decisively that Bashīr was a Follower. It is said he was born during the lifetime of the Prophet ﷺ, and also afterward. Ibn Khalafūn mentioned this. Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr in al-Tamhīd states decisively that he was born in the time of the Prophet ﷺ.

## Source unit 755 · printed entry 756

### English candidate

Bashīr ibn Fudayk, whose teknonym was Abū Ṣāliḥ. Ibn al-Sakan said: “He is said to have companionship, but companionship belongs only to his father.” Ibn Mandah said Bashīr had seen the Prophet and his father had companionship. Ibn Ḥibbān included him among the Companions and said he came to the Prophet ﷺ; his report is among his descendants. Al-Baghawī said: “It reached me from Fudayk ibn Sulaymān, from al-Awzāʿī, from al-Zuhrī, from Ṣāliḥ ibn Bashīr ibn Fudayk, that his father said: ‘I said, Messenger of God, is it the case that whoever does not emigrate perishes?’ He replied, ‘Establish prayer…’” Al-Bāwardī transmitted this route too, but it is an error. Al-Baghawī and Ibn Ḥibbān transmitted by way of al-Zubaydī, from al-Zuhrī, from Ṣāliḥ ibn Bashīr, from his father, that Fudayk came to the Prophet ﷺ and said, “Messenger of God…” Ibn Mandah transmitted another route from al-Zubaydī: from Ṣāliḥ, from his father, who said, “Fudayk came…” Thus “his father” in the first version means Fudayk: he is Bashīr’s father figuratively, being actually his grandfather. Everyone who included Bashīr among the Companions relied on the first version. Al-Zubaydī is more reliable than others from al-Zuhrī, and his version is correct. Had Ibn Mandah not stated decisively that Bashīr had seen the Prophet, this entry would more properly belong in the fourth section.

## Source unit 756 · printed entry 757

### English candidate

Bābawayh, the Persian scribe. Ibn Abī al-Dunyā said in Dalāʾil al-Nubuwwa: Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn Ayyūb related to us; Ibrāhīm ibn Saʿd related to us; Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq related to us: The Prophet ﷺ sent ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ḥudhāfa to Khosrow with a letter inviting him to Islam. Khosrow tore it up and wrote to his governor in Yemen, Bādhān: “Send two hardy men to this man and have them bring him to me.” Bādhān sent his quartermaster Bābawayh, a scribe and accountant, with a Persian named Khusra to the Prophet ﷺ, ordering him to return with them. He told Bābawayh to observe the man and report. They came to al-Ṭāʾif, then Medina. Bābawayh said: “The king of kings, Khosrow, ordered King Bādhān to send someone to bring you. If you comply I shall write something that benefits you; if you refuse he will destroy you, your people, and your land.” He told them to return tomorrow. It was revealed to the Prophet ﷺ that God had empowered Khosrow’s son over him and he had killed him at a specified hour, night, and month. In the morning he told them. They asked whether to write it to Bādhān. He said: “Yes, and tell him: if you accept Islam, I shall confirm you in your rule.” He gave Khusra a belt containing gold and silver. They returned and told Bādhān. He said: “This is not a king’s speech. If true, he is surely a sent prophet.” Soon Shīrawayh’s letter arrived confirming Khosrow’s killing, ordering obedience from his subjects, and forbidding interference with the man about whom Khosrow had written. Bādhān and the Persian Abnāʾ in Yemen accepted Islam. Bābawayh told Bādhān: “I have never known anyone who inspired greater awe in me than he did.” Ibn Abī al-Dunyā also transmitted an extremely abbreviated version from ʿAlī ibn al-Jaʿd, from Abū Maʿshar, from Saʿīd al-Maqburī, but it did not name Khusra or Bābawayh.

## Source unit 757 · printed entry 758

### English candidate

Bāb ibn Dhī al-Jurra—with jīm bearing a kasra—the Ḥimyarī, one of the celebrated horsemen. In the year nineteen he took part with Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī in the conquest of Tustar. Abū Mūsā sent him with forty men to the fortress of Dastamūlā. He surprised it by night and found the guards drunk and the gate open. They rushed in and killed them, but the alarm was raised. Dhū al-Ritāq, commander of the fortress, met Bāb ibn Dhī al-Jurra. Bāb grappled with him to throw him down; Dhū al-Ritāq bit him and severed his finger, but Bāb did not release him until he had thrown him down and killed him. He then took possession of what the fortress contained. Al-Madāʾinī reported it. More will follow about him under the name ʿAbd al-Raḥmān.

## Source unit 758 · printed entry 759

### English candidate

Bādhān—with final nūn, though it is also said with mīm—the Persian, one of the Abnāʾ whom Khosrow sent to Yemen. He was ruler of Yemen in his time. Bādhān accepted Islam when Khosrow perished and sent notice of his Islam to the Prophet ﷺ, who confirmed him over his territories. When he died, the Prophet appointed his son Shahr ibn Bādhān over part of his jurisdiction. Ibn Isḥāq, Ibn Hishām, al-Wāqidī, and al-Ṭabarī reported this. Al-Bāwardī and others included him among the Companions. He will be mentioned in the entry on the grandfather of Jumayra under jīm. His reports are in the histories and sīra works. Al-Thaʿlabī said: “He was the first of the non-Arab kings to accept Islam and the first person appointed in Islam over Yemen.” Al-Fākihī said: Yaḥyā ibn Abī Ṭālib related to us; ʿAlī ibn ʿĀṣim related to us; Dāwūd related to us, from al-Shaʿbī: “The Prophet ﷺ wrote to Khosrow, who tore up his letter and wrote to Bādhān: ‘Send someone to order him to return to his people’s religion; if he refuses, fight him.’” He then related the report, which includes: “Bādhān left Yemen for the Prophet ﷺ, but the false prophet al-ʿAnsī caught him and killed him.”

## Source unit 769 · printed entry 770

### English candidate

Bishr ibn Rabīʿa, who is Bishr ibn Abī Ruhm al-Juhanī, the man associated with the Burial Ground of Bishr in Kufa. Ruhm is pronounced with ḍamma on its first letter and sukūn on the unpointed ḥāʾ; al-Amīr vocalized it and said that he was Bishr ibn Abī Ruhm. He mentioned that Bishr witnessed al-Yamāma. Al-Marzubānī listed him in his Muʿjam as he is named at the head of this entry and said that he was one of the cavalrymen. He is the one who said to ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb after the battle of al-Qādisiyya:

‘May God guide you—remember the blows of our swords
at the gate of Qudays, when wheeling for attack was difficult.
Whenever we finished clashing with one battalion,
we advanced upon another, moving like mountains.’

He says in it:

‘With the Commander of the Faithful are extra grants,
and with al-Muthannā are silver and silk.’

Abū ʿUbayda related from Yūnus and Abū al-Khaṭṭāb that the reason for this poem was that Saʿd distributed the spoils, but a remainder was left. ʿUmar wrote to him: ‘Distribute it among the bearers of the Qurʾān.’ ʿAmr ibn Maʿdīkarib came to him, and Saʿd asked, ‘How much of the Book of God do you have?’ He replied, ‘Jihad kept me too occupied to memorize it.’ Saʿd said, ‘You have no share in this.’ Bishr al-Khathʿamī then came to him. Saʿd asked, ‘How much do you have?’ He replied, ‘In the name of God, the All-Merciful, the Ever-Merciful.’ Saʿd gave him nothing, so Bishr recited the poem just quoted. ʿAmr recited another poem. Saʿd wrote to ʿUmar about them, and ʿUmar said, ‘Give them something on account of their valor.’ Saʿd gave each of them two thousand.

Diʿbil said in Ṭabaqāt al-Shuʿarāʾ: ‘Bishr al-Khathʿamī, the man associated with the Burial Ground of Bishr, said to ʿUmar’—and he cited the first two verses, followed by:

‘That evening, the people wished that one of them
might be lent a bird’s two wings and fly away.’

He said: When Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ collected the land tax, a surplus remained. He wrote to ʿUmar, who ordered him to distribute it among the reciters of the Qurʾān, and he did so. When the following year came, Saʿd wrote to ʿUmar: ‘They were seven, but now they have become seventy.’ ʿUmar wrote back: ‘Distribute it among those distinguished by valor and effectiveness against the enemy.’ Bishr al-Khathʿamī wrote this poem to ʿUmar. ʿUmar then wrote to Saʿd: ‘Include him among the men of valor and give him precedence.’ Saʿd did so.

## Source unit 770 · printed entry 771

Bishr ibn ʿĀmir ibn Mālik ibn Jaʿfar ibn Kilāb, a paternal cousin of the poet Labīd ibn Rabīʿa. He lived into the Islamic period, and his father had Companionship. ## Source unit 774 · printed entry 775

### English candidate

Bishr ibn Quḥayf. Ibn Manda mentioned him among the Companions but said, ‘I know of neither Companionship nor sight of the Prophet for him.’ Al-Bukhārī listed him among the Followers. Abū Nuʿaym said, ‘He had no Companionship. Aḥmad ibn Sayyār listed him among the Companions only because of a report transmitted by way of Muḥammad ibn Jābir, from Simāk, from him, in which he said: “I used to attend prayer with the Prophet ﷺ, and he would turn away in whichever direction his face was.”’ Simāk ibn Ḥarb in fact transmitted this from him, from al-Mughīra ibn Shuʿba; the error came from Muḥammad ibn Jābir. Ibn Ḥibbān listed him among the trustworthy Followers. Ibn Abī Ḥātim said: ‘He transmitted from ʿUmar and al-Mughīra ibn Shuʿba.’ Ibn Saʿd said: Yazīd related to us, from Shuʿba, from Simāk, from Bishr ibn Quḥayf, who said: ‘I came to ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb and said, “I have come to pledge allegiance to you.” He replied, “Have you not already pledged allegiance to my commander?” I said, “Yes.” He said, “If you have pledged allegiance to my commander, you have pledged allegiance to me.”’ This chain is sound. It indicates that Bishr had no Companionship, although he did live into the Prophetic period. His delegation came during ʿUmar’s days, showing that he was already an adult in the Prophet’s lifetime ﷺ.

<div dir="rtl" lang="ar">

## Source unit 775 · printed entry 776

### English candidate

Bishr ibn Quṭba ibn Sinān ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Judʿān ibn Nawfal ibn Faqʿas al-Asadī al-Faqʿasī. It is also said that he was Bishr ibn al-Ḥārith and that Quṭba was his mother’s name; she was a daughter of Sinān. He was a poet, cavalryman, and mukhaḍram. He witnessed al-Yamāma during Abū Bakr’s reign with Khālid ibn al-Walīd and said about it:

‘I go out at evening and morning in Khālid’s battalion,
on a lean mount made hollow-flanked by war.’

These are among verses mentioned by al-Marzubānī. Al-Zubayr ibn Bakkār mentioned him in Khālid’s biography and said: ‘I found a document in al-Ḍaḥḥāk’s handwriting which named Bishr ibn Quṭba and traced his lineage to al-Ḥārith, then completed it as ibn Judʿān ibn Nawfal ibn Faqʿas.’ It also says: ‘Bishr ibn Quṭba said on the Day of ʿAqrabāʾ in al-ʿArḍ of al-Yamāma, while he was with Khālid ibn al-Walīd’—and he quoted the poem, including:

‘When the Sword of God said, “Charge them,”
we charged, caring nothing for the command of the hinderer.
I say to my soul after its heart grew faint:
“Steady—why be afraid when there is cause for fear?”
Stand with the shepherd whom Muḥammad charged,
and though the hypocrite’s soul lies, speak true.’

## Source unit 778 · printed entry 779

### English candidate

Bashīr—on the pattern of ʿaẓīm—ibn Kaʿb ibn Ubayy al-Ḥimyarī, one of the commanders at al-Yarmūk. Sayf mentioned in al-Futūḥ, through his chains, that when Abū ʿUbayda departed from al-Yarmūk and encamped outside Damascus, he left Bashīr ibn Kaʿb ibn Ubayy al-Ḥimyarī at al-Yarmūk with a body of cavalry; then Sayf related a lengthy account. This man unquestionably lived through both the pre-Islamic and Islamic periods.

As for Bushayr ibn Kaʿb al-ʿAdawī, he was a Basran Follower who transmitted from ʿImrān ibn Ḥuṣayn and others. His reports are in the two Ṣaḥīḥs, and his name has ḍamma on its first letter. Ibn ʿAsākir placed the first account in this second man’s biography, and al-Mizzī followed him in al-Tahdhīb, but this is questionable. Ibn Fatḥūn, in his supplement to al-Istīʿāb, listed the first man among those named Bashīr, with fatḥa on the first letter. والله أعلم.

<div dir="rtl" lang="ar">

## Source unit 781 · printed entry 782

### English candidate

Bughayḍ ibn ʿĀmir ibn Shammās ibn Laʾy ibn Anf al-Nāqa, Jaʿfar ibn Qurayʿ ibn ʿAwf ibn Kaʿb ibn Saʿd ibn Zayd Manāt ibn Tamīm, al-Tamīmī al-Saʿdī. He was one of the chiefs of Banū Tamīm in the pre-Islamic period and lived into Islam. None of the transmitted routes says that he came as a delegate to the Prophet ﷺ. He is mentioned during ʿUmar’s caliphate. Abū al-Faraj al-Iṣbahānī related, by way of Abū ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Aʿrābī, Abū ʿUbayda, Yūnus ibn Ḥabīb, and other traditionists, that the Prophet ﷺ appointed al-Zibriqān ibn Badr ibn Imriʾ al-Qays ibn Khalaf ibn Bahdala ibn ʿAwf ibn Kaʿb over the alms of Banū Tamīm. Abū Bakr then retained him in that office. He later came to ʿUmar with his people’s alms. At Qarqarā he met the poet al-Ḥuṭayʾa, accompanied by his two sons Aws and Sawāda, his daughters, and his wife. Al-Zibriqān recognized him and asked, “Where are you bound?” He replied, “Iraq, so that I may find someone who will support my dependants and to whom I may devote my praise.” He said, “You have found him.” “Who?” “Me.” “Who are you?” “Al-Zibriqān ibn Badr. Take my letter to Umm Badra.” She was a daughter of Ṣaʿṣaʿa ibn Nājiya, al-Farazdaq’s paternal aunt, and al-Zibriqān’s wife. He went to her. News reached Bughayḍ ibn ʿĀmir, his brothers, and his paternal cousins, among them Bughayḍ ibn Shammās, ʿAlqama ibn Hawdha, Shammās ibn Laʾy, al-Mukhabbal, and others. They contended with al-Zibriqān ibn Badr for leadership, and al-Zibriqān and ʿAlqama had exchanged satires. They secretly told Umm Badra that al-Zibriqān wanted to marry al-Ḥuṭayʾa’s daughter and had ordered her to honor him for that reason. Umm Badra consequently treated him coldly. Bughayḍ and his family invited al-Ḥuṭayʾa to them, saying, “We will give you better protection than al-Zibriqān,” and tempted him with food and promises, so he moved to them. When al-Zibriqān returned and learned what had happened, he rode to them and demanded, “Return my protected guest to me.” They refused and nearly went to war. The clan attended, and they agreed to let al-Ḥuṭayʾa choose; he chose Bughayḍ and his group. It is also said that al-Zibriqān complained against them to ʿUmar, who ordered them to let the poet choose. Al-Ḥuṭayʾa kept praising them without attacking al-Zibriqān until al-Zibriqān sent for a poet of al-Namir ibn Qāsiṭ named Dithār ibn Shaybān, who satirized Bughayḍ and his household. When al-Ḥuṭayʾa heard Dithār’s verse, zeal for his protectors seized him and he composed the long poem containing: “What fault was Bughayḍ’s—may you be fatherless—
concerning a destitute man who came driving on the last of the people?” This led al-Zibriqān to complain to ʿUmar against al-Ḥuṭayʾa and to ʿUmar’s imprisoning him, followed by the well-known events. Abū Ḥātim al-Sijistānī also mentioned Bughayḍ among the long-lived, from al-Aṣmaʿī, and cited from the poem: “What fault was Bughayḍ’s when he saw a man
in want, who settled in a rugged, distant place?
Whoever does good will not lack its recompense;
kindness shall not vanish between God and humankind.”

<div dir="rtl" lang="ar">

بغيض بن عامر بن شماس بن لأي بن أنف الناقة جعفر بن قريع بن عوف بن كعب بن سعد بن زيد مناة بن تميم التميمي السعدي كان من رؤساء بني تميم في الجاهلية وأدرك الإسلام ولم يرد في شيء من الطرق أنه وفد على النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم وله ذكر في خلافة عمر وروى أبو الفرج الأصبهاني من طريق أبي عبد الله بن الأعرابي وأبي عبيدة ويونس بن حبيب وغيرهم من أهل الأخبار أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم ولي الزبرقان بن بدو بن امرئ القيس بن خلف بن بهدلة بن عوف بن كعب صدقات بني تميم ثم اقره أبو بكر على عمله ثم قدم على عمر بصدقات قومه فلقيه الحطيئه الشاعر بقرقرى ومعه أبناه أوس وسواده وبناته وامرأته فعرفه الزبرقان فقال أين تريد قال العراق لاصادف من يكفيني عيالي واصفيه مدحى فقال لقد لقيته قال من قال أنا قال من أنت قال الزبرقان بن بدر فسر إلى أم بدرة وهي بنت صعصعه بن ناجية عمة الفرزدق وهي امرأة الزبرقان بكتابى فسار إليها فبلغ ذلك بغيض بن عامر وإخوته وبنى عمه منهم بغيض بن شماس وعلقمه بن هوذة وشماس بن لأي والمخبل وغيرهم وكانوا ينازعون الزبرقان بن بدر الرياسة وكانت بين الزبرقان وبين علقمة مهاجاة فدسوا إلى أم بدرة أن الزبرقان يريد أن يتزوج بنت الحطيئة ولذلك أمرك أن تكرميه فجفته أم بدرة فأرسل بغيض وأهله إلى الحطيئة أن ائتنا فنحن أحسن لك جوارا من الزبرقان فاطمعوه ووعدوه فتحول إليهم فلما جاء الزبرقان بلغه الخبر فركب إليهم فقال لهم ردوا علي جاري فأبوا حتى كاد أن يكون بينهم حرب فحضرهم أهل الحي فاصطلحوا على أن يخيروه فاختار بغيضا ورهطه ويقال أن الزبرقان استعدى عليهم عمر فأمرهم أن يخيروه قال فجعل الحطيئة يمدحهم من غير أن يتعرض للزبرقان فلم يزل كذلك حتى أرسل الزبرقان إلى شاعر من النمر بن قاسط يقال له دثار بن شيبان فهجا بغيضا وآل بيته فلما سمع الحطيئة شعر دثار حمى لجيرانه فقال أبياته التي منها <br />
 ما كان ذنب بغيض لا ابالكم <br />
 في بائس جاء يحدو آخر الناس وهي طويلة فكان من استعداء الزبرقان عمر على الحطيئة وحبسه إياه وكان ما كان وذكره أبو حاتم السجستاني في المعمرين عن الأصمعي وذكر من القصيدة قوله <br />
 ما كان ذنب بغيض أن رأى رجلا <br />
 ذا فاقة حل في مستوعر شاس <br />
 من يفعل الخير لا يعدم جوازيه <br />
 لن يذهب العرف بين الله والناس

## Source unit 783 · printed entry 784

### English candidate

Bakkāʾ the monk, one of the people of Syria. He lived into Islam and testified to the Prophet’s messengership ﷺ, though no delegation by him is mentioned. Al-Haytham ibn ʿAdī reported in the historical accounts, from Saʿīd ibn al-ʿĀṣ: “When my father, al-ʿĀṣ ibn Saʿīd ibn al-ʿĀṣ, was killed on the day of Badr, I was in the guardianship of my paternal uncle Abān ibn Saʿīd ibn al-ʿĀṣ. He went to Syria as a merchant, remained for a year, and returned. He had frequently reviled the Messenger of God ﷺ. The first thing he asked was, ‘What has become of Muḥammad?’ My paternal uncle ʿAbd Allāh answered, ‘By God, he is mightier and more elevated in standing than ever.’ Abān fell silent and did not revile him as he had before. Then he prepared food and summoned the notables of Banū Umayya. He told them: ‘I was in a village where I saw a monk called Bakkāʾ. He had not descended to the ground for forty years. One day he came down, and the people gathered to look at him. I approached and said I had a need, so he met me privately. I said, “I am of Quraysh, and a man among us has emerged claiming that God sent him.” “What is his name?” “Muḥammad.” “How long since he emerged?” “Twenty years.” “Shall I describe him?” “Yes.” He described him without missing a single feature. Then he said, “By God, he is the prophet of this nation, and by God he shall prevail.” He then entered his hermitage and told me, “Convey to him the greeting عليه السلام (“peace be upon him”).”’” This occurred in the time of al-Ḥudaybiya.

<div dir="rtl" lang="ar">

## Source unit 795 · printed entry 796

### English candidate

Bahīrā the monk. Ibn Mandah mentioned him, followed by Abū Nuʿaym. His story is well known in the works on the Prophet's campaigns, though I do not know whether he lived to see the prophetic mission. In some works of sīra, on al-Zuhrī's authority, he was a Jew of Taymāʾ. In al-Masʿūdī's Murūj al-Dhahab, however, he was a Christian of ʿAbd al-Qays called Jirjīs. As for his story, Ibn Isḥāq related in al-Maghāzī that Abū Ṭālib set out with a caravan to trade in Syria, and the Messenger of God ﷺ went with him. When the caravan stopped at Buṣrā, there was a monk there called Bahīrā, living in his cell and possessed of Christian learning. Caravans had often stopped there without his speaking to them. Bahīrā saw Muḥammad ﷺ with a cloud shading him, so he came down to them, prepared food, and gathered them to his place. Because of his youth, Muḥammad had stayed behind with their baggage. Bahīrā instructed them to summon him, and one of them brought him. Bahīrā began scrutinizing him closely and examining features of his body that matched the description he possessed. When they had finished, he questioned him about matters concerning his circumstances; Muḥammad answered, and what he said agreed with Bahīrā's knowledge. He then looked at his back and saw the Seal of Prophethood between his shoulder blades. Bahīrā turned to his uncle and said, 'Take your nephew back to his country and guard him against the Jews, for this nephew of yours is destined for a momentous affair.' Abū Ṭālib hurried him back toward his country. It is also said that a group of the People of Scripture saw the same signs in him that Bahīrā had seen and intended him harm. Bahīrā warded them off, reminded them of God and of the mention and description of him they found in Scripture, and told them that they would be unable to reach him. He persisted until they accepted what he said and withdrew. After completing his trade in Syria, Abū Ṭālib returned with him to his country. Abū Nuʿaym related in al-Dalāʾil from al-Wāqidī—as is also found in Ibn Saʿd's al-Ṭabaqāt through al-Wāqidī's isnad—that he was twelve years old at the time. He gave the story at great length and added that the group in question were Jews. This story has also come through a chain whose transmitters are trustworthy, in a report of Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī transmitted by al-Tirmidhī and others; the monk is not named there. It adds an objectionable phrase: 'Abū Bakr sent Bilāl after him.' What makes it objectionable is that Abū Bakr was not yet of an age or position to do so and had not bought Bilāl at that time—unless this final sentence is understood to have been detached from another report and inserted into this one. In any event, it is an error by one of its transmitters. Ibn Mandah also transmitted, from the Tafsīr of ʿAbd al-Ghanī ibn Saʿīd al-Thaqafī—one of the weak, abandoned transmitters—through his chains from Ibn ʿAbbās, that Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq accompanied the Prophet ﷺ when Abū Bakr was eighteen years old and the Prophet ﷺ was twenty, while they were bound for Syria on a trading journey. When they stopped at a place containing a lote tree, the Prophet sat in its shade, and Abū Bakr went to a monk called Bahīrā to ask him about something. The monk asked, 'Who is the man in the shade of the lote tree?' Abū Bakr answered, 'Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib.' The monk said, 'By God, this is a prophet. No one after Jesus son of Mary has taken shade beneath it except Muḥammad.' Conviction concerning him entered Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq's heart, and when the Prophet of God ﷺ was commissioned, Abū Bakr followed him. If sound, this may have occurred on another journey after the journey with Abū Ṭālib. In Abū Saʿīd al-Naysābūrī's Sharaf al-Muṣṭafā, the Prophet ﷺ also passed by Bahīrā when he went out on Khadīja's trading business accompanied by Maysara. Bahīrā said to him, 'I have recognized all the signs in you except the Seal of Prophethood, so uncover your back for me.' He uncovered his back, and Bahīrā saw it. He said, 'I bear witness that there is no god but God, and I bear witness that you are the Messenger of God, the unlettered Prophet whom Jesus son of Mary announced.' He then related the story at great length. الله أعلم. I have mentioned Bahīrā in this section only because the definition of a Companion does not apply to him: a Companion is a Muslim who met the Prophet ﷺ while believing in him and died in that state. Thus our stipulation 'a Muslim' excludes someone who met him believing in him before he was commissioned, such as this man. والله أعلم.

## Source unit 796 · printed entry 797

### English candidate

Buḥayna. ʿAbdān mentioned this person among the Companions and transmitted from ʿAbbās al-Dūrī, from Abū Nuʿaym, from ʿAbd al-Salām ibn Ḥarb, from Abū Khālid, from Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Thawbān, from Buḥayna, who said: The Prophet ﷺ passed by me while I was standing in prayer after the dawn prayer and said, 'Place a separation between the two.' Abū Mūsā said: This is how ʿAbdān entitled the entry and narrated the report. The correct version is what Khaythama ibn Sulaymān narrated from al-Sarī ibn Yaḥyā, from Abū Nuʿaym, with this isnad: 'from Ibn Buḥayna.' I say: Aḥmad ibn Ḥāzim ibn Abī ʿUrwa identified in his Musnad the person who made the error. He transmitted it from Abū Nuʿaym exactly as ʿAbbās had, and then added: 'Abū Nuʿaym told us: It is only Ibn Bujayna, but this is how he—meaning ʿAbd al-Salām—said it to us.' Abū Mūsā said: Yaḥyā ibn Abī Kathīr likewise narrated it from Ibn Thawbān in the correct form. He then cited it that way from the Musnad of Aḥmad.

## Source unit 801 · printed entry 802

### English candidate

Badhīma, the father of ʿAlī—the first letter bears fatḥa and the dotted dhāl bears kasra. He was mentioned among the Companions, but this is an error caused by an omission in the isnad. Ibn Mandah said that Ibn Ṣāʿid mentioned him among the Companions and narrated from Aḥmad ibn Manīʿ, from Ashʿath ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, from al-Walīd ibn Thaʿlaba, from ʿAlī ibn Badhīma, from his father, who said, 'I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ'—and he then related a report concerning supplication. Here ends Ibn Mandah's statement. Abū Nuʿaym also mentioned him and said, 'This is an error,' but did not explain the source of the error. It is the omission of Abū ʿUbayda ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd between ʿAlī and his father. The report actually belongs to the Musnad of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd. Misʿar made this clear in his narration from ʿAlī ibn Badhīma, from Abū ʿUbayda, from his father; al-Ḥākim transmitted it in al-Mustadrak. I will mention the report, إن شاء الله تعالى, in the biography of Sālim ibn ʿAwf ibn Mālik. Badhīma had neither companionship, direct sight of the Prophet, nor narration from him. Rather, he was one of the sons of the Persian kings. He was captured while still young in the fighting against the Persians, and Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ gave him to Jābir ibn Samura on the day of al-Madāʾin. Ibn Saʿd mentioned this in al-Ṭabaqāt.

<div dir="rtl" lang="ar">
