## Source unit 818 · printed entry 819

### English candidate

Bashīr ibn Zayd al-Anṣārī. Al-Ḥākim mentioned him, saying that his musnads are rare, and cited by way of Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq al-Balkhī: “ʿUmar ibn Qays ibn Bashīr related to me, from his father, from his grandfather, that the Prophet ﷺ said: ‘Cut off the fool.’” Al-Bayhaqī said in al-Shuʿab that al-Ḥākim erred in three or four respects. First, he said ʿUmar ibn Qays, whereas it is ʿAmr. Second, he said Bashīr—with open bāʾ followed by dotted shīn bearing a kasra—whereas it is Yusayr, with initial yāʾ bearing a ḍamma, followed by unpointed sīn, in the diminutive. Third, he raised the report to the Prophet, whereas it is mawqūf. Fourth, he made the man a Companion, whereas he merely lived into the period. I say: one error remains—he said Bashīr ibn Zayd, whereas it is Bashīr ibn ʿAmr; and he called him Anṣārī, whereas he is ʿAbdī, though Kinda is also given.

## Source unit 819 · printed entry 820

### English candidate

Bashīr ibn ʿAmr was born in the year of the Hijra. Bashīr said: “The Prophet ﷺ died when I was ten years old.” It is also related that he was his people’s registrar in the time of al-Ḥajjāj. He died in the year eighty-five. Abū ʿUmar reported only this, but he corrupted the name. This is the Bashīr ibn ʿAmr whom al-Bayhaqī identified in the preceding entry. He is the man called Usayr ibn Jābir, though it is said that this is someone else. Ibn Saʿd dated his death to eighty-five. Abū Nuʿaym said he was a registrar in al-Ḥajjāj’s time, then transmitted from ʿAmr ibn Qays, from his father, from his grandfather Bashīr: “The Prophet ﷺ was taken in death when I was ten years old.” Ibn Shāhīn also corrupted the name: he entered Bashīr ibn ʿAmr among the Companions under bāʾ, then cited through ʿAmr ibn Qays ibn Bashīr ibn ʿAmr, from his father, from his grandfather—who had lived into the Prophet’s time ﷺ—that whenever he received his stipend, he retained one year’s maintenance. The report is mawqūf. This is Yusayr ibn ʿAmr, also called Usayr with hamza. ʿAlī ibn al-Madīnī said: “The Basrans say Usayr ibn Jābir, while the Kufans say Usayr ibn ʿAmr.” Al-Bukhārī preferred the latter and indicated weakness in the view that called him Ibn Jābir. Others said Usayr ibn ʿAmr ibn Jābir. والله أعلم.

<div dir="rtl" lang="ar">

بشير بن عمرو ولد في عام الهجرة قال بشير توفي النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم وأنا بن عشر سنين وروى أنه كان عريف قومه في زمن الحجاج توفي سنة خمس وثمانين هكذا ذكره أبو عمر لم يزد على ذلك وصحف في هذا الاسم وهو بشير بن عمرو الذي نبه البيهقي عليه في الذي قبله وهو الذي يقال له أسير بن جابر وقيل هو غيره وأرخ بن سعد وفاته سنة خمس وثمانين وقال أبو نعيم كان عريفا في زمن الحجاج ثم روى عن عمرو بن قيس عن أبيه عن جده بشير وقال قبض النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم وأنا بن عشر سنين وقد صحف فيه أيضا بن شاهين فإنه ذكر في الصحابة في الموحدة بشير بن عمرو ثم ساق حديثا من طريق عمرو بن قيس بن بشير بن عمرو عن أبيه عن جده وكان قد أدرك النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم إنه كان إذا أخذ عطاءه أمسك نفقة سنة الحديث موقوف وهذا هو يسير بن عمرو ويقال أسير بالهمزة وقال علي بن المديني أهل البصرة يقولون أسير بن جابر وأهل الكوفة يقولون أسير بن عمرو ورجح البخاري الثاني وأشار إلى تليين قول من قال فيه بن جابر وقال غيره أسير بن عمرو بن جابر والله أعلم

## Source unit 822 · printed entry 823

### English candidate

Bushayr—with initial bāʾ bearing a ḍamma, in the diminutive—ibn Kaʿb al-ʿAdawī. Ibn Shāhīn and Ibn ʿAbdān mentioned him among the Companions. ʿAbdān said: “One of our shaykhs mentioned him, but we know of no companionship for him. He was a man who had read the scriptures.” He also said: “Ṭāwūs related from Ibn ʿAbbās that he told Bushayr ibn Kaʿb, ‘Repeat such-and-such a report.’” I say: Muslim transmitted that. ʿAbdān said: “ʿAbd al-Jabbār related to us; Sufyān related to us, from ʿAmr ibn Dīnār, from Ṭalq ibn Ḥabīb, who reported from Bushayr ibn Kaʿb: ‘Two young men came to the Messenger of God ﷺ and said, Messenger of God, do we act concerning that for which the pens have dried…?’” Ibn Shāhīn likewise transmitted it by two routes from Sufyān. Abū Mūsā said: “This gives the impression that Bushayr had companionship, but he did not; it is mursal; fuller witnesses insert ʿImrān ibn Ḥuṣayn between Bushayr and the young men.” I say: I previously explained that Ibn ʿAsākir confused him with another man called Bashīr ibn Kaʿb who witnessed Yarmūk. Had this Bushayr witnessed Yarmūk, he would have met the senior Companions, yet we find him transmitting from no one earlier than Abū Dharr and Abū al-Dardāʾ; it is also said that even his transmissions from them are mursal. والله أعلم.

## Source unit 830 · printed entry 831

### English candidate

Al-Tilb ibn Thaʿlaba ibn Rabīʿa ibn ʿAṭiyya ibn Ukhayf ibn Kaʿb ibn al-ʿAnbar ibn ʿAmr ibn Tamīm, al-Tamīmī al-ʿAnbarī. It is also said that he was the brother of Zaynab bint Thaʿlaba, and other versions of his lineage are reported. He had companionship and reports; Abū Dāwūd and al-Nasāʾī transmitted from him. The Messenger of God ﷺ sought forgiveness for him three times. His name has initial tāʾ bearing a fatḥa, lām bearing a kasra, and then a light bāʾ, though the bāʾ is also said to be doubled. Shuʿba pronounced the initial as thāʾ; the former is sounder. Aḥmad said that Shuʿba had a speech impediment. Ukhayf in his lineage has an initial hamza bearing a ḍamma, followed by dotted khāʾ, in the diminutive.

## Source unit 834 · printed entry 835

### English candidate

Tamīm ibn Usayd—also said Asad—ibn ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā ibn Jaʿwana ibn ʿAmr ibn al-Qayn ibn Razāḥ ibn ʿAmr ibn Saʿd ibn Kaʿb ibn ʿAmr al-Khuzāʿī. Ibn Saʿd said that he embraced Islam and kept company before the conquest of Mecca, and that the Prophet ﷺ sent him to renew the boundary markers of the Sanctuary. He then supplied a chain for this through Ibn Khuthaym, from Abū al-Ṭufayl, from Ibn ʿAbbās, from the Prophet ﷺ, and mentioned the report. Abū Nuʿaym transmitted it and added that Abraham had set the markers while Gabriel showed him their positions. Al-Fākihī transmitted by way of Ibn Jurayj, who said: Ibn Khuthaym informed me, from Muḥammad ibn al-Aswad ibn Khalaf; he mentioned it and added that Tamīm was the grandfather of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Muṭṭalib ibn Tamīm. Ibn Isḥāq transmitted in al-Maghāzī, in a report of Ibn ʿAbbās, that the Messenger of God ﷺ entered Mecca on the Day of the Conquest riding his mount and circumambulated upon it. He related the report and said that whenever the Prophet pointed toward an idol, it fell backward. Tamīm ibn Asad al-Khuzāʿī said about this:

‘In the idols are a lesson and a sign
for one who hopes for reward or punishment.’

Ibn Manda transmitted it by another route and said, ‘This is a strange report, uniquely transmitted by Yaʿqūb ibn Muḥammad al-Zuhrī.’

<div dir="rtl" lang="ar">

تميم بن أسيد وقيل أسد بن عبد العزى بن جعونة بن عمرو بن القين بن رزاح بن عمرو بن كعب بن عمرو الخزاعي قال بن سعد أسلم وصحب قبل فتح مكة وبعثة النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم يجدد انصاب الحرم ثم ساق بذلك سندا إلى بن خثيم عن أبي الطفيل عن بن عباس أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم فذكره وأخرجه أبو نعيم وزاد وكان إبراهيم وضعها يريه إياها جبريل إسناده حسن وروى الفاكهي من طريق بن جريج أخبرني بن خثيم عن محمد بن الأسود بن خلف فذكره وزاد وهو جد عبد الرحمن بن المطلب بن تميم وروى بن إسحاق في المغازي من حديث بن عباس قال دخل رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم مكة يوم الفتح على راحلة فطاف عليها فذكر الحديث قال فما يشير إلى ضم منها إلا وقع لقفاه وفي ذلك يقول تميم بن أسد الخزاعي <br />

## Source unit 837 · printed entry 838

### English candidate

Tamīm ibn Aws ibn Ḥāritha—or Khārija—ibn Sūd, also said Sawād, ibn Judhayma ibn Dhirāʿ ibn ʿAdī ibn al-Dār, Abū Ruqayya al-Dārī. He is famous among the Companions. He had been a Christian, came to Medina, and embraced Islam. He told the Prophet ﷺ the story of al-Jassāsa and the Antichrist, and the Prophet ﷺ related it from him on the pulpit. This was counted among Tamīm’s merits. Ibn al-Sakan said that he and his brother Nuʿaym embraced Islam in the year nine and both had Companionship. Ibn Isḥāq said that he came to Medina and campaigned with the Prophet ﷺ. Abū Nuʿaym said, ‘He was the monk of the people of Palestine and the worshipper of the people of Palestine.’ He was the first to light a lamp in the mosque; al-Ṭabarānī transmitted this in a report of Abū Hurayra. He was also the first to deliver narrative sermons, during ʿUmar’s reign; Isḥāq ibn Rāhawayh and Ibn Abī Shayba transmitted this.

He moved to Syria after ʿUthmān was killed and settled in Palestine. The Prophet ﷺ had granted him the village of ʿAynūn there; this is transmitted by many routes. He prayed extensively at night. Once he stood through the night repeating a single verse until morning: ‘Or do those who commit evil deeds suppose…’ [Qurʾān 45:21]. Al-Baghawī transmitted it in al-Jaʿdiyyāt with a sound chain to Masrūq, who said: ‘A man from Mecca said to me, “This is the standing-place of your brother Tamīm,”’ and related it. Al-Baghawī transmitted in al-Ṣaḥāba a story of his with ʿUmar containing a manifest charismatic gift for Tamīm and showing ʿUmar’s great respect for him. I shall mention it in the biography of Muʿāwiya ibn Ḥarmal in the section on the mukhaḍrams, إن شاء الله تعالى.

Ibn Ḥibbān said that he died in Syria and that his grave is at Bayt Jibrīn in Palestine. Al-Bukhārī said that Abū Hind al-Dārī was his brother, which was challenged; Ibn Ḥibbān, however, said that he was his maternal half-brother.

Notice: In al-Tajrīd, al-Dhahabī stated categorically that the man involved with the cup, concerning whom and his companion the verse was revealed—‘O you who believe, testimony between you when death approaches one of you…’ [Qurʾān 5:106]—was someone other than Tamīm al-Dārī. He attributed this to Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān. That is unsound, because al-Tirmidhī and others transmit from Ibn ʿAbbās, in the story of the cup, that the man was Tamīm al-Dārī.

## Source unit 840 · printed entry 841

### English candidate

Tamīm ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Qays ibn ʿAdī ibn Saʿd ibn Sahm al-Qurashī al-Sahmī. Al-Zubayr said that he was killed as a martyr on the Day of Ajnādayn. His maternal half-brother Saʿīd ibn ʿAmr al-Tamīmī was killed with him, and their mother was from Banū ʿĀmir ibn Ṣaʿṣaʿa. Al-Wāqidī called him Numayr—with an initial nūn bearing ḍamma and ending in rāʾ. It has already appeared that Ibn Isḥāq called him Bashīr ibn al-Ḥārith and stated that he emigrated to Abyssinia. Al-Balādhurī said: ‘Tamīm ibn al-Ḥārith emigrated in the second migration to Abyssinia, accompanied by a brother of his from Banū Tamīm named Maʿbad. ## Source unit 843 · printed entry 844

### English candidate

Tamīm ibn Zayd al-Anṣārī, father of ʿAbbād and, according to the majority, brother of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Zayd ibn ʿĀṣim al-Māzinī. It is also said that he was his maternal half-brother, while his father was Ghaziyya ibn ʿAbd ʿAmr ibn ʿAṭiyya ibn Khansāʾ; al-Dimyāṭī stated this categorically, following Ibn Saʿd. Ibn Ḥibbān said, ‘Tamīm ibn Zayd al-Māzinī had Companionship, and his report is transmitted through his son.’

Al-Bukhārī in his Tārīkh, Aḥmad ibn Abī Shayba, Ibn Abī ʿAmr al-Baghawī, al-Ṭabarānī, al-Bāwardī, and others all transmitted by way of Abū al-Aswad, from ʿAbbād ibn Tamīm al-Māzinī, from his father, who said: ‘I saw the Messenger of God ﷺ perform ablution and wipe water over his feet.’ Its transmitters are trustworthy. Abū ʿUmar made the anomalous statement that it is weak. Al-Baghawī said, ‘I know of no report transmitted by ʿAbbād from his father other than this one,’ and others followed him in that. This is open to question, for Ibn Manda transmitted two other reports from him. One concerns doubt, but Ibn Lahīʿa erred in it; it is known only from ʿAbbād’s paternal uncle.

The second we transmitted earlier in the Fawāʾid of al-ʿĪsawī, by way of al-Layth, from Hishām ibn Saʿd, from Ibn Shihāb, from ʿAbbād ibn Tamīm, from his father and paternal uncle: they saw the Prophet ﷺ lying on his back; and the report continues. It is well known from ʿAbbād through his paternal uncle, but nothing prevents ʿAbbād from having transmitted it from both men together. Al-Bāwardī transmitted it by way of Abū Bakr al-Hudhalī, from al-Zuhrī, with the wording ‘from ʿAbbād, from his father or his paternal uncle,’ expressing uncertainty. والله أعلم.

## Source unit 850 · printed entry 851

## Source unit 857 · printed entry 858

### English candidate

Tamām ibn al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib al-Hāshimī, a paternal cousin of the Prophet ﷺ and the youngest of the brothers. His mother was an umm walad. Al-ʿAbbās used to say, “Complete them with Tamām, and so they became ten.” Al-Zubayr ibn Bakkār related this. Abū ʿUmar said: “Every son of al-ʿAbbās had sight of the Prophet, while al-Faḍl and ʿAbd Allāh also heard from him.” Ibn al-Sakan said: “It is said that he was the youngest of his brothers and the strongest of Quraysh in physical force. No report from the Prophet ﷺ is preserved from him through an established route.” Ibn Ḥibbān placed him among the trustworthy Followers and said: “His report from the Prophet ﷺ is mursal; he related it only from his father.” I say: The transmitters differed in reporting it from Manṣūr. Abū ʿAlī al-Ṣayqal transmitted from Jaʿfar ibn Tamām, from his father, who said that the Messenger of God ﷺ said, “Use tooth-sticks.” Al-Thawrī and most of Manṣūr’s transmitters related it thus, and Aḥmad and others included it. ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Abbār related it from Manṣūr as “from Tamām, from his father”; al-Bazzār and al-Ḥākim included it. Shaybān related from Manṣūr, from Abū ʿAlī, from Jaʿfar ibn al-ʿAbbās, from his father; in another version from him it is “from Jaʿfar ibn Tamām, from his father.” It was also related from al-Thawrī, from Manṣūr, from al-Ṣayqal, from Qutham ibn Tamām—or Tamām ibn Qutham—from his father. Aḥmad included it from Muʿāwiya ibn Hishām, from al-Thawrī; Muʿāwiya had a poor memory. Tamām governed Medina in ʿAlī’s time, according to Khalīfa and others. [The source breaks off after: “He died in …”] I say: The ten brothers are al-Faḍl, ʿAbd Allāh, ʿUbayd Allāh, Qutham, Maʿbad, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, Kathīr, Ṣubayḥ, Mishar, and Tamām. All are agreed upon except the eighth and ninth: Hishām ibn al-Kalbī alone mentioned them. Al-Dāraquṭnī said in al-Ikhwa that he is not corroborated concerning them.

### Arabic authority

<div dir="rtl" lang="ar">

تمام بن العباس بن عبد المطلب الهاشمي بن عم النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أصغر الإخوة أمه أم ولد كان العباس يقول تموا بتمام فصاروا عشرة قاله الزبير بن بكار وقال أبو عمر كل ولد العباس له رؤية وللفضل وعبد الله سماع قال بن السكن يقال كان أصغر إخوته وكان أشد قريش بطشا ولا يحفظ له عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم رواية من وجه ثابت وقال بن حبان في ثقات التابعين حديثه عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم مرسل وإنما رواه عن أبيه قلت اختلف على منصور عن أبي علي الصيقل عن جعفر بن تمام عن أبيه قال قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم استاكوا هكذا رواه الثوري وأكثر أصحاب منصور وأخرجه أحمد وغيره ورواه عمر بن عبد الرحمن الأبار عن منصور فقال عن تمام عن أبيه أخرجه البزار والحاكم ورواه شيبان عن منصور عن أبي علي عن جعفر بن العباس عن أبيه وفي رواية عنه عن جعفر بن تمام عن أبيه وروى عن الثوري عن منصور عن الصقيل عن قثم بن تمام أو تمام بن قثم عن أبيه أخرجه أحمد عن معاوية بن هشام عنه ومعاوية سيء الحفظ ولي تمام المدينة في زمان علي قال حليفة وغيره ومات في قلت والاخوة العشرة هم الفضل وعبد الله وعبيد الله وقثم ومعبد وعبد الرحمن وكثير وصبيح ومسهر وتمام وكلهم متفق عليه الا الثامن والتاسع فتفرد بذكرهما هشام بن الكلبي قال الدارقطني في الإخوة لا يتابع عليه

## Source unit 860 · printed entry 861

### English candidate

Tabīʿ ibn ʿĀmir al-Ḥimyarī, the son of Kaʿb al-Aḥbār’s wife. He experienced the pre-Islamic period. Khalīfa placed him in the first generation of the people of Syria. Abū Bakr al-Baghdādī placed him in the highest generation of the people of Ḥimṣ, the one immediately following the Companions, and said: “He was a man who served as a guide for the Prophet ﷺ.” He said that Islam was presented to him, but he did not accept Islam until the Prophet ﷺ died; then he accepted Islam with Abū Bakr. Ibn Saʿd placed him in the second generation of the Syrians. Ibn Yūnus mentioned in his History of Egypt that he died in the year 101 AH. Al-Nasāʾī transmitted from him.

## Source unit 862 · printed entry 863

### English candidate

Tamīm ibn Muqbil ibn ʿAwf ibn Ḥunayf ibn Qutayba ibn al-ʿAjlān ibn Kaʿb ibn Rabīʿa ibn ʿĀmir ibn Ṣaʿṣaʿa, Abū Kaʿb. Al-Marzubānī mentioned him in the Dictionary of Poets and said: “He lived into Islam and accepted it, yet he continued to lament the people of the pre-Islamic age. He reached one hundred and twenty years of age.” He had an incident with ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb when he sought redress from him against the poet al-Najāshī, for the two exchanged satires. The account is famous. We transmitted it in the Book of Conversations, and Thaʿlab mentioned it in his Fawāʾid, by transmission from Abū al-Ḥasan ibn Miqsam, from him. He said: “Our authorities said: Tamīm ibn Muqbil sought ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb’s redress against al-Najāshī. He said, ‘Commander of the Faithful, he has satirized me, so give me redress against him.’ ʿUmar asked, ‘Najāshī, what did you say?’ He replied, ‘Commander of the Faithful, I said something in which I do not think I bear sin,’ and recited: ‘If God recompenses the people of baseness for breach of covenant,
may He recompense Banū al-ʿAjlān, the clan of Ibn Muqbil.
His tribe never betrays a covenant
nor wrongs people by a mustard seed.’ ʿUmar said, ‘Would that I were one of these people!’ He then recited: ‘They do not come to the water except in the evening,
when all who came to drink have left every watering place.’ ʿUmar said, ‘What harm is there to these people in when they come to drink?’ He then recited: ‘Al-ʿAjlān was named only for his saying,
“Take the bowl and milk, slave, and hurry!”’ ʿUmar said, ‘The best of the people is the one most useful to his family.’ Tamīm said, ‘Then ask him about his saying: “Those are the sons of a half-breed and the household of a base man,
the clan of the helpless, abject one.”’ ʿUmar said, ‘As for this, I will not excuse you for it.’ He imprisoned and flogged him.”

## Source unit 864 · printed entry 865

### English candidate

Tamīm ibn Warqāʾ al-Khathʿamī. He experienced the pre-Islamic period and was his people’s ʿarīf during ʿUmar’s rule. Muʿāwiya sent him to ʿUmar with the news of Caesarea’s conquest. Ibn ʿAsākir mentioned him in the biography of al-Ḥakam ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, by way of Hishām ibn ʿAmmār: Yazīd ibn Samura told us, from al-Ḥakam ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī al-ʿAṣmāʾ, who had witnessed Caesarea. He said: “Muʿāwiya besieged it for seven years. The Byzantine fighting men receiving stipends there numbered one hundred thousand. Al-Naṭṭāq showed them a vulnerable point; he was one of the hostages. He brought them in through a conduit wide enough for a camel carrying its load to walk through. It was Sunday, and they were in church. They became aware of nothing until the cry ‘God is greatest!’ arose, and that was their destruction.” Yazīd ibn Samura said: “They sent news of the victory to ʿUmar with Tamīm ibn Warqāʾ, the ʿarīf of Khathʿam. ʿUmar rose and said, ‘Behold, Caesarea has been taken by force.’”

## Source unit 865 · printed entry 866

### English candidate

Tulayd ibn Kilāb al-Laythī. Al-Dhahabī added him in al-Tajrīd, saying: “His report is in the Musnad of Aḥmad: ‘The statement of Dhū al-Khuwayṣira: Be just.’ Ibn Isḥāq related it from Abū ʿUbayda ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿAmmār, from Miqsam, from a man, from him.” I say: The cited report occurs in the Musnad of ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ within the Musnad of Imam Aḥmad. Tulayd ibn Kilāb has no transmission in it; he is merely mentioned in it. Imam Aḥmad said: Yaʿqūb told us: my father told us, from Ibn Isḥāq: Abū ʿUbayda ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir told me, from Miqsam Abū al-ʿAbbās, the client of ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Nawfal, who said: “Tulayd ibn Kilāb al-Laythī and I set out until we came to ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ while he was circumambulating the House with his sandals suspended from his hand. We asked him, ‘Were you present with the Messenger of God ﷺ when the Tamīmī spoke to him on the day of Ḥunayn?’ He said, ‘Yes. A man from Banū Tamīm called Dhū al-Khuwayṣira approached,’” and he related the report at length. Al-Ṭabarānī likewise included it in al-Muʿjam al-Kabīr in the Musnad of ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ. It has therefore become clear that Miqsam received this report directly, orally, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ. Nothing in the context entails that Tulayd was a Companion or that he transmitted the report.

## Source unit 869 · printed entry 870

### English candidate

Tamīm, without a lineage. Ibn Mandah said: “It is said that he is al-Dārī, but that is not sound.” Mūsā ibn ʿAlī transmitted his report from Yazīd ibn al-Ḥuṣayn, from Tamīm, who said: “The Prophet ﷺ was asked whether Sabaʾ had been a man or a woman,” and he continued the report. Ibn Mandah said: “ʿAbd al-Wahhāb ibn ʿAbda related it thus, from Abū ʿAmr, from al-Layth, from him. Abū ʿAmr is unknown. Mūsā transmitted it from his father, from Yazīd ibn al-Ḥuṣayn, as mursal, without Tamīm in it.” I say: Ibn Mardawayh included it by way of Zayd ibn al-Ḥubāb, from Mūsā, in that form. Ibn Abī Khaythama, however, included it from ʿAbd al-Wahhāb ibn ʿAbda, from ʿUthmān ibn Kathīr, from al-Layth, from Mūsā ibn ʿAlī, from Yazīd ibn Ḥuṣayn, from Tamīm al-Dārī, that a man asked—and he related it. This rebuts Ibn Mandah on two counts. First, his statement that Abū ʿAmr was unknown: he has now been identified as ʿUthmān ibn Kathīr. Second, his statement, ‘It is said that he is Tamīm al-Dārī, but that is not sound’: Ibn Abī Khaythama explicitly stated that he was Tamīm al-Dārī. The fact that it was also transmitted as mursal does not undermine the identification of the named Tamīm as al-Dārī. والله أعلم. The report is well known from Furwa ibn Musayk, whose entry will come under the letter fāʾ; al-Tirmidhī included it. Something similar was also related from Ibn ʿAbbās; al-Tirmidhī alluded to it and Ibn Mardawayh gave it with a connected chain.

## Source unit 872 · printed entry 873

### English candidate

Thābit ibn Aqram ibn Thaʿlaba ibn ʿAdī ibn al-ʿAjlān al-Balawī, an ally of the Anṣār. Mūsā ibn ʿUqba mentioned him among the participants at Badr. Ibn Isḥāq said in al-Maghāzī: Muḥammad ibn Jaʿfar ibn al-Zubayr related to me from ʿUrwa, who said: Thābit ibn Aqram then took the banner—meaning during the expedition of Muʾta—after Ibn Rawāḥa was killed, and handed it to Khālid ibn al-Walīd. Ibn Mandah likewise narrated it from Abū al-Yusr through a weak isnad. Al-Wāqidī narrated from Abū Hurayra, who said: 'I witnessed Muʾta, and Thābit ibn Aqram told me that I had not witnessed Badr with them and that they had not been granted victory through superior numbers.' The authorities on the Prophet's campaigns agree that Thābit ibn Aqram was killed during Abū Bakr's reign by Ṭulayḥa ibn Khuwaylid al-Asadī. After Ṭulayḥa accepted Islam, ʿUmar said to him, 'How can I love you when you killed the two righteous men ʿUkkāsha ibn Miḥṣan and Thābit ibn Aqram?' Ṭulayḥa replied, 'God honored them at my hand and did not abase me at theirs.' ʿUrwa contradicted this account. Al-Ṭabarānī transmitted by way of Ibn Luhayʿa, from Abū al-Aswad, from ʿUrwa, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ dispatched a detachment to a place before al-Ghamra in Najd, appointing Thābit ibn Aqram its commander, and Thābit ibn Aqram was struck down there. On its face, this means that he was killed during the Prophet's ﷺ lifetime. The words 'was struck down' can, however, be interpreted to mean that he was wounded but did not die. I say: al-Ghamra begins with the dotted ghayn bearing fatḥa.

## Source unit 874 · printed entry 875

### English candidate

Thābit ibn al-Ḥārith al-Anṣārī. Ibn Yūnus supplied his lineage in Tārīkh Miṣr. He is also said to have been Ibn Ḥāritha. Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from his father: Thābit ibn al-Ḥārith al-Anṣārī narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he forbade the killing of a man who had witnessed Badr, saying, 'How do you know? Perhaps God has looked with favor upon the people of Badr.' Al-Ḥasan ibn Sufyān, Ibn Saʿd, and al-Ṭabarānī narrated by way of Ibn al-Mubārak, from Ibn Luhayʿa, from al-Ḥārith ibn Yazīd, from Thābit ibn al-Ḥārith al-Anṣārī, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ distributed the spoils of Khaybar and made an allotment to Sahla bint ʿĀṣim ibn ʿAdī al-Anṣārī and to a daughter whom she had borne. Its isnad is strong, because Ibn al-Mubārak's narration from Ibn Luhayʿa belongs to the strong body of Ibn Luhayʿa's hadith. Al-Baghawī transmitted something similar from Kāmil ibn Ṭalḥa, from Ibn Luhayʿa, who said, 'al-Ḥārith related to me.' Al-Baghawī said: 'I know of no report of his other than this.' I say: Al-Ṭabarānī has another report of his through this route, and Ibn Mandah has yet another, which he transmitted by way of Ibn Wahb, from Ibn Luhayʿa, from al-Ḥārith ibn Yazīd, from Thābit ibn al-Ḥārith al-Anṣārī, who said: A man from among us Anṣār had become a hypocrite. His nephew, called Warqa, came and said, 'O Messenger of God, my uncle has become a hypocrite; give me permission to strike off his head.' The Prophet replied, 'He witnessed Badr, and perhaps that will expiate his offense'—and he continued the report. This is the report to which Abū Ḥātim referred.

## Source unit 877 · printed entry 878

## Source unit 878 · printed entry 879

### English candidate

Thābit ibn al-Daḥdāḥ ibn Nuʿaym ibn Ghanm ibn Iyās, an ally of the Anṣār. He was of Balī and entered into alliance with Banū ʿAmr ibn ʿAwf. He is also called Thābit ibn al-Daḥdāḥa and bore the kunyahs Abū al-Daḥdāḥ and Abū al-Daḥdāḥa. Al-Ṭabarānī narrated by way of Ibn Isḥāq, who said: Mūsā ibn Yasār related to me, from Simāk ibn Ḥarb, from Jābir ibn Samura, who said: 'I saw the Messenger of God ﷺ at the funeral of Thābit ibn al-Daḥdāḥ'—and he continued the report. It is also in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim through Jābir ibn Samura, though Thābit is not named there: it says, 'We prayed over Ibn al-Daḥdāḥ,' and in another recension, 'over Abū al-Daḥdāḥ.' Al-Bāwardī narrated by way of Ibn Isḥāq, who said: Muḥammad ibn Abī ʿAdī related to me, from ʿIkrima or Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbās, that Thābit ibn al-Daḥdāḥa asked the Prophet ﷺ a question, whereupon the words 'They ask you about menstruation ...'—the verse—were revealed. Al-Wāqidī said concerning the expedition of Uḥud: ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmmār al-Khaṭmī related to me that Thābit ibn al-Daḥdāḥa came forward on the day of Uḥud and said, 'O company of the Anṣār, if Muḥammad has been killed, then God is Living and does not die, so fight for your religion.' He charged with the Muslims who were with him. Khālid stabbed him through, and he fell dead. Al-Wāqidī said: Some of our colleagues say instead that he survived, recovered from his wounds, and later died in his bed when the Prophet ﷺ returned from al-Ḥudaybiya. الله أعلم.

## Source unit 891 · printed entry 892

### English candidate

Thābit ibn al-Ṣāmit ibn ʿAdī ibn Kaʿb ibn ʿAbd al-Ashhal al-Anṣārī al-Ashhalī. Ibn al-Sakan and others mentioned him. Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from his father that he had companionship. Ibn Khuzayma narrated by way of Ibn Abī Ḥabīb, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Thābit ibn al-Ṣāmit, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: The Prophet ﷺ prayed in the mosque of Banū ʿAbd al-Ashhal wearing a cloak wrapped around himself to protect him from the cold of the ground. Ibn Mājah transmitted it through the same route, but his version reads 'from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Thābit' and omits 'from his father, from his grandfather,' thereby creating the false impression that ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān had companionship. Ibn al-Sakan said: 'It is said that Thābit ibn al-Ṣāmit died in the pre-Islamic period and that companionship belonged to his son ʿAbd al-Raḥmān.' Abū ʿUmar stated this categorically, following Ibn Saʿd. Ibn Saʿd said that there is an error in this hadith: either it should be from a son of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, from his father, from his grandfather; or it should be from his father, from the Prophet ﷺ, without 'from his grandfather.' The person who accompanied the Prophet ﷺ and narrated from him was ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Thābit, not his father. Ibn Saʿd's basis for this was Hishām ibn al-Kalbī's statement that Thābit ibn al-Ṣāmit died in the pre-Islamic period. In the biography of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Thābit it will be explained that the al-Ṣāmit who died in the pre-Islamic period was the father of ʿUbāda and was not Ashhalī. Ibn Qāniʿ made the unusual move of mentioning al-Ṣāmit, the father of this Thābit, among the Companions. He transmitted this report through another route from Ibn Shayba, saying, 'from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Thābit, from his father, from his grandfather.' It appears that the word ibn fell out of his narration and that it should be 'from a son of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān.'

### Arabic authority

<div dir="rtl" lang="ar">

ثابت بن الصامت بن عدي بن كعب بن عبد الأشهل الأنصاري الأشهلي ذكره بن السكن وغيره وقال بن أبي حاتم عن أبيه له صحبة وروى بن خزيمة من طريق بن أبي حبيب عن عبد الرحمن بن عبد الرحمن بن ثابت بن الصامت عن أبيه عن جده قال صلى النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم في مسجد بني عبد الأشهل وعليه كساء ملتفا به يقيه برد الأرض ومن هذا الوجه أخرجه بن ماجة لكن وقع عنده عن عبد الله بن عبد الرحمن بن ثابت وسقط منه عن أبيه عن جده فاوهم أن الصحبة لعبد الله بن عبد الرحمن وليس كذلك وقال بن السكن يقال إن ثابت بن الصامت مات في الجاهلية والصحبة لابنه عبد الرحمن وجزم بهذا أبو عمر تبعا لابن سعد قال بن سعد في هذا الحديث وهل أما أن يكون عن بن لعبد الرحمن بن عبد الرحمن عن أبيه عن جده وإما أن يكون عن أبيه عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم ليس فيه عن جده لأن الذي صحب النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم وروى عنه عبد الرحمن بن ثابت لابوه وعمدة بن سعد في ذلك قول هشام بن الكلبي أن ثابت بن الصامت مات في الجاهلية وسيأتي في ترجمة عبد الرحمن بن ثابت أن الصامت الذي مات في الجاهلية هو والد عبادة وليس هو اشهليا وأغرب بن قانع فذكر الصامت والد ثابت هذا في الصحابة وساق هذا الحديث من وجه آخر عن بن شيبة فقال عن عبد الرحمن بن ثابت عن أبيه عن جده فكأنه سقط من روايته بن وكأنه عن بن عبد الرحمن

## Source unit 894 · printed entry 895

### English candidate

Thābit ibn al-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Khalīfa ibn Thaʿlaba ibn ʿAdī ibn Kaʿb ibn ʿAbd al-Ashhal, al-Anṣārī al-Ashhalī. He witnessed the Pledge of al-Riḍwān, as is established in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim from Abū Qilāba’s report that Thābit told him this. Ibn Mandah mentioned that al-Bukhārī said he witnessed Badr. Abū Nuʿaym objected: “Al-Bukhārī only mentioned that he witnessed al-Ḥudaybiya.” I say: Al-Tirmidhī likewise said that he witnessed Badr. Ibn Shāhīn, on the authority of Ibn Abī Dāwūd, and Ibn al-Sakan, by way of Abū Bakr ibn Abī al-Aswad, said: “Thābit ibn al-Ḍaḥḥāk al-Ashhalī rode behind the Messenger of God ﷺ on the day of the Trench, was his guide to Ḥamrāʾ al-Asad, and was among those who pledged beneath the tree.” Abū ʿUmar, following al-Wāqidī, said: “He was born in the year 3 AH and died in the year 45 AH.” I say: This is an error. Perhaps he was born in the third year after the beginning of the prophetic mission, for how could someone who witnessed al-Ḥudaybiya in the year 6 AH and pledged there have been born three years after the Hijra and thus been three years old at al-Ḥudaybiya? It is more likely that the person born in the year 3 AH was the preceding Thābit. الله أعلم. Abū Ḥātim said: “It reached me from Ibn Numayr that he said: ‘He was the father of Zayd ibn Thābit.’” If he said that, he erred. Abū Qilāba did not meet Zayd ibn Thābit, so how could he have met Zayd’s father while saying, “Thābit ibn al-Ḍaḥḥāk told me”? I say: Perhaps Ibn Numayr did not mean what they understood from him. Perhaps he merely conveyed that Thābit had a son named Zayd, not that he was the father of the famous jurist Zayd ibn Thābit. Al-Baghawī related from Abū Mūsā Hārūn ibn ʿAbd Allāh that his kunya was Abū Zayd and that he died during the time of Ibn al-Zubayr. Al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Saʿd, and Abū Aḥmad al-Ḥākim dated his death similarly; some of them further specified the year 64 AH. ʿAmr ibn ʿAlī said that he died in the year 45 AH, perhaps following al-Wāqidī.

## Source unit 901 · printed entry 902

### English candidate

Thābit ibn ʿAmr ibn Zayd ibn ʿAdī ibn Sawād ibn Mālik ibn Ghanm ibn ʿAdī ibn al-Najjār. In Abū al-Aswad’s report from ʿUrwa, the genealogy differs after Sawād: he says, ‘Sawād ibn ʿIṣma.’ Abū ʿIṣma al-Anṣārī was their confederate; his origin was among Ashjaʿ. He then entered alliance with the Anṣār and was affiliated to them by filiation, as happened with many Arabs, such as al-Miqdād ibn al-Aswad. Otherwise, carrying the genealogy through to al-Najjār would entail that he was an Anṣārī by descent, not by alliance. He witnessed Badr and was martyred at Uḥud according to all of them except Ibn Isḥāq—so Abū ʿUmar said, following Ibn Jarīr. Yet Ibn Isḥāq did mention him among the participants at Badr and said that he was killed at Uḥud. Mūsā ibn ʿUqba did not mention him among those martyred at Uḥud.

## Source unit 902 · printed entry 903

### English candidate

Thābit ibn Qays ibn al-Khaṭīm ibn ʿAdī ibn ʿAmr ibn Sawād ibn Ẓafar, al-Anṣārī al-Ẓafarī. Ibn Shāhīn mentioned him, from Muḥammad ibn Ibrāhīm, from Muḥammad ibn Yazīd, from his authorities among the Companions. Abū ʿUmar said: “He is mentioned among the Companions. Saʿīd ibn al-ʿĀṣ appointed him over Kufa when ʿUthmān summoned Saʿīd because the people of Kufa complained about him. I know of no transmission from Thābit. His father was one of the great poets of the pre-Islamic period.” Muṣʿab al-Zubayrī said: “ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿUmāra al-Qaddāḥ told me that the Prophet ﷺ offered Islam to Qays ibn al-Khaṭīm while he was in Mecca. Qays asked him for time until he should reach Medina, but Qays was killed in one of the wars between al-Aws and al-Khazraj before the Hijra.” He said: “Among his descendants was Yazīd ibn Qays, after whom he took his kunya. Thābit ibn Qays received twelve wounds on the day of Uḥud. The Prophet ﷺ called him Ḥāsir that day and would say to him, ‘Ḥāsir, advance! Ḥāsir, fall back!’ as he struck with his sword before him. He witnessed the campaigns thereafter. ʿAlī appointed him over al-Madāʾin, and he remained there until al-Mughīra arrived as Muʿāwiya’s governor of Kufa and dismissed him. Thābit died during Muʿāwiya’s time.” Ibn Saʿd related something similar in al-Ṭabaqāt from Muṣʿab. Al-Qaddāḥ also transmitted from Muḥammad ibn Ṣāliḥ ibn Dīnār, through his chain, that Muʿāwiya disliked Thābit ibn Qays because of his participation in the wars alongside ʿAlī. The Anṣār gathered and wished to write to Muʿāwiya because he was withholding their entitlements. Thābit advised them that a single one of them should correspond with him, lest his response contain something they would dislike. He related a long account in which Thābit went to Muʿāwiya with their letter and an exchange took place between them. Al-Ḥarbī transmitted in Gharīb al-Ḥadīth, by way of Ibn Isḥāq, from ʿĀṣim ibn ʿUmar, who heard Anas say: “Al-Khazraj had killed Qays ibn al-Khaṭīm in the pre-Islamic period. When his son accepted Islam, they sent him his father’s weapons. He said, ‘Were it not for Islam, you would have repudiated what you had done.’” It is also said that the report in the Sunan from ʿAdī ibn Thābit, from his father, from his grandfather, means that the grandfather was this Thābit ibn Qays, since ʿAdī was the son of Abān ibn Thābit ibn Qays ibn al-Khaṭīm. Abū Aḥmad al-Dimyāṭī asserted this firmly, following some genealogists such as Ibn al-Kalbī. There is much disagreement about it. It is said instead that he was Thābit ibn ʿĀzib, brother of al-Barāʾ; or Thābit ibn ʿUbayd ibn ʿĀzib, son of al-Barāʾ’s brother; or that his grandfather’s name was ʿAdī ibn ʿAmr ibn Akhṭab; or that the grandfather was his maternal grandfather ʿAbd Allāh ibn Yazīd; or that he was Thābit ibn Dīnār; and other views are given. What counts against al-Dimyāṭī’s view is that the genealogists, including Ibn al-Kalbī and Ibn Saʿd, agree that Abān ibn Thābit ibn Qays died leaving no progeny.

## Source unit 904 · printed entry 905

### English candidate

Thābit ibn Qays ibn Shammās ibn Zuhayr ibn Mālik ibn Imriʾ al-Qays ibn Mālik ibn Thaʿlaba ibn Kaʿb ibn al-Khazraj, al-Anṣārī al-Khazrajī, the orator of the Anṣār. Ibn al-Sakan transmitted, by way of Ibn Abī ʿAdī, from Ḥumayd, from Anas, who said: “When the Messenger of God ﷺ arrived in Medina, Thābit ibn Qays delivered an address and said, ‘We will protect you from what we protect ourselves and our children; what then shall we receive?’ He said, ‘Paradise.’ They said, ‘We are satisfied.’” Jaʿfar ibn Sulaymān related from Thābit, from Anas: “Thābit ibn Qays was the orator of the Anṣār.” His kunya was Abū Muḥammad, though it is also said to have been Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān. The authors of the campaign works did not mention him among the Badrians; they said that his first battle was Uḥud and that he witnessed the battles thereafter. The Prophet ﷺ gave him the glad tidings of Paradise in a famous account transmitted by Mūsā ibn Anas from his father; Muslim included the core of the report. In al-Tirmidhī, through a fair chain from Abū Hurayra, raised to the Prophet, are the words: “What an excellent man Thābit ibn Qays is!” In al-Bukhārī in abbreviated form, and in al-Ṭabarānī at length, from Anas: “When the people broke ranks on the day of al-Yamāma, I said to Thābit ibn Qays, ‘Do you not see, uncle?’ I found him applying embalming perfume. He said, ‘This is not how we used to fight with the Messenger of God ﷺ. Wretched is the habit you have taught your matched opponents! God, I declare myself free before You of what these people brought and of what those people did.’ He then fought until he was killed. He was wearing a precious coat of mail. A Muslim man passed him and took it. Then, while another Muslim was asleep, Thābit came to him in his dream and said: ‘I charge you with an instruction. Beware of saying, “This is a dream,” and letting it go to waste. When I was killed, so-and-so took my coat of mail. His lodging is at the far end of the people. Beside his tent is a horse frisking on its tether. He overturned a pot over the coat of mail, and atop it is a saddle. Go to Khālid and tell him to take it. Tell Abū Bakr that I owe such-and-such a debt and that so-and-so is free.’ The man awoke, went to Khālid, and informed him. Khālid sent for the coat of mail, and it was brought to him. The man told Abū Bakr of his dream, and Abū Bakr executed Thābit’s bequest.” Al-Baghawī transmitted it at length through another route, from ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī, from the daughter of Thābit ibn Qays.

## Source unit 906 · printed entry 907

### English candidate

Thābit ibn Mukhlad ibn Zayd ibn Mukhlad ibn Ḥāritha ibn ʿAmr al-Anṣārī al-Khaṭmī. Ibn Shāhīn mentioned him among the Companions and said that he was killed on the day of al-Ḥarra. He said: “I heard ʿAbd Allāh ibn Sulaymān ibn al-Ashʿath say this.” Ibn Shāhīn transmitted, by way of Naṣr ibn ʿAlī, from Muḥammad ibn Bakr, from Ibn Jurayj, from Ibn al-Munkadir, from Abū Ayyūb, from Maslama ibn Mukhlad al-Anṣārī, raising it to the Prophet: “Whoever conceals a Muslim, God will conceal him,” and he continued the report. Aḥmad transmitted it in his Musnad from Muḥammad ibn Bakr through this chain, but said “from Maslama ibn Mukhlad.” The report is well known from Maslama, and he has an account concerning it with Abū Ayyūb that we transmitted in al-Khaṭīb’s Book of the Journey.

## Source unit 909 · printed entry 910

### English candidate

Thābit ibn al-Nuʿmān ibn Umayya ibn Imriʾ al-Qays ibn Thaʿlaba ibn ʿAmr ibn ʿAwf ibn Mālik ibn al-Aws, whose kunya was Abū Ḥabba. He witnessed the conquest of Egypt, according to Ibn al-Barqī and Ibn Yūnus. He is not the Badrian, who by agreement descended from Kulfa ibn Thaʿlaba ibn ʿAmr ibn ʿAwf. Ibn Mandah erred by making the two one person. Ibn Isḥāq mentioned among those martyred at Uḥud Abū al-Ṣabāḥ ibn Thābit ibn al-Nuʿmān and gave this very genealogy. On that basis, Abū al-Ṣabāḥ’s father lived for a considerable time after him.

## Source unit 915 · printed entry 916

### English candidate

Thābit ibn Waqsh ibn Zughba ibn Zaʿūrāʾ ibn ʿAbd al-Ashhal, al-Anṣārī al-Ashhalī. Ibn Isḥāq mentioned in al-Maghāzī: ʿĀṣim ibn ʿUmar told me, from Maḥmūd ibn Labīd, who said: “When the Messenger of God ﷺ set out for Uḥud, Thābit ibn Waqsh and Ḥisl ibn Jābir—the father of Ḥudhayfa ibn al-Yamān—were left in the fortified houses with the women and children. They were two very old men. One said to the other, ‘May you be fatherless! What are we waiting for? We are only skulls today or tomorrow.’ They joined the Muslims so that they might be granted martyrdom. When they entered among the people, the polytheists killed Thābit ibn Waqsh. The Muslims’ swords closed around Ḥudhayfa’s father. Ḥudhayfa cried, ‘My father! My father!’ but they killed him without recognizing him. Ḥudhayfa said, ‘May God forgive you,’ and gave his blood-money in charity to the Muslims.” The account of Ḥudhayfa’s father in this incident is in the Ṣaḥīḥ through ʿĀʾisha’s report, but it does not mention Thābit.

## Source unit 929 · printed entry 930

### English candidate

Thaʿlaba ibn Ḥāṭib—or Ibn Abī Ḥāṭib—al-Anṣārī. Ibn Isḥāq mentioned him among those who built the Mosque of Harm. Al-Bāwardī, Ibn al-Sakan, Ibn Shāhīn, and others transmitted under the biography of the preceding man, by way of Maʿān ibn Rifāʿa, from ʿAlī ibn Zayd, from al-Qāsim, from Abū Umāma, that Thaʿlaba ibn Ḥāṭib al-Anṣārī said: ‘Messenger of God, pray to God to provide me with wealth.’ The Prophet ﷺ said, ‘A little for which you render thanks is better than much that you cannot bear.’ He then related the report at length: the Prophet ﷺ prayed for him, his wealth became abundant, he withheld the alms, and the Most High’s saying was revealed, ‘Among them are those who made a covenant with God: If He gives us of His bounty …,’ to the end of the passage. It says that the Prophet ﷺ died without accepting the alms from him; neither Abū Bakr nor ʿUmar accepted it, and he died during ʿUthmān’s caliphate. There is reason for scrutiny over whether the subject of this account—if the report is sound, and I do not think it is sound—was the Badrian mentioned immediately before. The distinction between them is reinforced by Ibn al-Kalbī’s statement that the Badrian was martyred at Uḥud. It is further supported by Ibn Mardawayh’s transmission in his Tafsīr, by way of ʿAṭiyya, from Ibn ʿAbbās concerning the cited verse: ‘A man of the Anṣār called Thaʿlaba ibn Abī Ḥāṭib came to a gathering and called them to witness, saying, “If He gives us of His bounty …”’ He related the account at length and called him Thaʿlaba ibn Abī Ḥāṭib, whereas there is agreement that the Badrian was Thaʿlaba ibn Ḥāṭib. It is established that he ﷺ said, ‘No one who witnessed Badr and al-Ḥudaybiya will enter the Fire,’ and that he related from his Lord that He said to the people of Badr, ‘Do whatever you wish, for I have forgiven you.’ How could someone of this standing be followed by God’s planting hypocrisy in his heart and revealing concerning him what was revealed? It therefore appears that he was someone else. والله أعلم.

### Arabic authority

<div dir="rtl" lang="ar">

ثعلبة بن حاطب أو أبي حاطب الأنصاري ذكره بن إسحاق فيمن بني مسجد الضرار وروى الباوردي وابن السكن وابن شاهين وغيرهم في ترجمة الذي قبله من طريق معان بن رفاعة عن علي بن زيد عن قاسم عن أبي أمامة أن ثعلبة بن حاطب الأنصاري قال يا رسول الله أدع الله أن يرزقني ما لا فقال النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قليل تؤدي شكره خير من كثير لا تطيقه فذكر الحديث بطوله في دعاء النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم له وكثرة ماله ومنعه الصدقة ونزول قوله تعالى ومنهم من عاهد الله لئن آتانا من فضله الآية وفيه أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم مات ولم يقبض منه الصدقة ولا أبو بكر ولا عمر وأنه مات في خلافة عثمان وفي كون صاحب هذه القصة إن صح الخبر ولا أظنه يصح هو البدري المذكور قبله نظر وقد تأكدت المغايرة بينهما بقول بن الكلبي إن البدري استشهد بأحد ويقوي ذلك أيضا أن بن مردويه روى في تفسيره من طريق عطية بن عباس في الآية المذكورة قال وذلك أن رجلا يقال له ثعلبة بن أبي حاطب من الأنصار أتى مجلسا فأشهدهم فقال لئن آتانا من فضله الآية فذكر القصة بطولها فقال إنه ثعلبة بن أبي حاطب والبدري اتفق على أنه ثعلبة بن حاطب وقد ثبت أنه صلى الله عليه وسلم قال لا يدخل النار أحد شهد بدرا والحديبية وحكى عن ربه أنه قال لأهل بدر اعملوا ما شئتم فقد غفرت لكم فمن يكون بهذه المثابة كيف يعقبه الله نفاقا في قلبه وينزل فيه ما نزل فالظاهر أنه غيره والله أعلم

## Source unit 934 · printed entry 935

Thaʿlaba ibn Zayd ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥarām ibn Ghanm ibn Kaʿb ibn Salima ibn Saʿd ibn ʿAlī ibn Sārida ibn Tazīd ibn Jusham ibn al-Khazraj, al-Anṣārī al-Khazrajī. ## Source unit 935 · printed entry 936

### English candidate

Thaʿlaba ibn Zayd al-Anṣārī, one of Banū ʿAmr ibn ʿAwf. Ibn Mandah said: ‘He is mentioned in the campaign literature.’ ʿAbd al-Ghanī ibn Saʿīd al-Thaqafī mentioned in his Tafsīr, through his chain to Ibn ʿAbbās, that Thaʿlaba was among those concerning whom the Most High’s saying was revealed, ‘Nor is there blame upon those who, when they came to you so that you might mount them …,’ to the end of the verse. ʿAbdān related from Aḥmad ibn Yasār that ‘Thaʿlaba ibn Zayd of Banū Ḥarām among the Anṣār was one of the Weepers.’ Abū Mūsā added him. I say: The man from Banū Ḥarām is the preceding entry, while the man from Banū ʿAmr ibn ʿAwf is the subject of this entry. It is possible that both belonged to the Weepers; it is also possible that the subject’s name was corrupted. Mujammiʿ ibn Ḥāritha named the Weepers but did not count among them Thaʿlaba ibn Zayd; rather, he counted ʿUlba ibn Zayd al-Ḥārithī. Ibn Mardawayh included this in his Tafsīr. والله أعلم.

## Source unit 942 · printed entry 943

### English candidate

Thaʿlaba ibn Ṣuʿayr—the ṣād and ʿayn are both unpointed, and the form is a diminutive—also called ibn Abī Ṣuʿayr ibn ʿAmr ibn Zayd ibn Sinān ibn Salāmān al-Quḍāʿī al-ʿUdhrī, an ally of Banū Zuhra. Al-Dāraquṭnī said that he had companionship and that his son ʿAbd Allāh had seen the Prophet. Ibn Abī ʿĀṣim, al-Bāwardī, and others narrated by way of Bakr ibn Wāʾil, from al-Zuhrī, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Thaʿlaba ibn Ṣuʿayr, from his father, concerning the alms of breaking the fast. Hammām alone transmitted it from Bakr. I say: Baḥr ibn Kunayz al-Saqqāʾ corroborated Bakr from al-Zuhrī; al-Ḥasan ibn Sufyān transmitted it, and Abū Nuʿaym transmitted it by way of him. Abū Dāwūd narrated the aforementioned report by way of al-Nuʿmān ibn Rāshid, from al-Zuhrī, who said: from Thaʿlaba ibn Abī Ṣuʿayr, from his father. In another recension with him: from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Thaʿlaba, or Thaʿlaba ibn ʿAbd Allāh. Ibn al-Sakan said: Thaʿlaba ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Ṣuʿayr al-ʿUdhrī; his audition is not soundly established. He then narrated with his chain to Ibn Maʿīn, who said: Thaʿlaba ibn Abī Ṣuʿayr saw the Prophet ﷺ. Ibn Shāhīn narrated by way of Yaḥyā ibn Khārija, from al-Zuhrī, who instead said: from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Thaʿlaba ibn Abī Ṣuʿayr. Ibn Shāhīn said that Yaḥyā ibn Khārija rendered it mursal. He will be mentioned again in the biography of his son ʿAbd Allāh ibn Thaʿlaba. Al-Bukhārī said in al-Tārīkh: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Thaʿlaba, from the Prophet ﷺ, mursal—unless it was from his father, which is more likely. As for Thaʿlaba ibn Abī Ṣuʿayr, he is not one of these. I say: this requires Thaʿlaba ibn Ṣuʿayr to be someone other than Thaʿlaba ibn Abī Ṣuʿayr. الله أعلم.

## Source unit 944 · printed entry 945

### English candidate

Thaʿlaba ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Anṣārī. It is said that he used to serve the Prophet ﷺ. Ibn Shāhīn and Abū Nuʿaym narrated at length by way of Sulaym ibn Manṣūr ibn ʿAmmār, from his father, from al-Munkadir ibn Muḥammad ibn al-Munkadir, from his father, from Jābir: a young man of the Anṣār called Thaʿlaba ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān used to serve the Prophet ﷺ. He sent him on an errand. Thaʿlaba passed the door of an Anṣārī man, saw the man's wife bathing, and looked at her repeatedly. He then feared that revelation would descend, so he fled headlong until he reached mountains between Mecca and Medina and settled there. The Prophet ﷺ missed him for forty days, which, they claimed, were the days concerning which they said, 'His Lord forsook him and detested him.' Then Gabriel descended to him and said, 'O Muḥammad, the fugitive among the mountains seeks refuge in Me from the Fire.' He sent ʿUmar to him, saying, 'Go—you and Salmān—and bring him to me.' A shepherd called Dufāfa met the two and said, 'Perhaps you seek the fugitive from Hell.' The source then mentions the report in full concerning their bringing him back, his illness, and his death from fear of his sin. Ibn Mandah, after narrating it in abridged form, said: Manṣūr alone transmitted it. I say: Manṣūr is weak, and his shaykh is weaker still. The narrative itself indicates the report's frailty, because the revelation of 'Your Lord has not forsaken you, nor has He detested you' occurred before the Hijra, without disagreement.

## Source unit 952 · printed entry 953

### English candidate

Thaʿlaba ibn Abī Mālik al-Quraẓī. His companionship is disputed. Ibn Maʿīn said that he had seen the Prophet. Ibn Saʿd said: Abū Mālik, whose name was ʿAbd Allāh ibn Sām, came from Yemen and belonged to Kinda. He married a woman of Qurayẓa and consequently became known as one of them. Muṣʿab al-Zubayrī said that Thaʿlaba was among those whose pubic hair had not yet grown on the Day of Qurayẓa, so he was spared just as ʿAṭiyya and others like him were spared. I say: ʿAṭiyya will be mentioned later. Al-Baghawī and others narrated by way of Ibn Isḥāq, from Abū Mālik ibn Thaʿlaba ibn Abī Mālik, from his father, that the people of Mahzūr came to the Prophet ﷺ. He ruled that when the water reached the ankles, the upstream holder was not to detain it. Al-Walīd ibn Kathīr corroborated Abū Mālik. Ibn Abī ʿĀṣim narrated a similar report by way of Ṣafwān ibn Sulaym, from Thaʿlaba; its transmitters are trustworthy. Ibn Mājah narrated it by another route, from Muḥammad ibn ʿUqba ibn Abī Mālik, from his paternal uncle Thaʿlaba ibn Abī Mālik. Ibn Ḥibbān included him among the trustworthy Followers. Abū Ḥātim said that he was a Follower and that his report was mursal. I say: his report from ʿUmar is in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī. A person whose father was killed at Qurayẓa, and who himself was on the verge of being killed but for the absence of pubic hair, could quite possibly have valid audition. Because of this possibility, I have included him here.

## Source unit 955 · printed entry 956

### English candidate

Thaʿlaba al-Anṣārī, father of ʿAbd Allāh. It is said that his father's name was Suhayl. Ibn Abī Ḥātim mentioned him. Al-Bāwardī and Abū Muslim al-Kajjī narrated by way of Khālid ibn al-Ḥārith, while al-Ḥākim in al-Mustadrak, al-Ḥasan ibn Sufyān, and Abū Aḥmad al-Ḥākim in al-Kunā narrated by way of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ḥumrān; both transmitters narrated from ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd ibn Jaʿfar, who said: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Thaʿlaba al-Anṣārī informed me, 'I heard ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Kaʿb say: I heard your father Thaʿlaba say: I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say, Any man who appropriates another man's right by a false oath will have a black spot of hypocrisy in his heart that nothing will alter until the Day of Resurrection.' In the Musnad of Baqī ibn Makhlad the name appears as Thaʿlaba ibn ʿAbd Allāh. الله أعلم. Abū Aḥmad al-Ḥākim related that al-Ḥusayn ibn Muḥammad al-Qabbānī said this Thaʿlaba was Abū Umāma al-Ḥārithī. The well-known view, however, is that Abū Umāma's name was Iyās ibn Thaʿlaba. Al-Baghawī, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Ibn Shāhīn, and more than one other compiler on the Companions categorically held that this was someone else. The two reports differ in both text and isnad, so it is possible that he was a different man. Abū Ḥātim and others stated the distinction categorically. والله أعلم.

<div dir="rtl" lang="ar">

ثعلبة الأنصاري والد عبد الله يقال اسم أبيه سهيل ذكره بن أبي حاتم روى الباوردي وأبو مسلم الكجي من طريق خالد بن الحارث والحاكم في المستدرك والحسن بن سفيان وأبو أحمد الحاكم في الكنى من طريق عبد الله بن حمران كلاهما عن عبد الحميد بن جعفر أخبرني عبد الله بن ثعلبة الأنصاري سمعت عبد الرحمن بن كعب يقول سمعت أباك ثعلبة يقول سمعت رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يقول أيما امرئ اقتطع حق امرئ بيمين كاذبة كانت نكتة سوداء من نفاق في قلبه لا يغيرها شيء إلى يوم القيامة ووقع في مسند بقي بن مخلد ثعلبة بن عبد الله فالله أعلم وحكى أبو أحمد الحاكم أن الحسين بن محمد القباني قال إن ثعلبة هذا هو أبو أمامة الحارثي لكن المعروف أن اسم أبي أمامة إياس بن ثعلبة وقد جزم بأنه غيره البغوي وابن أبي حاتم وابن شاهين وغير واحد ممن ألف في الصحابة وبين الحديثين مغايرة في المتن والإسناد فيحتمل أن يكون غيره وبالمغايرة جزم أبو حاتم وغيره والله أعلم

## Source unit 957 · printed entry 958

### English candidate

Thaʿlaba, without a patronymic. Ibn Mandah and Abū Nuʿaym mentioned him among the unnamed persons under 'Ibn Thaʿlaba.' They transmitted by way of Yaḥyā ibn Jābir, from Ibn Thaʿlaba, that he came to the Prophet ﷺ and said, 'O Messenger of God, ask God to grant me martyrdom.' The Prophet ﷺ said to him, 'Bring me some hairs.' He brought them, and the Prophet ﷺ told him, 'Bare your upper arm.' The Prophet bound them around his upper arm, then blew upon it and said, 'O God, make Thaʿlaba's blood inviolable to the polytheists and hypocrites.' Ibn al-Athīr said: thus their recensions read 'the blood of Thaʿlaba'; nothing in it indicates 'Ibn Thaʿlaba' except the beginning of the isnad. I say: Ibn Thaʿlaba's name was Ḍamra, and this report appeared previously in his biography under the letter ḍād. If this recension is established, the pronoun in the words 'that he came' would refer to Ibn Thaʿlaba, and Thaʿlaba would necessarily have to be included among the Companions. On that reading, this would be counted among the cases in which both a man and his father had companionship. The earlier recension under the letter ḍād, however, reads, 'O God, make the blood of Ibn Thaʿlaba inviolable,' with the additional word ibn. والله أعلم.

### Arabic authority

<div dir="rtl" lang="ar">

ثعلبة غير منسوب ذكره بن منده وأبو نعيم في المبهمات في بن ثعلبة وأخرجاه من طريق يحيى بن جابر عن بن ثعلبة أنه أتى النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم فقال له يا رسول الله أدع الله لي بالشهادة فقال النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم ائتني بشعرات فأتاه بها فقال له النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم اكشف عن عضدك قال فربطه في عضده ثم نفث فيه ثم قال اللهم حرم دم ثعلبة على المشركين والمنافقين قال بن الأثير كذا عندهما دم ثعلبة وليس فيه ما يدل على بن ثعلبة الا في أول الإسناد قلت بن ثعلبة اسمه ضمرة وقد تقدم هذا الحديث في ترجمته في حرف الضاد المعجمة فإن كانت هذه الرواية ثابتة فيكون الضمير في قوله إنه بن لثعلبة وتعين ذكره في الصحابة ويعد على هذا فيمن صحب هو وأبوه لكن الرواية الماضية في حرف الضاد فيها اللهم حرم دم بن ثعلبة بزيادة لفظة بن والله أعلم

## Source unit 961 · printed entry 962

### English candidate

Thumāma ibn Uthāl ibn al-Nuʿmān ibn Maslama ibn ʿUtba ibn Thaʿlaba ibn Yarbūʿ ibn Thaʿlaba ibn al-Duʾl ibn Ḥanīfa al-Ḥanafī, Abū Umāma al-Yamāmī. His report is in al-Bukhārī by way of Saʿīd al-Maqburī, from Abū Hurayra, who said: The Prophet ﷺ dispatched cavalry toward Najd. They returned with a man of Banū Ḥanīfa named Thumāma ibn Uthāl and tied him to one of the pillars of the mosque. The Prophet ﷺ came out and said, ‘Release Thumāma.’ He went to some date palms near the mosque, bathed, then entered the mosque and said, ‘I testify that there is no god but God and that Muḥammad is the Messenger of God.’ Al-Bukhārī also transmitted it at greater length.

Ibn Isḥāq transmitted it at length in the Maghāzī from Saʿīd al-Maqburī. Its beginning states that Thumāma, while still a polytheist, had confronted the Messenger of God ﷺ intending to kill him, so the Messenger of God ﷺ prayed to his Lord to give him power over Thumāma. After accepting Islam, Thumāma went to Mecca to perform ʿumra and said, ‘By Him in whose hand is my soul, not a single grain from al-Yamāma’—which was the agricultural provision of the people of Mecca—‘will come to you until the Messenger of God ﷺ permits it.’

Al-Ḥumaydī transmitted it from Sufyān, from Ibn ʿAjlān, from Saʿīd, from Abū Hurayra. Ibn Isḥāq also related that Thumāma remained steadfast in Islam when the people of al-Yamāma apostatized. He and those of his people who obeyed him departed and joined al-ʿAlāʾ al-Ḥaḍramī, fighting alongside him against the apostates of Bahrain. After they were victorious, Thumāma bought a robe that had belonged to the apostates’ leader. Some men of Banū Qays ibn Thaʿlaba saw him wearing it and, thinking that he had killed and despoiled their leader, killed him. He will be mentioned again in the biography of ʿĀmir ibn Salama al-Ḥanafī.

Ibn Manda transmitted by way of ʿAlbāʾ ibn Aḥmar, from ʿIkrima, from Ibn ʿAbbās, the story of Thumāma’s conversion, his return to al-Yamāma, his withholding provisions from Quraysh, and the revelation of the Most High’s words: ‘We had certainly seized them with punishment, but they neither humbled themselves to their Lord nor entreated Him’ [Qurʾān 23:76]. Its chain is fair. Wathīma mentioned that Thumāma took a fine stand during the apostasy and cited verses of his rebuking Banū Ḥanīfa, among them:

I think of leaving speech, but then I am brought back / to speech by the favor of the Prophet Muḥammad.
I thanked him for freeing me from the fetter after / I had seen the shadow of a keen Indian sword.

Thumāma ibn ʿAdī al-Qurashī. He was mentioned earlier in the biography of Thaqaf ibn ʿAmr, where it was stated that he was among the earliest Emigrants. Abū Mūsā related from al-Ṭabarī that he witnessed Badr. Ibn al-Sakan said that he was said to have Companionship and that he was governor of Ṣanʿāʾ.

Al-Bukhārī in his Tārīkh and Ibn Saʿd transmitted, with a sound chain to Abū Qilāba, from Abū al-Ashʿath al-Ṣanʿānī, who said: When news of the killing of ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān reached Thumāma ibn ʿAdī—who was governor of Ṣanʿāʾ al-Shām and had Companionship—he wept, and his weeping lasted a long time. When he recovered, he said, ‘This is when the caliphate of prophecy was torn away.’ Al-Bāwardī transmitted it by another route from Ayyūb, from Abū Qilāba. Ibn Manda transmitted by way of al-Naḍr ibn Maʿbad, from Abū Qilāba: Abū al-Ashʿath al-Ṣanʿānī related to me that Thumāma governed Ṣanʿāʾ and was one of the Companions of Muḥammad the Prophet ﷺ; and he related the report.

## Source unit 967 · printed entry 968

### English candidate

Thawbān, client of the Messenger of God ﷺ, a well-known Companion. It is said that he was an Arab: a Ḥakamī from Ḥakam ibn Saʿd of Ḥimyar; and it is said that he was from al-Sarāh. The Messenger of God ﷺ bought him and then emancipated him, and he served him until he died. Thawbān then moved to al-Ramla and afterward to Ḥimṣ, where he died in the year fifty-four. Ibn Saʿd and others stated this.

Ibn al-Sakan transmitted by way of Yūsuf ibn ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd, who said: ‘I met Thawbān, and he related to me that the Messenger of God ﷺ prayed for his family. I said, “Am I one of the Household?” On the third occasion he replied, “Yes, so long as you do not stand at the door of a ruler’s residence or go to an emir and ask him.”’

Abū Dāwūd transmitted by way of ʿĀṣim, from Abū al-ʿĀliya, from Thawbān, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said, ‘Who will guarantee me that he will not ask people for anything, and I will guarantee him Paradise?’ Thawbān said, ‘I will.’ Thereafter he would not ask anyone for anything.

## Source unit 981 · printed entry 982

### English candidate

Thawr ibn Tilda—also said to be Thawb, with a bāʾ. There is disagreement over its vocalization. Ibn al-Kalbī said that the latter is like thawb, the singular of thiyāb, while al-Dāraquṭnī, following al-Haytham ibn ʿAdī, vocalized the former as Thuwar, with ḍamma on the thāʾ and fatḥa on the wāw. As for his father’s name, al-Haytham and Ibn al-Kalbī gave it as Tilda, with kasra on the tāʾ and sukūn on the lām, whereas al-Dāraquṭnī gave it as Talda, with fatḥa on the tāʾ. He is also called Tulayda, in the diminutive. He belonged to Banū Wāliba ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Thaʿlaba ibn Dūdān ibn Asad ibn Khuzayma. It is also said that Tilda, or Tulayda, was his mother or a slave woman who nursed him, and that his father’s name was Rabīʿa; Sayf mentioned this in al-Futūḥ.

Abū Ḥātim al-Sijistānī included him among the long-lived and related that he appeared before Muʿāwiya, who asked, “Whom among my forefathers did you meet?” He replied, “I met Umayya ibn ʿAbd Shams after he had gone blind, with his servant Dhakwān leading him.” Muʿāwiya said, “Stop! He was in fact his son.” Thawr replied, “That is something you people have claimed.” Muʿāwiya asked, “Which of these men most resembles Umayya?” He replied, “This one,” pointing to ʿAmr ibn Saʿīd ibn al-ʿĀṣ ibn Umayya, known as al-Ashdaq.

Abū Mūsā mentioned part of this account in al-Dhayl by way of Abū Yaʿqūb al-Sarrāj, who had included Thawr among the Companions, through ʿĀṣim ibn Abī al-Najūd. ʿĀṣim said: “We—that is, Banū Asad ibn Khuzayma—were one-seventh of the Emigrants on the day of Badr, and among us was a man called Thawr ibn Tilda who reached one hundred and twenty years of age.” He then related part of the account. Abū Mūsā supposed that ʿĀṣim’s words “among us” were connected to “we were on the day of Badr,” which would make the subject one of the Badrians. This is not as he supposed. Rather, ʿĀṣim meant to enumerate his people’s distinctive merits: he first said that they amounted to one-seventh of the Emigrants, then said that this long-lived man was among them. Were the words taken in the literal manner understood by Abū Mūsā, ʿĀṣim himself would also be a Badrian because he said “we”; yet he was a young Follower whose transmissions are mostly from Followers.

Al-Dāraquṭnī transmitted in al-Muʾtalif, by way of Abū Bakr ibn ʿAyyāsh from ʿĀṣim, that Thawr ibn Tilda said, “I lived to see three Wālibas.” He said that Thawr had reached two hundred and forty years. Ibn al-Kalbī cited this verse of his:

“A man may have lived for ninety years,
all the way to two hundred—yet all of it is passing away.”

He said: “I do not know how long he lived after reciting this to Muʿāwiya.” Sayf ibn ʿUmar mentioned that he was present during the conquests, witnessed al-Qādisiyya, and recited poetry about it. Al-Marzubānī also cited poetry of his which al-Āmidī attributed to someone else, as will come under the notice of Nusayr ibn Thawr al-ʿIjlī in the letter nūn, إن شاء الله تعالى.

## Source unit 983 · printed entry 984

### English candidate

Thawr ibn Mālik al-Kindī. He lived in the time of the Prophet ﷺ and accompanied Muʿādh ibn Jabal in Yemen. Muʿādh appointed him deputy over Kinda when news reached him of the Prophet’s ﷺ death. ## Source unit 991 · printed entry 992

### English candidate

Thābit ibn Masʿūd. ʿAbdān mentioned him briefly and said that he is known only from the report of Ṣafwān ibn Muḥriz. Saʿīd ibn Yaʿqūb al-Sarrāj also mentioned him among the Companions and transmitted for him, by way of Ḥammād, from Thābit al-Bunānī, from Ṣafwān ibn Muḥriz, who said: “I was praying behind the Station, and beside me was a man from among the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ. We thought him—Thābit said—to be Ibn Masʿūd. Whenever I raised my voice in recitation, he lowered his, and I never saw a neighbor with finer neighborliness. Whenever I stumbled, he prompted me. When I finished, he entered the circumambulation; he then caught up with me, took my hand, and said, ‘The spirits are marshalled troops …’” and the rest of the report.

Abū Mūsā said in al-Dhayl: “Thus he gave it.” It is astonishing that two ḥadīth masters should concur in this error. The correct parsing is: “We think him—Thābit,” meaning al-Bunānī, “to have been Ibn Masʿūd.” Ibn Masʿūd is the second object of “we think him,” and the intended person is ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd. I say: al-Bāwardī agreed with the two of them in this, headed an entry “Thābit ibn Masʿūd,” and transmitted the report in his entry by way of Ḥammād from Thābit.

As for Abū ʿUmar, he wrote: “Thābit ibn Masʿūd. Ṣafwān ibn Muḥriz said: ‘My neighbor was a man from among the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ; I think him to have been Thābit ibn Masʿūd. I never saw better neighborliness than his,’” and he related the report. This is his wording. By deleting Thābit, the transmitter from Ṣafwān, his version requires that Ṣafwān himself be the one who supposed the man to be Ibn Masʿūd. Al-Dhahabī criticized Abū ʿUmar for that in al-Tajrīd. I say: I still hesitate about this because of Ṣafwān ibn Muḥriz, for I do not think he met Ibn Masʿūd. الله أعلم.

<div dir="rtl" lang="ar">

ثابت بن مسعود ذكره عبدان مختصرا وقال لا يعرف له ذكر الا في حديث صفوان بن محرز وذكره سعيد بن يعقوب السراج في الصحابة وأخرج له من طريق حماد عن ثابت البناني عن صفوان بن محرز قال كنت أصلي خلف المقام وإلى جنبي رجل من أصحاب النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم نحسبه ثابت بن مسعود قال وكنت إذا جهرت بالقراءة خفض صوته فلم أر جارا أحسن من جواره وكنت إذا تتعتعت فتح علي فلما انصرفت دخلت الطواف فلحقني فأخذ بيدي فقال إن الأرواح جنود مجندة الحديث قال أبو موسى في الذيل كذا أورده والعجب من حافظين كيف يتواردان على هذا الوهم فإن الصواب نحسبه ثابت وهو البناني بن مسعود فابن مسعود مفعول ثان لنحسبه والمراد به عبد الله بن مسعود قلت وقد وافقهما الباوردي على ذلك وترجم لثابت بن مسعود وأخرج الحديث في ترجمته من طريق حماد بن ثابت وأما أبو عمر فقال ثابت بن مسعود قال صفوان بن محرز كان جاري رجلا من أصحاب النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أحسبه ثابت بن مسعود فلم أر أحسن جوارا منه وذكر الخبر هذا لفظه وقد اقتضى له حذف ثابت الراوي له عن صفوان الجزم بأن الذي ظنه بن مسعود هو صفوان وقد عاب الذهبي في التجريد ذلك على أبي عمر قلت وبقي عندي فيه وقفة من جهة صفوان بن محرز لأني لا أحسبه أدرك بن مسعود فالله أعلم

## Source unit 993 · printed entry 994

### English candidate

Thābit ibn Maʿbad. A Follower who transmitted a report without a Companion link—or connected it—and it became inverted for one of its transmitters. Ibn Mandah mentioned him, explained the source of the error, and said: ʿAmr ibn Khālid transmitted from ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿAmr, from ʿAbd al-Malik ibn ʿUmayr, from a man of Kalb, from Thābit ibn Maʿbad, that a man asked the Prophet ﷺ about a woman of his people whose beauty pleased him; then the report. This is how ʿAmr gave it. ʿAlī ibn Maʿbad and others transmitted it from ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿAmr, from ʿAbd al-Malik, from Thābit ibn Saʿīd, from a man of Kalb, in this form. Ibn Mandah said: “This is correct; ʿAmr ibn Khālid inverted it.” End quotation.

In al-Bukhārī’s al-Tārīkh: “Thābit ibn Maʿbad. ʿAbd al-Malik ibn ʿUmayr transmitted from him; his report is disconnected. He is counted among the Kūfans.” Ibn Ḥibbān said among the Followers: “Thābit ibn Maʿbad, from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb; ʿAbd al-Malik transmitted from him.” Ibn Mandah said: “A Follower counted among the people of Kufa.”

## Source unit 994 · printed entry 995

### English candidate

Thābit ibn al-Mundhir ibn Ḥarām ibn ʿAmr, of Banū Mālik ibn al-Najjār ibn Aws. He witnessed Badr. This is how Ibn Mandah gave it. He then transmitted with his chain to Ibn Isḥāq, who said, while naming those of Banū Mālik ibn al-Najjār who witnessed Badr: “Ibn Aws, Thābit ibn al-Mundhir,” and mentioned him. Abū Nuʿaym objected: “This is an obvious error, for al-Najjār is the son of Thaʿlaba ibn Mālik. The correct text is what Ibrāhīm ibn Saʿd and others transmitted from Ibn Isḥāq: ‘Among Banū ʿAmr ibn Mālik ibn al-Najjār, Aws ibn Thābit ibn al-Mundhir ibn Ḥarām witnessed Badr.’” End quotation.

It is as though the copyist moved the word ibn before Aws, producing that grave error. How did it escape this imam that Thābit ibn al-Mundhir—the father of Ḥassān and his brothers—did not live to see Islam, and that al-Najjār is the forefather of the famous Anṣārī clan and is not called “al-Najjār ibn Aws”? Mūsā ibn ʿUqba correctly listed Aws ibn Thābit among the Badrians in al-Maghāzī, and several others did likewise, as already discussed in his entry.

Al-Ṭabarānī also erred in this. He wrote “Thābit ibn al-Mundhir ibn Ḥarām” and transmitted with his chain to Ibn Lahīʿa, from Abū al-Aswad, from ʿUrwa, in naming those of Banū Mālik ibn al-Najjār who witnessed Badr: “Thābit ibn al-Mundhir,” and so forth. Abū Nuʿaym claimed that the error lay with Ibn Lahīʿa. الله أعلم. A parallel error by Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr will come under the entry for Ḥāritha ibn Mālik.

## Source unit 997 · printed entry 998

### English candidate

Thābit ibn Yazīd al-Anṣārī. Al-Bāwardī and Abū Nuʿaym mentioned him among the Companions and transmitted, by way of Sharīk, from Abū Isḥāq, from ʿĀmir ibn Saʿd, who said: “I entered upon Qaraẓa ibn Kaʿb, Thābit ibn Yazīd, and Abū Masʿūd al-Anṣārī while slave girls and other things were with them. I said, ‘Do you do this when you are Companions?’ They replied, ‘Entertainment at weddings was permitted to us.’” I say: this Thābit ibn Yazīd is Ibn Wadīʿa. Whoever made them two persons erred. Abū Dāwūd al-Ṭayālisī transmitted this report in his Musnad from Shuʿba, from Abū Isḥāq, and gave the name as Thābit ibn Wadīʿa. This is the form preserved through many routes from Abū Isḥāq.

Even more remarkable is that the name Wadīʿa became corrupted for Ibn Abī Ḥātim into Wadāʿa, and he distinguished that person from Thābit ibn Yazīd ibn Wadīʿa. His exact words are: “Thābit ibn Yazīd ibn Wadāʿa, a Kūfan who had companionship. Al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib, Zayd ibn Wahb, and ʿĀmir ibn Saʿd transmitted from him.” Before that he had written “Thābit ibn Yazīd ibn Wadīʿa” and mentioned roughly the same information; and before that he had written “Thābit ibn Zayd, who had companionship, from whom ʿĀmir ibn Saʿd transmitted.” Thus he turned one man into three.

## Source unit 1016 · printed entry 1017

### English candidate

Jābir ibn Sufyān, of Banū Zurayq of al-Khazraj, confederate of Muʿammar ibn Ḥabīb al-Jumaḥī. The father of Jābir and Junāda had entered into alliance with Muʿammar and settled in Mecca. He then embraced Islam and emigrated to Abyssinia, after which he and his two sons, Jābir and Junāda, arrived in the two ships from the land of Abyssinia. Ibn Isḥāq stated this. ## Source unit 1018 · printed entry 1019

### English candidate

Jābir ibn Samura ibn Junāda ibn Jundab ibn Ḥujayr ibn Riʾāb ibn Ḥabīb ibn Suwāʾa ibn ʿĀmir ibn Ṣaʿṣaʿa al-ʿĀmirī al-Suwāʾī, a confederate of Banū Zuhra. His mother was Khālida bint Abī Waqqāṣ, sister of Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ. Both he and his father had companionship. The compilers of the Ṣaḥīḥ works transmitted reports from him. Sharīk transmitted from Simāk, from Jābir ibn Samura, who said: “I sat with the Prophet ﷺ more than one hundred times.” Al-Ṭabarānī transmitted it. In the Ṣaḥīḥ, from him: “I prayed with the Prophet ﷺ more than two thousand times.” Ibn al-Sakan said that his kunya was Abū ʿAbd Allāh; it is also said to have been Abū Khālid. He settled in Kufa and built a house there. He died while Bishr governed Iraq, in the year seventy-four. Salm ibn Junāda transmitted from his father that ʿAmr ibn Ḥurayth led the funeral prayer over him.

## Source unit 1022 · printed entry 1023

### English candidate

Jābir ibn Ṭāriq ibn Abī Ṭāriq ibn ʿAwf al-Aḥmasī—with two undotted letters—al-Bajalī. He is sometimes ascribed to his grandfather and called Jābir ibn ʿAwf; he is also called Jābir ibn Abī Ṭāriq. Al-Bukhārī said that he had companionship. His report is in al-Nasāʾī with a sound chain. Al-Baghawī said: “I know no other report of his.” Ibn al-Sakan transmitted by way of Ismāʿīl ibn Abī Khālid, from Ḥakīm ibn Jābir—who was among the people of al-Qādisiyya—from his father, and related a report. In al-Shīrāzī’s al-Alqāb it appears without the words “who was among the people of al-Qādisiyya”: a Bedouin praised the Prophet ﷺ until foam appeared at the corners of his mouth, whereupon he said: “Keep speech brief, for splitting speech into affected branches is among Satan’s bombast.”

Ibn Ḥibbān distinguished Jābir ibn Ṭāriq al-Aḥmasī from Jābir ibn ʿAwf al-Aḥmasī. Of the first he said: “He lived in Kufa and used to dye with red.” Of the second: “He had companionship and was Ḥakīm’s father.” Ibn Fatḥūn likewise added Jābir ibn Ṭāriq as a supplement to Abū ʿUmar, who had included Jābir ibn ʿAwf. All of that is error: he is one man.

## Source unit 1025 · printed entry 1026

### English candidate

Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Riʾāb ibn al-Nuʿmān ibn Sinān ibn ʿUbayd ibn ʿAdī ibn Ghanm ibn Kaʿb ibn Salama al-Anṣārī al-Sulamī, one of the six who attended the First ʿAqaba. Ibn Isḥāq said: ʿĀṣim ibn ʿUmar ibn Qatāda related to me, from elders of his people, who said: when the Prophet ﷺ met the six men of the Anṣār—Asʿad ibn Zurāra, Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Riʾāb, Quṭba ibn ʿĀmir, Rāfiʿ ibn Mālik, ʿUqba ibn ʿĀmir ibn Zayd, and ʿAwf ibn Mālik—they accepted Islam. They then mentioned the report. Mūsā ibn ʿUqba, from Ibn Shihāb, and Abū al-Aswad, from ʿUrwa, mentioned him among those who attended Badr. Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said in his biography: he has a report transmitted by al-Kalbī, from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from him; I know of no other. I say: rather, reports from Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Riʾāb have come by weak routes. Al-Baghawī, Ibn al-Sakan, and others narrated by way of al-Wāziʿ ibn Nāfiʿ, from Abū Salama, from Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Riʾāb, that the Prophet ﷺ said, 'Michael passed by me among a group of angels'—the report. Al-Baghawī said: al-Wāziʿ is extremely weak. He also said: I know of no other musnad report from Jābir. I say: rather, he has another. Al-Bukhārī mentioned in al-Tārīkh, by way of Ibn Isḥāq, from al-Kalbī, from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Riʾāb, the story of Abū Yāsir ibn Akhṭab. Yūnus ibn Bukayr narrated it in al-Maghāzī from Ibn Isḥāq, from Muḥammad ibn Abī Muḥammad, from ʿIkrima or Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbās and Jābir ibn Riʾāb: Abū Yāsir ibn Akhṭab passed by the Prophet ﷺ while he was reciting the Opening of the Book and 'Alif Lām Mīm. That is the Book, in which there is no doubt'; the source then mentions the story. It appears that Jābir was attributed to his grandfather. Ibn Shāhīn and Ibn Mardawayh likewise narrated by way of Hammām, from al-Kalbī, concerning the saying of God Most High, 'God effaces what He wills and confirms.' Al-Kalbī said, 'He effaces from provision.' I asked, 'Who related this to you?' He replied, 'Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Jābir ibn Riʾāb, from the Prophet ﷺ.'

## Source unit 1026 · printed entry 1027

### English candidate

Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr ibn Ḥarām ibn Kaʿb ibn Ghanm ibn Kaʿb ibn Salama al-Anṣārī al-Sulamī. He was variously given the kunyahs Abū ʿAbd Allāh, Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, and Abū Muḥammad. He was one of the prolific transmitters from the Prophet ﷺ, and a group of Companions narrated from him. Both he and his father had companionship. In al-Ṣaḥīḥ he reported that he was among those who attended al-ʿAqaba. Al-Bukhārī narrated in his Tārīkh, with a sound chain from Abū Sufyān, from Jābir, who said: 'I used to draw water for my companions on the Day of Badr.' By way of Ḥajjāj ibn al-Ṣawwāf, from Abū al-Zubayr, Jābir related: 'The Messenger of God ﷺ personally went on twenty-one campaigns; I attended nineteen of them.' Al-Wāqidī rejected the aforementioned narration of Abū Sufyān from Jābir. Muslim narrated by way of Zakariyyā ibn Isḥāq, from Abū al-Zubayr, who heard Jābir say: 'I went on nineteen campaigns with the Messenger of God ﷺ.' Jābir said: 'I attended neither Badr nor Uḥud; my father prevented me. After he was killed, I never stayed behind.' Jābir also said: 'The Messenger of God ﷺ asked forgiveness for me twenty-five times on the Night of the Camel.' Aḥmad and others transmitted it by way of Ḥammād ibn Salama, from Abū al-Zubayr, from him. In Wakīʿ's Muṣannaf, Hishām ibn ʿUrwa said that Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh had a teaching circle in the Prophet's Mosque from which knowledge was taken. Al-Baghawī narrated by way of ʿĀṣim ibn ʿUmar ibn Qatāda: Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh came to us after losing his sight, having touched his head and beard with some yellow dye. By way of Abū Hilāl, from Qatāda: Jābir was the last of the Messenger of God's Companions ﷺ to die in Medina. Al-Baghawī said: that is an error; the last of them was Sahl ibn Saʿd. Yaḥyā ibn Bukayr and others said that Jābir died in 78. ʿAlī ibn al-Madīnī said that Jābir died after living to an advanced age and had instructed that al-Ḥajjāj not lead his funeral prayer. I say: this agrees with al-Haytham ibn ʿAdī's statement that he died in 74. Al-Ṭabarī and al-Bukhārī's Tārīkh contain evidence for it: al-Ḥajjāj attended his funeral. It is also said that he died in 73, and it is said that he lived ninety-four years.

## Source unit 1027 · printed entry 1028

### English candidate

Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh—also said to be ibn ʿUbayd ibn Jābir—al-ʿAbdī. Aḥmad narrated the Book of Beverages, and al-Baghawī narrated from him, by way of al-Ḥārith ibn Murra, from Nufays, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jābir al-ʿAbdī, who said: 'I was among the delegation who came to the Messenger of God ﷺ from ʿAbd al-Qays, although I was not one of them; I was merely with my father. The Messenger of God ﷺ forbade them to drink from certain vessels'—the report. It also says that, after the Prophet ﷺ, he performed the pilgrimage with his father and came to al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī. He greeted him, and al-Ḥasan welcomed him. He asked al-Ḥasan about date beverage prepared in an earthenware jar, and al-Ḥasan permitted it. His father said to al-Ḥasan, 'After the Messenger of God ﷺ forbade it?' He answered, 'Yes; after your departure, he granted a concession for it.' Its chain is fair. I did not find it in Aḥmad's Musnad. Abū Nuʿaym transmitted it by way of al-Qaṭīʿī, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal, from his father. Ibn al-Athīr strangely set it out with the Musnad's chain; apparently, when he saw Abū Nuʿaym's chain, he assumed that, whereas it is actually in Aḥmad's Book of Beverages. Al-Bāwardī narrated by way of al-Naḍr ibn Shumayl, from Ḥabīb ibn Abī Juwayra al-Ṭufāwī, who said: Qays related to me, 'I set out for the pilgrimage and met a man from ʿAbd al-Qays called ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jābir. He said, I performed the pilgrimage with my father, and we took the Medina road. My father said, Shall we not stop to visit the Mother of the Believers? I said, Yes. We went up to her, and my father said to her while I listened: I was among the delegation who came from Bahrain. Did you hear the Messenger of God ﷺ state anything new about beverages after us? She replied, No.'

Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh, of the Anṣār. Abū al-Fatḥ al-Yaʿmurī mentioned him in al-Sīra al-Nabawiyya among those whom the Prophet ﷺ sent back on the Day of Uḥud.
