## Source unit 1208 · printed entry 1209

### English candidate

Junāda ibn ʿAwf ibn Umayya ibn Qalaʿ ibn ʿAbbād ibn Ḥudhayfa ibn ʿAbd ibn Fuqaym ibn ʿAdī ibn Zayd ibn ʿĀmir ibn Thaʿlaba ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Mālik ibn Kināna, Abū Thumāma al-Kinānī. Ibn Isḥāq, early in the Sīra, mentioned the pre-Islamic practice of calendrical intercalation and its hereditary officeholders, until he said: ‘Islam arose while Junāda ibn ʿAwf held the office’; he did not state that Junāda embraced Islam. Al-Suhaylī said: I found a report indicating that he did embrace Islam. He attended the pilgrimage in ʿUmar’s time and saw the people crowding around the Black Stone. He said, ‘People, I have granted it protection from you.’ ʿUmar struck him with his whip and said, ‘Woe to you! God has abolished the practices of the Age of Ignorance.’ Hishām ibn al-Kalbī related that Junāda intercalated the calendar for forty years, and said that his memory was the most enduring and his tenure the longest. Al-Zubayr said in the Book of Genealogy: The first to intercalate after al-Qalammas was Ḥudhayfa ibn ʿAbd ibn Fuqaym ibn ʿAdī—he was al-Qalammas ibn ʿĀmir ibn Thaʿlaba—then ʿAbbād ibn Ḥudhayfa, then Qalaʿ ibn ʿAbbād, then Umayya ibn Qalaʿ, then ʿAwf ibn Umayya, then Junāda, whom Islam overtook. It is said that he intercalated for forty years. Al-Zubayr also mentioned from Abū ʿUbayda that Islam arose while Abū Thumāma Junāda ibn ʿAwf held the office. Then he transmitted from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan, from Maʿmar, from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, that the first intercalator was al-Ḥārith ibn Thaʿlaba ibn Mālik ibn Kināna and the last was Abū Thumāma, here called Umayya ibn ʿAwf ibn Junāda ibn ʿAwf ibn ʿAbbād ibn Qalaʿ ibn Fuqaym ibn ʿAdī ibn ʿĀmir ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Thaʿlaba. All of these back to al-Ḥārith practiced intercalation.

### Arabic authority

<div dir="rtl" lang="ar">

جنادة بن عوف بن أمية بن قلع بن عباد بن حذيفة بن عبد بن فقيم بن عدي بن زيد بن عامر بن ثعلبة بن الحارث بن مالك بن كنانة أبو ثمامة الكناني ذكر بن إسحاق في أوائل السيرة أمر النسئ والنسأة إلى أن قال وقام الإسلام على جنادة بن عوف ولم يذكر أنه أسلم قال السهيلي وجدت له خبرا يدل على أنه أسلم فإنه حضر الحج في زمن عمر فرأى الناس يزدحمون على الحجر الأسود فقال أيها الناس إني قد أجرته منكم فخفقه عمر بالدرة وقال ويحك إن الله قد أبطل أمر الجاهلية وحكى هشام بن الكلبي أنه نسأ أربعين سنة قال وكان أبعدهم ذكرا وأطولهم أمدا وقال الزبير في كتاب النسب أول من نسأ بعد القلمس حذيفة بن عبد بن فقيم بن عدي وهو القلمس بن عامر بن ثعلبة ثم بعده عباد بن حذيفة ثم قلع بن عباد ثم أمية بن قلع ثم عوف بن أمية ثم جنادة فأدركه الإسلام يقال إنه نسأ أربعين سنة وذكر أيضا عن أبي عبيدة أن الإسلام قام على أبي ثمامة جنادة بن عوف ثم نقل عن محمد بن الحسن عن معمر عن بن أبي نجيح عن مجاهد أن أول من نسأ الحارث بن ثعلبة بن مالك بن كنانة وآخر من نسأ أبو ثمامة واسمه أمية بن عوف بن جنادة بن عوف بن عباد بن قلع بن فقيم بن عدي بن عامر بن الحارث بن ثعلبة كل هؤلاء إلى الحارث قد نسأ

Al-Muʿāfā ibn Zakariyyā mentioned in his al-Jalīs, by way of Saʿd ibn ʿĀmir, from Qābūs ibn Abī Ẓabyān, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: I saw the Messenger of God ﷺ spreading apart what was between al-Ḥusayn’s thighs and kissing his penis. Companionship has been claimed for Jundub on the first chain’s reading, where ‘from his grandfather’ refers to Abū Ẓabyān’s father; however, the better-attested alternate route makes Ibn ʿAbbās the eyewitness. ## Source unit 1218 · printed entry 1219

### English candidate

Jundub ibn Zuhayr ibn al-Harith ibn Kathir ibn Sabʿ ibn Malik al-Azdi al-Ghamidi. He is also said to have been Jundub ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Zuhayr al-Ghamidi. Ibn al-Kalbi mentioned in the Tafsir, from Abu Salih, from Ibn ʿAbbas, that when Jundub ibn Zuhayr al-Ghamidi prayed, fasted, or gave alms and it was mentioned, he took pleasure in that. Then the verse was revealed: ‘So whoever hopes to meet his Lord, let him do righteous work’—to the end of the verse. He is also mentioned in the entry on ʿUmayr ibn al-Harith al-Azdi: he came to the Prophet ﷺ in a group from his people that included Jundub ibn Zuhayr, Mikhnaf ibn Sulaym, ʿAbd Allah ibn Sulaym, Jundub ibn Kaʿb, and others. ʿAli ibn Saʿd transmitted in al-Taʿa wa-l-Maʿsiya, by way of Muqatil, from ʿIkrima, from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: A man of Azd called Jundub ibn Zuhayr al-Ghamidi stood before the Messenger of God ﷺ and said, ‘May my father and mother be your ransom! I leave your presence, but neither wealth nor child brings coolness to my eye until I return and look at you; and I shall indeed be with you amid the throngs of the Resurrection.’ He then related a long report about the terrors of the Day of Resurrection. Muqatil is weak. Ibn Saʿd transmitted with a chain of his that Jundub was with ʿAli on the Day of the Camel. Khalifa transmitted by way of ʿAli ibn Zayd, from al-Hasan, that Jundub ibn Zuhayr was with ʿAli at Siffin. Al-Mufaddal al-Ghallabi likewise mentioned him in his History, and Abu ʿUbayd said that on that day he commanded the infantry. Ibn Durayd mentioned in his Amali, with his chain to Abu ʿUbayda, from Yunus, who said: ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr had drawn us up in ranks on the Day of the Camel. A crier from among ʿAli’s companions, sounding like a sincere adviser, came out to us and said, ‘Young men of Quraysh, I warn you against two men: Jundub ibn Zuhayr al-Ghamidi and al-Ashtar. You cannot stand before their swords. As for Jundub, he is a man of medium stature who trails his coat of mail until it effaces his tracks.’ Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said: al-Zubayr mentioned that this Jundub ibn Zuhayr was the slayer of the sorcerer, but the correct view is that he was someone else. There is disagreement over Jundub ibn Zuhayr’s Companionship, and his hadith was criticized because of al-Sari ibn Ismaʿil. I say: al-Zubayr, transmitting from his uncle in Kitab al-Muwaffaqiyyat, distinguished Jundub ibn Zuhayr from Jundub ibn Kaʿb, the slayer of the sorcerer Ibn Kabsha. Ibn al-Kalbi likewise distinguished them.

## Source unit 1224 · printed entry 1225

### English candidate

Jundub ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Sufyan al-Bajali, then al-ʿAlaqi, Abu ʿAbd Allah. He is sometimes ascribed to his grandfather and called Jundub ibn Sufyan. He lived in Kufa and then Basra, which he entered with Musʿab ibn al-Zubayr. The people of both garrison towns transmitted from him. I say: Shahr ibn Hawshab, one of the people of Syria, also transmitted from him, saying, ‘Jundub ibn Sufyan told me.’ Ibn al-Sakan said: The people of Basra say ‘Jundub ibn ʿAbd Allah,’ while the people of Kufa say ‘Jundub ibn Sufyan’—except Sharik alone. He is called Jundub al-Khayr. Ibn al-Kalbi rejected that. Al-Baghawi said: He is called Jundub al-Khayr, Jundub al-Faruq, and Jundub ibn Umm Jundub. Ibn Hibban said: He is Jundub ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Sufyan, and whoever says ‘ibn Sufyan’ has ascribed him to his grandfather. It has also been said that he is Jundub ibn Khalid ibn Sufyan, but the former is sounder. Al-Tabarani related approximately the same. In al-Tabarani, by way of Abu ʿImran al-Jawni, Jundub said to him: ‘In the time of the Messenger of God ﷺ, I was a boy approaching puberty.’ In Sahih Muslim, by way of Safwan ibn Muhriz, Jundub ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Bajali sent word to ʿAsʿas ibn Salama during the civil strife of Ibn al-Zubayr: ‘Gather for me a group of your brothers.’ In al-Tabarani, by way of al-Hasan, who said: ‘I sat with Jundub during the governorship of Musʿab’—meaning Ibn al-Zubayr.

## Source unit 1226 · printed entry 1227

Jundub ibn ʿAmmar ibn Nuʿaym ibn Shihab ibn Laʾm ibn ʿAmr ibn Tarif al-Taʾi, then al-Lami. Ibn al-Kalbi gave his lineage and said that he was a poet who witnessed al-Qadisiyya. Al-Marzubani mentioned him in Muʿjam al-Shuʿaraʾ and said that he came in a delegation to the Prophet ﷺ and later witnessed al-Qadisiyya. He is the author of the lines:

The fault-finders claim that Jundub’s she-camel,
at Liwa al-Qarya, has been rubbed bare and grown weary.

The fault-finders lie. Had they seen her resting place
at al-Qadisiyya, they would have said, ‘She persisted, then submitted.’

Were a tambour struck beneath her throat
by a hoarse-voiced man, she would yearn when he sang.

## Source unit 1227 · printed entry 1228

### English candidate

Jundub ibn ʿAmr ibn Humama al-Dawsi, an ally of Banu Umayya. Musa ibn ʿUqba, from Ibn Shihab, and Abu al-Aswad, from ʿUrwa, mentioned him among the Companions killed on the Day of Ajnadayn. Ibn Mandah said: No hadith of his is known. Al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar transmitted in Kitab al-Nasab, by way of ʿAbd al-ʿAziz ibn ʿImran, from Mihriz ibn Jaʿfar, from his grandfather, who said: Jundub ibn ʿAmr ibn Humama al-Dawsi arrived as an Emigrant and then went on to Syria. He left his daughter Umm Aban in ʿUmar’s care and said, ‘If you find a suitable match for her, marry her to him, even for the strap of his sandal; otherwise keep her until you return her to the homeland of her people.’ While staying with ʿUmar she called him her father, until he married her to ʿUthman. She bore him ʿAmr ibn ʿUthman during ʿUmar’s reign. He will also be mentioned in the entry on al-Tufayl ibn ʿAmr. Ibn al-Kalbi said: He is Jundub ibn ʿAmr ibn Humama ibn al-Harith ibn Rafiʿ ibn Rabiʿa ibn Thaʿlaba ibn Luʾayy ibn ʿAmir ibn Ghanm ibn Dahman ibn Munahhib ibn Daws. His father was one of the judges of the Arabs. Ibn Durayd said: Al-Sakan ibn Saʿid told us, from Muhammad ibn ʿAbbad, from al-Sharqi, and from Mujalid, from al-Shaʿbi, who said: We were with Ibn ʿAbbas while he sat at the edge of Zamzam giving legal opinions to the people. A Bedouin stood before him and said, ‘You have given them rulings; now give us one.’ He said, ‘Present it.’ The man asked, ‘What is the meaning of the poet’s words:

For the man of judgment, before today, the staff is not struck;
and man was taught only so that he might learn?’

Ibn ʿAbbas answered: ‘That was ʿAmr ibn Humama al-Dawsi. He judged among the Arabs for three hundred years. When he grew old, they assigned to him the seventh—or the ninth—of his sons. Whenever he forgot, the son struck the staff for him. When death came to him, his people gathered around him, and he counselled them with an excellent testament containing wisdom.’

جندب بن عمرو بن حممة الدوسي حليف بني أمية ذكره موسى بن عقبة عن بن شهاب وأبو الأسود عن عروة فيمن قتل يوم أجنادين من الصحابة قال بن منده لا يعرف له حديث وروى الزبير بن بكار في كتاب النسب من طريق عبد العزيز بن عمران عن محرز بن جعفر عن جده قال قدم جندب بن عمرو بن حممة الدوسي مهاجرا ثم مضى إلى الشام وخلف ابنته أم أبان عند عمر وقال إن وجدت لها كفؤا فزوجها ولو بشراك نعله وإلا فأمسكها حتى تلحقها بدار قومها فكانت عند عمر تدعوه أباها إلى أن زوجها من عثمان فولدت له عمرو بن عثمان في عهد عمر وسيأتي له ذكر في ترجمة الطفيل بن عمرو قال بن الكلبي هو جندب بن عمرو بن حممة بن الحارث بن رافع بن ربيعة بن ثعلبة بن لؤي بن عامر بن غانم بن دهمان بن منهب بن دوس وكان أبوه من حكام العرب قال بن دريد حدثنا السكن بن سعيد عن محمد بن عباد عن الشرقي وعن مجالد الشعبي قال كنا عند بن عباس وهو في ضفة زمزم يفتي الناس إذ قام إليه أعرابي فقال أفتيتهم فأفتنا قال هات قال ما معنى قول الشاعر <br />
 لذي الحكم قبل اليوم ما تقرع العصا <br />
 وما علم الإنسان الا ليعلما فقال له بن عباس ذاك عمرو بن حممة الدوسي قضى بين العرب ثلاثمائة سنة فكبر فألزموه السابع أو التاسع من ولده فكان إذا غفل فرع له العصا فلما حضره الموت اجتمع إليه قومه فأوصاهم بوصية حسنة فيها حكم

</div>

## Source unit 1228 · printed entry 1229

### English candidate

Jundub ibn Kaʿb ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Juzʾ ibn ʿĀmir ibn Mālik ibn Dahmān al-Azdī al-Ghāmidī, Abū ʿAbd Allāh. He is sometimes ascribed to his grandfather. He is Jundub al-Khayr, the man who killed the sorcerer. He was discussed earlier in the notice of Jundub ibn Zuhayr. Ibn Ḥibbān said: “Jundub ibn Kaʿb al-Azdī had Companionship.” Abū Ḥātim said: “Jundub ibn Kaʿb, the killer of the sorcerer; he is also called Jundub ibn Zuhayr,” thus making them one person. Ibn Saʿd transmitted from Hishām ibn al-Kalbī: Lūṭ ibn Yaḥyā told us that the Prophet ﷺ wrote to Abū Ẓabyān al-Azdī of Ghāmid, inviting him and his people. He responded with a group of his people, among them Mikhnaf, ʿAbd Allāh and Zuhayr the sons of Sulaym, and ʿAbd Shams ibn ʿAfīf ibn Zuhayr. These came to him in Mecca. Jundub ibn Zuhayr, Jundub ibn Kaʿb, and al-Ḥajar ibn al-Muraqqaʿ came to him in Medina. Later, al-Ḥakam ibn Mughafal came with the forty. Al-Bukhārī transmitted in his History, by way of Khālid al-Ḥadhdhāʾ from Abū ʿUthmān, who said: There was a man in al-Walīd’s presence performing tricks. He slaughtered a person and severed his head. We were astonished; then he restored his head. Jundub al-Azdī came and killed him. By way of ʿĀṣim from Abū ʿUthmān, it says that Jundub ibn Kaʿb killed him. Al-Bayhaqī transmitted in al-Dalāʾil, by way of Ibn Wahb, from Ibn Lahīʿa, from Abū al-Aswad, that al-Walīd ibn ʿUqba was governor of Iraq and a sorcerer performed before him. He would strike off a man’s head, then cry out to him; the man would stand outside while his head returned to him. The people said, “Glory be to God! He gives life to the dead!” A righteous man among the Emigrants saw him and watched. The next day he wrapped his sword beneath his clothes. The sorcerer began the same performance; the man drew his sword, struck off the sorcerer’s head, and said, “If he is truthful, let him revive himself.” Al-Walīd ordered that the man be imprisoned. The jailer was called Dīnār and was righteous. He admired the man’s conduct and told him, “Go. May God never question me about you.” Another route from Burayda will come in the notice of Zayd ibn Ṣūḥān. Ibn al-Kalbī said that the sorcerer was named Bustānī. In al-Istīʿāb he is Abū Bustān. Ṣāʿid the lexicographer said in al-Fuṣūṣ that his name was Baṭrūnā. Ibn al-Sakan transmitted, by way of Yaḥyā ibn Kathīr, the associate of al-Baṣrī: My father told me; al-Jurayrī told us, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Burayda, from his father, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ traveled at night with his Companions and kept saying, “Jundub—and what a Jundub!” until morning. His Companions said to Abū Bakr, “He has uttered two words whose meaning we do not know.” Abū Bakr asked him, and he said, “He will strike one blow and thereby become a nation unto himself.” He said: When ʿUthmān became caliph, he appointed al-Walīd ibn ʿUqba over Kufa. Al-Walīd seated a man who practiced sorcery and showed them that he could give life and cause death. He then related the story of Jundub killing him. The matter was referred to ʿUthmān, who told Jundub, “You have brandished a sword in Islam. Were it not for what I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say about you, I would strike you with the finest sword in Medina.” He ordered Jundub sent to Jabal al-Dukhān. In al-Istīʿāb, by another route, Jundub’s nephew struck the jailer and released his uncle from prison. He said concerning that:

“Is Jundub imprisoned for striking down the sorcerer,
while the earliest Companions of the Prophet are killed?”

Al-Tirmidhī transmitted by way of al-Ḥasan from Jundub ibn Kaʿb, who said: “The prescribed punishment for a sorcerer is a stroke with the sword.” Al-Tirmidhī judged it more likely to be a stopped report. Al-Ṭabarānī included the report about the sorcerer’s punishment in the notice of Jundub ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Bajalī, but the correct view is that he is someone else. Ibn Qāniʿ and al-Ḥasan ibn Sufyān transmitted it by two routes from al-Ḥasan, from Jundub al-Khayr: he came to a sorcerer and struck him with the sword until he died, saying, “I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say”—then he cited it.

وما جندب حتى أصبح فقال أصحابه لأبي بكر لقد لقظ بكلمتين ما ندري ما هما فسأله فقال يضرب ضربة فيكون أمة وحده قال فلما ولي عثمان ولي الوليد بن عقبة الكوفة فأجلس رجلا يسحر يريهم أنه يحيي ويميت فذكر قصة  ويقتل أصحاب النبي الأوائل وروى الترمذي من طريق الحسن عن جندب بن كعب قال حد الساحر ضربه بالسيف ورجح أنه موقوف أخرج الطبراني حديث حد الساحر في ترجمة جندب بن عبد الله البجلي والصواب أنه غيره وقد رواه بن قانع والحسن بن سفيان من وجهين عن الحسن عن جندب الخير أنه جاء إلى ساحر فضربه بالسيف حتى مات وقال سمعت رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يقول فذكره

## Source unit 1229 · printed entry 1230

### English candidate

Jundub ibn Makīth—his first letter is open, and his final letter is a three-dotted thāʾ—ibn ʿAmr ibn Jarād ibn Yarbūʿ ibn Ṭuḥayl ibn ʿAdī ibn al-Rabʿa ibn Rushdān al-Juhanī, brother of Rāfiʿ ibn Makīth. Ibn Saʿd said that the Messenger of God ﷺ appointed him over the alms of Juhayna. Al-Baghawī transmitted, by way of Ibn Isḥāq from Yaʿqūb ibn ʿUtba, from Muslim ibn ʿAbd Allāh, from Jundub ibn Makīth, who said: “The Messenger of God ﷺ dispatched Ghālib al-Laythī with a raiding party, and I was among them.” He then related the story at length. Al-ʿAskarī said that he is Jundub ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Makīth, ascribed to his grandfather. Others distinguished the two, making the second a nephew of the first; Ibn al-Athīr preferred that view. Yet some routes of the report cited by Ibn Isḥāq, as transmitted by al-Ṭabarānī, read “from Jundub ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Juhanī.”

## Source unit 1231 · printed entry 1232

### English candidate

Jundub ibn al-Nuʿmān al-Azdī, Abū ʿAzīz. Ibn ʿAsākir said in his History: I read in the book of Abū al-Ḥasan al-Rāzī: Abū Naṣr Ẓafar ibn Muḥammad ibn Ẓafar ibn ʿUmar ibn Ḥafṣ ibn ʿUmar ibn Saʿīd ibn Abī ʿAzīz al-Azdī told me: I heard my father relate from his father Ẓafar, from his father ʿUmar, from his father Ḥafṣ, from his father ʿUmar, from his father Saʿīd ibn Abī ʿAzīz, who said: Abū ʿAzīz Jundub ibn al-Nuʿmān al-Azdī came to the Prophet ﷺ, embraced Islam, and practiced Islam well. The Prophet made him the representative of his people. He then migrated to Syria during the caliphate of ʿUmar, settled in Damascus, and his house became known as Dār al-Nakhla. He was buried there, as were his son Saʿīd and his son ʿUmar ibn Saʿīd. Then Ḥafṣ ibn ʿUmar ibn Saʿīd moved to Zamalkā and settled there. Its chain is singular; I know of no mention of its transmitters except in this report. Abū ʿUmar mentioned him briefly among the kunyās, but said “Abū ʿAzīz ibn Jundub”; he then said it is also reported that he was Jundub.

## Source unit 1234 · printed entry 1235

### English candidate

Jundaʿ ibn Ḍamra ibn Abī al-ʿĀṣ al-Jundaʿī al-Ḍamrī, or al-Laythī. Ibn Isḥāq said in the Sīra, from Yazīd ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Qusayṭ, from men of his people, who said: When the Prophet ﷺ migrated to Medina, Jundaʿ ibn Ḍamra ibn Abī al-ʿĀṣ was a Muslim man who found the delay too long. He then related the report containing Jundaʿ’s words to his sons, “Take me out of Mecca.” He departed as an emigrant but died on the road. God then revealed concerning him: “Whoever leaves his home as an emigrant to God and His Messenger...” [Qurʾan 4:100]. This is the well-known version from Ibn Isḥāq. Ḥammād ibn Salama transmitted it from Ibn Isḥāq as “Jundub ibn Ḍamra,” and al-Wāqidī stated that form decisively. Ibn Mandah transmitted, by way of Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh, from Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna, from Ibn Ṭāwūs, from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: “A man of Banū Layth named Jundub ibn Ḍamra”—then he related it. Abū Yaʿlā and Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted, by way of Ashʿath from ʿIkrima, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: “Ḍamra ibn Jundub departed.” Ibn Mandah transmitted by way of al-Ḥakam ibn Abān from ʿIkrima, from Ibn ʿAbbās, as “Ḍamra, or Ibn Ḍamra.” Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted it by that route as “Ḍamra,” without uncertainty. Al-Fākihī transmitted by way of Ibn Jurayj: “Jundub ibn Ḍamra.” He said that a client of Ibn ʿAbbās said “Ḍamra.” By way of Ibn ʿUyayna, from ʿAmr ibn Dīnār, from ʿIkrima, it says “a man of Banū Bakr,” and then gives the report. Ibn ʿUyayna said: “It reached us that he was Ḍamra ibn Jundub.” Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: “Ḍamra ibn al-ʿĪṣ,” and he is also reported as saying “Abū Ḍamra ibn al-ʿĪṣ.” والله أعلم. Al-Balādhurī and al-Sarrāj transmitted, by way of Abū Bishr, from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, who said: “A man of Khuzāʿa called Ḍamra ibn al-ʿĪṣ, or al-ʿĪṣ ibn Ḍamra ibn Zanbāʿ.” Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmitted by way of Sālim al-Afṭas from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr: “Abū Ḍamra ibn al-ʿĪṣ departed.” ʿAbd al-Ghanī ibn Saʿīd al-Thaqafī transmitted in his Tafsīr, by way of ʿAṭāʾ and al-Ḍaḥḥāk from Ibn ʿAbbās: “Ḍamḍam ibn ʿAmr departed.” Another transmitter said “Ḍamra ibn ʿAmr.” Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr mentioned him by the previously cited route of Ashʿath as “Ḍamra ibn Jundub”; he is also called Ibn Ḥabīb and Ibn Anas. Al-Wāqidī mentioned, by way of ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī from Ibn ʿAbbās, that he said: “Ḥabīb ibn Ḍamra.”

## Source unit 1235 · printed entry 1236

### English candidate

Jundaʿ al-Anṣārī al-Awsī. Ḥammād ibn Salama transmitted from Thābit, from an unnamed son of ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Nawfal, from his father, from Jundaʿ al-Anṣārī, who said: I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say, “Whoever deliberately lies about me, let him take his seat in the Fire.” Abū Nuʿaym transmitted it. Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said that Ḥāritha ibn Nawfal narrated from Jundaʿ; that is what he said. Ibn al-Jawzī went far astray by giving him, in the introduction to al-Mawḍūʿāt, a notice as Jundaʿ ibn Ḍamra. It appears that he followed Ibn Mandah in that, for Ibn Mandah conflated him with the preceding man. This is an error: the preceding man died during the lifetime of the Messenger of God ﷺ, as stated above, and did not live long enough to transmit. Jundaʿ is also mentioned in the notice of Judjud.

## Source unit 1237 · printed entry 1238

### English candidate

Jandal, also called Jandala ibn Naḍla ibn ʿAmr ibn Bahdala. His report is among the signs of prophethood—a fair report; this is how Abū ʿUmar put it in abridged form. Abū Saʿd al-Naysābūrī transmitted in Sharaf al-Muṣṭafā that he came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: “O Messenger of God, I was a poet who composed rajaz, and I had a companion from among the jinn. He came upon me suddenly and said:

‘Arise! The lamp of religion has appeared
in a truthful, refined, trustworthy man.
Set out on a trusty she-camel
that walks over level plains and rugged ground.’

I awoke terrified and said, ‘What did he say? By the One who levels the earth and imposes the obligations, Muḥammad has indeed been sent through length and breadth. He arose amid the great sanctities and migrated to secure Tayba.’” He said: “So I journeyed, and suddenly an unseen caller was saying:

‘O rider urging his mount
toward the Messenger, you have indeed been guided aright.’

It was my companion from the jinn.” He related the story until he said: “The Prophet ﷺ presented Islam to him, and he accepted Islam.”

## Source unit 1246 · printed entry 1247

### English candidate

Jahjāh ibn Saʿīd, also said to be ibn Qays and also ibn Masʿūd, al-Ghifārī. He witnessed the Pledge of al-Riḍwān at al-Ḥudaybiyya. The Two Shaykhs transmitted from Jābir: “We were on the expedition of Banū al-Muṣṭaliq when a man of the Emigrants struck a man of the Helpers from behind”—the report concerning the revelation of God Most High’s saying, “The mightier will surely expel the humbler from it” [Qur’an 63:8]. Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr stated that the Emigrant was Jahjāh and the Helper was Sinān. Al-Wāqidī mentioned that he witnessed the expedition of al-Muraysīʿ and that he and Sinān ibn Wabra quarreled until they called their respective tribal groups to their aid. Jahjāh was a hired man of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb. He related the story. He was mentioned earlier in the notice of Juʿāl.

Ibn Abī Shayba transmitted by way of ʿUbayd al-Agharr, from ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasār, from Jahjāh al-Ghifārī, that he arrived with a group of his people who intended to accept Islam. They attended the sunset prayer with the Messenger of God ﷺ. When he had given the salutation, he said, “Let each man among you take the hand of the man sitting beside him.” He then related the report that, before Jahjāh accepted Islam, he drank the milk yields of seven ewes, whereas after he accepted Islam he could not finish the milk yield of a single ewe. The report is rare; Mūsā ibn ʿUbayda alone transmitted it from ʿUbayd. Al-Tirmidhī alluded to it under the chapter heading.

Jahjāh lived into the caliphate of ʿUthmān. Al-Bāwardī transmitted by way of al-Walīd ibn Muslim, from Mālik and others, from Nāfiʿ, from Ibn ʿUmar, who said: Jahjāh al-Ghifārī came up to ʿUthmān while he was on the pulpit, took his staff, and broke it. Before a full year had elapsed with Jahjāh still alive, God sent a consuming lesion into his hand, and he died of it. Ibn al-Sakan transmitted the same by way of Sulaymān ibn Bilāl and ʿAbd Allāh ibn Idrīs, from ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿUmar, from Nāfiʿ, from Ibn ʿUmar. He also transmitted by way of Fulayḥ ibn Sulaymān, from his paternal aunt, from her father and her paternal uncle, that those two had been present with ʿUthmān. He said: Jahjāh ibn Saʿīd al-Ghifārī went up to him, took the staff from his hand, placed it across his knee, and broke it. The people shouted at him, and ʿUthmān came down and entered his house. God smote the Ghifārī in his knee, and a year had not elapsed before he died. We have transmitted it in al-Muḥāmaliyyāt by way of Ḥammād ibn Zayd, from Yazīd ibn Ḥāzim, from Sulaymān ibn Yasār, with a report about Jahjāh al-Ghifārī similar to the first. Ibn al-Sakan said: “He died less than a year after ʿUthmān.”

## Source unit 1247 · printed entry 1248

### English candidate

Jahr, Abū ʿAbd Allāh, without a lineage given. Al-Ṭabarānī and Ibn Qāniʿ transmitted from a single shaykh, by way of ʿUthmān ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Waqqāṣī, from al-Zuhrī, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jahr, from his father Jahr, who said: “I recited behind the Prophet ﷺ, and he said, ‘Jahr, let your Lord hear you, but do not let me hear you.’” Al-Ṭabarānī transmitted it under the letter jīm and said “from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jahr.” Ibn Qāniʿ transmitted it under the letter ḥāʾ and said “from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ḥajar.” Abū Aḥmad al-ʿAskarī transmitted it by a route from al-Waqqāṣī and said “from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jābir.” These are three versions, of which the first is the strongest.

I read in Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr’s hand, in a marginal note on Ibn al-Sakan’s book: “Among those whom Ibn al-Sakan did not mention is Jahr. He related to us…” He then gave his chain by another route to ʿUthmān ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Makhzūmī—namely, the aforementioned al-Waqqāṣī—with the same report. He said: “No report is transmitted from Jahr other than this one.” I say: al-Waqqāṣī is weak.

Al-Nuʿmān ibn Rāshid contradicted him, transmitting it from al-Zuhrī, from Abū Salama, from Abū Hurayra, who said: The Prophet ﷺ heard ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ḥudhāfa praying and reciting aloud during the day, so he said, “ʿAbd Allāh, let God hear you, but do not let us hear you.” Aḥmad, Ibn Abī Khaythama, and al-Ḥākim Abū Aḥmad transmitted it in al-Kunā. We heard it with a short chain in the fourth part of the hadith collection of Abū Jaʿfar ibn al-Bakhtarī, by this route.

## Source unit 1248 · printed entry 1249

### English candidate

Jahm ibn Qutham al-ʿAbdī. He is mentioned in the notice of Maṭar ibn Hilāl al-ʿAnazī, in the report of al-Zāriʿ that he came as a delegate to the Prophet ﷺ with Jahm ibn Qutham. Abū ʿUmar al-Kindī mentioned that the Prophet ﷺ gave Māriya’s sister to Jahm al-ʿAbdī, and she bore him Zakariyyā ibn Jahm. Ibn Zūlāq said: “The well-known account is that he gave her to Ḥassān.”

I say: Abū ʿUmar al-Kindī took what he mentioned from Ibn Isḥāq’s Maghāzī. Ibn Isḥāq said there: al-Zuhrī related to me, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAbd al-Qārī, that the Messenger of God ﷺ sent Ḥāṭib ibn Abī Baltaʿa to al-Muqawqis. He related the story, which includes: “He presented him with two slave women. One of them was the mother of Ibrāhīm; as for the other, he gave her to Jahm ibn Qutham al-ʿAbdī. She was the mother of Zakariyyā ibn Jahm, who served as deputy to ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ.”

Al-Bayhaqī transmitted in al-Dalāʾil by way of Abū Bishr al-Dūlābī, then through the transmission of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam, from his father, from Yaḥyā ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ḥāṭib, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: “The Messenger of God ﷺ sent me to al-Muqawqis.” He related the story, which includes: “He presented three slave women.” In this report, however, he said: “He gave one of them to Abū Jahm ibn Ḥudhayfa.”

## Source unit 1249 · printed entry 1250

## Source unit 1252 · printed entry 1253

### English candidate

Jahm, without a lineage given. Ibn Abī Gharza transmitted in his Musnad by way of Layth, from Mujāhid, from Abū Wāʾil, that Dhū al-Kalāʿ claimed that he heard Jahm say: “I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say, ‘Al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥusayn are the two leaders of the youths of Paradise.’” Its chain is weak. ## Source unit 1255 · printed entry 1256

### English candidate

Juhayish—ending in a dotted consonant—in the diminutive form. It is also said with the first letter bearing fatḥa, the hāʾ bearing kasra, and the yāʾ quiescent; and it is also said with the first letter bearing fatḥa and the hāʾ quiescent, followed by a bāʾ. Ibn al-Amīn ibn Uways al-Nakhaʿī was categorical about this last form.

Ibn Mandah transmitted by way of ʿAmmār ibn ʿAbd al-Jabbār, from Ibn al-Mubārak, from al-Awzāʿī, from Yaḥyā ibn Abī Salama, from Abū Hurayra, who said: Juhayish ibn Uways al-Nakhaʿī came to the Messenger of God ﷺ with a group of his companions from Madhḥij. They said, “O Messenger of God, we are a clan of Madhḥij.” He then related a long report that contains poetry, including:

“O Messenger of God, you are confirmed as truthful;
blessed are you as one rightly guided, and blessed as a guide.
You laid down for us the upright monotheistic faith, after
we had worshipped false gods like asses.”

Al-Khaṭṭābī included the report in full in Gharīb al-Ḥadīth and explained its obscure expressions.

Ibn Saʿd said in al-Ṭabaqāt, in the section on the delegation of al-Nakhaʿ: Hishām ibn Muḥammad ibn al-Sāʾib al-Kalbī related to us, from his father, from the elders of al-Nakhaʿ, who said: Al-Nakhaʿ sent two of their men to the Prophet ﷺ as delegates announcing their acceptance of Islam: Arṭāh ibn Shuraḥbīl ibn Kaʿb and al-Juhayish, whose name was al-Arqam, of the Banū Bakr ibn ʿAmr ibn ʿAwf ibn al-Nakhaʿ. They set out until they came to the Messenger of God ﷺ. He presented Islam to them; they accepted it and pledged allegiance to him on behalf of their people. The Messenger of God ﷺ admired their bearing and their fine appearance. He asked, “Have you left behind among your people any who are like you?” They replied, “O Messenger of God, we have left behind among our people seventy men, every one of whom is better than us. Every one of them decides matters and sees affairs through; none of them lets us share in a matter when it arises.” The Messenger of God ﷺ supplicated good for the two of them and for their people, and said, “O God, bless al-Nakhaʿ.” He gave Arṭāh a banner, and then the source related his story.

Al-Dhahabī said in al-Tajrīd: “He is said to be al-Khuzāʿī. He is mentioned in a report that seems fabricated.”

## Source unit 1257 · printed entry 1258

Juhaym ibn al-Ṣalt ibn Makhrama ibn al-Muṭṭalib ibn ʿAbd Manāf al-Muṭṭalibī. Ibn Saʿd said: “He accepted Islam after the Conquest, and I know of no transmission from him.” Al-Balādhurī said the same and added that he learned writing in the pre-Islamic period; Islam came while he already wrote, and he wrote for the Messenger of God ﷺ. Ibn Isḥāq said in al-Maghāzī: When the Messenger of God ﷺ reached Tabūk, Yuḥanna ibn Ruʾba came to him. He concluded a treaty with him, and the Messenger of God ﷺ wrote him a document that remains in their possession. At its end is: “Written by Juhaym ibn al-Ṣalt.”

He is also the man who, during the days of Badr, saw a man on horseback saying, “ʿUtba and Shayba, the two sons of Rabīʿa, have been killed.” He then related the story. At its end Abū Jahl said, “And this is a prophet from the Banū ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib!”

The author of al-Tārīkh al-Ṣamādiḥī said: “Al-Zubayr and Juhaym ibn al-Ṣalt used to record the property collected as alms.”

## Source unit 1260 · printed entry 1261

### English candidate

Jawdan al-ʿAbdi, without a recorded lineage. Ibn Shahin transmitted by way of Shuʿayb ibn Safwan, from ʿAtaʾ ibn al-Saʾib, from al-Ashʿath ibn ʿUmayr, from Jawdan, who said: The delegation of ʿAbd al-Qays came to the Messenger of God ﷺ and asked him about drinks—the hadith. Ibn Mandah said: ʿAtaʾ ibn al-Saʾib transmitted it from his father, from Jawdan. Ibn Hibban transmitted in Rawdat al-ʿUqalaʾ by way of Wakiʿ, from Sufyan, from Ibn Jurayj, from al-ʿAbbas ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Mina, from Jawdan, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: ‘Whoever apologizes to his brother and his apology is not accepted bears the equivalent of the sin of an unjust toll collector.’ Ibn Hibban said: If Ibn Jurayj heard it, it is a fair, rare report. Ibn Majah and al-Tabarani transmitted it by this route. Abu Dawud transmitted it in al-Marasil from Sahl ibn Salih, from Wakiʿ, but said: from Ibn Jawdan, from his father. Ibn Abi Hatim said: I asked my father about him, and he said, ‘Jawdan is unknown and had no Companionship.’ End quotation. ## Source unit 1266 · printed entry 1267

### English candidate

Jaʿda ibn Hubayra ibn Abi Wahb ibn Wahb ibn ʿAmr ibn ʿAʾidh ibn ʿImran ibn Makhzum, al-Qurashi al-Makhzumi. His mother was Umm Haniʾ bint Abi Talib. He was born during the lifetime of the Prophet ﷺ and transmitted reports directly from him without stating an intermediary. ʿAli appointed him governor of Khurasan. Ibn Mandah said: His Companionship is disputed. Al-Bukhari said: He had Companionship. Al-Azdi and others listed him among those from whom only one Companion transmitted. Al-Hakim said in his History: It is said that he saw the Prophet. Ibn Hibban said: I know nothing sound concerning his Companionship upon which I can rely. Al-Baghawi said: He was born during the lifetime of the Prophet ﷺ but did not have Companionship. Ibn al-Sakan said approximately the same. Al-Ajurri said: I asked Abu Dawud, ‘Did Jaʿda ibn Hubayra see the Prophet?’ He answered, ‘He heard nothing from the Prophet ﷺ.’ I say: As for his having seen him, that is certain, because he was born during the lifetime of the Prophet ﷺ, was the son of his paternal cousin, and Umm Haniʾ’s special closeness to the Prophet ﷺ is well known. Al-Tabarani transmitted by way of Ibn Jurayj, from Abu al-Zubayr, who reported from Mujahid, who reported from Jaʿda ibn Hubayra, who said: ‘The Messenger of God ﷺ forbade me to wear a gold ring’—the hadith. Al-Hafiz al-Diyaʾ included it in al-Mukhtara by way of al-Tabarani because al-Bawardi had transmitted it from al-Tabarani’s shaykh, with the same chain, from Jaʿda, but there Jaʿda said: ‘My maternal uncle ʿAli forbade me’—and he related the report. The hadith is well known through ʿAli by another route in the Sahih. Al-Tabarani included another hadith under the entry for an otherwise unidentified Jaʿda ibn Hubayra, which says: ‘A slave belonging to Banu ʿAbd al-Muttalib who prayed and did not sleep was mentioned in the presence of the Prophet ﷺ’—the hadith. It is disconnected. Al-Bukhari and others said: Jaʿda died during the caliphate of Muʿawiya. I say: It will be stated in the entry on Umm Haniʾ that he encountered the Prophet ﷺ. Were that established, it would invalidate the statement of those who denied his Companionship. I have already indicated this in the first section.

## Source unit 1273 · printed entry 1274

### English candidate

Al-Jabban, without a recorded lineage. He was nicknamed ‘the Coward’ because of his bravery, and I do not know his personal name. He witnessed the conquest of Tustar with Abu Musa and lived into the Islamic period. Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shayba said: Qurad Abu Nuh told us: ʿUthman ibn Muʿawiya al-Qurashi told us, from his father, from ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakra, who said: When Abu Musa encamped with the army against al-Hurmuzan at Tustar—then he related the story. In it, Mujazzaʾa ibn Thawr entered from the water channel into the city with three hundred men, but only eighty-six men came safely through it. He said to them, ‘I shall not go back until I have brought in those of you who remain.’ A man of Kufa called al-Jabban—so called because of his courage—said to him, ‘Someone other than you should do this, Mujazzaʾa. You are responsible only for yourself, so proceed with what you were ordered to do.’ He answered, ‘You are right.’ Mujazzaʾa proceeded with them to the gate and stationed them there. He then went with a detachment to the wall. A non-Arab soldier from the Persian cavalry descended against him and stabbed Mujazzaʾa, incapacitating him. Mujazzaʾa told the men, ‘Proceed to your commander; let nothing distract you.’ They threw a saddlecloth over him so that they would know his location and went on. The Muslims became numerous upon the wall and opened the gate. Abu Musa came forward—then he related the remainder of the hadith.

## Source unit 1275 · printed entry 1276

Jubayr ibn Nufayr—with nun and faʾ, in the diminutive—ibn Malik ibn ʿAmir al-Hadrami, Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman. He is well known as one of the senior Successors, and his father had Companionship. Al-Bawardi and Ibn al-Sakan transmitted by way of ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Jubayr ibn Nufayr, from his father Jubayr, who transmitted from his own father Nufayr: ‘I lived through the pre-Islamic period. I say: He erred in that. Its cause was that the report reached him in a version saying that Jubayr ibn Nufayr came in a delegation to the Prophet ﷺ. The correct form is ‘from Jubayr ibn Nufayr, from his father,’ as will appear.

## Source unit 1276 · printed entry 1277

### English candidate

Jadd Jumayra—with two jīms; he is also called Kharkhusra, with two dotted consonants and an unpointed sīn—the Persian. He was Bādhān’s envoy to the Prophet ﷺ at Khosrow’s command, and he later accepted Islam. Abū Saʿīd al-Naysābūrī related in The Nobility of al-Muṣṭafā, by way of Ibn Isḥāq, from al-Zuhrī, from Abū Salama ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, who said: When the letter of the Messenger of God ﷺ reached Khosrow, he read it and tore it up. He then wrote to Bādhān, his governor in Yemen: ‘Send to me two robust men from your service to bring this man in the Ḥijāz to me.’ Bādhān sent his steward, Abānūh, who was a scribe and accountant in the Persian script, and with him he sent a Persian man called Jadd Jumayra. He gave the two of them a letter to the Messenger of God ﷺ commanding him to proceed with them to Khosrow. He told his steward, ‘Observe the man and what he is, speak to him, and bring me news of him.’ They set out until they reached al-Ṭāʾif, where they found some Qurayshī merchants. They asked them about him, and they replied, ‘He is in Yathrib.’ The merchants rejoiced and said, ‘Khosrow has now set himself against him; you have been spared the man.’ The two then set out until they reached Medina. Abānūh spoke to him and said, ‘Khosrow has written to Bādhān ordering him to send someone to bring you to him, and he has sent me so that you will depart with me.’ He said, ‘Go back, and come to me tomorrow.’ When they came to him the next morning, the Messenger of God ﷺ informed them that God had killed Khosrow and had given his son Shīrawayh power over him on such-and-such a night of such-and-such a month. They said, ‘Do you know what you are saying? Shall we write this to Bādhān?’ He said, ‘Yes. Tell him also: If you accept Islam, I shall grant you what is under your authority.’ Then he gave Jadd Jumayra a belt that had been presented to him, containing gold and silver. They returned to Bādhān and told him. He said, ‘By God, these are not the words of a king. Let us wait and see what he said.’ Before long, a letter from Shīrawayh reached him: ‘To proceed: I killed Khosrow out of anger for Persia, because he had deemed lawful the killing of its nobles. Take for me the obedience of those under your authority, and do not harass the man concerning whom Khosrow wrote to you in any way.’ When Bādhān read it, he said, ‘This man is surely a messenger-prophet.’ He accepted Islam, and all the Abnāʾ descended from the Persians who were in Yemen accepted Islam. Abū Nuʿaym al-Aṣbahānī likewise related it in The Proofs, from Ibn Isḥāq without an isnād, but he called the subject Kharkhusra and agreed in naming his companion Abānūh.

## Source unit 1284 · printed entry 1285

### English candidate

Jurayba—with a jīm and a bāʾ, in the diminutive—ibn al-Ashaym ibn ʿAmr ibn Wahb ibn Dithār ibn Fuqʿus, al-Asadī and then al-Fuqʿusī. Al-Āmidī said: He was one of the devils of Banū Asad and one of their poets in the pre-Islamic period; then he accepted Islam and said:

I was given one religion in place of another long-established;
as for religion, I had been as though in a dream.
O Sustainer of religion, make us upright and we shall be upright;
if I encounter a sinful act, I shall not go near it.

Al-Marzubānī said that he was pre-Islamic and that he said:

A ransom for the marked horsemen,
beneath the battle dust, are my maternal and paternal uncles.
We challenged them, ‘Come down and fight!’ but they did not come;
and the challenge ‘Come down and fight!’ was to them a fortress.

Ibn al-Kalbī mentioned him but added nothing beyond describing him as a poet. His lineage back to Fuqʿus will come by a route exactly as it appears here.

## Source unit 1288 · printed entry 1289

### English candidate

Jushaysh al-Daylamī—with two dotted consonants after the jīm, in the diminutive; al-Dāraquṭnī recorded its vocalization. He was among those who assisted in killing al-Aswad the Liar. Al-Ṭabarī mentioned him, and Ibn Fatḥūn added him as an omission. In Sayf’s Book of the Ridda, the Prophet ﷺ sent to the family of Jushaysh, to Dādhawayh, and to Fayrūz, ordering them to fight al-Aswad al-ʿAnsī. He transmitted it by two routes from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said that the envoy charged with that was Wabra ibn Yuḥannis. Al-Wāqidī likewise mentioned it in The Ridda, in a report from Hammām ibn Munabbih. Sayf also said: al-Mustanīr ibn Yazīd related to us, from ʿUrwa ibn Ghaziya al-Duthaynī, from al-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Fayrūz, from Jushaysh al-Daylamī, who said: ‘Wabra ibn Yuḥannis came to us with a letter of the Prophet ﷺ ordering us in it to remain steadfast in our religion, rise to war, and take action against al-Aswad the Liar.’ He then related at length the story of their killing al-Aswad. At its end he said: ‘Then I proclaimed the call to prayer and threw his head down to them. Wabra gave the signal for the prayer, and then we launched the raid. We wrote the news to the Prophet ﷺ while he was alive, although revelation had reached him that very night and he had informed his Companions of it. Our messengers arrived after his death before Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, and he was the one who answered our letters.’ End. It will come in the notice of Dādhawayh that he was one of those who assisted in killing al-Aswad.

### Arabic authority

<div dir="rtl" lang="ar">

جشيش الديلمي بمعجمتين بعد الجيم مصغرا قيده الدارقطني كان ممن أعان على قتل الأسود الكذاب ذكره الطبري واستدركه بن فتحون وفي كتاب الردة لسيف بعث النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم آل جشيش وإلى داذويه وإلى فيروز يأمرهم بمحاربة الأسود العنسي أخرجه من وجهين عن بن عباس قال وكان الرسول بذلك وبرة بن يحنس وكذا ذكره الواقدي في الردة من رواية همام بن منبه وقال سيف أيضا حدثنا المستنير بن يزيد عن عروة بن غزية الدثيني عن الضحاك بن فيروز عن جشيش الديلمي قال قدم علينا وبرة بن يحنس بكتاب النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم الله وسلم يأمرنا فيه بالقيام على ديننا والنهوض في الحرب والعمل على الأسود الكذاب فذكر قصة قتلهم الأسود بطولها وفي آخرها ثم ناديت بالأذان وألقيت إليهم رأسه وأقام وبرة الصلاة ثم شننا الغارة وكتبنا إلى النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم بالخبر وهو حي قد أتاه الوحي من ليلته وأخبر أصحابه بذلك وقدمت رسلنا بعده على أبي بكر الصديق فهو الذي أجابنا على كتبنا انتهى وسيأتي في ترجمة داذويه أنه من جملة من أعان على قتل الأسود

## Source unit 1290 · printed entry 1291

### English candidate

Jaʿda al-Sulamī. He lived through the pre-Islamic period and has a story in Medina during ʿUmar’s time. Al-Āmidī mentioned him and said: He was amorous, a companion of women; he would converse with them, make them laugh, and joke with them, so they would gather at his place. He would take a woman and hobble her legs, then order her to walk. She would trip and fall, becoming exposed, and they would laugh together at that. News of this reached Buqayla al-Ashjaʿī while he was campaigning during ʿUmar’s reign, so he wrote to him:

Carry a message to Abū Ḥafṣ—
from a trustworthy brother: my waist-wrapper is your ransom.
Our young she-camels—may God guide you—
have kept us occupied away from you during the siege.
Whose young she-camels have been left hobbled
behind Salʿ amid the interlacing thickets?
Young she-camels of Banū Kaʿb ibn ʿAmr,
and of Aslam, Juhayna, or Ghifār.
A white, tall and vigorous man hobbles them;
what an evil hobbling for the choice herd!

ʿUmar then sent for Jaʿda and exiled him. The story is well known, though it has also been transmitted about someone else; الله أعلم. I read in Ibn ʿAsākir’s History, by way of Jaʿfar ibn Khanzāba, with an isnād of his to al-Aṣmaʿī: Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ related to us, saying: In Medina there was a man of Banū Sulaym called Jaʿda. Women would come to converse with him on the outskirts of Medina. He would take a woman and hobble her, saying, ‘A stallion leaps while hobbled.’ When she leapt, she would fall and become exposed. News of this reached some people on one of the campaigns, and a man among them wrote to ʿUmar and cited the poem. ʿUmar said, ‘Bring me Jaʿda ibn Sulaym.’ He was brought. Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib used to say, ‘I was among the young boys who dragged Jaʿda to ʿUmar.’ When ʿUmar saw him, he said, ‘I testify that you are white and shayẓamī, just as he described.’ He beat him and exiled him to Oman.

## Source unit 1297 · printed entry 1298

### English candidate

Al-Julanda—with the first letter vocalized u, the lam vocalized a, the nun unvocalized, and the dal vocalized a—king of Oman. Wathima mentioned in al-Ridda, on the authority of Ibn Ishaq, that the Prophet ﷺ sent Amr ibn al-As to call him to Islam. He said: ‘What has led me to this unlettered Prophet is that he commands no good without being the first to embrace it, and forbids no evil without being the first to abandon it. He prevails but does not exult insolently; when overcome, he does not rave. He keeps covenants and fulfills promises. I bear witness that he is a prophet.’ Then he recited verses, among them:

Amr brought me that after which
no part of the truth remains; a sincere adviser is sincere.

I said to him: ‘You have added nothing by bringing what
al-Julanda of Oman proclaims in Oman.’

O Amr, I have openly submitted to God;
in the two valleys a clear-voiced herald proclaims it.

It will come in the notice of Jayfar ibn al-Julanda, under this letter, that Amr was sent to him. It is possible that both father and son were sent to. Al-Madaʾini mentioned that one of the Persian kings commanded al-Julanda ibn Abd al-Aziz al-Azdi, who in the pre-Islamic period was called Abd Jamal; he then related his story.

## Source unit 1299 · printed entry 1300

### English candidate

Jamra ibn Shihab, a mukhadram. He has a story with Umar that we transmitted in the Fawaʾid of Abu al-Qasim ibn Bishran, by way of Musa ibn Uqba, from Nafi, from Ibn Umar, who said: Umar ibn al-Khattab asked a man, ‘What is your name?’ He replied, ‘Jamra [Ember].’ He asked, ‘Son of whom?’ He replied, ‘Son of Shihab [Flame].’ He asked, ‘From whom?’ He replied, ‘From al-Huraqa [the Burning].’ He asked, ‘Where is your dwelling?’ He replied, ‘Al-Harra [the lava field].’ He asked, ‘Which part of it?’ He replied, ‘Dhat Laza [the Place of Blazing Fire].’ Umar said, ‘Go to your family, for they have burned.’ The man returned and found that his family had burned. Abd al-Razzaq transmitted from Mamar, from al-Zuhri, from Ibn al-Musayyab, who said: Umar said—and he related a similar account. Malik transmitted in al-Muwatta from Yahya ibn Said that Umar ibn al-Khattab asked a man, ‘What is your name?’ He replied, ‘Jamra,’ and he related a similar account. It has another route, transmitted by Abu Bilal al-Ashari from Khalid al-Ashari, from Mujalid, from a shaykh who had lived through the pre-Islamic period; he said: ‘I was with Umar when a man came to him’—and he related a similar account. Ibn Durayd said in al-Akhbar al-Manthura: Abu Hatim al-Sijistani related to us from Abu Ubayda ibn al-Muthanna, who said: ‘Shihab ibn Jamra al-Juhani came in a delegation to Umar.’ Thus he mentioned it in reverse order. The first version is more likely. Ibn al-Kalbi mentioned him in al-Jami, saying: Jamra ibn Shihab ibn Diram ibn Malik al-Juhani; and he related his story with Umar.

## Source unit 1306 · printed entry 1307

### English candidate

Jahma ibn Awf al-Dawsi. Abu Mikhnaf Lut ibn Yahya mentioned him among the long-lived and said: He lived for three hundred and sixty years and reached the Islamic period. Whenever he heard someone say, ‘There is no god but God,’ he would say, ‘In my old age I have indeed lived to see people who utter this profession.’ He would pass through a valley entirely filled with doum palms and say, ‘I used to pass through this valley when there was not a tree in it.’ He lived until his eyebrows drooped over his eyes. He is the one who said:

I grew old, and life stretched long, until there befell me
the plight of one snake-bitten by a night’s vipers, without farewell.

It was not illness that wore me down; rather there followed
upon me years of summering and spring pasture.

Three hundred years have passed in full,
and here I am hoping they will become four.

I recount the reports of generations that have passed,
yet inevitably one day I shall be borne away to my place of falling.

## Source unit 1310 · printed entry 1311

### English candidate

Jayfar—on the pattern of Jafar, but with a ya in place of the ayn—ibn al-Julanda al-Azdi, king of Oman. Abu Umar mentioned him briefly. Al-Askari said: Neither he nor his brother saw the Prophet ﷺ. The notice of his father has already appeared. Ibn Sad transmitted by way of Amr ibn Shuayb, from a client of Amr ibn al-As, who said: I heard Amr ibn al-As say, ‘I embraced Islam in the presence of the Negus’; he then related the story of his emigration and said: ‘The Messenger of God ﷺ sent me to Jayfar and Ubayd, the two sons of al-Julanda. They were in Oman, and Jayfar was the king of the two; they were of Azd.’ He related the story of their conversion and said that they allowed him free access to the alms tax. He remained in Oman until the Prophet ﷺ died. Abdan transmitted, with a sound chain to al-Zuhri, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abd al-Qari, that the Messenger of God ﷺ sent Amr ibn al-As to Jayfar and Abbad, the two sons of al-Julanda, the two rulers of Oman. Amr went to them; they embraced Islam, and many people embraced Islam with them. He imposed the poll tax on those who did not embrace Islam. I say: There is no contradiction between this and the previously mentioned mission to al-Julanda. Nothing prevents al-Julanda from having grown old and delegated authority to his two sons. والله أعلم.

## Source unit 1313 · printed entry 1313

Jabir ibn Ayyash. Abu Nuaym said: ‘No hadith of his is known.’ He cited him briefly. This is how Ibn al-Athir expressed it, but he was mistaken. Rather, Abu Nuaym said, in the course of the notice of Jabir ibn Yasir ibn Uways—who was the grandfather of Ayyash and Jabir, the two sons of Abbas ibn Jabir—‘No mention or transmission of his is known.’ Ibn al-Athir thought that the words ‘and Jabir ibn Ayyash’ had been coordinated with the names Abu Nuaym had mentioned. ## Source unit 1314 · printed entry 1314

Jabir ibn al-Numan [an erroneous heading for Haritha ibn al-Numan]. He said: Ali ibn Hashim related to us; Ibn Abi Fudayk related to us; Muhammad ibn Uthman related to us, from his father, from Jabir ibn al-Numan, with this report. ## Source unit 1322 · printed entry 1322

### English candidate

Jabala ibn Sharāḥīl, the brother of Ḥāritha. Ibn Mandah gave him a separate notice, but Abū Nuʿaym rejected that and said: ‘Rather, he is Jabala ibn Ḥāritha, the brother of Zayd, who was mentioned earlier; Ḥāritha is his father, not his brother.’ This is correct. I say: The cause of the mistake is that, at the end of the story of Zayd ibn Ḥāritha transmitted by way of his descendants—as will come in the notice of his father Ḥāritha—it says: ‘Ḥāritha said, “My son, as for me, I shall support you with my very self. I testify that there is no god but God and that Muḥammad is the Messenger of God.” Thus Ḥāritha ibn Sharāḥīl believed, while the others refused and returned to the desert. Then his brother Jabala returned and believed in the Prophet ﷺ.’ Ibn Mandah took the pronoun in ‘his brother’ to refer to Ḥāritha because he is the nearest antecedent, whereas Abū Nuʿaym took it to refer to Zayd because the report is about him. Both are possible. What Abū Nuʿaym said is more likely, however, because Jabala ibn Ḥāritha is known by name and companionship among the Companions, unlike Zayd’s paternal uncle, who is named nowhere but this ambiguous report. الله أعلم. Moreover, even this report is anomalous and contrary to the well-known account: when Zayd ibn Ḥāritha chose the Prophet ﷺ, his father and paternal uncle were content, left him, and returned. That is how the sīra authorities mention it, and Ibn Mardawayh likewise related it in his Tafsīr by way of al-Kalbī, from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Ibn ʿAbbās.

## Source unit 1325 · printed entry 1325

### English candidate

Jubayr ibn al-Ḥārith, the Bedouin. Al-Afshahrī mentioned in The Benefits of His Journey, with a lengthy isnād leading to the emir Abū al-Makārim ʿAbd al-Karīm ibn the emir Naṣr al-Daylamī, who said: ‘I was in the service of the Abbasid imam al-Nāṣir. He went out hunting, galloped in pursuit of game, and some of his intimates followed him. We came to barren land where there was a small group of Bedouins. Their elders came forward, having recognized the caliph, kissed the ground, and presented whatever food they could. They said, “Commander of the Faithful, we have a treasure with which to honor you.” He asked, “What is it?” They replied, “All of us are descendants of a single man. He is still alive and provided for; he lived during the time of the Messenger of God ﷺ and was present with him at the digging of the Trench.” He asked, “What is his name?” They replied, “Jubayr ibn al-Ḥārith.” He said, “Show him to me.” They lowered him in a cradle like an infant.’ He then related something like the story of Raṭan the Indian. This was in the year 576. I have given the story in full in Lisān al-Mīzān.

## Source unit 1327 · printed entry 1327

### English candidate

Al-Jaḥḥāf ibn Ḥakīm ibn ʿĀṣim ibn Sibāʿ ibn Khuzāʿī ibn Muḥārib ibn Hilāl ibn Fālij ibn Dhakwān ibn Thaʿlaba ibn Buhtha ibn Sulaym, al-Sulamī, the famous horseman and participant in the celebrated conflicts during the reign of ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān. Ibn al-Athīr added him as an omission from his predecessors and adduced as evidence his words in some verses describing the horses of Banū Sulaym:

They were present with the Prophet, marked,
at Ḥunayn, their hooves bloodied.

I say: This does not indicate that he was a Companion. He was merely boasting of his people, Banū Sulaym, who were numerous on the day of Ḥunayn. The story of al-ʿAbbās ibn Mirdās al-Sulamī concerning that is well known. I found that Ibn al-Athīr had a predecessor in this view, but one more learned than he undertook to refute it. Ibn ʿAsākir related with a sound chain to Muḥammad ibn Sallām al-Jumaḥī, who said: Abān al-Aʿraj said to me, ‘Al-Jaḥḥāf lived during the pre-Islamic period.’ I asked him, ‘Why do you say that?’ He replied, ‘Because of his line,’ and cited this verse. Muḥammad ibn Sallām said: ‘I told him, “He meant only the horses of his people, Banū Sulaym.” Later I mentioned that to ʿĀṣim ibn al-Sarī, and he said: “Qays ibn al-Haytham related to me that he gave Ḥakīm ibn Umayya a slave woman, and she bore al-Jaḥḥāf to him in an upper room of our house.”’ End. It thereby became known that he was born a considerable time after the Prophet ﷺ. Abū Tammām claimed in al-Ḥamāsa that the cited verses belonged to someone else, namely al-Ḥuraysh ibn Hilāl al-Qurayʿī. الله أعلم. Ibn Sayyid al-Nās said in The Names of the Companion Poets: ‘Ibn al-Amīn added him as an omission from Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr; I copied this from his own hand. He said that Hishām mentioned him and that he had poetry concerning the conquest of Mecca.’ What I saw in the Sīra, from Ibn Isḥāq, says: ‘A speaker from Banū Jadhīma—and some say a woman called Salmā—said,’ then cited a poem beginning:

Had the people not said to the people, ‘They have submitted,’
Sulaym would that day have met a butting foe.

He said that al-ʿAbbās ibn Mirdās answered her—or, it is said, al-Jaḥḥāf ibn Ḥakīm:

Leave off your talk of error; we suffice
to butt the ram of battle, today as yesterday.

[The remaining verses.] I say: This likewise does not indicate companionship; he said it only to boast of his people, as noted above.

## Source unit 1340 · printed entry 1340

### English candidate

Jaʿfar Abū Zamʿa al-Balawī, a Companion who pledged beneath the Tree and then settled in Egypt. His name is disputed: it was said to be Jaʿfar and said to be ʿAbd. Ibn al-Athīr added him as an omission and said: ‘Abū Mūsā mentioned him under ʿAbd but did not mention him under Jaʿfar.’ End. I say: Ibn al-Athīr made a clear error concerning him. Abū Mūsā’s exact words were: ‘ʿAbd ibn Zamʿa al-Balawī, among those who pledged beneath the Tree; he settled in Egypt. His name is disputed. Jaʿfar [al-Mustaghfirī] said, “It is said that his name was ʿAbd.”’ End. It appears that Ibn al-Athīr’s copy contained a corruption. The Jaʿfar from whom Abū Mūsā quoted was al-Mustaghfirī. ## Source unit 1342 · printed entry 1342

### English candidate

Jafar ibn Nastur al-Rumi, one of the liars who claimed Companionship hundreds of years after the Prophet ﷺ. I read his notice in Mughaltay’s handwriting as an addition to Ibn al-Athir. Ibn al-Dabbagh likewise added him to Ibn Abd al-Barr, and al-Dhahabi also added him in al-Tajrid, but said: ‘The chain to him is darkness upon darkness, and the texts are false. He is an impostor—or he never existed.’ He was reportedly seen in the vicinity of Farab, in the land of the Turks, in the year 350. I say: I could not bring myself to place him in the first section. A copy has reached us by way of Mansur ibn al-Hakam, the ascetic of Farghana, from him. Among its contents is his statement: Jafar ibn Nastur al-Rumi related to me, saying: ‘I was with the Prophet ﷺ during the expedition to Tabuk. His whip fell from his hand, so I dismounted from my horse, picked it up, and handed it to him. He said, “May God greatly prolong your life.” I then lived for three hundred and twenty years.’ Abu Hurayra ibn al-Dhahabi informed us by authorization: Ishaq ibn Yahya al-Amidi reported to us; Yusuf ibn Khalil reported to us; Masud al-Jammal reported to us; Abu Ali al-Haddad reported to us; Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Amr al-Waiz al-Qumisi reported to us by dictation; Abu Shuja Umar ibn Ali al-Iraqi reported to us; Mansur ibn al-Hakam reported to us. Also among them is the fabricated report: ‘Whoever walks barefoot to do good, it is as though he walked upon the ground of Paradise’—the hadith. I also heard some of his hadith at the end of the Mashyakha of Shahda bint al-Ibari. Further discussion will come in the notice of Nastur al-Rumi. Al-Silafi said: Abd Allah ibn Umar ibn Khalaf al-Qarawi informed us in Mecca in the year 497; Ali ibn al-Husayn ibn Ismail al-Kashghari informed us; Abu Dawud Sulayman ibn Nuh ibn Muhammad al-Marghinani informed me; Mansur ibn al-Hakam the jurist informed us—and he mentioned the copy. It comprises eleven hadiths, including the two reports just mentioned and this report: ‘We were seated before the Prophet ﷺ while he was cleaning his teeth with a tooth-stick. He gestured with his right hand and then with his left. We said, “O Messenger of God, we see no one; to whom are you gesturing?” He said, “Gabriel and Michael were before me. I gestured to Gabriel, and he said, ‘Hand it to Michael, for he is older than I.’”’ The copy was also transmitted, and it came by way of Abu al-Muzaffar Maymun ibn Mahmud: al-Sharif Abd al-Jalil related to me, from Umar ibn al-Husayn al-Kashghari, from Ibn Nastur, from his father. It will come under the letter nun.

جعفر بن نسطور الرومي أحد الكذابين الذين ادعوا الصحبة بعد النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم بمئين من السنين قرأته بخط مغلطاي مستدركا على بن الأثير وكذا استدركه بن الدباغ على بن عبد البر وكذا استدركه الذهبي في التجريد لكن قال الإسناد إليه ظلمات والمتون باطلة وهو دجال أو لا وجود له رؤى بناحية فاراب من أرض الترك في سنة خمسين وثلاث مائة قلت لم تطب نفسي بإخراجه في القسم الأول وقد وقعت لنا نسخة من طريق منصور بن الحكم الزاهد الفرغاني عنه فمنها قال حدثني جعفر بن نسطور الرومي قال كنت مع النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم في غزوة تبوك فسقط السوط من يده فنزلت عن جوادي وأخذته فدفعته إليه فقال مد الله في عمرك مدا فعشت بعدها ثلاثمائة وعشرين سنة أخبرنا أبو هريرة بن الذهبي إجازة أنبأنا إسحاق بن يحيى الآمدي أنبأنا يوسف بن خليل أنبأنا مسعود الجمال أنبأنا أبو علي الحداد أنبأنا أحمد بن محمد بن عمرو الواعظ القومسي إملاء أنبأنا أبو شجاع عمر بن علي العراقي أنبأنا منصور بن الحكم ومنها من مشى إلى خير حافيا فكأنما مشى على أرض الجنة الحديث وسمعت من حديثه أيضا في آخر مشيخته شهدة بنت الإبري وستأتي في ترجمة نسطور الرومي وقال السلفي أخبرنا عبد الله بن عمر بن خلف القروي بمكة سنة سبع وتسعين وأربعمائة أخبرنا علي بن الحسين بن إسماعيل الكاشغري أخبرني أبو داود سليمان بن نوح بن محمد المرغيناني أخبرنا منصور بن الحكم الفقيه فذكر النسخة وهي أحد عشر حديثا منها الحديثان المذكوران ومنها كنا جلوسا بين يدي النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم يستاك فأشار بيده اليمني ثم اليسرى فقلنا يا رسول الله ما نرى أحدا إلى من تشير قال كان جبرائيل وميكائيل بن يدي فأشرت إلى جبرائيل فقال ناول ميكائيل فإنه أكبر مني وروى النسخة أيضا وجاء من طريق أبي المظفر ميمون بن محمود حدثني الشريف عبد الجليل عن عمر بن الحسين الكاشغري عن بن نسطور عن أبيه وسيأتي في النون

## Source unit 1343 · printed entry 1343

Jufi ibn Sad al-Ashira, of Madhhij. It was said that he came to the Prophet ﷺ as part of the delegation of Jufa during the days in which the Prophet ﷺ died. This is how Ibn Abi Hatim mentioned him in his book. Abu Umar followed him, copying the statement from him without criticizing it. Ibn al-Athir said: ‘This is among the strangest things a scholar could say. Jufi ibn Sad al-Ashira died a very long time before the Prophet ﷺ; indeed, between Jufi and some of those who accompanied the Prophet there are ten or more fathers.’ I say: What I think happened is that Ibn Abi Hatim saw in the campaign literature the heading ‘Delegation of Jufi ibn Sad al-Ashira, of Madhhij.’ Authors customarily use the names of tribes as headings and then name the delegates from them. He seems to have imagined that wafd was wafada, with the fa vocalized a, and concluded from it that Jufi ibn Sad al-Ashira himself was the delegate. That is not so: he turned the noun into a verb and the name of the tribe into the delegate’s name. Abu Umar deserves more blame for this than Ibn Abi Hatim.

## Source unit 1345 · printed entry 1345

### English candidate

Jamd al-Kindi. Ibn Mandah transmitted by way of Hammad, from Asim, that Jamd al-Kindi said: ‘For a large dish to be brought to me and for me to eat from it is dearer to me than to be given glad tidings of a boy.’ The Prophet ﷺ was informed of that and said, ‘They are the fruit of the heart.’ Abu Nuaym said: ‘The well-known account is that al-Ashath was the speaker. Perhaps he likened al-Ashath’s lack of compassion to inanimate matter and nicknamed him Jamd.’ I say: That is not so. Rather, what is known is that al-Ashath was given glad tidings of a boy born to the daughter of Jamd al-Kindi, whereupon he said what he said. Jamd was one of the four kings who apostatized and were killed during the caliphate of Abu Bakr. His daughter was married to al-Ashath.

## Source unit 1354 · printed entry 1354

### English candidate

Jawn ibn Qatada ibn al-Awar ibn Saida ibn Awf ibn Kab ibn Abd Shams ibn Zayd Manat ibn Tamim al-Tamimi, a Successor. Some transmitters erred by making a hadith from him connected after dropping the name of a Companion—Salama ibn al-Muhabbiq. Al-Baghawi and others therefore mentioned him among the Companions. His father was a Companion and will come in his proper place. Al-Baghawi said: ‘My grandfather—namely, Ahmad ibn Mani—and Shuja ibn Makhlad related to us; they said: Hushaym related to us.’ Ibn Qani transmitted by way of al-Hasan ibn Arafa, and Ibn Mandah by way of Yahya ibn Ayyub; both transmitted from Hushaym: Mansur informed us, from al-Hasan, from Jawn ibn Qatada al-Tamimi, who said: ‘We were with the Prophet ﷺ on one of his journeys. One of his Companions passed by a hanging waterskin containing water and wanted to drink. The owner of the waterskin said to him, “It is the hide of a dead animal.” They mentioned that to the Prophet, and he said, “Drink, for tanning a dead animal’s hide is its purification.”’ Al-Baghawi said: ‘This is how Hushaym transmitted it, taking it no further than Jawn ibn Qatada; Jawn had no Companionship.’ Ibn Mandah said: ‘Hushaym erred in it. Jawn had neither Companionship nor sight of the Prophet. Qatada transmitted it from al-Hasan, from Jawn, from Salama ibn al-Muhabbiq.’ Abu Nuaym said: ‘Zakariya ibn Yahya ibn Zahamawayh transmitted it from Hushaym and included Salama ibn al-Muhabbiq in the chain.’ He then gave it by that route and said: ‘Zahamawayh rendered it accurately. The transmitter from him, Aslam ibn Suhayl al-Wasiti, was one of the senior hadith masters and scholars of Wasit. It is therefore clear that the person who erred was someone other than Hushaym.’ Al-Mizzi objected that Ibn Mandah’s statement was correct, that the error was Hushaym’s, and that Zahamawayh’s transmission was anomalous. I say: It is possible that Hushaym transmitted it incorrectly several times and correctly once. Abu Muhammad ibn Hazm was deceived by the apparent form of Hushaym’s chain. He transmitted by way of al-Tabari, from Muhammad ibn Hatim, from Hushaym, and related it as Ahmad ibn Mani and those who followed him had done. He said: ‘This is a sound hadith, and Jawn’s Companionship is established.’ Abu Bakr ibn Muawwaz objected: ‘This is an error. Jawn is an unknown Successor; no one is known to have transmitted from him except al-Hasan. His transmission of this hadith is in fact from Salama ibn al-Muhabbiq. Muhammad ibn Hatim erred in it.’ I say: He was not correct in attributing the error to Muhammad ibn Hatim. As for his statement that Jawn was unknown, Abu Talib and al-Athram transmitted it from Ahmad ibn Hanbal. Abu al-Hasan ibn al-Bara transmitted from Ali ibn al-Madini: ‘Jawn is known, even though no one but al-Hasan transmitted from him.’ Yet in another place he counted Jawn among al-Hasan’s unknown shaykhs. Jawn ibn Qatada also transmitted from al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam and witnessed the Battle of the Camel with him. As for Qatada’s route, to which Ibn Mandah alluded, Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Nasai, Ibn Hibban, and al-Hakim transmitted it. Their reports do not differ in including Salama ibn al-Muhabbiq in its chain. والله أعلم.

## Source unit 1355 · printed entry 1355

### English candidate

Ḥābis ibn Daghina al-Kalbī. He has a report among the signs of prophecy and was a Companion. That is how Abū ʿUmar cited him in summary. The report was related by Hishām ibn al-Kalbī from a hadith of ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim, who said: ‘I had a hired herdsman from Kalb called Ḥābis ibn Daghina. One day, while I was in the open area before my dwelling, he came to me terrified at heart and said, “Take charge of your camels.” I asked, “What alarmed you?” He replied, “While I was in the valley, an old man appeared from a cleft in the mountain opposite me, his head like a vulture’s. He descended from a place from which an eagle would descend, moving at ease and unalarmed, until his feet came to rest at the valley floor. As I stood in awe of what I saw, he said:

O Ḥābis ibn Daghina, O Ḥābis,
do not let whisperings assail your heart.
This is the radiance of light in the fire-kindler’s palm;
incline toward truth and do not deal deceitfully.

Then he vanished. I brought my camels home that evening and afterward pastured them in a valley other than that one. Then I lay down. Suddenly a rider spurred me, and I awoke to find that it was my companion, saying:

O Ḥābis, hear what I say and you will be guided;
one lost and bewildered is not like one rightly guided.
Do not abandon the straightest road;
religion has been superseded by the religion of Aḥmad.

By God, everything then went dark for me. I recovered after some time.’ He related the remainder of the story. At its end, Ḥābis said, ‘ʿAdī, God has tested my heart for Islam.’ Then he left me, and that was the last I saw of him.

## Source unit 1356 · printed entry 1356

### English candidate

Ḥābis ibn Rabīʿa al-Tamīmī. Ibn Ḥibbān said: ‘Ḥābis al-Tamīmī was a Companion.’ Ibn al-Sakan said that he is counted among the Basrans. His son Ḥayya—with a heavily pronounced yāʾ—related from him that he heard the Prophet ﷺ say, ‘The evil eye is real.’ Aḥmad, al-Tirmidhī, Ibn Khuzayma, and al-Bukhārī in both his Tārīkh and al-Adab al-Mufrad transmitted it, all by way of Yaḥyā ibn Abī Kathīr from Ḥayya, from his father Ḥābis. Shaybān, however, related from Yaḥyā, from Ḥayya, from Abū Hurayra; the first is sounder. Ibn al-Sakan said: ‘He is said to have been a Companion. The transmissions from Yaḥyā ibn Kathīr differ concerning him, and we have found the report only by his route.’ Al-Baghawī said: ‘I know no report of his but this one.’ Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said that the isnād of his hadith is confused, and named his father Rabīʿa. I say: In some routes it occurs as Ḥayya ibn Ḥābis—or ʿĀbis. Another form of the disagreement is what Ibn Abī ʿĀṣim and Abū Yaʿlā transmitted by another route from Yaḥyā ibn Abī Kathīr: ‘Ḥayya ibn Ḥābis related to me: I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ ...’ The words ‘from his father’ fell from it. Abū Mūsā mentioned him at the end of the section for unpointed ḥāʾ as ‘Ḥayya,’ with a yāʾ, indicated the error in it, and said that the correct form is ‘from Ḥabba,’ with a bāʾ, from his father, from the Prophet ﷺ.

## Source unit 1358 · printed entry 1358

### English candidate

Ḥābis ibn Saʿd ibn al-Mundhir ibn Rabīʿa ibn Saʿd ibn Yathribī al-Ṭāʾī. Ibn Saʿd and Abū Zurʿa al-Dimashqī included him among the Companions who settled in Syria. Ibn Sumayʿ placed him in the first class of Companions. Al-Bukhārī said that he lived during the time of the Prophet ﷺ. Aḥmad transmitted by way of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ghābir, who said: Ḥābis ibn Saʿd entered the mosque before dawn—he had lived during the time of the Prophet ﷺ—and saw people praying in the mosque’s portico. He said, ‘Show-offs! Frighten them away. The angels pray at the front of the mosque before dawn.’ This is a sound mawqūf report in its chain. Ibn al-Sakan said that some transmitted from him a hadith in which he was claimed to be a Companion. Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Khalīfa, and others mentioned him and said that he was killed at Ṣiffīn while with Muʿāwiya. It therefore appears that they regarded him as the preceding man, although al-Bāwardī and others distinguished them. Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr mentioned that he was known among the Syrians as al-Yamānī. Some scholars of historical reports transmitted that ʿUmar said to him, ‘I wish to appoint you judge of Ḥimṣ.’ He then related the story of Ḥābis’s dream in which the sun and moon fought, and he was with the moon. ʿUmar told him, ‘You were with the effaced sign; you shall hold no office for me.’

## Source unit 1360 · printed entry 1360

### English candidate

Ḥājib ibn Zurāra ibn ʿUdas ibn Zayd ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Dārim, al-Dārimī al-Tamīmī, the father of ʿUṭārid. He will be mentioned in the notice of Ṣafwān ibn Usayd under the unpointed letter ṣād. That notice contains the story of his acceptance of Islam and says that the Prophet ﷺ appointed him over the alms of Banū Tamīm. He was mentioned earlier in the notice of Aktham ibn Ṣayfī in the third section, and he will be mentioned in the notice of Khālid ibn Mālik. Al-Marzubānī said that he was chief of Banū Tamīm on several occasions. He was the man who pledged his bow to Khosrow as security for a great sum of money and fulfilled the pledge. The following is recited as his boast:

Among us are Ibn Māʾ al-Muzn and Ibn Muḥarriq,
until Bujayr and Ḥājib appeared among them—
three kings reared in our chambers, all of them;
and from us comes boasting that is no lie.

## Source unit 1373 · printed entry 1373

### English candidate

Al-Harith ibn Aws ibn Muadh ibn al-Numan al-Ansari, then al-Awsi, the son of the brother of Sad ibn Muadh, chief of al-Aws. His mention is established in a sound hadith transmitted by Ahmad through Alqama ibn Waqqas from Aisha, who said: ‘I went out on the day of the Trench and heard a sound. I turned, and there was Sad ibn Muadh, accompanied by his nephew al-Harith ibn Aws, carrying his shield’—and she related the hadith. Ibn Hibban declared it sound. Abu Umar said that he witnessed Badr and was martyred on the day of Uhud at twenty-eight years of age. I say: In this he followed Ibn al-Kalbi, and it is an error. One of the genealogists challenged it, saying: ‘I did not find him among the martyrs killed at Uhud.’ I say: It is possible that the man martyred at Uhud was someone else, because Uhud occurred some time before the Trench. Ibn Ishaq did mention al-Harith ibn Aws ibn Muadh among those martyred at Uhud, but he did not say that he was the nephew of Sad ibn Muadh; thus he is a different man. As for Sad's nephew, he also participated in the killing of Kab ibn al-Ashraf. In the notice of Abu Naila, under the letter nun in the section on kunyas, it will come that Sad ibn Muadh said to him: ‘Take my nephew al-Harith ibn Aws with you.’ It is established in al-Bukhari, in the hadith of Jabir, that Muhammad ibn Maslama came with two men: Abu Qays ibn Jabir and al-Harith ibn Aws. This is he. والله أعلم.

### Arabic authority

<div dir="rtl" lang="ar">

الحارث بن أوس بن معاذ بن النعمان الأنصاري ثم الأوسي بن أخي سعد بن معاذ سيد الأوس ثبت ذكره في حديث صحيح أخرجه أحمد من طريق علقة بن وقاص عن عائشة قال خرجت يوم الخندق فسمعت حسا فالتفت فإذا أنا بسعد بن معاذ ومعه بن أخيه الحارث بن أوس يحمل مجنه الحديث وصححه بن حبان وقال أبو عمر شهد بدرا واستشهد يوم أحد وهو بن ثمان وعشرين سنة قلت تبع في ذلك بن الكلبي وهو وهم تعقبه بعض أهل النسب فقال لم أجده في قتلى أحد الشهداء قلت يحتمل أن يكون المستشهد بأحد غيره لأن أحدا قبل الخندق بمدة وقد ذكر بن إسحاق فيمن استشهد بأحد الحارث بن أوس بن معاذ لكن لم يقل إنه بن أخي سعد بن معاذ فهو غيره أما بن أخي سعد فقد شهد أيضا قتل كعب بن الأشرف فسيأتي في ترجمة أبي نائلة في حرف النون من الكنى أن سعد بم معاذ قال له أذهب معك بابن أخي الحارث بن أوس وثبت في البخاري من حديث جابر أن محمد بن سلمة جاء معه برجلين أبو قيس بن جابر والحارث بن أوس فهو هذا والله أعلم

</div>

## Source unit 1388 · printed entry 1388

Al-Ḥārith ibn al-Ḥārith al-Ghāmidī, whose kunya was Abū al-Makhāriq. Ibn al-Sakan said he was counted among the people of Ḥimṣ. Al-Bukhārī in al-Tārīkh, Abū Zurʿa al-Dimashqī, al-Baghawī, Ibn Abī ʿĀṣim, and al-Ṭabarānī related through al-Walīd ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Jurashī: al-Ḥārith ibn al-Ḥārith al-Ghāmidī told me: I said to my father, while we were at Minā, ‘What is this gathering?’ He said, ‘These people have gathered around a Ṣābiʾ of theirs.’ I craned up to look, and there was the Messenger of God ﷺ calling the people to the oneness of God while they answered him back. The hadith continues. Al-Bukhārī and Ibn al-Sakan also related, through Shurayḥ ibn ʿUbayd, from al-Ḥārith ibn al-Ḥārith, Kathīr ibn Murra, and others, concerning the leaders being from Quraysh. Al-Bukhārī said: Khālid ibn Maʿdān related it from al-Ḥārith ibn al-Ḥārith al-Ghāmidī. Ibn al-Sakan related it through Sulaym ibn ʿĀmir from al-Ḥārith ibn al-Ḥārith al-Ghāmidī. He had reached the Prophet ﷺ and related hadiths from him. Abū al-Qāsim ibn ʿĪsā, in Ṭabaqāt al-Ḥimṣiyyīn, reported from Muḥammad ibn ʿAwf that he said, ‘How likely he is to have been one of the people of Ḥimṣ.’ He then mentioned that Sulaym ibn ʿĀmir, Khālid ibn Maʿdān, and Shurayḥ ibn ʿUbayd transmitted from him; that he had an allotment at Tamr ʿAyn; and that he witnessed the engagement at Rāhiṭ.

## Source unit 1392 · printed entry 1392

### English candidate

Al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥāṭib ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Maʿmar ibn Ḥabīb ibn Wahb ibn Ḥudhāfa ibn Jumaḥ al-Qurashī al-Jumaḥī. His father emigrated to Abyssinia, where al-Ḥārith and Muḥammad were born to him; al-Zuhrī said this. Musʿab’s wording indicates that al-Ḥārith was born before the emigration to Abyssinia and that his brother Muḥammad was the one born to his father there. Ibn Manda erred when he reported from Ibn Isḥāq, among those who emigrated to Abyssinia, ‘al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥāṭib.’ What is in Ibn Isḥāq’s Maghāzī and Ibn Hishām’s abridgment of it is ‘Ḥāṭib ibn al-Ḥārith.’ Al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥāṭib transmitted from the Prophet ﷺ; his report is in Abū Dāwūd and al-Nasāʾī. Ḥusayn ibn al-Ḥārith al-Jadalī and others transmitted from him. Muṣʿab al-Zubayrī said: Marwān appointed him over the alms functions—that is, in Medina—and he served Marwān’s son ʿAbd al-Malik over Mecca. Ibn Ḥibbān, however, listed him among the Successors and erred, because the explicit wording of his hadith is: ‘The Messenger of God ﷺ charged us …’

## Source unit 1397 · printed entry 1397

### English candidate

Al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥassān—also said to be ibn Yazīd—al-Bakrī al-Dhuhlī. It is also said that his name was Ḥurayth, perhaps as a diminutive. Aḥmad, al-Tirmidhī, al-Nasāʾī, and Ibn Māja transmitted reports from him. In some routes of his hadith, he is said to have come in a delegation to the Prophet ﷺ. Abū Wāʾil, Simāk ibn Ḥarb, and Iyāḍ ibn Laqīṭ transmitted from him. Al-Baghawī said he lived in the desert. Al-Ṭabarānī related through Simāk ibn Ḥarb that al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥassān married. When a man consummated a marriage, he would remain secluded for several days. He was asked about that, and replied, ‘By God, a woman who keeps me from the dawn prayer in congregation is an evil woman.’ His hadith states that his arrival occurred in the days when the Messenger of God ﷺ dispatched ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ on the expedition of Dhāt al-Salāsil. I found in al-Futūḥ that when al-Aḥnaf conquered Khurāsān, he sent al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥassān to Sarakhs; he may therefore be this man.

## Source unit 1408 · printed entry 1408

### English candidate

Al-Harith ibn Abi Rabia ibn al-Mughira ibn Abd Allah ibn Umar ibn Makhzum al-Makhzumi. Ibn Manda transmitted, by way of Qasim al-Jarmi, from al-Thawri, from Ismail ibn Ibrahim ibn Abi Rabia, from his father, from al-Harith ibn Abi Rabia, that when the Prophet ﷺ arrived in Mecca he borrowed thirty thousand from him—the hadith. This hadith is known as the report of his brother Abd Allah ibn Abi Rabia; Ibn al-Mubarak transmitted it in that form from al-Thawri through this chain. Hatim ibn Ismail transmitted it from Ismail ibn Ibrahim ibn Abd Allah ibn Abi Rabia, from his father, from his grandfather. Ibn Abi Asim transmitted it by way of Ibn Abi Fudayk, from Musa and Ismail, the two sons of Ibrahim, from their father, from Abd Allah ibn Abi Rabia. It is possible that both Abd Allah and al-Harith possessed the hadith. الله أعلم.

Al-Harith ibn Zayd al-Ansari al-Saidi.
