## Source unit 1425 · printed entry 1425

### English candidate

Al-Harith ibn Suwayd ibn al-Samit al-Ansari al-Awsi. His brother al-Jallas was mentioned earlier under jim. Ibn al-Athir said: The transmitters agree that he was the one who killed al-Mujadhdhar ibn Ziyad, and the Prophet ﷺ killed him in retaliation. His categorical assertion warrants examination, for al-Adawi, Ibn al-Kalbi, and al-Qasim ibn Sallam asserted that the incident concerned his brother al-Jallas; the well-known view, however, assigns it to al-Harith. Abd al-Razzaq in his Tafsir and Musaddad in his Musnad, both from Jafar ibn Sulayman, and al-Bawardi, Ibn Manda, and others by way of Jafar, from Humayd al-Araj, from Mujahid, related that al-Harith ibn Suwayd had been a Muslim, then apostatized and joined the unbelievers. Thereupon this verse was revealed: ‘How shall God guide a people who disbelieved after their faith?’ A man carried it to him and recited it. Al-Harith said: ‘By God, you are truthful, and God is the most truthful of those who speak truth.’ He then embraced Islam. Abd ibn Humayd and al-Firyabi transmitted by way of Ibn Nujayh, from Mujahid, concerning this verse: ‘It was revealed about a man of Banu Amr ibn Awf’; and by way of al-Suddi: ‘It was revealed about al-Harith ibn Suwayd, one of Banu Amr ibn Awf.’ Al-Nasai, Ibn Hibban, and al-Hakim transmitted by way of Dawud ibn Abi Hind, from Ikrima, from Ibn Abbas: ‘A man embraced Islam and then apostatized’; and he related a similar account without naming him. Al-Tabari transmitted it by way of Dawud in both connected and mursal forms. In the version of Ahmad ibn Mani, from Ali ibn Asim, from Dawud, the wording is: ‘A man of the Ansar apostatized’; and he related the hadith in connected form. The reason he killed al-Mujadhdhar was that al-Mujadhdhar had killed his father, Suwayd ibn al-Samit, in the pre-Islamic period. Al-Harith caught al-Mujadhdhar off guard on the day of Uhud, killed him, and fled. Concerning this, Hassan ibn Thabit said:

‘O Harith, were you in a drowse from the sleep of your forebears,
or—woe to you—were you deluded by Gabriel?
Or were you, O son of Ziyad, when you killed him
unawares in the open expanse of earth, unknown?’

Ibn Abd al-Barr has: ‘Al-Harith ibn Suwayd, also said to be ibn Muslim al-Makhzumi, apostatized and joined the unbelievers, whereupon “How shall God guide a people...” was revealed’—the verse. I say: The well-known view is that he was an Ansari.

### Arabic authority

<div dir="rtl" lang="ar">

## Source unit 1426 · printed entry 1426

### English candidate

Al-Harith ibn Shurayh ibn Dhuayb ibn Rabia ibn al-Harith ibn Numayr ibn Amir al-Numayri. Al-Bukhari said in al-Tarikh: He came to the Prophet ﷺ in the delegation of Banu Numayr. Al-Bawardi and Yaqub ibn Sufyan transmitted by way of Yahya ibn Rashid, from Dalham ibn Dahtham, from Aid ibn Rabia al-Qurayi, from Qurra ibn Damus, from al-Harith ibn Shurayh, that he set out for the Prophet ﷺ; and he related a long hadith that will come in the notice of Yazid ibn Umayr. Qays ibn Hafs transmitted it from Dalham ibn Dahtham, from Qurra—who was in the delegation—and related something similar; it will come under qaf. Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi transmitted by way of Aidh ibn Rabia, who said: I asked al-Harith ibn Shurayh, ‘What did the Messenger of God ﷺ say to you concerning items of common use?’ He replied: ‘Stone, iron, and water.’ Ibn al-Sakan transmitted it at length. Umar ibn Shabba has ‘Shurayh ibn al-Harith,’ which is inverted.

### Arabic authority

<div dir="rtl" lang="ar">

الحارث بن شريح بن ذؤيب بن ربيعة بن الحارث بن نمير بن عامر النميري قال البخاري في التاريخ وفد على النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم في وفد بني نمير وروى الباوردي ويعقوب بن سفيان من طريق يحيى بن راشد عن دلهم بن دهثم عن عائد بن ربيعة القريعي عن قرة بن دعموص عن الحارث بن شريح أنه انطلق إلى النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم فذكر حديثا طويلا سيأتي في ترجمة يزيد بن عمير ورواه قيس بن حفص عن دلهم بن دهثم عن قرة وكان في الوفد فذكر نحوه وسيأتي في القاف وروى الحكيم الترمذي من طريق عائذ بن ربيعة قال قلت للحارث بن شريح ما قال لك رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم في الماعون قال الحجر والحديد والماء وأخرجه بن السكن مطولا ووقع عند عمر بن شبة شريح بن الحارث وهو مقلوب

### English candidate

Al-Harith ibn al-Simma—with the unpointed letter vocalized i and the mim doubled—ibn Amr ibn Atik ibn Amr ibn Amir ibn Malik ibn al-Najjar, father of Abu Juhaym. Musa ibn Uqba, Ibn Ishaq, and others mentioned him among the people of Badr. They said that he broke a bone at al-Rawha, so the Prophet ﷺ sent him back and allotted him his share. He is the one who said:

‘O Lord, al-Harith ibn al-Simma
has set out through a trackless waste, a waste,
driving onward with the Prophet, guide of the community.’

Ibn Ishaq related in al-Maghazi that he was martyred at Bir Mauna; Abu al-Aswad, from Urwa, mentioned the same. Ibn Shahin said that the Prophet ﷺ established brotherhood between him and Suhayb ibn Sinan. Al-Tabarani transmitted by way of Asim ibn Amr, from Mahmud ibn Labid, who said: Al-Harith ibn al-Simma said, ‘On the day of Uhud, while he was in the ravine, the Prophet ﷺ asked me about Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf. I said: I saw him beside the mountain. He said: The angels are fighting alongside him’—the hadith. I say: Those who claimed that he was Abu Juhaym—such as Muslim in al-Kuna and those who followed him—erred. The correct view is that Abu Juhaym was his son.

## Source unit 1429 · printed entry 1429

### English candidate

Al-Harith ibn Abi Dirar ibn Habib ibn al-Harith ibn Aidh ibn Malik ibn al-Mustaliq, Abu Malik al-Khuzai, then al-Mustaliqi, father of Juwayriya, Mother of the Believers. Ibn Ishaq mentioned in al-Maghazi that he came to Medina with his daughter's ransom after she had been captured and the Messenger of God ﷺ had married her. When he reached al-Aqiq, he looked at the camels, took a liking to two of them, and concealed them in a mountain pass. Then he came and said: ‘Muhammad, this is my daughter's ransom.’ He said: ‘Where are the two camels you concealed at al-Aqiq?’ Al-Harith said: ‘I bear witness that there is no god but God and that you are the Messenger of God. By God, no one but God knew of that.’ He embraced Islam; two of his sons and some of his people embraced Islam with him. Ibn Aidh mentioned this in al-Maghazi, from Muhammad ibn Shuayb, from Abd Allah ibn Ziyad, with a disconnected chain. Ahmad, al-Tabarani, Mutayyan, Ibn al-Sakan, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted by way of Isa ibn Dinar the muezzin, from his father, who heard al-Harith ibn Abi Dirar say: ‘I came to the Messenger of God ﷺ, and he invited me to Islam, so I entered it’; then he related a long hadith containing the account of al-Walid ibn Uqba when he came to him as a collector of alms, and the revelation of His word, exalted is He: ‘O you who believe, if an iniquitous man comes to you with a report, ascertain...’—the verse.

## Source unit 1433 · printed entry 1433

### English candidate

Al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Juhanī. Ibn Saʿd and others related his report through Saʿīd ibn Khālid al-Juhanī, who said: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Qays sent me to al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Juhanī. ## Source unit 1440 · printed entry 1440

### English candidate

Al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā ibn Rifāʿa ibn Mallān ibn Nāṣira ibn Qaṣaba ibn Naṣr ibn Saʿd ibn Bakr ibn Hawāzin al-Saʿdī, husband of Ḥalīma, the wet nurse of the Prophet ﷺ. Ibn Saʿd said his kunya was Abū Dhuʾayb. Ibn Isḥāq mentioned in al-Sīra: My father told me, from men of Banū Saʿd ibn Bakr, who said: Al-Ḥārith, the foster father of the Prophet ﷺ, came to Mecca. Quraysh said to him, ‘Do you not hear what your son is saying—that people will be resurrected after death?’ He said, ‘My son, what is this that you are saying?’ He replied, ‘Yes. When that day comes, I shall take you by the hand and make you recognize what you say today.’ Al-Ḥārith later embraced Islam, and his Islam was good. He used to say, ‘If my son takes me by the hand, he will not let me go until he admits me to Paradise.’ I say: Ibn Saʿd has another mursal report in which this episode happened to al-Ḥārith’s son. He related through Yaḥyā ibn Abī Kathīr, from Isḥāq ibn ʿAbd Allāh, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ had a foster brother. He said to the Prophet ﷺ—meaning after the prophetic mission—‘Do you think there will be a resurrection?’ The Prophet ﷺ replied, ‘By Him in whose hand is my soul, I shall take you by the hand on the Day of Resurrection and make you recognize it.’ When he later believed in the Prophet ﷺ, he would sit weeping and say, ‘I hope that the Prophet ﷺ will take me by the hand on the Day of Resurrection.’ It is possible that this happened to both father and son. Some named the son ʿAbd Allāh and mentioned him among the Companions. Ibn Saʿd likewise named him when listing Ḥalīma’s children. His notice will appear under al-Shaymāʾ in the letter shīn among the women’s names. Abū Dāwūd related through ʿUmar ibn al-Ḥārith that ʿUmar ibn al-Sāʾib told him that it had reached him that the Messenger of God ﷺ was seated when his foster father approached; he spread part of his garment for him, and the man sat upon it. The hadith continues. Ibn Isḥāq mentioned that it had reached him that al-Ḥārith embraced Islam only after the death of the Prophet ﷺ. الله أعلم. It is also said that he was Abū Kabsha, the foster guardian of the Prophet ﷺ, whose notice will appear under the kunyās.

## Source unit 1442 · printed entry 1442

### English candidate

Al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAbd Kulāl ibn Naṣr ibn Sahl ibn ʿArīb ibn ʿAbd Kulāl ibn ʿUbayd ibn Fahd ibn Zayd al-Ḥimyarī, one of the qayls of Yemen. The Prophet ﷺ wrote to him, as will appear under the biography of his brother Shuraḥbīl and elsewhere. Al-Hamdānī said in al-Ansāb: The Prophet ﷺ wrote to al-Ḥārith and his brother and ordered his messenger to recite ‘Lam Yakun’ to both of them. Al-Ḥārith then came to him in a delegation, embraced Islam, and he set him free and spread his cloak for him. Before al-Ḥārith entered, he said, ‘A man of noble grandfathers and bright cheeks will enter upon you from this mountain pass.’ It would seem to be this man. End. The reports that have converged, however, say that he sent word of his Islam and remained in Yemen. Ibn Isḥāq said: On the Messenger of God’s ﷺ return from Tabūk, a letter came to him from the kings of Ḥimyar announcing their Islam; among them was al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAbd Kulāl. The Prophet ﷺ had sent al-Muhājir ibn Abī Umayya to al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAbd Kulāl, and he embraced Islam and wrote poetry to the Prophet ﷺ, saying:

Your religion is the religion of truth; within it is purity,
and you command what it contains of truth.

Al-Dāraquṭnī likewise related it through Nāfiʿ from Ibn ʿUmar, and Abū al-Ḥasan al-Madāʾinī likewise mentioned it in his Book of the Envoys of the Prophet ﷺ.

## Source unit 1458 · printed entry 1458

### English candidate

Al-Harith ibn Amr al-Ansari, paternal uncle of al-Bara ibn Azib; it is also said, his maternal uncle. Ahmad transmitted by way of Ashath ibn Sawwar, from Adi ibn Thabit, from al-Bara, who said: Al-Harith ibn Amr passed by after the Messenger of God ﷺ had tied a banner for him. I said, ‘Uncle, where are you going?’ He said: ‘The Messenger of God ﷺ sent me to a man who had married his father's wife and ordered me to strike off his head.’ Ibn al-Sakan transmitted it through this route with the wording, ‘My paternal uncle al-Harith ibn Amr passed by me.’ Abd al-Razzaq transmitted it through the same route as, ‘I met my paternal uncle,’ without naming him. He transmitted it by another route from Ashath as, ‘I met my maternal uncle’; Ibn Maja likewise included it. A group transmitted it from Adi ibn Thabit, but disagreed over its chain: it is said, from him, ‘I heard al-Bara’; and it is said, from him, from Yazid ibn al-Bara, from his father. The latter is the transmission of Abu Maryam Abd al-Ghaffar ibn Qays, from Adi ibn Thabit, from Yazid, from his father: ‘I met my maternal uncle, who had a banner with him. I asked, Where are you going?’—and he related the hadith without naming him.

## Source unit 1459 · printed entry 1459

### English candidate

Al-Harith ibn Amr ibn Thalaba; it is also said, al-Harith ibn Amr ibn al-Harith ibn Iyas ibn Amr ibn Sahm ibn Nadla ibn Ghanm ibn Thalaba ibn Man ibn Malik ibn Asur, al-Bahili, then al-Sahmi. His kunya was Abu Misqaba—with the mim vocalized a, the unpointed letter unvocalized, and the qaf and ba vocalized a. The author of al-Kamal miscopied it, and al-Mizzi followed him—as I read in Mughaltay's handwriting—as ‘Abu Safina.’ He settled in Basra and transmitted a hadith included by al-Bukhari in al-Adab and by Abu Dawud and al-Nasai, which al-Hakim declared sound. Some transmitted it at length by way of Zurara ibn Karim ibn al-Harith ibn Amr, who said: ‘I came to the Prophet ﷺ at Mina or Arafat while the people had gathered around him’—the hadith; and by way of Yahya ibn Zurara: ‘My father informed me, from his grandfather al-Harith.’ Al-Baghawi transmitted it by way of Yahya ibn al-Harith: ‘My father informed me, from his grandfather al-Harith, who had lived in both the pre-Islamic and Islamic periods’; then he mentioned part of the hadith concerning seeking forgiveness, the fara, and the atira. His son Abd Allah ibn al-Harith and his grandson Zurara ibn Karim ibn al-Harith transmitted from him. Something concerning him will come in the notice of Karim ibn al-Harith under kaf.

## Source unit 1462 · printed entry 1462

### English candidate

Al-Harith ibn Awf ibn Abi Haritha al-Muzani, one of the horsemen of the pre-Islamic age. Abu Ubayd mentioned in Kitab al-Dibaj evidence that he embraced Islam; others likewise mentioned it. Abu Ubayd said: The long wars of the Arabs were three: the war of the two sons of Qayla, al-Aws and al-Khazraj; the war of Dahis and al-Ghabra between Banu Abs and Fazara; and the war of the two sons of Wail, Bakr and Taghlib. Then the two guarantors assumed liability for their blood payments; the two guarantors were Kharija ibn Sinan and al-Harith ibn Awf. God sent the Prophet ﷺ while something of their blood payments remained incumbent on al-Harith ibn Awf, and he waived it in Islam. The Prophet ﷺ sought his daughter in marriage. He said: ‘I do not deem her suitable for you; she has an ailment,’ though she had none. He returned and found that she had developed leprosy. Her paternal cousin Yazid ibn Jamra al-Muzani married her, and she bore him Shabib, who became known as Ibn al-Barsa; al-Barsa's name was Qursafa. Al-Rushati mentioned this. Another authority said that her father said, ‘She has whiteness’—the Arabs euphemize leprosy as whiteness—whereupon he said, ‘Then let her be so,’ and she became leprous from that moment. Al-Waqidi said: Abd al-Rahman ibn Ibrahim al-Madani related to me from his shaykhs that a delegation of Banu Murra, thirteen men headed by al-Harith ibn Awf, arrived as the Messenger of God ﷺ was returning from Tabuk. They lodged in the house of the daughter of al-Harith, then came to the Messenger of God ﷺ while he was in the mosque. Al-Harith said: ‘Messenger of God, we are your people and kin; we are from Luayy ibn Ghalib’—and he related the account. Al-Zubayr said: My paternal uncle Musab related to me that al-Harith ibn Awf came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: ‘Send with me someone to call people to your religion; I shall guarantee his safety.’ He sent two men of the Ansar with him, but al-Harith's clan acted treacherously toward one and killed him. Hassan said:

‘O Harith, whoever among you betrays the protection owed his neighbor—
Muhammad does not betray’—and he continued with the verses.

Al-Harith came, apologized, paid the blood money for the Ansari, and said: ‘Muhammad, I seek your protection from Hassan's tongue.’

<div dir="rtl" lang="ar">

الحارث بن عوف بن أبي حارثة المزني من فرسان الجاهلية ذكر أبو عبيد في كتاب الديباج ما يدل على أنه أسلم وكذا ذكره غيره قال أبو عبيد أيام العرب الطوال ثلاثة حرب أبني قيلة الأوس والخزرج وحرب داحس والغبراء بين بني عبس وفزارة وحرب ابني وائل بكر وتغلب ثم حمل الحاملان دماءهم والحاملان خارجة بن سنان والحارث بن عوف فبعث الله النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم وقد بقي على الحارث بن عوف شيء من دمائهم فأهدره في الإسلام وكان النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم خطب إليه ابنته فقال لا أرضاها لك أن بها سوءا ولم يكن بها فرجع فوجدها قد برصت فتزوجها بن عمها يزيد بن جمرة المزني فولدت له شبيبا فعرف بابن البرصاء واسم البرصاء قرصافة ذكر ذلك الرشاطي وقال غيره وقال أبوها إن بها بياضا والعرب تكنى عن البرص بالبياض فقال لتكن كذلك فبرصت من وقتها وقال الواقدي حدثني عبد الرحمن بن إبراهيم المدني عن أشياخه قالوا قدم وفد بني مرة ثلاثة عشر رجلا رأسهم الحارث بن عوف وذلك منصرف رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم من تبوك فنزلوا في دار بنت الحارث ثم جاءوا إلى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم وهو في المسجد فقال الحارث يا رسول الله إنا قومك وعشيرتك إنا من لؤي بن غالب فذكر القصة وقال الزبير حدثني عمي مصعب أن الحارث بن عوف أتى النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم فقال ابعث معي من يدعو إلى دينك فأنا له جار فأرسل معه رجلان من الأنصار فغدر به عشيرة الحارث فقتلوه فقال حسان <br />

Abu Salih and Hammad ibn Khalid transmitted from Muawiya through that chain: ‘I have not forgotten that I saw the Messenger of God ﷺ placing his right hand upon his left in prayer.’ Al-Baghawi and Samawayh included it. Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi and Zayd ibn al-Hubab transmitted it from Muawiya in the same way, except that they said, with uncertainty, ‘Ghatif ibn al-Harith or al-Harith ibn Ghatif.’ Ibn Abi Shayba and Ibn al-Sakan included it. Ibn Wahb and Rushdayn ibn Sad transmitted it from Muawiya as Abu Salih did, without uncertainty, but inserted Abu Rashid al-Hubrani between Yunus and al-Harith. Ibn Manda, al-Bawardi, and Ibn Shahin included it. Ibn Manda said: Mentioning Abu Rashid in it is an addition. Main transmitted from Muawiya: ‘Ghudayf ibn al-Harith,’ with the dotted dad. Ibn Manda included it and said: The first is sounder. Ibn al-Sakan transmitted from Ibn Main that he said: The correct form is al-Harith ibn Ghatif. Ibn al-Sakan said: Whoever says Ghudayf in this report has made a scribal error, for Ghudayf ibn al-Harith is another man whose kunya is Abu Asma.

## Source unit 1471 · printed entry 1471

### English candidate

Al-Harith ibn Qays ibn Adi al-Sahmi. Mention of his son al-Harith has already occurred. As for this man, Ibn Abi Khaythama transmitted by way of Nasr ibn Muzahim, from Maruf ibn Kharrabudh, who said: Preeminence in the pre-Islamic period came to ten men of Quraysh and then continued in Islam. He listed them until he said: ‘Among Banu Sahm was al-Harith ibn Qays; arbitration and the funds were entrusted to him.’ I say: It is possible that the words ‘then continued in Islam’ mean through their descendants, so this does not prove that he had companionship. Then I found that Ibn Abd al-Barr had mentioned approximately what Ibn Abi Khaythama mentioned and added that he embraced Islam and emigrated to Abyssinia with his sons al-Harith, Bishr, and Muammar. Ibn al-Athir objected that al-Zubayr and Ibn al-Kalbi mentioned him among the mockers. In al-Tajrid he added: ‘No one mentioned that he embraced Islam except Abu Umar.’ I say: Indeed, Abu Ubayd, Musab, al-Tabari, and others also mentioned him among them. There is nothing to prevent him from having repented, accompanied the Prophet, and emigrated; thus the two statements do not conflict. As for His word, exalted is He, ‘We have sufficed you against the mockers,’ it does not explicitly indicate that some of them did not repent. This is supported by Ibn Ishaq's having mentioned for each mocker the death that befell him: he mentioned the death of al-Harith ibn Talatila, then transmitted by way of Ikrima and Said ibn Jubayr and said ‘al-Harith ibn Ghaytala.’ As for Ikrima, he said ‘al-Harith ibn Qays.’ Ibn Ishaq, transmitting from Yazid ibn Ruman, from Urwa, identified him as a Khuza'i; thus he is not the Sahmi. والله أعلم.

### Arabic authority

<div dir="rtl" lang="ar">

## Source unit 1477 · printed entry 1477

### English candidate

Al-Harith ibn Kalada ibn Amr ibn Abi Ilaj ibn Abi Salama ibn Abd al-Uzza ibn Ghira ibn Awf ibn Qusayy al-Thaqafi, the physician of the Arabs. Ibn Ishaq said in al-Maghazi: Someone whom I do not suspect related to me, from Abd Allah ibn Makram, from a man of Thaqif, who said: When the people of al-Taif embraced Islam, a group of them spoke concerning those slaves—meaning those who had gone down to the Prophet ﷺ, embraced Islam, and been emancipated. The Prophet ﷺ said: ‘Those are God's freedmen.’ Al-Harith ibn Kalada was among those who spoke concerning them. Another authority said: Al-Azraq, a client of al-Harith, was among them. Abu Dawud transmitted by way of Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, from Sad ibn Abi Waqqas, who said: I fell ill, and the Prophet ﷺ came to us and said: ‘You have a disorder of the heart. Go to al-Harith ibn Kalada, the brother of Thaqif, for he practices medicine. Tell him to take seven dates, crush them with their pits, and administer them to you as a medicine inserted at the side of the mouth.’ Ibn Manda transmitted by way of Ismail ibn Muhammad ibn Sad, from his father, who said: Sad fell ill, and the Prophet ﷺ visited him and said: ‘I hope that God will heal you.’ Then he said to al-Harith ibn Kalada: ‘Treat Sad for what afflicts him’; and he related the report. Ibn Abi Hatim said: His Islam is not soundly established. This hadith demonstrates the permissibility of seeking medical assistance from protected non-Muslims. I say: I found a report of his that we transmitted in the ninth part of al-Amali al-Muhamiliyya and in al-Askari's al-Tashif, by way of Sharik, from Abd al-Malik ibn Umayr, from al-Harith ibn Kalada. He was the most skilled physician of the Arabs and would sit in a maqnaa of his. He was asked about that and said: ‘The sun alters the odor, wears out clothing, and brings forth latent illness.’ Al-Askari said: Maqnaa, with qaf and nun, is a place the sun does not reach; and his word tathful, with dotted tha and fa vocalized i, means ‘it changes it.’ Reports about al-Harith's medicine are numerous. Among them is what al-Jawhari related in al-Sihah: Umar asked al-Harith ibn Kalada, the physician of the Arabs, ‘What is the remedy?’ He replied: ‘Al-azm’—meaning dietary restraint. Then I found it transmitted in Ibrahim al-Harbi's Gharib al-Hadith by way of Ibn Abi Najih: Umar asked him, and he related it. It also appears in Abd al-Malik ibn Habib's al-Tibb al-Nabawi in a mursal report of Urwa ibn al-Zubayr from Umar. Dawud ibn Rashid transmitted from Amr ibn Maruf, who said: When al-Harith was near death, the people gathered around him and said, ‘Counsel us.’ He said: ‘Marry only a young woman; eat fruit only when it is ripe; let none of you seek treatment while his body can bear the illness; use depilatory lime every month, for it removes phlegm; whoever eats the midday meal should sleep afterward; and whoever eats the evening meal should walk forty paces.’ His story with Khosrow is famous, so we shall not prolong this notice with it. It is said that the cause of his death was that he saw a snake and said: ‘A learned man's knowledge may sometimes take the place of medicine, and his wisdom suffice in place of an antidote.’ Someone said to him: ‘Abu Wail, will you not take this in your hand?’ Pride moved him to stretch his hand toward it. It bit him, and he fell at once; they had not left before he died.

<div dir="rtl" lang="ar">

الحارث بن كلدة بن عمرو بن أبي علاج بن أبي سلمة بن عبد العزى بن غيرة بن عوف بن قصي الثقفي طبيب العرب قال بن إسحاق في المغازي حدثني من لا اتهم عن عبد الله بن مكرم عن رجل من ثقيف قال لما أسلم أهل الطائف تكلم نفر منهم في أولئك العبيد يعني الذين نزلوا إلى النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم فأسلموا فأعتقهم فقال النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أولئك عتقاء الله وكان ممن تكلم فيهم الحارث بن كلدة قال غيره وكان فيهم الأزرق مولى الحارث وروى أبو داود من طريق بن أبي نجيح عن مجاهد عن سعد بن أبي وقاص قال مرضت فأتانا النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم فقال انك مفئود ائت الحارث بن كلدة أخا ثقيف فإنه يتطبب فمره فليأخذ سبع تمرات فليلدك بهن وروى بن منده من طريق إسماعيل بن محمد بن سعد عن أبيه قال مرض سعد فعاده النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم فقال إني لأرجو أن يشفيك الله ثم قال للحارث بن كلدة عالج سعدا مما به فذكر الخبر قال بن أبي حاتم لا يصح إسلامه وهذا الحديث يدل على جواز الاستعانة بأهل الذمة في الطب قلت وجدت له رواية روينا في الجزء التاسع من الأمالي المحاملية وفي التصحيف للعسكري من طريق شريك عن عبد الملك بن عمير عن الحارث بن كلدة وكان أطب العرب وكان يجلس في مقنأة له فقيل له في ذلك فقال الشمس تثفل الريح وتبلى الثوب وتخرج الداء الدفين قال العسكري المقنأة بالقاف والنون الموضع الذي لا تصيبه الشمس وقوله تثفل بالمثلثة والفاء المكسورة أي تغيره وأخبار الحارث في الطب كثيرة منها ما حكاه الجوهري في الصحاح أن عمر سأل الحارث بن كلدة وكان طبيب العرب ما الدواء قال الأزم يعني الحمية ثم وجدته مرويا في غريب الحديث لإبراهيم الحربي من طريق بن أبي نجيح قال سأل عمر فذكره وفي كتاب الطب النبوي لعبد الملك بن حبيب من مرسل عروة بن الزبير عن عمر وروى داود بن رشيد عن عمرو بن معروف قال لما احتضر الحارث اجتمع الناس إليه فقالوا أوصنا فقال لا تتزوجوا الا شابة ولا تأكلوا الفاكهة الا نضيجة ولا يتعالجن أحدكم ما احتمل بدنه الداء وعليكم بالنورة في كل شهر فإنها مذهبة للبلغم ومن تغدى فلينم بعده ومن تعشى فليمش أربعين خطوة وقصته مع كسرى مشهورة فلا نطيل بها ## Source unit 1479 · printed entry 1479

### English candidate

Al-Harith ibn Malik ibn Qays ibn Udh ibn Jabir ibn Abd Manaf ibn Shuja ibn Amir ibn Layth ibn Bakr al-Kinani al-Laythi, known as Ibn al-Barsa. She was his mother; it is also said, his father's mother. He lived in Mecca and then Medina. Al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Hibban transmitted his hadith and declared it sound, as did al-Daraqutni, by way of al-Shabi, from him. He said: I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say on the day of the conquest: ‘Mecca will not be attacked after today until the Day of Resurrection.’ Al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar transmitted by way of Miswar ibn Abd al-Malik al-Yarbui, from his father, from Said ibn al-Musayyab, who said: Ibn al-Barsa al-Laythi was one of Marwan ibn al-Hakam's companions and would converse with him at night. They discussed the fay in Marwan's presence and said: ‘The fay is God's wealth, and Umar placed it where it belonged.’ Marwan said: ‘The fay is the wealth of the Commander of the Faithful Muawiya; he distributes it to whomever he wishes.’ Ibn al-Barsa left and met Sad ibn Abi Waqqas and informed him. Said said: Sad met me while I was heading for the mosque and said, ‘Follow me.’ I followed him until we entered upon Marwan, and he spoke harshly to him; and he related the account. Marwan said: ‘Who do you think told this old man?’ They said: ‘Ibn al-Barsa.’ He had him brought and ordered him stripped to be beaten. The doorkeeper entered to ask permission for Hakim ibn Hizam. Marwan said: ‘Give him back his clothes and send him out, lest this other old man become agitated against us’; and he related the account at length. It indicates that al-Harith remained alive into Muawiya's caliphate. This is the well-known genealogy of al-Harith. Ahmad, in his Musnad, transmitted his raised hadith and reported from Sufyan that he said al-Harith was a Khuzai.

## Source unit 1480 · printed entry 1480

### English candidate

Al-Harith ibn Malik al-Ansari. Ibn al-Mubarak transmitted his hadith in al-Zuhd from Mamar, from Salih ibn Mismar: the Prophet ﷺ said, ‘Harith ibn Malik, how are you this morning?’ He replied: ‘This morning I am truly a believer.’ He said: ‘Every statement has a reality. What is the reality of your faith?’ He replied: ‘My soul has turned away from this world; I have kept vigil through my night and gone thirsty through my day. It is as though I see my Lord's Throne, as though I see the people of Paradise visiting one another there, and as though I hear the howling of the people of the Fire.’ He said: ‘A believer whose heart God has illumined.’ This chain is mudal. Abd al-Razzaq likewise transmitted it from Mamar, from Salih ibn Mismar and Jafar ibn Burqan: the Prophet ﷺ spoke to al-Harith. He also transmitted it in al-Tafsir from al-Thawri, from Amr ibn Qays al-Malai, from Yazid al-Sulami, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said to al-Harith, ‘How are you this morning, Harith?’ He replied: ‘Among the believers.’ He said: ‘Know what you are saying’; and he related something similar. At its end he added: ‘Messenger of God, ask God to grant me martyrdom.’ He prayed for him. A raid was then made on Medina's grazing animals; he went out, fought, and was killed. It also came through other connected routes. Al-Tabarani transmitted it by way of Said ibn Abi Hilal, from Muhammad ibn Abi al-Jahm, and Ibn Manda by way of Sulayman ibn Said, from al-Rabi ibn Lut—both from al-Harith ibn Malik al-Ansari—that he came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: ‘Messenger of God, I am truly among the believers.’ He replied: ‘Consider what you are saying’—the hadith. At its end: ‘Whoever would be pleased to look upon one whose heart God has illumined, let him look upon al-Harith ibn Malik.’ Ibn Manda said: Zayd ibn Abi Unaysa transmitted it from Abd al-Karim ibn al-Harith, from al-Harith ibn Malik. Jarir ibn Utba ibn Abd al-Rahman transmitted from his father, from Anas ibn Malik, that the Prophet ﷺ entered the mosque, and there was al-Harith ibn Malik; he nudged him with his foot and related the hadith. Al-Bayhaqi transmitted in al-Shuab by way of Yusuf ibn Atiyya al-Saffar—who is extremely weak—from Anas: the Prophet ﷺ met al-Harith one day and said: ‘How are you this morning, Harith?’ He replied: ‘This morning I am truly a believer’—the hadith at length. At its end he said: ‘Harith, you have known, so adhere.’ Al-Bayhaqi said: This is rejected. Yusuf confused it, sometimes saying al-Harith and sometimes Haritha. Abu Asim Khushaysh ibn Asram said in his Kitab al-Istiqama: Abd al-Aziz ibn Aban related to us; Malik ibn Mighwal informed us, from Fudayl ibn Ghazwan, who said: A raid was made on Medina's grazing animals. Al-Harith ibn Malik went out, killed eight of them, and then was killed. He is the one to whom the Prophet ﷺ said: ‘How are you this morning, Haritha?’ Ibn Abi Shayba transmitted it from Ibn Numayr, from Malik ibn Mighwal, as a raised report, without mentioning Fudayl ibn Ghazwan. Ibn Said said, after transmitting it from al-Husayn ibn al-Hasan al-Marwazi, from Ibn al-Mubarak: ‘I do not know Salih ibn Mismar to have supplied a chain for more than one hadith.’ This hadith is not established through a connected chain.

## Source unit 1490 · printed entry 1490

### English candidate

Al-Harith ibn Muawiya ibn Zamaa al-Kindi. His companionship is disputed. Ibn Manda included him among the Companions, and Abu Nuaym followed him, relying on the hadith of al-Miqdam al-Rahawi, who said: Ubada ibn al-Samit, Abu al-Darda, and al-Harith ibn Muawiya were sitting together. Abu al-Darda said, ‘Which of you remembers the day when the Messenger of God ﷺ prayed facing a camel from the spoils?’ Ubada said, ‘I do,’ and he related the hadith. Abu Nuaym said: Abu Salam transmitted it from al-Miqdam al-Kindi, who named al-Harith ibn Muawiya al-Kindi. Ibn Sad and Abu Zura al-Dimashqi placed him in the first class of the Followers of Syria. Abu Mushir counted him among the senior associates of Abu al-Darda, and al-Ijli said that he was one of the senior Followers. Al-Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Hatim, Ibn Sumay, and Ibn Hibban also listed him among the Followers. Abu Wahb al-Kulai transmitted from Makhul, from al-Harith ibn Muawiya al-Kindi, who said: ‘Abu Jandal ibn Sahl and I used to perform ablution,’ followed by an account concerning wiping over leather socks. Yaqub ibn Sufyan also transmitted by way of Sulaym ibn Amir, from al-Harith ibn Muawiya, that he came to Umar, who asked him, ‘What has brought you? How did you leave the people of Syria?’ followed by an account. What seems most likely is that he was one of the Mukhadramun. The first hadith does not explicitly establish companionship. والله أعلم.

## Source unit 1492 · printed entry 1492

Al-Ḥārith ibn Muʿammar—with the consonant doubled—ibn Ḥabīb ibn Wahb ibn Ḥudhāfa ibn Jumaḥ al-Jumaḥī, the father of Ḥāṭib and grandfather of al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥāṭib, who was discussed shortly before. ## Source unit 1494 · printed entry 1494

### English candidate

Al-Ḥārith ibn Naḍr al-Sahmī, or al-Ḥārith ibn Sahm al-Baṣrī. Al-Zubayr ibn Bakkār cited poetry of his about the Anṣār in al-Muwaffaqiyyāt, through Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq, in the account of the Portico of Banū Sāʿida. It begins:

Alas for my people, for the fickleness of their minds,
and for my waiting for feet to slip.
Before, they were among those who called to God,
and they were the reins of Islam.
Truly, this authority, rather than us, belongs to Quraysh,
and Quraysh are the people of sound judgment.

Wathīma mentioned that when the Emigrants and the Anṣār disputed over the caliphate, al-Ḥārith ibn al-Naḍr al-Anṣārī stood to address his people. He cited the first and third verses and added: ‘Fear God, assembly of al-Aws and al-Khazraj, and fear the consequences of the days.’ He also cited other poetry of his about appointing Khālid ibn al-Walīd to command the fighting against the apostates at al-Yamāma. This conflicts with the name of his father and the lineage given by al-Zubayr. الله أعلم.

## Source unit 1502 · printed entry 1502

### English candidate

Al-Harith ibn Nawfal ibn al-Harith ibn Abd al-Muttalib ibn Hashim al-Hashimi, father of Abd Allah, who was nicknamed Bubah—with two ba letters both bearing fatha, the second geminated. Ibn Hibban mentioned him among the Companions and said that the Prophet ﷺ appointed him over some of the administrative affairs of Mecca. Al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar said the same. Ibn Abi Khaythama said: Musab related to us that al-Harith ibn Nawfal had companionship and transmission, and that during the Prophet’s ﷺ lifetime he had a son, Abd Allah, nicknamed Bubah. Al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar said: Nawfal was the eldest of his father’s children. Among his own children was al-Harith, from whom his kunya was taken, and al-Harith was his eldest son. Al-Bukhari transmitted in al-Tarikh by way of Abd Allah ibn al-Harith that his father held authority over Mecca. Ibn al-Sakan and al-Tabarani transmitted by way of Asim ibn Ubayd Allah, from Abd Allah ibn al-Harith ibn Nawfal, from his father, who said: When the Prophet ﷺ heard the caller to prayer, he would repeat what the caller said. When the caller said, ‘Come to prayer,’ he would say, ‘There is no power and no strength except through God.’ Al-Harith has other hadiths. Al-Nasai transmitted by way of Abu Mijlaz, from al-Harith ibn Nawfal, from Aisha: ‘I used to rub semen from the garment of the Messenger of God ﷺ.’ Al-Mizzi stated that this is the present al-Harith. Ibn Hibban, however, treats him as a different man: he mentioned al-Harith ibn Nawfal ibn al-Harith among the Companions, but mentioned the narrator from Aisha among the Followers. That remains the more cautious view. Ibn al-Kalbi related that he was the occasion for the revelation of God Most High’s saying, ‘But God would not punish them while you are among them’ [Quran 8:33], to the end of the verse. Abu Hatim said that he died in Basra near the end of Uthman’s caliphate. Ibn Sad said: Ali ibn Isa ibn Abd Allah ibn Abd Allah ibn al-Harith informed me that al-Harith ibn Nawfal accompanied the Prophet ﷺ, who appointed him over one of his jurisdictions in Mecca. Abu Bakr, Umar, and Uthman confirmed him in office. He then moved to Basra, marked out a house there, and died there near the end of Uthman’s caliphate. Another member of his household said that he died during Muawiya’s time and resembled the Prophet ﷺ. Al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar, however, gave this last statement in the entry on al-Harith’s brother, Abd Allah ibn Nawfal.

### Arabic authority

<div dir="rtl" lang="ar">

الحارث بن نوفل بن الحارث بن عبد المطلب بن هاشم الهاشمي والد عبد الله الملقب ببة بموحدتين مفتوحتين الثانية ثقيلة ذكره بن حبان في الصحابة وقال ولاه النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم بعض أعمال مكة وكذا قال الزبير بن بكار وقال بن أبي خيثمة حدثنا مصعب قال الحارث بن نوفل له صحبة ورواية وولد له في عهد النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم عبد الله الملقب ببة وقال الزبير بن بكار كان نوفل أسن ولد أبيه وكان له من الولد الحارث وبه كان يكنى وهو أكبر ولده وروى البخاري في التاريخ من طريق عبد الله بن الحارث أن أباه كان على مكة وروى بن السكن والطبراني من طريق عاصم بن عبيد الله عن عبد الله بن الحارث بن نوفل عن أبيه قال كان النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم إذا سمع المؤذن قال كما يقول فإذا قال حي على الصلاة قال لا حول ولا قوة الا بالله وله أحاديث أخر وأخرج النسائي من طريق أبي مجلز عن الحارث بن نوفل عن عائشة كنت أفرك المني من ثوب رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم فذكر المزي أنه الحارث هذا وعند بن حبان أنه غيره فإنه ذكر الحارث بن نوفل بن الحارث في الصحابة وذكر الراوي عن عائشة في التابعين وهو الأظهر وذكر بن الكلبي أنه سبب نزول قوله تعالى @QB@ وما كان الله ليعذبهم وأنت فيهم @QE@ الآية وقال أبو حاتم مات بالبصرة في آخر خلافة عثمان قال بن سعد أخبرني علي بن عيسى بن عبد الله بن عبد الله بن الحارث قال صحب الحارث بن نوفل النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم فاستعمله على بعض عمله بمكة وأقره أبو بكر وعمر وعثمان ثم انتقل إلى البصرة واختط بها دارا ومات بها في آخر خلافة عثمان وقال غيره من أهل بيته مات زمن معاوية وكان يشبه النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم وأما الزبير بن بكار فذكر هذا الكلام الأخير في ترجمة أخيه عبد الله بن نوفل

## Source unit 1503 · printed entry 1503

### English candidate

Al-Harith ibn Abi Hala, brother of Hind ibn Abi Hala and stepson of the Prophet ﷺ. His lineage will come in his brother’s entry. Ibn al-Kalbi and Ibn Hazm related that he was the first person killed in God’s path, beneath the Yemeni Corner. Al-Askari said in al-Awail: When God commanded His Prophet ﷺ to proclaim what he had been commanded, he stood in the Sacred Mosque and said, ‘Say: There is no deity but God, and you will prosper.’ They rose against him, and a cry for help reached his family. Al-Harith ibn Abi Hala came upon him and struck at them; they turned upon al-Harith and killed him, so he was the first martyr. In Sayf’s al-Futuh, through Sahl ibn Yusuf from his father, Uthman ibn Mazun said: ‘The first counsel the Prophet ﷺ gave us, when al-Harith ibn Abi Hala was killed and we were forty men in Mecca, each one steadfast upon the same position as the others…’; then he related the hadith.

## Source unit 1506 · printed entry 1506

### English candidate

Al-Harith ibn Hisham ibn al-Mughira ibn Abd Allah ibn Amr ibn Makhzum, Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Qurashi al-Makhzumi, brother of Abu Jahl and paternal cousin of Khalid ibn al-Walid. His mother was Fatima bint al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. His hadith is in the two Sahih collections, from Aisha: al-Harith ibn Hisham asked the Prophet ﷺ, ‘How does revelation come to you?’—the hadith. In a recension of Ahmad and al-Baghawi it occurs from Aisha, from al-Harith ibn Hisham. Ibn Majah transmitted another hadith of his by way of Muhammad ibn Ishaq, from Abd Allah ibn Abi Bakr, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Harith ibn Hisham, from his father: the Prophet ﷺ married Umm Salama in Shawwal—the hadith. Al-Zubayr said that he was a distinguished and renowned nobleman, and Kab ibn al-Ashraf the Jew praised him. Al-Harith ibn Hisham attended Badr with the polytheists and was among those who fled. Hassan ibn Thabit reproached him, saying:
‘If what she related to me was false, / then you escaped as al-Harith ibn Hisham escaped;
he left his loved ones instead of fighting for them, / and escaped with the head of a swift mare and its bridle.’
Al-Harith answered him:
‘God knows I did not leave off fighting them / until they struck my horse with frothing scarlet blood;
I knew that, if I fought even one man, / I would be killed while my stand would not harm my enemy;
so I turned away from them, though the loved ones were among them, / hoping to avenge them on a day lying in wait.’
It is said that these verses are the finest lines spoken in excuse for flight. Al-Zubayr said that he then attended Uhud as a polytheist, until he accepted Islam on the day Mecca was conquered; thereafter his Islam was good. He said: My paternal uncle related to me that in Umar’s time al-Harith departed Mecca for Syria with his family and wealth. The people of Mecca followed him, and he said, ‘Had I exchanged one abode for another with you, I would not have wanted anyone in place of you; but it is the migration to God.’ He continued fighting in Syria until God granted him a good end. He is also mentioned in the entry on Suhayl ibn Amr. Al-Waqidi said: In the view of our learned authorities on the campaigns, al-Harith ibn Hisham died in the Plague of Amwas. Al-Madaini said that he was martyred on the Day of Yarmuk; Ibn Sad likewise related this from Habib ibn Abi Thabit. As for Ibn Lahia’s report from Yazid ibn Abi Habib, from al-Zuhri, from Abu Bakr ibn Abd al-Rahman, that al-Harith ibn Hisham entered into a written emancipation contract with a slave of his, followed by a story in which they brought the dispute before Uthman: its apparent sense is that al-Harith lived into Uthman’s caliphate. Ibn Lahia, however, is weak, and the adjudication may have been delayed until after al-Harith’s death. Al-Zubayr said that al-Harith left no child except his son Abd al-Rahman. He was brought, together with Najiya bint Utba ibn Sahl ibn Amr, to Umar, who said, ‘Marry the bereft survivor to the bereft survivor; perhaps God will spread descendants from the two of them.’ God then spread many descendants from them. Al-Harith was proverbial for preeminence, so much so that the poet said:
‘Did you suppose, when you were taken captive, that your father / in glory was al-Harith ibn Hisham—
the foremost of Quraysh in noble deeds and largesse / in both the Age of Ignorance and Islam?’
Al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar said in al-Muwaffaqiyyat, by way of Muhammad ibn Ishaq, in the account of the portico of Banu Saida: Al-Harith ibn Hisham stood up. He was then the chief of Banu Makhzum, with no one considered his equal except those who had precedence in service with the Messenger of God ﷺ. He said, ‘By God, were it not for the Messenger of God’s ﷺ statement, “The leaders are from Quraysh,” we would be no less entitled to it than the Ansar, and they would be worthy of it. But it is a statement in which there is no doubt. By God, if only one man from all Quraysh remained, God would place this matter in him.’ Al-Harith used to charge in combat against the unbelievers while chanting:
‘I believe in my Lord and in the Prophet;
I am certain of resurrection after death;
how vile a person who makes this life his settled home.’

## Source unit 1507 · printed entry 1507

### English candidate

Al-Harith ibn Abi Wajza ibn Abi Amr ibn Umayya ibn Abd Shams ibn Umayya al-Umawi. Al-Baladhuri said that Abu Wajza’s name was Tamim and that he lived to a great age. Al-Waqidi and al-Zubayr related that he witnessed Badr with the polytheists and that Sad ibn Abi Waqqas took him captive. Abu Hatim al-Sijistani said in Kitab al-Muammarin: They said that al-Harith had a certain roughness and was dark-skinned and tall. He prayed behind Umar and heard him recite, ‘As though they were propped-up timbers.’ He said, ‘Are you alluding to me, Ibn al-Khattab? By God, I will never pray behind you again.’ Al-Marzubani alluded to this report in Mujam al-Shuara and added that al-Harith lived until his legs left him unable to stand. He said concerning that: ‘I have grown old, and the nights have worn me down;
whoever lives as long as I have wakes beset by cares and unable to rise.
My utmost end, though I live another twenty pilgrimages,
is extinction; time leaves no one immortal.’ Al-Baladhuri also related that Umar heard al-Harith ibn Abi Wajza praising Khalid ibn al-Walid, so he forbade him and said, ‘Love of vainglory corrupts religion.’ I say: I have not seen this al-Harith mentioned in the books composed on the Companions, though he meets their criteria: he was a grown man during the Prophet’s ﷺ lifetime and lived into Umar’s caliphate. As has already been explained, no Qurashi remained an unbeliever in Mecca after the Conquest; rather, all of them witnessed the Farewell Pilgrimage with the Prophet ﷺ, as Ibn Abd al-Barr expressly stated.

## Source unit 1509 · printed entry 1509

### English candidate

Al-Harith ibn Wahb—or, it is said, Wahban—of the Banu Adi ibn al-Duil. He headed a delegation; that has already appeared in the entry on Usayd ibn Abi Iyas under the letter hamza. Al-Harith ibn Wahb also had an episode with Umar, which al-Zubayr related in al-Muwaffaqiyyat from Yahya ibn Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn Thawban, from Muhriz ibn Jafar, the client of Abu Hurayra, from his father. He said: Umar removed Abu Musa from Basra, along with Qudama ibn Mazun, Abu Hurayra, and al-Harith ibn Wahb, one of the Banu Layth ibn Bakr, and took half of their wealth. He then related the episode. In it Umar said to al-Harith, ‘What of the slaves and young she-camels that you sold for one hundred dinars?’ He replied, ‘I set out with spending money of my own and traded with it.’ Umar said, ‘By God, we did not send you to trade with the Muslims’ property.’ He then ordered him to bring the money. Al-Harith said, ‘By God, I will never perform another office for you.’ Umar replied, ‘Steady now—until I appoint you again.’

## Source unit 1510 · printed entry 1510

### English candidate

Al-Harith ibn Yazid ibn Unaysa; it is also said Ibn Nubaysha, and also Ibn Abi Unaysa, of the Banu Muays ibn Amir ibn Luayy, the Qurashi Amirite. Ibn Ishaq related in al-Sira from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Harith ibn Abd Allah ibn Ayyash, who said: Al-Qasim ibn Muhammad said to me, ‘This verse—“It is not for a believer to kill a believer except by mistake” [Quran 4:92]—was revealed concerning your grandfather Ayyash ibn Abi Rabia and al-Harith ibn Zayd, the brother of the Banu Muays ibn Amir. Al-Harith used to harm them in Mecca while he was an unbeliever. When the Companions emigrated, al-Harith embraced Islam without their knowing of his Islam and set out as an emigrant. When he reached the outer part of al-Harra, Ayyash ibn Abi Rabia met him, thought that he was still upon his polytheism, and struck him with his sword until he killed him. Then this verse was revealed.’ Al-Baladhuri, Abu Yala, al-Harith ibn Abi Usama, and Abu Muslim al-Kajji all transmitted it by way of Hammad ibn Salama, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, but this version has Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Qasim from his father, calls him al-Harith ibn Yazid ibn Abi Unaysa, and says that al-Harith had helped bind Ayyash ibn Abi Rabia. Ayyash therefore swore that, if an opportunity against him arose, he would kill him; the report then continues at length. Al-Kalbi gave it at length in his Tafsir, with wording indicating that al-Harith came as a Muslim to the Prophet ﷺ before Ayyash encountered him. Ibn Jarir transmitted by way of Ibn Jurayj, from Ayyash, from Ikrima, who said that al-Harith ibn Yazid ibn Unaysa used to torture Ayyash ibn Abi Rabia together with Abu Jahl; he then related a similar account. Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted in al-Tafsir by way of Said ibn Jubayr that Ayyash ibn Abi Rabia swore that he would kill al-Harith ibn Yazid, a client of the Banu Amir ibn Luayy, and related a similar report. Al-Tabarani transmitted the story at length by way of al-Suddi without naming him, and also by way of Mujahid without naming him. The latter’s context indicates that he met the Prophet ﷺ after embracing Islam, then went out and was killed by Ayyash. والله أعلم. On this basis his status as a Companion is sound. Ibn Abi Hatim said in al-Jarh wa-l-Tadil: Al-Harith ibn Yazid ibn Abi Unaysa was the man whom Ayyash ibn Abi Rabia killed at al-Baqi after his arrival in Medina; this was after Uhud. Ibn Abd al-Barr included him in two places, calling his father Zayd in one and Yazid in the other, and thus thought them two men. They are one. والله أعلم.

## Source unit 1512 · printed entry 1512

### English candidate

Al-Harith ibn Yazid al-Juhani. Abdan said: I heard Ahmad ibn Sayyar say, ‘No hadith of his is known; he is only mentioned in the hadith of Abu al-Yasar.’ He was alluding to what Abdan himself and Abd al-Ghani ibn Said transmitted in al-Mubhamat by way of Ibn Wahb, from Yunus, from Ibn Shihab, from Jabir, who said: Abu al-Yasar said, ‘Al-Harith ibn Yazid al-Juhani owed me money and delayed me for a long time,’ followed by the hadith. Its transmitters are trustworthy, though its chain is disconnected. Its basis is in Sahih Muslim from Ubada ibn al-Walid ibn Ubada ibn al-Samit, who said: My father and I went out seeking knowledge among this clan of the Ansar. The first person we met was Abu al-Yasar, who said: ‘So-and-so son of so-and-so al-Harami owed me money,’ followed by the hadith. I say: Al-Harami is written with both consonants undotted, and he belonged to the Ansar; it is possible that he was a Juhani ally of the Ansar. I also found a hadith transmitted by al-Harith himself, but its chain is weak. Abu Musa included it in al-Dhayl by way of Bishr ibn Umara, from al-Ahwas ibn Hakim, from al-Harith ibn Ziyad, from al-Harith ibn Yazid al-Juhani, who said: The Prophet ﷺ used to forbid urinating in collected, stagnant water.

## Source unit 1515 · printed entry 1515

### English candidate

Al-Harith, without a lineage. Al-Bukhari said: ‘If he is not Ibn Nawfal, I do not know who he is.’ His son Abd Allah transmitted from him. Ibn Abd al-Barr said: Al-Harith, Abu Abd Allah, transmitted from the Prophet ﷺ concerning prayer over the deceased. Alqama ibn Marthad transmitted it from Abd Allah ibn al-Harith, from his father. Ibn al-Athir said: ‘He is al-Harith ibn Nawfal; Abu Umar repeated him to no benefit.’ End of quotation. Yet certainty that he is Ibn Nawfal is remarkable. The hadith is found in al-Baghawi, Ibn Shahin, al-Bawardi, al-Tabarani, and others through routes all turning on Layth ibn Abi Sulaym, from Alqama, from Abd Allah ibn al-Harith, from his father. In none of their recensions does it state that he is al-Harith ibn Nawfal, although they placed the hadith in the entry on al-Harith ibn Nawfal. Thus it remains a possibility; as for certainty, no. Consequently Ibn Abd al-Barr is not to be blamed.

Haritha ibn Humayr al-Ashjai, an ally of the Banu Salama. ## Source unit 1526 · printed entry 1526

### English candidate

Haritha ibn Suraqa ibn al-Harith ibn Adi ibn Malik ibn Amir ibn Ghanm ibn Adi ibn al-Najjar, the Ansari Najjari. His mother was al-Rubayyi bint al-Nadr, the paternal aunt of Anas ibn Malik. He was martyred on the Day of Badr. Ahmad and al-Tabarani transmitted by way of Hammad ibn Salama, from Thabit al-Bunani, from Anas; al-Bukhari and al-Nasai transmitted through more than one route from Humayd, from Anas; and al-Tirmidhi transmitted by way of Said, from Qatada, from Anas. They all agreed that he was killed on the Day of Badr. In Thabit’s version, he went out as a spectator and was struck. His mother came to the Prophet ﷺ and said, ‘You know Haritha’s place with me,’ followed by the hadith, in which it says that he is in al-Firdaws. Ibn Ishaq, Musa ibn Uqba, and Abu al-Aswad likewise listed him among the Muslims who witnessed Badr and were killed there. The authorities on the military campaigns did not differ concerning this. Ibn Manda relied upon what occurs in one recension of Hammad ibn Salama and said that he was martyred on the Day of Uhud. Abu Nuaym rejected that and, as was his habit, did so emphatically. In al-Tabarani’s recension by way of Hammad and al-Baghawi’s by way of Humayd, it likewise occurs that he was killed on the Day of Uhud. الله أعلم. The first view is authoritative.

Ḥāritha ibn Qaṭan ibn Zābir ibn Ḥiṣn ibn Kaʿb ibn ʿUlaym ibn Junāb al-Kalbī. Its chain will come in the notice of Ḥaml ibn Saʿd—that he is al-Kalbī—إن شاء الله تعالى. It states that he ﷺ wrote a document for Ḥāritha ibn Qaṭan: ‘This is a document from Muḥammad, Messenger of God, to the people of Dūmat al-Jandal and the adjoining clans of Kalb, with Ḥāritha ibn Qaṭan: the exposed, rain-watered palms are for us, and the sheltered palms are for you; the running-water crop is subject to a tenth, and the deep-well crop to half a tenth.’ He then related the document.

## Source unit 1534 · printed entry 1534

### English candidate

Ḥāritha ibn al-Nuʿmān ibn Nafaʿ ibn Zayd ibn ʿUbayd ibn Thaʿlaba ibn Ghanm ibn Mālik ibn al-Najjār al-Anṣārī. Mūsā ibn ʿUqba and Ibn Saʿd mentioned him among those who attended Badr. Ibn Isḥāq also mentioned him, except that he named his grandfather Rāfiʿ. Ibn Saʿd said that his kunyah was Abū ʿAbd Allāh.

Al-Nasāʾī transmitted by way of al-Zuhrī, from ʿUrwa, from ʿĀʾisha, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: ‘I entered Paradise and heard a recitation. I asked, “Who is this?” and was told, “Ḥāritha ibn al-Nuʿmān.”’ The Messenger of God ﷺ said, ‘Such is filial devotion.’ Ḥāritha was dutiful to his mother. Aḥmad also has it by way of Maʿmar, from al-Zuhrī, from ʿUrwa or someone else, with the wording: ‘He was the most dutiful of people to his mother.’ Its chain is sound.

Aḥmad and al-Ṭabarānī transmitted by way of al-Zuhrī: ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĀmir ibn Rabīʿa informed me, from Ḥāritha ibn al-Nuʿmān, who said: ‘I passed the Messenger of God ﷺ while Gabriel was sitting with him at al-Maqāʿid, and I greeted him. When I returned, he asked, “Did you see the one who was with me?” I said, “Yes.” He said, “That was Gabriel, and he returned your greeting.”’ Its chain is also sound.

Ibn Shāhīn transmitted by way of al-Masʿūdī, from al-Ḥakam, from al-Qāsim, that Ḥāritha came to the Prophet ﷺ while he was speaking privately with a man and did not offer a greeting. Gabriel said, ‘Had he greeted us, we would have returned it.’ He asked Gabriel, ‘Do you know him?’ Gabriel replied, ‘Yes. This man is one of the eighty who held firm on the day of Ḥunayn. God has undertaken to provide for them and their children in Paradise.’ Al-Ḥārith transmitted it by another route from al-Masʿūdī, but said: ‘from al-Qāsim, from al-Ḥārith ibn al-Nuʿmān.’ That is what he said. Al-Ṭabarānī transmitted it by way of Ibn Abī Laylā, from al-Ḥakam, but said: ‘from Ibn ʿAbbās,’ and then related something similar. Ḥāritha has another report with Aḥmad and others.

Al-Bukhārī transmitted in al-Tārīkh, by way of Thābit, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rabāḥ, that Ḥāritha ibn al-Nuʿmān said to ʿUthmān: ‘If you wish, we will fight in your defense.’ Miqsam ibn Saʿd said that he lived into the caliphate of Muʿāwiya and died during it after losing his sight.

Al-Ṭabarānī and al-Ḥasan ibn Sufyān transmitted by way of Muḥammad ibn Abī Fudayk, from Muḥammad ibn ʿUthmān, from his father, who said that Ḥāritha ibn al-Nuʿmān—and in one of al-Ṭabarānī’s recensions, ‘from Ḥāritha ibn al-Nuʿmān’—had lost his sight. He therefore laid a cord from his place of prayer to the door of his chamber. Whenever a poor person came, he would take something from his basket, then take hold of the cord until he could hand it to him. His family would say, ‘We will do it for you,’ but he would reply, ‘I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say: “Handing something to a poor person wards off calamitous ends.”’

## Source unit 1535 · printed entry 1535

### English candidate

Ḥāritha ibn Wahb al-Khuzāʿī. His mother was Umm Kulthūm bint Jarwal ibn Mālik al-Khuzāʿiyya, so he was the maternal brother of ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿUmar. He transmitted from the Prophet ﷺ, from Ḥafṣa bint ʿUmar, and from others. Four reports of his are in the two Ṣaḥīḥ collections, including his statement: ‘The Prophet ﷺ led us in a two-rakʿa prayer at Mina when the people were at their safest and most numerous.’ Abū Isḥāq al-Sabīʿī, Maʿbad ibn Khālid, and others narrated from him.

## Source unit 1536 · printed entry 1536

### English candidate

Ḥāzim ibn Ḥarmala ibn Masʿūd al-Ghifārī. He has a report concerning frequent recitation of the ḥawqala. His client Abū Zaynab narrated from him. Ibn Māja, Ibn Abī ʿĀṣim in al-Wuḥdān, al-Ṭabarānī, and others all included him under the unpointed ḥāʾ. Its chain is fair. Ibn Qāniʿ listed him under the dotted khāʾ and thereby made a copyist’s error.

## Source unit 1537 · printed entry 1537

### English candidate

Ḥāzim ibn Ḥarām al-Judhāmī, one of the desert people of Syria. Al-Bāwardī, al-Dūlābī, and al-ʿUqaylī transmitted by way of Sulaymān ibn ʿUqba ibn Shabīb ibn Ḥāzim, from his father, from his grandfather, from his father Ḥāzim, who said: ‘I came to the Prophet ﷺ with game that I had hunted in al-Urdunn and presented it to him. He accepted it, clothed me in an Adeni turban, and asked me, “What is your name?” I said, “Ḥāzim.” He said, “Rather, you are Muṭʿim.”’ Some transmitters abridged it. There is disagreement over his father’s name: Ḥarām, with two unpointed letters, or Ḥizām, with kasra on the first letter followed by zāy. They agreed that he was al-Judhāmī, with ḍamma on jīm followed by dotted dhāl. Abū ʿUmar, however, said al-Khuzāʿī, with ḍamma on dotted khāʾ followed by zāy. The first is correct.
